units.la: DUo, de patria publice scripturis, scopuli non cautè minus, quàm religiosè sunt vitandi, Blanditia & Stupor. Ut enim patriae nomen in se ελκυστικόν τι habet, adeóque, ut cum Poëta loquar; dulcedine cunctos
units.tr: There are two rocks to be avoided, and to be avoided no less carefully than devoutly, when writing publicly about one's homeland: flattery and complacency. For the name of one's country has in itself something attractive [ελκυστικόν τι], and so, to borrow the poet's words:

units.la: Ducit, & immemores non sinit esse sui;
units.tr: It draws all by its sweetness, and does not let them forget themselves.

units.la: ita argumenta eadem suppeditat, illa etiam magnopere extollendi, quae alii, tanquam χυδαῖα & abjecta, contemnunt. Rempublicam non tam Platonicam, quàm vere Christianam optimus quisque Civis suâ esse cupit. Hoc tamen nevo qui laborant, veniam facilè merentur, quòd talem sistant Patriam, qualem esse optant: Rectius interim & sibi, & publico consulturi, si vel aliis tam arduam relinquant Spartam, vel boni potius Historici, quàm nimis officiosi Civis faciant officium. Sed & Stupore non in patriam modò, verùm in ipsum etiam coelestem Patrem peccant; quotquot bona, & beneficia, largissima Ejus manu data, grato animo non agnoscunt, neque pio praeconio celebrant, turpissimaeque adeò ingratitudinis reatum contrahunt. Scelus hoc non semel Judaeis exprobratum legimus, tum ab aliis, tum ab Esaja praesertim, Veteris Testamenti Evangelista. Nolebant animadvertere, degeneres Judaei, se vineam illam esse spiritualem, divinitus plantatam, nec de exspectato fructu multum erant soliciti, donec, ex justissima indignatione, caelestis exclamaret Pater familias: Quid faciendum amplius vineae meae, quod non fecerim in ea? Quamobrem, cùm exspectâssem ut ederet uvas, edidit labrusras? Jam itaque notum faciam vobis, vobis, quid facturus sim vineæ meæ: amovebo sepimejus, ut sit depastioni, disrumpam maceriam ejus, ut sit conculcationi, c.6.v.5. Hac exitiali ἀναθεματισμῷ factum, ut non videret Nazareth, se arctis suis pomœriis Eum continere, quem cæli cœlorum alias capere non poterant. Si Bethlehem Ephratæa sua novisset bona, nunquam Principem vitæ passa fuisset in caula, non aula, primum suum quærere domicilium. Eadem ratione, si maximis componere liceat minora, multi, dubio procul, ardentiori Deo gratias agendi ferventur studio, si, beneficia, sibi, Patriæ, suis, collata digna memorique repeterent recordatione. Hæc me causa impulit, cur liberalius paulo & liberius, non tamen vel inscijs vel invitis Vobis, de Patria, statu cumprimis ejus Ecclesiastico, & Scholastico, semel atque iterum, & publice diffcruerim, & Origines hasce Carolinas luci jam exposuerim. Satis, fateor, multa dixi, quæ Patriam ornare utcunque possunt, neque tamen velim quemquam existimare, blandiendi, aut sumum domesticum vendendi animo, quicquam irrepsisse. Tabulæ adsunt authenticæ, quibus probare minime fuerit difficile, nihil à me esse dictum, quod prolixè, & operosè domi forisque ab aliis non fuerit scriptum. Paulo vero diligentius Antiquitatis nostræ Tigurinæ forulos excusi, tum ut boni Civis facerem officium, tum etiam, ut ad gratiarum actionem, magismagisque Deo pendendam, calcaria nostris adderem. Vobis vero, Viri Reverendi & Clarissimi, Collegæ honoratissimi; hæc qualiacunque μελετήματα sacra esse volui, ut publice testarer, non eximia tantum in Patriam, Ecclesiam & Scholam Tigurinam, Vestra esse merita; sed & singularem in literas & literatos favorem, atque affectum. Et à quibus vel patrocinium amplius, vel judicium æquius huic meo, si non prolixo, non usque adeo tamen vel facili, vel inutili labori exspectarem, quàm ab iis, qui Ecclesiæ & Scholæ nostræ res, juvant & amant? Dignum videbatur Ecclesiasticæ & Scholasticæ nostræ Historiæ compendium, ab Octingenta propemodum annis deductum, & ex monumentis authenticis, ipsa vetustate venerandis, MSS. ἀνεκδότως collectum, ut illorum inscriberetur Nomini, qui sibi haec non ingrata futura, quotidiana probant praxi, quique Suis, Suorumq; studiis id cum laude sunt consecuti, ut non postremum in Bibliotheca Tigurina occupent locum. Placuit Magno nostro Bullingero, Heroi incomparabili, superioris seculi anno LXXIV. d. 21. Decembris elaboratissimas suas Antiquitates, opus vere aureum, Venerando Ecclesiae Capitulo inscribere, ut aeternum posteritati, fraternae conjunctionis & conversationis relinqueret momentum: Liceat & mihi idem; seculo propemodum vergente; non effectus Bullingeriani (quid enim mihi, infanti, cum Hercule?) sed qualiscunque afsectus testimonio posteritati relinquere, & sincerum me Collegij vestri fuisse cultorem, & Historiae etiam patriae vel mediocrem amatorem. Neque pagellarum numerus offendat. Artis etiam spatiis non Pictores modo, sed & Geographi multa ostendunt; digitumque ad amplissima saepe intendunt. Sed desino apud eos prolixe praefari, qui me meaque explorate habent perspecta. Valete, praeclara Ecclesiae & Scholae patriae lumina, eique porro favete, qui sincero animo est,
units.tr: In the same way it supplies arguments that men are eager to magnify, which others, as vulgar and base [χυδαῖα], despise. Every good citizen wishes his commonwealth to be not so much Platonic as truly Christian. Those who labour under this fault, however, easily win pardon, since they set before us a country such as they wish it to be. It would be wiser, both for themselves and for the public, either to leave so arduous a Sparta to others, or to act as a good historian rather than as an overly dutiful citizen. But complacency also sins not only against the homeland but against the heavenly Father himself: all who do not gratefully acknowledge the good things and benefits given by His most bountiful hand, and do not celebrate them with pious praise, incur the guilt of the most shameful ingratitude. We read that this crime was often charged against the Jews, both by others and especially by Isaiah, the evangelist of the Old Testament. The degenerate Jews did not notice that they were that spiritual vineyard, divinely planted, and they were little concerned about the fruit expected of it, until the heavenly Father of the household cried out in most just indignation: "What more was there to do for my vineyard that I had not done for it? Why, when I looked for it to yield grapes, did it yield wild grapes? Now therefore I will make known to you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away its hedge, that it may be grazed, and break down its wall, that it may be trodden down," c.6.v.5. By this deadly curse [ἀναθεματισμῷ] it came about that Nazareth did not see that its narrow boundaries held Him whom the heavens of heavens could not otherwise contain. Had Ephratan Bethlehem known its own blessings, it would never have allowed the Prince of life to seek his first dwelling in a stall rather than a palace. By the same reasoning, if it is allowed to compare small things with great, many people undoubtedly would be kindled with a more ardent zeal for giving thanks to God, if they recalled with worthy and grateful remembrance the benefits bestowed on themselves, on their homeland, and on their own people. This is the reason that has moved me to speak more freely and openly, yet not against your wishes or without your knowledge, about our homeland, and especially about its ecclesiastical and scholastic condition, both once and again, publicly; and to set forth these Carolinian Origins to the light. I confess I have said many things that may in some way adorn the homeland; yet I would not have anyone think that anything crept in from a desire to flatter or to sell domestic smoke. Authentic records are at hand, by which it will be very easy to prove that I have said nothing that has not been written at length and with care by others at home and abroad. I have, indeed, laboured a little more diligently in searching the little chests of our Tigurine antiquity, partly to perform the duty of a good citizen, and partly so that I might add spurs to our people for giving thanks and paying honour to God ever more. To you, Reverend and Most Distinguished Gentlemen, my most honoured colleagues, I wished these to be sacred exercises [μελετήματα], whatever their worth, so that I might publicly bear witness that your services to the homeland, the Church, and the Tigurine School are not only outstanding, but that you also have a singular favour and affection for letters and men of letters. And from whom could I more justly expect either more support for this my work, if not lengthy, yet not so very easy or useless, or a fairer judgement, than from those who help and love the affairs of our Church and School? It seemed fitting to inscribe to the names of those who approve by their daily practice that these things will be welcome to them, and who have attained this with praise through their own labours and studies, a compendium of our ecclesiastical and scholastic history, traced back almost eight hundred years and gathered unpublished from authentic monuments, venerable for their very antiquity, manuscripts, so that it may hold no small place in the Tigurine library. In the year 1574, on 21 December, our great Bullinger, the incomparable hero, was pleased to dedicate his most elaborate Antiquities, a truly golden work, to the venerable chapter of the Church, so that he might leave to posterity an enduring monument of brotherly union and fellowship. Let me also, as the century nears its close, do the same: not to leave to posterity the achievements of Bullinger (for what have I, a child, to do with Hercules?), but at least a testimony of my affection, and that I was a sincere devotee of your college and a modest lover of our homeland's history. Nor let the number of pages give offence. Painters and geographers alike show many things within the limits of their art, and often point the finger at vast matters. But I will stop speaking at length before those who know me and my affairs thoroughly. Farewell, illustrious lights of the Church and School of our homeland; and continue to favour whoever is of sincere mind.

units.tr: pastor at Abbatissa in the Church of Zurich. Their names, a horrible and impious anthropolatry [Ἀνθρωπολατρεία], of which the ancients wrote at length, they turn into gods; they assign divine honours and religious worship to mortals, and now even to the dead, to ashes and dust, a foul meal for worms and food for eternal hell; and so, as the Apostle complains, they worship the creature besides the Creator. Neither the time allowed nor your attentive expectation requires me to recount how this has crept into Christianity little by little, and how far it has departed from the footsteps of the ancients. For this panegyric is dedicated not to the censure of the errors that prevail in the Church, but to the praise of Charles the Great, patron of our great college.

units.la: Non sit quidem nobis religio (liceat verbis loqui augusti Ecclesiæ Africanæ Episcopi, Aurelij Augustini) humanorum operum cultus, meliores enim sunt ipsi artifices, qui talia fabricantur, quos tamen colere non debemus. Non sit nobis religio cultus bestiarum; meliores enim sunt extremi homines, quos tamen colere non debemus. Non sit nobis religio cultus hominum mortuorum, quia si pie vixerint, non sic habentur, ut tales quærant honores, sed illum à nobis coli volunt, quo illuminante lætantur, meriti sui nos esse conservos. Honorandi ergo sunt propter imitationem, non adorandi propter religionem. Neq; ergo nos vel Martyribus vel Sanctis (ut ejusdem Patris mutuemus suffragium) Templa sicut Diis, sed memorias sicut mortuis, quorum apud Deum vivunt Spiritus, fabricemus. Sit memoria eorum apud nos in benedictionem. Vivat eorum post funera virtus. Et certè vivunt, viventque deinceps, quicunque de Ecclesiis, & Scholis Christianorum bene sunt meriti. Non licet exemplis agere pluribus, sed neque libet multo verborum anfractu obscurare, quod Sole meridiano clarius apparet.
units.tr: There is indeed no religion for us in the worship of human works (to borrow the words of Augustine, the illustrious bishop of the African Church): for the craftsmen who make such things are better than they, yet we ought not to worship them. Nor is there religion for us in the worship of beasts; for the lowest men are better than they, and yet we ought not to worship them. Nor is there religion for us in the worship of dead men; for if they lived piously, they do not regard themselves as such that they seek such honours, but they wish to be worshipped by us in that light in which they rejoice, that we are their fellow servants by their merit. They are therefore to be honoured for imitation, not adored for religion. Therefore let us not build for martyrs or saints (to borrow the same Father's support) temples as for gods, but memorials as for the dead, whose spirits live with God. May the memory of them be a blessing among us. May their virtue live on after their funerals. And indeed they live, and will live from now on, all who have deserved well of the Churches and Schools of the Christians. It is not allowed to deal with many examples, nor is it pleasant to obscure with a long winding of words what is clearer than the midday sun.

Aliter Pseudoprophetæ suo assentantur,aliter blanditur successoribus & asseclis,utrorumque tamen memoria iis superstitiosè religiosa est,& venerabilis. Gentilismus defunctorum
units.tr: {a} The memory of the just shall be for a blessing: this is an oracle of Holy Scripture. For so the wisest of kings, Solomon, speaks in his divine Book of Proverbs. Neither the religion we owe to the sacred letters nor the faith, which allows nothing unaccountable, lets us doubt the truth of this axiom, nor does the consensus of all nations suggest it. The Jewish synagogue has adopted the custom of not even mentioning the dead, whom they consider holy, unless this very title of honour is added. Hence, whenever the Jews run on in praise of their teachers who have ceased to live, they do not dare to omit this formula of reverence, which is a sin requiring atonement. The Muhammadans, as elsewhere so also here, imitators of the Jews, not only do the same things as the synagogue but outstrip it by many parasangs. For lest they seem to hold all the saints in the same place, they distinguish them by different formulas of good prayer. They flatter their false prophets in one way, and fawn upon their successors and followers in another; yet the memory of both is for them superstitiously religious and venerable. The heathen custom of the dead

units.la: A omnibus contubernis, Monachorum & Episcoporum aedibus pueros docerent. Vivit Carolus M. Europae delicium, hostium terror, amicorum solatium, totius orbis miraculum; sed & eheu! tam mortalitatis exemplum, quàm infirmitatis humanae speculum. Nam, ne parasitari videamur, ita magni Imperatoris mirabimur virtutes, ut tamen hominem fuisse, à quo proinde humani nihil alienum, ne quidem monendum censeamus. Pietatis, eruditionis, cultus religiosi ingenuus aestimator, suos tamen habuit naevos, quos charitatis & reverentiae pallio simpliciter tegere, quàm prolixè vel seculi vitio, vel nimio in sedem Romanam affectu, vel perversa Imperatoris clementia abutentium indole, vel declarandae gratitudinis desiderio, excusare, arctissimis horulae spatiis inclusi, malumus. Vivit Carolus Parisiis; vivit Reginoburgi liberalissimus Academiarum fundator & conservator. Vivit Moguntiae, Coloniae, Treviri, Salisburgi, Seduni amplissimorum Collegiorum Author & Patronus. Vivit & Tiguri, vixitque non superstes tantum ante annos octingentos, quando ipsam hanc urbem invisere, in illa aliquandiu morari, adeoque praesentiâ illam suâ illustrare voluit; sed & humanis exemtus, idemque immortalitatis Candidatus, immortalem quoque gloriam nobiscum reliquit.
units.tr: in all monasteries, and in the houses of bishops, they should teach boys. Charles the Great lives on, the delight of Europe, the terror of enemies, the solace of friends, the wonder of the whole world; but alas, he is as much an example of mortality as a mirror of human weakness. For, lest we seem to flatter, we shall admire the virtues of the great Emperor in such a way that we think it unnecessary even to remind people that he was a man, to whom nothing human was alien. He was a noble judge of piety, learning and religious worship, yet he had his blemishes, which we prefer to cover simply with the cloak of charity and reverence, rather than explain at length, whether by the vice of the age, by excessive affection for the Roman see, by the nature of those who abused the Emperor's clemency, or by the desire to show gratitude, though we are shut in by the narrowest limits of an hour. Charles lives on at Paris; he lives at Regensburg as the most generous founder and preserver of academies. He lives at Mainz, Cologne, Trier, Salzburg and Sion as the author and patron of most ample colleges. He lives also at Zurich, and he lived here not only as a survivor eight hundred years ago, when he wished to visit this very city, to stay in it for some time, and thus to illustrate it with his presence; but also, now taken from human life, he is a candidate for immortality and has left immortal glory with us.

units.la: Ut enim Maximus Imperator, meliorique adeo seculo dignus, de Ecclesia & Schola Tigurina praeclarè fuit meritus; ita non abs re Majorum authoritate introductum, successorumque consuetudine confirmatum est, ut hoc ipso Caroli die & Gratitudinis tanto Maecenati debitae, & officii quoque nostri, publico sermone, moneamur.
units.tr: For just as the greatest Emperor, worthy of an even better age, deserved splendidly well of the Church and School of Zurich, so it has not been without reason, introduced by the authority of our ancestors and confirmed by the custom of their successors, that on this very day of Charles, both for the gratitude owed to so great a patron and for our own duty, we should be admonished by a public discourse.

units.la: Quando verò dicendi ex hoc suggestu mihi vices, iterum, post tristissimam nostram, ex turris capraríae ruina, acceptam cladem, sunt demandatae, easdem pro virili ita sustinebo, ut si non effectu facundiae & eruditionis laudem; affectu saltem obsequii gratiam merear. Et quanquam nec momolis, nec artis sit magnæ, eam vobis Imperatoris memoriam, quam nulla unquam tempora obliterabunt, nulla hominum delebit oblivio, commendare ; judicio tamen amplissimus patet campus, ex locupletissimo Historiæ Carolinæ ea tantùm depromendi cornu copiæ, quæ ad rem maximè faciunt, præsentique hac nostra digna sunt Panegyri. Fuerit ergo aliis, alia occasione, Carolus noster, ex tot victoriis, & triumphis deportatis, ab Aquitanis, Longobardis, Saxonibus, Saracenis, Bojaris, Avaris & Hunnis, Normannis, aliisque hostibus immanissimis, Heros fortis. Fuerit ex præclara illa, pro Ecclesiæ conservatione, cura, pro tot Synodis & decretis, quibus impia nonnunquam & periculosa dogmata proculcata sunt, & superstitiosa imaginum adoratio damnata penitus, Ecclesiæ nutricius, & Patronus insignis. Nobis, hac vice, Scholasticus erit magnus. Absit, augusto hoc nomine animal hic somniemus rixosum, superbum, audax, loquutulejum, qualia ex Sorbona antehac prodierunt, & Schola Lombardi. Imperatorem sistimus incomparabilem, qui, cùm rebus gestis toto orbe fuerit Magnus, in Scholarum tamen & Academiarum, vel procurandis vel promovendis commodis, Mæcenas & liberalissimus esse voluit, & maximus. Et quem, ut Orationis nostræ scopum vel verbo judicemus, Tigurina quoque Schola authorem suum grato agnoscit animo & altorem. Habent Scholæ & Academiæ florentissimæ præcones suos & illices, quibus vel remotissimarum sæpe attrahant nationum florem ; antiquitatem, privilegia, splendorem in publicis honoribus & exercitiis, & si quæ sunt alia honestæ invitationis irritamenta, Regum, Principum, Rerum publicarum authoritate concessa. Hanc aliis non invidemus fortunam : Scholam modò Tigurinam, etiam illi nôrint, & incunabula sua debere Carolo Magno, & ea paulatim consecutam, a tempore præsertim Reformationis, ornamenta, quibus, ipsis annuentibus
units.tr: When the turn to speak from this platform has been given to me again, after our most sorrowful disaster from the fall of the Capraria tower, I shall sustain the duty as far as I can, so that, if not by the effect of eloquence and learning, at least by the feeling of obedience I may earn your favour. And although it is neither the work of a small nor of a great art to commend to you the memory of the Emperor, which no times will ever obliterate and no oblivion of men will destroy, nevertheless the field is wide open to judgment, and from the very rich history of Charles I may draw forth the horn of plenty of those things that bear most on the matter and are worthy of this present panegyric. Let our Charles be a brave hero on another occasion, with the many victories and triumphs he won over the Aquitanians, Lombards, Saxons, Saracens, Bohemians, Avars and Huns, Normans, and other most savage enemies. Let him be the nurse of the Church and its distinguished patron, for his splendid care for the preservation of the Church, for so many synods and decrees by which impious and sometimes dangerous doctrines were trampled down, and the superstitious adoration of images was utterly condemned. For us, on this occasion, he shall be a great scholar. Far be it that under this august name we should dream of a quarrelsome, proud, bold, babbling animal of the kind that formerly came forth from the Sorbonne and the school of Lombard. We set before us an incomparable Emperor, who, though he was great in his deeds throughout the world, wished also to be, and to be the greatest, a patron and most generous benefactor in procuring or promoting the advantages of schools and academies. And, that we may judge by a word the aim of our oration: the Zurich School also acknowledges its author and nourisher with a grateful mind. Flourishing schools and academies have their heralds and enticements, by which they often draw the flower of very remote nations: antiquity, privileges, splendour in public honours and exercises, and whatever other incentives of honourable invitation are granted by the authority of kings, princes and commonwealths. We do not envy others this fortune; let those who know also know that the Zurich School owes its cradle to Charles the Great, and that it gradually attained, especially from the time of the Reformation, the ornaments by which, with their own approval,

units.la: Qui Scholæ Tigurinæ author, tibus adversariis, aliis per orbem Scholis, celeberrimis etiam dubiam reddidit palmam. Nolumus cum cujusquam ingratiis aut invidia, (pridem enim suum cuique tribuere, & honore antevertere quemvis didicimus) laudem Scholae nostrae asserere; quin potius, quòd forte nec ipsi, nec alii bona nostra satis perspecta habuerint, illis, qui superstites jam ad gubernacula sedent Scholastica, remq; literariam juvare sunt parati, animum intendimus addere, ut illius porrò Gymnasij magno animo curam gerere pergant, cui vel à solo Carolo Magno antiquitatis & authoritatis momentum, antecessorum verò eruditione, pietate, rerum usu, nominis celeberritate imitationis irmensum accedit calcar. Et quamvis vel de consiliis Reformatorum Irenicis (quid deinceps sperandum de illis sit, sive Penelopes tela, sive saxo Sisyphi,) & quousque in iis perventum fuerit, vel de Epidemicis Academiarum & Scholarum morbis, disserturus, alió cursum Orationis dirigere constitui; huc tamen eundem, cum illi, cui plura debeo, ita visum fuerit, libenter obliquavi. Duabus autem universa Scholae nostrae Historia commodissimè includitur periodis, quarum illa trivialem nobis eam exhibet, haec Academiam. Illa Reformationem antecedit, haec eandem sequitur. Utramque pro merito non dicam vivis coloribus exprimere, sed supremis lineamentis adumbrare, cum unius horae pensum non sit; de illa tantum Schola Tigurinorum veteri, qualis fuit à Carolo Magno, ad Reformationem, triviali, verba facere fert animus. Quod dum crasla praesto Minerva, attentos animos, arrectásque aures tantò mihi de vobis confidentius polliceor, quanto veatrae humanitatis fiducia fretus cathedram hanc ascendi obsequentior. Vestra jussa, monita vestra fraterna. Tuum praesertim, Venerande D. Antistes, vestra consuetudo dicere me voluerunt, non de passere Catulli, Psittaco Statii, luto Majoragii, Puteani ovo; sed de ocello vestro,
units.tr: The founder of the Zurich school, in spite of many adversaries and other most celebrated schools throughout the world, has rendered the palm of victory doubtful. We do not wish to claim praise for our school out of any ingratitude or envy (for we have long learned to give each his due and to put anyone's honour before our own). Rather, because perhaps neither they nor others have had a sufficiently clear view of our assets, we are prepared to help those who now sit at the helm of the school and the cause of learning, and we intend to encourage them to keep caring for that gymnasium with a great spirit. For it has the weight of antiquity and authority from Carolo Magno alone, and from its predecessors' learning, piety, practical experience and renown there comes a mighty spur to imitation. Although I had intended to discuss the Irenic proposals of the Reformers (what may be hoped for from them in future, whether they are Penelope's web or Sisyphus's stone, and how far they have got), or the epidemic diseases of academies and schools, I have decided to turn my discourse elsewhere. Nevertheless, since he to whom I owe very much has thought it fitting, I have gladly turned it in this direction. The whole history of our school is most conveniently contained in two periods: the first presents it to us as trivialem, the second as Academiam. The first antecedit the Reformation, the second sequitur it. I shall not say that I can express each in lively colours as it deserves, but only sketch them in outline, since it is not a task for one hour. My intention is to speak only de illa old Zurich school, such as it was from Carolo Magno to the Reformation, in its triviali form. While Minerva is present in this way, I promise you attentive minds and pricked-up ears, and I promise this with all the more confidence as I have mounted this chair more willingly, trusting in your kindness. Your commands and your brotherly admonitions, and especially yours, Venerable Antistes, your custom has wished me to speak, not about Catullus's sparrow, Statius's parrot, Majoragius's mud or Puteanus's egg, but about your little eye, your darling, the Zurich school, the armoury of the state, the seminary of the Church, the storehouse of the whole fatherland. Therefore, what you wish to be recalled here, as usual, from me, I ask you to receive with kindly ears and well-disposed minds, with whatever respect I can and ought to show.

units.la: Propositio De Scholae Tigurinae origine. vestro, delicio vestro, Schola Tigurina, Reipublicæ armamentario, Ecclesiæ Seminario, patriæ universæ Promtuario. Quod igitur commemorari hic, more solito, àme voluistis, ut benevolis illud excipiatis auribus, animisque pronis, qua & possum, & debeo observantia rogo.
units.tr: Proposition: On the origin of the Tigurine School. Your own, your darling, the Tigurine School, the armoury of the Commonwealth, the seminary of the Church, the storehouse of the whole fatherland. Since you have wished this to be mentioned here, as is our custom, I ask you to receive it with kindly ears and willing minds, with the respect that I both can and ought to show.

units.la: Accersere; ut ipsam, bono cum Deo, rei aciem invadamus; non Parisiensis tantum Academicæ; sed & Scholæ Tigurinorum trivialis originem, ab ipso Carolo Magno, μέγα λίαν αἴ]ημα! Accersimus tamen, & jure quidem. Id qua occasione, quoque successu, atque progressu ab eo, inter tot Imperii curas, hostium impetus, regiminis stupenda incrementa, tentatum simul prudenter, & executioni datum fuerit feliciter, paulo plenius eruderabimus. Exulceratissimis & corruptissimis Carolum M. vixisse temporibus, quibus ubique terrarum, ut morum corruptela, ita artium disciplinarumque inscitia, atque ignorantia, longè latèque dominata, & veluti pestis, sive lues quædam fuerit grassata, ætatis illius historiæ, fluctuare nos non sinunt. Sed eamus in rem præsentem. Latina Lingua (cæteras enim, ceu barbaras, barbaris relinquebant) in qua proram & puppim suæ constituebat Clerus fortunæ, vix ea hinc inde sacerdotes erant instructi supellectili, quæ ad obeundum munus; nec molestum, nec fusæ aut reconditæ eruditionis indigum; requirebatur. Unde nova illa casuum examina, ex turpissimis sacrificulorum hallucinationibus Grammaticis nata, an qui, quod in Bavaria ea ipsa accidisse scribit ætate Aventinus, baptismi Candidatum aqua lustrica tincturus dixisset: Baptizo te in nomine Patria, Filia, & Spiritus Sancti, ipsum non polluisset, aut irritum reddidisset initiationis Sacramentum? Quæ quæstio cum inter primos acriter agitaretur Bojarorum Antistites, ad sedem tandem devoluta fuit Romanam. Sed & Artium liberalium nomenclatura eidem adeò ignota fuit Seculo, ut cum Johannes Mairofius, & Claudius Clemens Scoti in Franciam appulissent, operamque suam Carolo Magno, in tradendis liberalibus artibus obtulissent, ipse Carolus, quasi re nova attonitus, Alcuini demum Suadela permoveri potuerit, ut Parisiensis hac occasione Academia ortum suum haberet atque initium. Philosophi erant primi illi Doctores; unde factum postea, ut non Lutetiæ tantum, sed & Heidelbergæ; quæ filia Parisiensis Academiæ appellabatur; summa semper Facultatis Philosophicæ fuerit, & illic etiamnum sit authoritas. Mathematicas disciplinas ultra receptas hypotheses extendere, impune non licuit. Quibus de Antipodibus vel obiter Philosophari, aut quicquam rusipari venit in mentem, in præsentissimam illi non cujusvis erroris, sed hæreseos inciderunt suspicionem. Id quod Sacerdos quidam, Vergilius, magno suo tum expertus erat malo, quem hoc solo nomine & Bonifacius, Pontificis ad Germanos emissarius, & Zacharias Papa, non acri tantum censura perstrinxerunt, sed & Sacerdotio ceu indignum exauctorandum statuerunt. Ubi ipsa Theologia ingressi fuerimus adyta, quantam, optime Deus, hoc Seculo illa passa fuit cladem? Doctores, qui in Scholis Systemata pro ratione illius ævi, jam tum infecti & inficeti scripserunt, non a pura modo illa, & simplici veterum disciplinæ phraseologia, sed & in ipsa quoque tractatione Methodi necessarias neglexerunt leges. Præivit Johannes Damascenus, Scholasticorum sive Prodromus, sive Patriarcha, vir neque ingenio obtusio, neque laboris impatiens, scriptis quippe clarus, & qui Theologiam mole magis vastam, quam vel suis absolutam partibus, vel Ecclesiarum publicæ ædificationi accommodatam posteritati reliquit. Articulis enim momentosissimis, & ut cum Tertulliano loquar, Salutis devoratoriis, de Libero arbitrio, officio Christi, fide, &c. prætermissis, spinosas multas & intricatas rebus Theologicis quæstiones immiscuit; privatas
units.tr: To fetch the matter from afar: let us, with God's blessing, attack the subject itself, and set out to trace the origin not only of the Parisian Academy but also of the trivial School of the Tigurines, from Charles the Great himself. This is a very bold claim [μέγα λίαν αἴτημα]! Yet we do lay claim to it, and rightly so. By what occasion, with what success and progress this was attempted by him, prudently, amid so many cares of the Empire, the attacks of enemies and the amazing growth of his rule, and happily carried into effect, we shall explain a little more fully. That Charles the Great lived in most corrupt and ulcerated times, when, throughout the world, a corruption of morals and an ignorance and inexperience of the arts and disciplines reigned far and wide, and when a kind of plague or pestilence had spread, the history of that age does not allow us to pass over. But let us go to the matter at hand. Latin (for the other languages they left to the barbarians, as barbarous) was the language in which the clergy set the prow and stern of their fortune; the priests were scarcely equipped with such equipment, here and there, as was required to discharge their office without difficulty and without needing a broad or deep learning. Hence those new examinations of cases, born of the shameful blunders of the little priests in grammar: if someone, as Aventinus writes happened in Bavaria in that same age, meaning to dip the candidate for baptism in holy water, had said: "I baptize you in the name of the Father, the Daughter, and the Holy Spirit," would he not have polluted the Sacrament of initiation itself, or rendered it void? This question, while it was being hotly debated among the first bishops of the Boii, was finally referred to the Roman See. But the nomenclature of the liberal arts was so unknown to the same century that when Johannes Mairofius and Claudius Clemens, Scots, had landed in France and offered their services to Charles the Great for teaching the liberal arts, Charles himself, astonished as at a new thing, could at last be moved only by the persuasion of Alcuin, so that the Parisian Academy might have its origin and beginning on this occasion. Those first teachers were philosophers; hence it came about afterwards that not only at Paris but also at Heidelberg, which was called the daughter of the Parisian Academy, the highest authority always belonged to the Faculty of Philosophy, and it still has that authority there. To extend the mathematical disciplines beyond the accepted hypotheses was not allowed with impunity. Whoever happened to philosophize even briefly about the Antipodes, or to let slip anything on the subject, fell under the immediate suspicion not of some ordinary error but of heresy. This is what a certain priest, Virgil, experienced to his great cost at that time; him Boniface, the Pope's emissary to the Germans, and Pope Zacharias not only assailed with harsh censure for this alone, but also decided should be deposed from the priesthood as unworthy. And when we enter the sanctuary of theology itself, what a great blow, good God, did that discipline suffer in this century! The teachers who wrote systems for the schools, in the manner of that age, already infected and infecting, neglected not only the pure and simple phraseology of the ancient discipline but also the necessary laws of method in the very treatment of their subject. John of Damascus went before them, forerunner or patriarch of the Schoolmen, a man neither dull in intellect nor impatient of labour, famous indeed for his writings, who left to posterity a theology more vast in bulk than either complete in its parts or suited to the public edification of the Churches. For, passing over the most momentous articles, and (to use Tertullian's words) those that devour salvation, concerning free will, the office of Christ, faith, and so on, he mixed in many thorny and intricate questions about theological matters, and he forced upon the articles of faith the private opinions of teachers.

units.la: Doctorum opiniones, ut fidei articulos obtrusit : In citandis & explicandis Scripturis Sacris vel jejunus, vel rarus, stylum non à Scripturæ modò fontibus diversum, sed & à recepta consuetudine alienum sequi, adeóque subtilis, quàm perspicui & solidi Theologi officium facere maluit. Theologiæ exegeticæ cultores Scholis Christianorum pene eliminatos dixeris, adeò ejus obscura hac ætate rudera apparent. In Epicuri enim potius, quàm Christi Schola Ecclesiarum Antistites educati, otióque, deliciis, ac voluptatibus diffluentes, literis sacris ultimum ignominiosissimumque dixerunt vale. Rarissimi, quasi nantes in gurgite vasto, erant viri literati, qui ad hanc Josephi fracturam animum utcunq; adverterunt. Hinc pudenda Linguarum, artiumque liberalium nata inscitia, religionis execrabilis ignorantia, superstitiosorum rituum luxuries, errorum & impietatum lerna atque sententina. Quam quidem fundo Theologico calamitatem partim Regum & Imperatorum Orientalium desidia, & religionis neglectus, partim Episcoporum & Sacerdotum socordia attulit. Accesserunt Gentium Barbarorum, Gothorum, Hunnorum, Longobardorum, Saracenorum inopinati successus, quorum assiduis infestisque incursionibus libri literæque, tam sacræ, quàm profanæ, in Republica Christiana fere omnes interierunt. Hæc facies cadaverosæ & desperatæ propemodum fuit Ecclesiæ, rerum potiente Carolo Magno, quem ad dispellendas Ægyptiacas illas, & plus quàm Cimerias tenebras, ceu novum Solem Θεὸς ἐκ μηχανῆς emisit; & veluti alterum Josiam, qui scripta a blattis & tineis, quarum prædæ diu satis erant expositæ, vindicaret, excitavit. Etenim, ut magno, & excelso Augustissimus Imperator fuit ingenio, ita omnem impendit operam, ut res Christianæ rectius indies haberent, studium cumprimis Theologicum tantùm non sopitum & sepultum, vel mediocri nitori (pristinum enim sperare difficulter poterat,) restitueretur.Prima itaq; ejus cura fuit,ut contextum sacrum haberet Ecclesia ad ipsos fontes examinatum; Vet.& N.Test. libros omnes,amanuensium imperitia, Lecto- rum oscitantia,Interpretum inscitia,temporum injuria depravatos ,correctos iterum, novumq; Testamentum in Linguam Germanica legeret traductum. Proximum erat,ut ea pro cathedra paulatim plebi per annum commendarentur Scripturæ ιλήμματα, quæ nucleum Historiæ Evangelicæ proponerent & medullam. Hinc textus Dominicales,quos vocant, & ætate, & authoritate Caroli Magni excerptos & introductos nonnulli conjiciunt, quod, ut ut non satis sit certum,illud tamen vel Casinensia monumenta extra controversiam collocare nos jjubent, Paulum, cognomento VVinfridum, Diaconum Aquilejensem, Monachum Cafinenfem, Caroli nostri jussu Historias & Lectiones, per totum annum singulis Sanctorum festivitatibus convenientes compilasse, quæ Eclogæ etiamnum in Ecclesia Romana, etsi superstitione auctæ, reservantur. Cúmque Reipublicæ Christianæ multum interesse optimus Princeps intelligeret, ut & Ministri Ecclesiis præficerentur idonei, & plebs ad conciones sacras audiendas quoquo modo, adigeretur, & Scholæ deinceps vel superiores, vel inferiores extruerentur, vires suas, ne quid detrimenti hic res Christi paterentur; convertit libenter & liberaliter. Et de Ecclesia quidem Ministris, Episcopis seu Pastoribus, refert Aventinus, in Episcoporum Senatum haud temere quemquam Carolum adlegisse, eruditionem ac bonitatem in illis cooptandis potissimum spectasse. Neminem nisi antea sibi probatum, probéque cognitum creavisse. De cura vero plebis Ecclesiasticæ ex antiquissimo Msc. Palatino, Capitulare Caroli ad manus nostras nuper demum venit, ubi sect. 17. legimus, ut in Dominicis diebus conventus & placita publica non faciant, nisi pro magna necessitate, aut hostilitate cogente; sed omnes ad Ecclesiam recurrant, ad audiendum verbum Dei, & orationibus, vel justis operibus vacent, similiter & infestivitatibus præclaris Deo & Ecclesiæ conventui deserviant, & secularia placita dimittant. Scholas denique, cùm animadverteret, tutissimum eas pellendæ ignorantiæ esse alexipharmacum, & certissimum administrandæ Reipublicæ prognosticum, primus inter Christianos Imperatores Occidentales, curâ suâ amplecti voluit. Atque hac occasione Schola Tigurina primùm caput, timidiusculè tamen, κοὴ μὴ μετὰ πολλῆς φαντασίας exerere cæpit. Ut enim ne hodie quidem, in tanta luce, Imperatores, Reges, Respublicæ Academias ubique habent, sive, ut pro ætatis illius loquar consuetudine, Studia generalia, seu Universitates; sed & Scholas triviales, literarum primitiis destinatas, sive in Collegiis, piis ejusmodi usibus consecratis; sive extra Collegia, quæ constituto tempore discipulos suos, primis literaturæ rudimentis imbutos, carceribus quasi dimittunt, Professorumque curæ & industriæ limandos postea, atque expoliendos tradunt; ita & Carolum M. non Academias tantùm; sed & Scholas triviales, Gymnasia, Pædagogea, instituto laudatissimo, erexisse, observamus. Testes, ut de Academiis nihil addamus, sunt tot Monasteria, liberalissimi Caroli liberalitate extructa, non ut fucorum fruges consumere natorum speciosa essent receptacula; sed apicularum florilegarum utilissima alvearia. Neque enim, ut Mutij de Carolo M. utamur verbis, alio proposito tot fundavit Monasteria, nisi ut juventus bene in illis institura, utilis esset exemplo & doctrina hominibus, & qui in illis consenescere, mundi stultitia & pompa contemta, contemplationi & orationi se tradentes, statuerent, docerent morum probitatem, veramque religionem populum. Testis est Collegium Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ, quod cùm Majores jam ejus feliciter fundâssent, maximisque privilegiis, muneribus, donis, exemtionibus ornâssent, liberalitatem ille non modò eorundem habuit ratam, eamque tabulis confirmavit atque stabilivit; sed & immane quantum auxit. Hinc, hinc, inquam, Scholæ Tigurinæ derivanda origo. Sed prout, (ita Medicorum filii, ex Hippocrate suo monent) omnia singularum partium corporis humani stamina simul ponuntur, inque prima fœtus formatione cunctorum membrorum delineatio eodem oritur progressu, (perpetuò enim vis illa formatrix laborat, nec, donec metam suam attigerit, conquiescit) non omnia tamen simul absolvuntur; verùm successivè alterum inconsequenta perfectione excipit alterum, ita & Schola quoque nostra prima simul vidit lineamenta, perfectio tamen, distinctis postea sive gradibus, sive terminis, sive etiam ætatibus demum fuit subsecuta.
units.tr: The opinions of the doctors he pushed forward as articles of faith. In citing and explaining the Holy Scriptures he was either ignorant or rarely used them. He preferred to follow a style that was not only different from the sources of Scripture but also foreign to accepted usage, and so he chose to do the work of a subtle theologian rather than a clear and solid one. You might say that the cultivators of exegetical theology have been almost eliminated from the schools of the Christians, so obscure and ruinous does it appear in this age. For the bishops of the Churches were educated in the school of Epicurus rather than of Christ, and, dissolving in leisure, luxury and pleasures, they bade a final and most shameful farewell to the sacred letters. The learned men who did in some way attend to this breach in Josephus were very rare, like swimmers in a vast whirlpool. Hence came the shameful ignorance of languages and liberal arts, the detestable ignorance of religion, the luxuriance of superstitious rites, and a sink and cesspool of errors and impieties. This calamity in theology was brought about partly by the sloth of the Eastern kings and emperors and their neglect of religion, and partly by the carelessness of the bishops and priests. To these were added the unforeseen successes of the barbarian peoples, the Goths, Huns, Lombards and Saracens, by whose constant and hostile incursions nearly all books and writings, sacred and profane alike, perished in the Christian commonwealth. Such was the face of the Church, almost corpse-like and desperate, when Charles the Great took charge of affairs. To disperse those Egyptian and more than Cimmerian shadows, he sent him forth like a new sun, a god from the machine [Θεὸς ἐκ μηχανῆς], and as another Josiah he roused himself to rescue the writings that had been exposed for a long time as prey to moths and worms. For just as the most august emperor was of great and lofty genius, so he devoted all his effort to ensuring that Christian affairs stood more rightly day by day, and that theological study, almost lulled to sleep and buried, was restored to at least a moderate brilliance (for it could hardly hope to recover its former splendour). His first concern therefore was that the Church should have a sacred text examined at its very sources: all the books of the Old and New Testament, depraved by the unskilfulness of scribes, the drowsiness of readers, the ignorance of translators and the injury of time, were corrected again, and the New Testament was made to be read in the German tongue. The next step was that the lessons of Scripture, which set forth the kernel and marrow of the Gospel history, should gradually be commended to the people through the year from the pulpit. Hence some conjecture that the so-called Dominical texts were selected and introduced in the age and by the authority of Charles the Great; and although this is not sufficiently certain, the monuments of Cassino at least bid us place beyond controversy that Paul, surnamed Winfrid, deacon of Aquileia and monk of Cassino, by the command of our Charles compiled histories and lessons, suited to the feasts of the saints throughout the whole year. These selections are still preserved in the Roman Church, though swollen with superstition. And since the best Prince understood that it greatly mattered to the Christian commonwealth both that suitable ministers should be placed over the Churches and that the common people should be compelled in some way to hear the sacred sermons, and that schools, both higher and lower, should be built, he turned his powers to these things gladly and generously, lest the cause of Christ suffer any harm here. Concerning the ministers of the Church, the bishops or pastors, Aventinus reports that Charles did not lightly choose anyone into the senate of bishops; he looked chiefly to learning and goodness in choosing them. He appointed no one unless he had first been tested by him and well known to him. Concerning the care of the ecclesiastical common people, a Capitulary of Charles has lately come into our hands from a very ancient Palatine manuscript, where in section 17 we read: On the Lord's days let them hold no public assemblies or courts, unless compelled by great necessity or hostility; but let all run to the Church to hear the word of God, and be occupied with prayers or good works; and likewise on the famous festivals let them serve God and the assembly of the Church, and dismiss secular business. Finally, since he noticed that schools were the safest antidote for banishing ignorance and the most certain omen for governing the commonwealth, he was the first among Western Christian emperors to take them under his care. And on this occasion the Tigurine School began to put forth its first head, though rather timidly, not without great show [κοὴ μὴ μετὰ πολλῆς φαντασίας]. For even today, in so great a light, emperors, kings and commonwealths do not have academies everywhere, or, to speak in the usage of that age, general studies or universities; they also have elementary schools, destined for the first fruits of letters, whether in colleges consecrated to such pious uses, or outside colleges, which at an appointed time let out their pupils, as it were from prison, when they have been steeped in the first rudiments of learning, and hand them over to be filed and polished afterwards by the care and industry of professors. So we observe that Charles the Great erected not only academies but also elementary schools, gymnasia and pedagogies, by a most praiseworthy plan. To say nothing more of the academies, the many monasteries, built by the generosity of the most generous Charles, are witnesses: they were not made as splendid receptacles for drones to consume the fruits, but as most useful hives of the flower-gathering bees. For, to use the words of Muzio on Charles the Great, he did not found so many monasteries for any other purpose than that the youth, well trained in them, might be useful by example and teaching to men, and that those who grew old in them, scorning the folly and pomp of the world, devoting themselves to contemplation and prayer, might teach the people uprightness of life and true religion. The College of the Church of Zurich is a witness: when its elders had already happily founded it and adorned it with the greatest privileges, duties, gifts and exemptions, he not only approved their generosity but confirmed and established it by charters, and greatly increased it. From this, I say, from this the origin of the Tigurine School is to be derived. But just as, the sons of the physicians warn us from their Hippocrates, all the elements of the parts of the human body are laid down together, and in the first formation of the foetus the outline of all the limbs arises in the same progress (for that forming power is always at work and does not rest until it reaches its goal), yet not all are completed at once, but one thing follows another in succession with unfinished perfection, so our School too first saw its outlines together, but perfection followed afterwards, divided into degrees, or periods, or indeed ages.

units.la: Prima ætas, à fundatione, sive ab anno Christi 810. ad millesimum, ducentesimum, aut præter propter, rudis adhuc, & respectu regiminis penè informis, infantia vocari potest.
units.tr: The first age, from its foundation, or from the year of Christ 810 to about the year 1200, may be called infancy, still rude and, with respect to its government, almost unformed.

units.la: Secunda, à millesimo ducentesimo, ad millesimum trecentesimum, succrescentem adolescentiam, adeóque formatam jam & satis compactam Scholam nobis nostram exhibet.
units.tr: The second, from 1200 to 1300, presents to us our School as a growing adolescence, and now formed and sufficiently compact.

units.la: Tertia, ab anno millesimo, trecentesimo ad quadringentesimum eandem, Virilem quidem, ætatis ratione, sed literaturæ respectu languentem admodum & deformatam refert.
units.tr: The third, from the year 1300 to 1400, presents it as mature indeed in point of age, but very languid and deformed in respect of learning.

units.la: Quartam denique ab anno 1400, ad 1525. quo Zwinglius Scholastici etiam regiminis, Nieslino Scholastico defuncto, provinciam suscepit, reformatam vocare licebit. Et quanquam Senectus sit Scholæ Tigurinorum trivialis, si tempus spectes & annos, fragrantissimum tamen ætatis spirat florem, si rei literariæ laetissimis incrementis aslurgentem segetem.
units.tr: The fourth and last, from the year 1400 to 1525, in which Zwingli took up the office of the scholastic government after the death of the schoolmaster Niesli, may be called reformed. And although old age is the common lot of the Tigurine schools, if you look at the time and the years, yet it breathes the most fragrant flower of its age, if you look at the growing crop of literary affairs rising in the happiest increase.

units.la: Jure prima Scholæ nostræ periodus infantia nomen habet, & ejus quidem, quę sub magni Curatoris tutela erat. Nam eo ipso, quòd Carolus noster solenni instrumento, tabulis authenticis, Tiguri conscriptis, & Antecessorum privilegia, Fratribus (hæc enim primis Canonicis ubique in vetustissimis Ecclesiæ nostræ monumentis tribuitur nomenclatura) Canonica sive regulari disciplina viventibus, non confirmavit tantum tùm; sed & ingentem beneficiorum cumulum addidit, Scholæ Tigurinæ prima posuit stamina. Octodecim tum numero erant Fratres, non larvati, resti pendula, vesti, Æsopicæ instar corniculæ, versicolore, distinctis familiarum characteribus notati, quales esse solent hodie, qui Benedicti, Francisci, Dominici regulas jactant, eorumque adorant ἐϑελοπρεσβοσϑεγοκείας; sed, qui Canonem seu normam Scripturæ sacræ tam vita, quàm doctrina exprimere jussi, mutuas charitatis & officii in docendo, canendo, monendo, consolando sibi porrexerunt dexteras. Sed quid hoc ad rhombum? Carolina constitutio Canonicorum tantùm meminit, regulari disciplina viventium, die noctuq; indesinenter Dei laudes implentium; de Scholit οὐδὲ γῇ, οὐδὲ μῦ. Non diffitemur, Honoratissimi Auditores, e ruderibus, & obscuris quidem prima hæc Scholæ Carolinæ fundamenta eruenda. Sint verò obscura; certa interim sunt, non dum gradibus perfectæ, annis provectæ; sed natæ demum & in lucem productæ sobolis. Cur enim, salvo Testatoris sensu & scopo, in Carolina fundatione Scholæ nostræ, etsi vagientis, incunabula quærere dubitemus? Num quidquam Collegiorum, aut Monasteriorum, Carolinæ debemus liberalitati, quod Scholarum usum non habuerit? Cur ergo soli illud Tigurino Collegio, & in ea quidem Ecclesia, quæ & antiquissima erat, & per totam Diœcesin Constantiensem, post Episcopalem, ipso sic determinante Johanne XXII. Pontifice, primo derogemus? Huc accedit, quòd, præter, antiquissimum Donationis Instrumentum, Catalogus in archivo custoditur Decani, & primorum Canonicorum Carolinorum, cui ipsa etiam officii eorum annexa est ratio. Diserte autem ibi & strictè iis injungitur, ut sub vita Canonicorum (liceat Emphaticos repetere barbarismos) cum terminatione decimationum, à curtibus in hac Parochia eorum, subscriptarum, aliorumq; in montibus & vallibus habitantium hominum, sicut usque in avum dum dum mundus manet, mos est, ibidem populis Catholicæ fidei ac Christianitatis omni tempore ministerium, quærerent & haberent. Et ut alii post illos cum ipsis decimationibus & aliis professionibus Ecclesiæ illius consisterent semper. Canonicis ergo, & primis quidem, ratione officii incumbebat, Tigurinis,ut omni tempore Ministerium quærerent & haberent. Id vero qua ratione & commodius & compendiosius fieri poterat, quàm si, non Ecclesiastica tantum exhortatione redderent auditores suos περὶ τῶν ψυχῶν; sed & Scholastica institutione tales paulatim parerent vel successores, vel Collaboratores, qui ex Caroli mente & mandato, ad tam splendidam obeundam spartam apti redderentur atque idonei. {1}Neque enim tanta alibi tum temporis vel Scholarum, vel Academiarum erat frequentia, ut mitti promiscuè possent Studiosi ad mercatum literarium: satis erat, si domi quisque suæ in Collegiis, Monasteriis ea haberet adminicula, quæ ad mediocrem Latinitatis & Musicæ notitiam sufficerent. Quin, toto in Occidente, sola ante Carolum M. Bononia, suâ superbiit Academiâ, jam ante seculo V. extructa, posteàque, cùm temporis flexu & fluxu collaberetur, à Carolo restaurata; reliqua per orbem institutio ordinaria aliunde, quàm ex Collegiis & Monasteriis expectanda non erat. Id quod, si temporis ratio permitteret, paulò prolixius à nobis, exemplis Scholarum in Cænobiis Bannocorensi, Heilbrunensi, Lexoviensi, Theolegiensi, Malmesburiensi, Campidonensi, Hirsaugensi, Fuldensi, aliisque probatu pro sive esset. Quæ consuetudo, ubique recepta, gravissimo nobis argumento est, Collegio etiam nostro Scholam fuisse annexam. Denique si, quòd supra memorata Donationis appendix, exigit, de continuatione & propagatione Ministerii soliciti esse debuerunt Canonici nostri, quo tam periculosæ aleæ negotium, & quod optionis eorum non erat, imponi iis, aut imperari potuisset jure, nisi subsidia, seminaria,
units.tr: Rightly the first period of our School has the name infancy, and indeed of that which was under the tutelage of a great guardian. For by the very fact that Charles our Lord, by a solemn instrument, authentic charters drawn up at Zurich, not only confirmed the privileges of his predecessors to the Brethren (for this is the name given to the first canons everywhere in the most ancient monuments of our Church), living under canonical or regular discipline, but also added a huge heap of benefices, he laid the first foundations of the Tigurine School. There were then eighteen Brethren in number, not masked, not hanging by a thread, not marked with varied and distinct family badges like Aesop's little crow, such as there are commonly today, who boast of the rules of Benedict, Francis and Dominic and worship their will-worship [ἐθελοθρησκείας]. Rather, they were ordered to express the canon or rule of Holy Scripture in life as well as doctrine, and they extended to one another the right hands of mutual charity and duty in teaching, singing, admonishing and consoling. But what has this to do with the matter? The Carolingian constitution speaks only of canons, living under regular discipline, unceasingly day and night filling God's praises; nothing about the schools, neither earth nor mouse [οὐδὲ γῇ, οὐδὲ μῦ]. We do not deny, Most honourable hearers, that these first foundations of the Carolingian school must be dug out from rubble and obscurity. Let them be obscure; yet they are certain, not yet perfected by degrees, not advanced in years, but the offspring at last born and brought into the light. For why should we hesitate, saving the sense and purpose of the founder, to seek the cradle of our School in the Carolingian foundation, though it is still wailing as an infant? Do we owe any of the colleges or monasteries to Charles's generosity that did not have the use of a school? Why then should we, first, deny this to the Tigurine College alone, in a Church which was both very ancient and, throughout the whole diocese of Constance, second only to the episcopal one, as Pope John XXII himself so determined? Moreover, apart from the most ancient deed of gift, a catalogue is kept in the archive of the Dean and of the first Carolingian canons, to which is also attached the very reasoning of their office. And there they are clearly and strictly enjoined that, during the life of the canons (let me repeat the emphatic barbarisms) with the collection of the tithes from the farms of this parish of theirs listed below, and of the other men dwelling on the mountains and in the valleys, as has been the custom from time immemorial as long as the world remains, they should seek and have a ministry for the Catholic faithful peoples and Christians at all times there. And that others after them should always remain with those same tithes and other obligations of that Church. So the canons, and the first ones especially, were bound by reason of their office to seek and have a ministry at all times for the Tigurines. But in what way could this be done more fittingly and more economically than if they not only ministered to their hearers concerning their souls by ecclesiastical exhortation, but also through scholastic instruction gradually produced successors or colleagues who, according to the mind and command of Charles, would be made apt and fit to undertake so splendid a task? For at that time there was not such a crowd of schools or academies elsewhere that students could be sent promiscuously to the literary market; it was enough if each in his own colleges and monasteries had those aids that sufficed for a moderate knowledge of Latin and of music. Indeed, throughout the whole West, before Charles the Great only Bologna prided itself on its academy, built already in the fifth century, and afterwards, when it was falling into ruin with the turning and flowing of time, it was restored by Charles; for the rest of the world, ordinary instruction was not to be expected from anywhere but the colleges and monasteries. This, if the nature of the time allowed, we could demonstrate rather more fully by examples of schools in the abbeys of Bangor, Heilbronn, Lisieux, Tholey, Malmesbury, Campidonum, Hirsau, Fulda, and others that might be proved. This custom, received everywhere, is a most weighty argument that a school was also attached to our College. Finally, if, as the appendix to the aforesaid donation requires, our canons had to be anxious about the continuation and propagation of the ministry, then the matter of so dangerous a venture, which was not left to their choice, could not rightly have been imposed on them or ordered of them, unless there had been aids and seminaries...

units.la: {1} Canonicis cura Ministerii incumbebat.
units.tr: {1} The care of the ministry rested upon the canons.

units.la: {2} Ejusdem propagatio. naria, promtuaria ejusmodi, quales sunt Scholae & Collegia, laborantibus tulissent suppetias? Et quanquam vel ex annalibus nostris, vel reliquis Collegii documentis antiquissimis, quibus docendi vices in infantia illa fuerint commissae, perspicue satis non possit elici; verisimile tamen est, Fratres, sive Canonicos operas suas partitos fuisse, adeo ut Curatorum alii sive Plebanorum, alii Praeceptorum officium sigillatim explerent; privata vero cultus exercitia, pensa Canonica, pariter absolverent. Imo, ut propius accedamus, a vero non abhorret, eandem, si non perfectione & accuratione, conatu certe & intentione, fuisse docendi Methodum, quae in aliis sive Aulis, sive Collegiis inde ab aliquot, & quidem in ipso Papatu, obtinuit seculis. Postquam enim, ut de Hebraeorum & Arabum Collegiis per Orientem plurimis & celebratissimis, nihil dicamus, toto orbe divisi Britanni, literariae hujus palaestrae fecissent initium, vestigiis mox eorum Itali Bononiae & Romae, Hispani vero Salamantica, Vallesoleti, & Compluti, in Germania Electores Palatini insistentes; ad exemplum, & imitationem, ut opinor, Caroli nostri, Collegia magno numero, tanto cum successu & applausu, religiose instituerunt, ut Monasteriorum pedetentim nomen vilescere, imo sordere, Collegiorum vero authoritas eminere caeperit. Sed haec alius & otii, & fori sunt.
units.tr: {2} The propagation of the same. Were not storehouses and granaries of this kind, such as schools and colleges are, able to give aid to those who were struggling? And although it cannot be clearly enough gathered either from our annals or from the other most ancient documents of the College as to whom the duties of teaching were committed in that infancy, it is nevertheless likely that Fratres, that is, the canons, divided up their labours, so that some carried out the office of Curati or Plebani (parish priests), and others that of Praeceptores (teachers) separately; while they performed the private exercises of worship and the canonical duties alike. Indeed, to come closer to the point, it is not far from the truth that the method of teaching was the same, if not in perfection and exactness, at least in effort and intention, as that which has prevailed for some centuries in other courts and colleges, and indeed even under the Papacy itself. For after the Britons, scattered across the whole world, had made a beginning of this literary arena (not to mention the many and celebrated colleges of the Hebrews and Arabs in the East), the Italians soon followed in their footsteps at Bologna and Rome, the Spaniards at Salamanca, Valladolid and Alcalá, and in Germany the Electors Palatine; and following, I think, the example and imitation of our Charles, the colleges were founded in great numbers, with such success and applause, that the name of the monasteries gradually began to lose value, and even to fall into contempt, while the authority of the colleges began to stand out. But these matters belong to another time and another forum.

units.la: Habuistis Scholam Tigurinam rudem hactenus & informem, ejusque adeo infantiam, serperastris suis & septis Collegii inclusam: Adolescentia nunc sequitur, sive Schola jam formata, ab anno 1200. ex quo tempore, caput, omnium luci expositia, extulit. Postquam enim tum ex Imperatorum, Regumque amplissimis privilegiis, tum etiam speciosissimis Indulgentiarum chartis, Collegii authoritas majores acquisivisset vires; Collegarum paulatim distinctius distribui necesse fuit munera, ita ut rediturum alii Ecclesiasticorum, adeoque que Oeconomiæ, alii Scholarum, alii supellectilis librariæ, alii cantus Ecclesiastici, alii thesaurorum sive ornamentorum cultui destinatorum demandaretur cura. Unde Scholastici, hac ætate, Cantoris, Thesaurarii, Ædilis, axiomata. Et ut, quam de Scholis potissimum orsi sumus telam, pertexamus, in hanc ipsam Scholæ periodum secundam, electio sive constitutio Scholastici incidit, cujus, ceu Rectoris primarii, officii partes erant, Scholis prospicere, Præceptorem, & eu quidem, qui è re maximè esset ordinare. Primus, quantu ex documentis Collegii assequi potui, Scholæ Carolinæ Rector fuit Magister Bertoldus, Canonicus & Constantiensis, & Tigurinus, quem an. Ch. 1271. cum consensu Eberhardi, Episcopi Constantiensis, Henricus de Klingenberg, & Capitulum Ecclesiæ Thuricensis Canonicè elegerunt, eidemque & Successoribus Scholasticis, secundum aliarum ab antiquis temporibus Ecclesiarum consuetudinem, plenam & liberam concesserunt facultatem de Scholis & Rectore earum ordinandi, prout visum fuerit expedire maximè honori Dei & utilitati Ecclesiæ. Quam quidem ei Præpositus (retineo ipsa instrumenti veteris verba) & Capitulum tribuerunt authoritatem, secundum communem & approbatam, ab antiquis temporibus, consuetudinem aliarum Ecclesiarum, in quibus consuevit hujusmodi dignitatis officium ordinari. Constitutio hæc paulò post, anno 1273. alio repetita & confirmata fuit diplomate. Utque primo huic Rectori, de suorum quoque laborum vel aliquo constaret sive præmio, sive salario, Præpositi & Capituli decreto sancitum fuit, ut quatuor singulis annis ab eo, qui Præceptor à Rectore Scholæ esset constitutus, argenti marca, in recognitionem subjectionis & Magistratus penderentur, quo tamen onere triennio post Præceptores, cum tanti pulverem illum Scholasticum redimere, dubio procul, detrectassent, fuerunt sublevati, & Præpositura ipsa certum ex reditibus Ecclesiasticis Scholastico assignavit salarium. Bertholdus vero noster, ut & gratum Capitulo testaretur animum, & successoribus commodum relinqueret hospitium, ipsas, quae à Scholastico nomen postea acceperunt, aedes Conradi Wellonis, Militis, ab Ulrico de Regenspergo Viro Nobili emtas, Collegio donavit. Atque sic Schola nostra, etsi trivialis, & in primis fere rudimentis occupata, emersit tandem atque in apricum prodiit, idque, quod probe observandum, exemplo aliarum Ecclesiarum, quae, ut Instrumentum nostrum loquitur, ab antiquis temporibus suos habebant Scholasticos, id est, Scholarum Praesides, & Rectores. Ut vel hinc iterum, Scholas olim Ecclesiis & Collegiis individuo nexu fuisse sociatas, pateat, splendoremque potius externum, & quae, venientibus accessit annis, pompam, quam ipsas defuisse scholas, certum sit. Hanc in Ecclesia Tigurina dignitatem Scholasticam ad Reformationem usque continuasse, & honoratam quidem, ex annalibus nostris domesticis evidentissime liquet. Nota sunt nomina Marquardi Gnurferi, Nicolai à Rechberg, Rugeri Manes, Nicolai Martini, Johannis Meizeleri, Diethelmi Sturmii, Johannis Nieslini Collegii nostri Scholasticorum, quorum plerique à natalibus potius, quam publicis nobiles erant librorum aut scriptorum documentis. Scholasticorum vero provincia iis paulatim dignitatis & authoritatis crevit accessionibus, ut Praeceptorem vel Doctorem Capituli consensu semel admissum & probatum, vel retinere Scholastici potuerint, si fecit officium, vel exauctorare, si negligentior fuit aut remissior. Quemadmodum vero ea superiorum seculorum toto orbe fuit barbaries, Linguarum ignorantia, sanae Philosophiae neglectus, Bibliorum contemtus, Theologiae prosanatio, ut ne Cathedrae quidem Theologicae quicquam praeter Lombardum, Gratianum, Aristotelem creparent, ita quid miremur, Scholam hanc nostram, vel infra mediocritatem, studia si attendas & literas (privilegiis enim ab Imperatoribus, Regibus, Principibus, Pontificibus, Cardinalibus, ipso Magistratu Tigurino concessis, quæ & immunitatem ab omnibus oneribus civilibus, & summum vitæ necisque jus largiebantur, ne celeberrimis quidem per Galliam, Germaniam, Italiam inferius erat Collegium nostrum Academiis) substituisse, eo contenta, ut tales Ecclesiæ suæ formaret Ministros, qui legendo & cantando recepta peragere possent sacra. Unde, quod iterum nobis ex Collegii statutis per Rodolphum de VVartensee restauratis mutuandum, primarium Doctoris puerorum erat officium, ut Scholæ (expressa Scholarum, sive gradibus & pensis, sive locis distinctarum fit mentio) & Chorum Collegii legendo & cantando fideliter regeret. Hæc enim tam abstrusa Theologiæ illius, ut postea audiemus, fuerunt mysteria. Et quandoquidem Cantus Ecclesiasticus magis magisque Clero Romano placuit; præcipuamque cultus sacri partem constituit, Musices Professores, quos Cantores illi appellarunt, obvii ubique erant; quibus tamen Collegium hactenus Tigurinum caruisse, tantum non miramur. Aliarum itaque more Ecclesiarum invitatum, a.Ch. 1259. Cal. Maji Cantoris officium Præpositus & Capitulum, Conrado de Mure, primum demandat, Episcopus vero Constantiensis, Eberhardus electionem confirmat, & eo quidem privilegio, ut eandem dignitatem, quam Cantores Majoris Ecclesiæ Basileensis habuerunt, in festionibus, processionibus, & aliis, Cantor etiam Tigurinus in Ecclesia sua obtineret. Erat hic Conradus de Mure, Vir, pro ratione illius ætatis, haud vulgariter doctus, cordatus, quique magna apud Rodolphum Habspurgicum valebat gratia, nec ullius in universo per multos annos Collegio memini, cujus æquè fuerit celebrata fama per orbem: id quod non modò Felicis Malleoli, ejusdem Collegii Canonici, & Cantoris, adeoque & Successoris, calculo; sed & monumentis ejus litterariis, à Gesnero nostro recensitis, probare perquàm facile fuerit. Et
units.tr: You have had the Tigurine School hitherto rough and shapeless, and its infancy was thus enclosed within the walls and fences of the College. Now its adolescence follows, that is, a school already formed, from the year 1200, from which time it raised its head, exposed to the light of all. For after the authority of the College had acquired greater strength, both from the most ample privileges of emperors and kings and also from the most splendid charters of indulgences, it became necessary to distribute the duties among the fellows more distinctly, so that the care of the clergy and thus of the economy was assigned to some, of the schools to others, of the book furniture to others, of ecclesiastical song to others, and of the treasures or ornaments destined for worship to still others. Hence the titles Scholasticus, Cantor, Thesaurarius, Aedilis arose in this age. And to continue the thread with which we began, concerning the schools in particular, in this second period of the school the election or appointment of the Scholasticus fell, whose duty, as that of the chief Rector, was to provide for the schools, and to appoint a teacher, and indeed one who would be most suitable for the business. The first Rector of the Carolina school, as far as I have been able to follow from the documents of the College, was Magister Bertoldus, canon of Constance and a Tigurine, whom in the year of Christ 1271, with the consent of Eberhard, Bishop of Constance, Henry of Klingenberg and the chapter of the Church of Zurich canonically elected, and to him and his successors as Scholastici, according to the custom of other churches from ancient times, they granted full and free power of ordering the schools and their Rector, as they should judge most expedient for the honour of God and the usefulness of the Church. The provost (I retain the very words of the old instrument) and chapter granted him this authority, according to the common and approved custom of other churches from ancient times, in which the office of this dignity has been wont to be ordered. This arrangement was soon afterwards, in the year 1273, repeated and confirmed by another charter. And so that this first Rector should have some reward or salary for his labours, it was decreed by the decree of the provost and chapter that four marks of silver should be paid each year by the one who was appointed teacher by the Rector of the school, in acknowledgement of subjection and of the magistracy; but after three years the teachers, since they doubtless shrank from buying off that scholastic burden at so high a price, were relieved of it, and the provostship itself assigned a fixed salary to the Scholasticus out of the ecclesiastical revenues. Our Berthold, moreover, both to show a grateful spirit to the chapter and to leave a convenient dwelling to his successors, gave to the College the house itself, which later took its name from the Scholasticus, bought from Ulrich of Regensberg, a noble man, which had belonged to Conrad Wello, a knight. And thus our school, though only elementary and occupied for the most part with the first rudiments, emerged at last and came out into the light; and this, which must be carefully noted, on the example of other churches, which, as our instrument says, from ancient times had their own Scholastici, that is, presidents and rectors of the schools. So that from this too it may again be clear that the schools were long ago joined to churches and colleges by an indivisible bond, and that it is certain that the external splendour and the pomp which came with the passing years were added to the schools, not that the schools themselves were lacking. That this dignity of Scholasticus continued in the Tigurine Church until the Reformation, and was held in honour, is most clearly evident from our domestic annals. The names of Marquard Gnurfer, Nicholas of Rechberg, Roger Manes, Nicholas Martin, John Meiseler, Diethelm Sturm, John Nieslin, Scholastici of our College, are well known, most of whom were noble by birth rather than by the records of public books or writings. But the province of the Scholastici grew for them by such gradual additions of dignity and authority that they could either retain a teacher or doctor once admitted and approved with the consent of the chapter, if he performed his office, or dismiss him, if he was more negligent or remiss. But just as in those centuries there was throughout the world barbarism, ignorance of languages, neglect of sound philosophy, contempt for the Bible, and profanation of theology, so that the theological chairs prattled of nothing but Lombard, Gratian and Aristotle, why should we wonder that this school of ours, if you consider its studies and its letters, was placed below mediocrity? (For by privileges granted by emperors, kings, princes, pontiffs, cardinals and the Tigurine magistracy itself, which bestowed both immunity from all civil burdens and the supreme right of life and death, our College was in no way inferior to the most famous academies throughout France, Germany and Italy.) It was content with this: that it should form such ministers for its Church as could carry out the accepted rites by reading and singing. Hence, what we may again borrow from the statutes of the College restored by Rudolf of Wartensee, the chief duty of the teacher of the boys was that he should faithfully direct the schools (the word scholarum is mentioned expressly, distinguished either by grades and tasks or by places) and the choir of the College by reading and singing. For such were the abstruse mysteries of that theology, as we shall hear later. And since ecclesiastical song pleased the Roman clergy more and more, and constituted the chief part of sacred worship, music professors, whom they called Cantores, were to be found everywhere; yet that the Tigurine College had hitherto lacked them we hardly wonder. Accordingly, invited after the manner of other churches, in the year of Christ 1259, on the first of May, the provost and chapter first committed the office of Cantor to Conrad of Mure, and the Bishop of Constance, Eberhard, confirmed the choice, and indeed with this privilege: that the Tigurine cantor should hold in his own church the same dignity which the cantors of the major church of Basel held, in the sessions, processions and other things. This Conrad of Mure was a man, by the standard of that age, not commonly learned, wise, and he had great favour with Rudolf of Habsburg; and I do not remember any man in the College over many years whose fame was equally celebrated throughout the world: which can be easily proved not only from the judgement of Felix Malleolus, canon of the same College and cantor and thus his successor, but also from his literary monuments, listed by our Gesner. And

units.la: C ex Geßnero quidem nostro discimus, scripsisse cum diversis Poëtarum fabulis magnum volumen ; Carmen de naturis animalium, Libellum de Sacramentis ; Felicis & Regulæ passionem, de propriis nominibus fluviorum & montium, Cathedrale Romanum, Laudes B. Virginis, Clypearium Theutonicorum ; Catalogum Romanorum Pontificum & Imperatorum : Comendatitiam Rodolphi Regis Romanorum, Musicam, &c. Utinam vero scripta ejus omnia religiosiori fide & diligentia in hunc usque diem fuissent servata, magnam, sine dubio, lucem & profanæ & Ecclesiasticæ afferre possent Historiæ ! Nihil vero, quod sciam, superest nobis, quàm Fabularium ejus, sive Dictionarium MSc. in Bibliotheca Carolina repositum ; & carmina de Rodolfo I. Imperatore Habspurgico, ab Abbate Murensi, Dominico, non itapridem edita ; quæ veluti in tabella Heroicas nobis Optimi Principis adumbrant virtutes. Cæteris omnibus, si non periculosè, ægrè certè nos carere, cur dissimulemus ? Atque sic alterum Schola, ex nova hac professione Cantoris, habuit incrementum ; tertium sequitur, Librarii sive Bibliothecarii munus. Cùm enim & compendiosissimum, & usu probatissimum, eruditionis comparandæ subsidium sint libri, quorum beneficio mortui etiam, non modò impunè & licitè, sed & utiliter consuluntur, Præceptores communes, longissimis absentes spatiis interrogantur, ignorantia pellitur, dubia soluuntur, scientia augetur, ab ultima retrò antiquitate receptum fuisse, reperimus, ut quicunque bonis literis, humanioribusque pariter ac sacris studiis cautum probè voluerunt, rectéque consultum, Bibliothecas colligerent, & publica quædam rei literariæ armamentaria instruerent. Neque enim à privatis exspectari facilè debet, quod publicos requirit sumptus. Id quod eò magis tum, ob defectum artis typographicæ, erat necessarium, quò difficilius & carius, quæ manu tantùm descripta erant, acquiri atque coëmi debuerunt.
units.tr: From our Gesner indeed we learn that he wrote, along with various fables of the poets, a large volume; a poem on the natures of animals, a little book on the Sacraments; the Passion of Felix and Regula, on the proper names of rivers and mountains, the Roman Cathedral, the Praises of the Blessed Virgin, the Shields of the Germans; a Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs and Emperors, a letter of recommendation for Rudolf, King of the Romans, Music, etc. Would that all his writings had been preserved with more religious faith and diligence down to this day! They could undoubtedly have shed great light on both secular and ecclesiastical history! As far as I know, however, nothing remains to us except his Fabularium, or Dictionary, a manuscript deposited in the Carolina Library, and the poems on Rudolf I, the Habsburg emperor, published not long ago by the abbot of Mure, Dominic; which, as in a picture, set before us the heroic virtues of that best of princes. Why should we pretend that we lack all the rest, if not dangerously, at least with great difficulty? And so the school had a second increase from this new office of Cantor; a third follows, the office of Librarian or Bibliothecarius. For since books are the most compendious and most proven aid for acquiring learning, by whose help even the dead, not only with impunity and lawfully but also profitably, are consulted as common teachers, are questioned though far absent across the longest distances, ignorance is driven away, doubts are resolved, knowledge is increased, we find that from the most remote antiquity it was the practice that whoever wished well and rightly for good letters, both the humane and the sacred studies alike, gathered libraries and set up certain public arsenals of literature. For what requires public expense can hardly be expected from private persons. This was all the more necessary at that time, because of the lack of the art of printing, since things that had been copied only by hand were harder and more costly to acquire and to buy.

units.la: Nova ergò Collegio nostro Bibliothecæ & Bibliothecarii accessit cura. Initio quidem, fateor, Bibliothecarii munus novitate magis acceptum, quàm molestia onerosum erat. Quantæ enim, quæso, molis erat, de iis tantùm libris, quorum usus vel publici altaris, vel Chori terminabatur spatiis, prospicere, illos curare, reficere, conservare; quod leges Collegii, an.
