Ch. 1259. conscriptæ, & Librario, seu, ut ibidem vocatur, Custodi armarii librorum latæ, jubebant? Si quæ rariora erant κειμήλια, Thesaurarii illa fidei commendabantur. Id quod factum observavimus, an. Chr. 1333. Thesaurario Rodolfo Brunio, in cujus supellectili Ecclesiastica non aurea tantùm & argentea vasa, vestes pretiosissimæ, sed & libri quidam occurrunt, Caroli nempe (ut ne totius repetitione Catalogi aut Elenchi Thesauri Ecclesiastici, qui etiamnum ad manus est, vos occupem) Omeliarum libri duo, qui tamen, ipsam postea auxerunt Bibliothecam; Psalterium Caroli, ejusdem libellus Orationum, aureis exaratus literis, & Historia Carolina, musicè scripta. Quin ipsa à Carolo magno, Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ Biblia in Pergameno dono fuisse oblata, constans veterum fuit fama. Hæc Bibliothecæ Carolinæ fuerunt auspicia; ex qua sive incendiis, sive mutuationibus, tempore præsertim Concilii Constantiensis, sive, (quæ Rodolphi de VVartensee Præpositi querela est,) incuriâ, perdita & amissa esse, penè omnia, merito dolemus. Missale tamen de anno 1270. Msc. & superstitiosæ illius ætatis, & varietatis simul rituum Ecclesiasticorum in Ecclesia Romana, testis locupletissimus, vel hodie in Bibliothecæ nostræ forulis ostendi potest. Et certè, si votis quid proficeretur, optandum utique esset, vel Caroli saltem Libellum Orationum, sive Ἀχολόγιον, Psalterium, duos Homiliarum libros ideo superesse, ut tum grassantis superstitionis deformitatem, tum etiam emicantis in ipsis Papatus tenebris veritatis clariùs intueremur strictura. Sed redeamus ad Bibliothecarium. thecarium nostrum. Molestius paulò pòst & laboriosius esse coepit Bibliothecarii onus, cùm, aucto hinc inde bonarum literarum desiderio, numerus quoque librorum crescceret in ipsa Bibliotheca, & eò usque quidem, ut huc, tanquam ad aram & ultimum asylum, publico & privato occupati nomine, confluxisse videantur: quod, ut ne fraudi esset manifestæ, recens comparatæ supellectili, alias & strictiores quidem Bibliothecarius accepit leges; quæ ex Collegii Statutis ita habent:Librarius omnes sibi traditos libros Ecclesiæ fideliter conservârit, quod & facturũ fideliter juravit: Libri reficiendi & innovandi communibus expensis inventur. Habeat omnes libros in Registro, nec alicui accommodet, nisi habeat aliquod memoriale. Extra muros non accommodabit nisi cum consensu Capituli. Et ne libri amittantur, debet Præpositus annuatim cum duobus aliis Canonicis intrare librariam, & visitare libros secundum registrum, & si liber defuerit, debet solvi. Hæc, Scholæ Tigurinæ ætatis secundæ, erant incrementa; hæc publica munera, quæ ut à Schola jam constituta abesse non possunt, ita ejusdem statum formatum luculentissimè probant. Quid enim fuerit absurdius, quid ineptius, quàm inde penè à Carolo Magno admittere Rectorem, subordinatos Præceptores, Bibliothecarios, Scholas & in iis discipulos, dubiam tamen velle reddere aut controversam antiquissimam Gymnasii nostri originem?
units.tr: So our College acquired a new library and a new librarian to look after it. At first, I admit, the office of librarian was welcomed for its novelty more than it was burdensome. For what great effort, I ask you, was it to watch over, repair and preserve those books alone whose use was confined to the space of the public altar or the choir? The statutes of the College, drawn up in 1259 and given to the librarian, or, as the same text calls him, the keeper of the book cupboard, required exactly this. If any books were rarer treasures [κειμήλια], they were entrusted to the treasurer. We find this done in 1333, when Rodolf Brun was treasurer. Among his ecclesiastical equipment there appear not only gold and silver vessels and very costly vestments but also certain books: two books of Homilies of Charles, to save you a recital of the whole catalogue or list of the ecclesiastical treasury, which is still at hand. These two later increased the library itself. There was also a Psalter of Charles, his little book of Prayers, written in gold letters, and a History of Charles, written in musical notation. Indeed, it has been a constant tradition of the old writers that the Bible on parchment was given to the Church of Zurich by Charlemagne himself. These were the beginnings of the Carolingian library. From it, through fires, through loans, especially at the time of the Council of Constance, or (as the provost Rudolf von Wartensee complained) through carelessness, almost everything has been lost and mislaid, and we rightly grieve over it. Still, a Missal of 1270, in manuscript, a most abundant witness both of that superstitious age and of the variety of ecclesiastical rites in the Roman Church, can be shown even today on the shelves of our library. And certainly, if wishes achieved anything, it would be greatly to be hoped that at least Charles's little book of Prayers, or Agologium, his Psalter and the two books of Homilies had survived, so that we might see more clearly, under our scrutiny, both the ugliness of the superstition then rampant and the truth shining forth in the very darkness of Papacy. But let us return to our librarian. The burden of the librarian began a little later to be more troublesome and laborious, when, as the desire for good letters grew on every side, the number of books also increased in the library itself, and to such an extent that they seem to have flowed here, as to an altar and a last refuge, in the name of both the public and private persons. So that this should not be to the detriment of the manifest, the librarian received, for the newly acquired furniture, other and rather stricter laws. These, from the statutes of the College, read as follows: The librarian shall faithfully keep for the Church all books delivered to him, as he has also sworn to do faithfully. Books are to be repaired and renewed at common expense. He shall have all books entered in the register, and shall lend none unless he has some memorial in return. He shall lend none outside the walls except with the consent of the Chapter. And so that no books are lost, the provost shall each year, with two other canons, enter the library and inspect the books according to the register; and if a book is missing, it must be paid for. These were the growths of the Zurich School in its second age; these public offices, which cannot be absent from a school already established, prove its formed condition most clearly. For what could be more absurd, what more foolish, than to admit, from almost the time of Charlemagne, a rector, subordinate teachers, librarians, schools and pupils in them, and yet wish to make doubtful or controversial the most ancient origin of our gymnasium?

units.la: Ne igitur vel temporis prodigi, vel patientiæ Vestræ nimium securi, iis, quæ luce sua clarent, diutiùs immoremur, ad tertiam periodum, quæ Scholæ nostræ trivialis virilem ætatem, successionis tamen potiùs, temporis, & annorum, quàm vigoris & studiorum respectus, ostendit, accedimus. Planè ut multos videas, quorum adolescentia aliquid minatur præclari, qui tamen pravo postea corrupti exemplo, ubi virilem togam induerint, spem turpiter fallunt, totóque adeò Cœlo & animo à se ipsis mutantur, ita etiam Collegium nostrum Carolinum
units.tr: So, lest we either waste time or rely too much on your patience, let us not linger longer over things that shine with their own light, but approach the third period, which shows the manly age of our elementary school. Its maturity is measured by succession, time and years rather than by vigour and zeal. Just as you may see many whose youth promises something splendid, but who afterwards, corrupted by a bad example, when they have put on the manly toga, shamefully disappoint their hope, and are wholly changed, in heaven and in mind, from what they were, so too our Carolingian College, once it swelled with privileges, wealth, authority, splendour and immunities, cast off almost all care for letters and all literature.

units.la: C. Virilis ætas. rolinum postquam turgeret privilegiis, opibus, auctoritate, splendore, inmunitatibus, literarum propemodum curam & literaturae abjecit omnem. Haec enim regnis illa est, & torpescens aetas, quae gravissimas de ignorantia & desidia Collegii Malleolo nostro extorsit querelas. Domi rerum suarum Canonici tantum sategerunt, curriculam curarunt, literis & literatis πολεμον ἀσπονδον indixerunt. Foras ad Academias exteras, quae magnam jam ubique famam acquisiverunt, nullos miserunt. Heidelberga sane, non usque adeo remota, satis jam florens, & Theologorum, qui tum vivebant, qua factis, qua scriptis celebris, a nostratium tamen, ante annum 1406, nemine, quantum antehac ex matricula Academica collegi, frequentata fuit. Non deerant Collegio nostro subsidia Scholae augendae necessaria, non Antecessorum exemplum, non Collegarum desiderium, non vicinorum irritamentum. Beneficiorum pluralitas (geminam enim aut tergeminam abuno tum devorari otioso ventre offam, religioni non ducebatur) otii tranquillitas, laboris fuga, voluptatum illecebrae, & siquae sunt alia, virtutis & eruditionis impedimenta, non unam modo Collegio intulerunt calamitatem. Studia enim si intueamur, ingenua Malleoli confessio est, inde ab obitu Conradi de Muri (obiit autem an. Chr. 1281. 3. Cal. April.) ad annum usque Christi 1452. annorum 171. spatio, ne unum quidem ex toto Clero Ecclesiae Tigurinae quicquam esse meditatum, quod vel memoriae esset dignum. Quam querelam non semel magno cum animi dolore diligentissimus author inculcat. In officii, superstitiosi, & praesenti fere pecunia conducti, functione, cremulae ubique manus, oculi somno correpti, animi si non profani, tepidi saltem, & qui externis tantum commodis sua metiebantur omnia, turpissime se prodebant. In quam iterum negligentiam acerbissime, ut merebatur, invectus est, idem Decretorum Doctor, vir & plurimae lectionis, & magnae næ, apud exteros etiam Principes, authoritatis, Felix Malleolus, tum alibi, tum præsertim in Passionali, quo toto pene asserit tractatu, Canonicos sui temporis ineptos plerosque fuisse, & officii immemores, ingloria ventris mancipia. Et quanquam non negamus, ingenio paulo excitatiori & vehementiori aliquid forte excidisse, quod affectus dictárint turbati, ambigendum tamen non est, quin justissimæ querelæ causas habuerit sufficientes, & eas quidem, quæ clerum in contemtum induxerunt abjectissimum. Unde idem, quem modò citavimus lib. de libert. Ecclesiast. Factos esse, inquit, Sacerdotes & Clericos contemptibiles, præsertim dum literatura, vita & moribus essent vacillantes. Hæc ubique, de Seculi illius moribus & infscitia, obvia est querela. Desinant igitur recentiores quidam nasutuli veteri errori, ex multitudine librorum, patrocinium quærere. Hoc enim si Ecclesiæ & Scholæ Tigurinæ præsides ante ducentos uti voluissent argumento annos, quam imprudenter suo se jugulássent gladio? Inerti plerique torpebant otio, in diem viventes, aliis librorum vel tractationem, vel Editionem relinquebant. Quæ quidem Collegii, Ecclesiæ & Scholæ procerum vita deses, Dioecesi Tigurinæ pluribus nominibus fuit detrimentosa. Cùm enim ne Præceptores quidem sæpe vel literas nôssent vel nare, quid à discipulis illi, & futuris etiam Collegis poposcerint? Admittendi ad curam animarum non tenebantur rigore examinis, Græcorum Dialectis, Latinorum elegantiis, Orientalium monstrosis characteribus, locorum Theologicorum varietate, fontium inspectione; aliisve Theologiæ Candidato dignis speciminibus. Illi omnium tulerant puncta, qui (ut flosculos illorum technologicos retineamus) bene poterant legere, competenter exponere, & sententiare, in computo practicare, cantare, & si quæ sunt alia, non dicam Prisciani ludibria, sed Scholæ potius Trivialis & fori, quàm empli Texercitia. Ridicula ista magis videantur, an lalacrymis digna, difficulter dixero! Illud certum est, vix talia fidem meritura apud posteritatem, nisi rerum gestarum Historia scrupulum omnem atq; difficultatem tolleret. Uno liceat exemplo praxin hujus quidem virilis, sed otiosae & segnescentis ob oculos ponere aetatis. Leonhardus Brun, (in Nidharti haec, Praepositi, adeoque Malleoli inciderunt tempora) de Ulma, vel Echingen ad Examen pro cura (id est, Ministerio, Curatos enim Ministros suos appellare solebant, prout an. Chr. 1443. Ecclesiae ad lacum Tigurinum Horgensis Curatum, hunc Leonhardum fuisse, reperio) examinatus bene legit, competenter exponit & sententiat, computum ignorat, male cantat, & in aliis curam concernentibus competenter respondet: fiat admissio. Haec rigida Majorum sunt examina, quae illis etiam, qui ad Ministerium Ecclesiasticum adspirabant, erant imperata. O caecam noctem! O propudiosam ignorantiam! Sed quorsum tam diu in tenebris istis moremur? Ad lucem properemus, & Solem, qui ultima Scholae Trivialis periodo, eminus suos spargit radios. Quemadmodum enim, ubi intempesta nox meridiem suum, ut cum Plauto loquar, attigit, oriturno mox phosphoro proxima est; ita quo crassiores superiori aevo fuerunt tenebrae, eo propiores Reformationi tam Ecclesiarum, quam Scholarum Antecessores nostros vixisse, eventus probavit. Ea igitur, quae ultima a Seculo 15. sequitur Scholae Tigurinae aetas, cum variis quidem adhuc ignorantiae luctari debuit monstris; multis tamen parasangis praecedentium seculorum fortem superavit. Jam enim Schola nostra eo surrexit, ut ad seria magis paulatim contenderet studia; domi viros eruditos aleret, exteros alliceret, domesticos foras mitteret, eosdemque opimis stipendiis excitaret, praemiis etiam, quod vel indicasse satis sit, ornaret. Et primo quidem habuit hac aetate Tigurum non paucos viros doctos, cives maximè Patritios & nobiles ea apud alios authoritate, ut ipsi per eos patriæ nomen conciliari potu erit atque fama. Dubitatis? Malleolum Vestrum considerate; qui libris suis adeò innotuit, ut memoria ejus posteritati etiam fuerit veneranda. Nam & Gallus, Gaultherius Jesuita, in Catalogum Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum eum retulit, & Germanus, non longè post excessum ejus, vitam Lingua Germanica ἐγκωμιαστικῶς ita edidit, ut non studia minus ipsius, quàm mores, liberalitatem præsertim in pauperes, non tamen validos mendicantes; ne voto quidem adstrictos; commendaret. Theologica, Juridica, Historica, Physica ita tractavit, ut quamvis multa & accuratius & melius dicere potuisset, grassantis tamen barbariei flagellum fuerit. Extat Catalogus operum ejus, prolixus satis, in Gesnero nostro. Sed & Felix Schmid, Tigurinus patriâ, professione Monachus, sede Ulmensis, magno se studio Posteritati commendavit, cum Annalibus suis Suevicis, cum descriptione peregrinationis Orientalis, Bernhardi Breittenbach, Ecclesiæ Moguntinæ Decani.
units.tr: C. The manly age. For this is the sluggish age, which wrung from our Malleolus the most serious complaints about the ignorance and idleness of the College. The canons attended only to their own affairs at home, to their revenues, and declared an unending war against letters and learned men. Abroad they sent no one to the foreign academies, which had already won great fame everywhere. Heidelberg, indeed, not so distant, was already flourishing well and was famous for its theologians then living, both for their deeds and their writings; yet, as far as I have gathered from the academic register, before 1406 no one of our countrymen attended it. Our College lacked none of the resources needed to enlarge the school, not the example of its predecessors, not the wishes of its colleagues, not the stimulus of its neighbours. But the plurality of benefices (for they did not consider it a matter of conscience to devour two or three of these morsels at once in an idle belly), the calm of leisure, the flight from labour, the allurements of pleasures, and whatever other hindrances there are to virtue and learning, brought more than one calamity upon the College. If we look at its studies, it is the frank confession of Malleolus that from the death of Conrad von Muri (he died on 29 March 1281) to the year of Christ 1452, over a span of 171 years, not one man of the whole clergy of the Church of Zurich had planned anything that was worth remembering. This complaint the most diligent author presses more than once with great grief of mind. Lazy in their office, which was superstitious and hired for almost ready money, their hands ever in the cups, their eyes seized by sleep, their minds, if not profane, at least lukewarm, and measuring everything by external advantages, they most shamefully betrayed themselves. Against this negligence he inveighed again most bitterly, as it deserved: the same Doctor of Decretals, a man of wide reading and of great authority even among foreign princes, Felix Malleolus, both elsewhere and especially in his Passionale*, in almost the whole of which treatise he asserts that the canons of his time were for the most part useless, forgetful of their duty, inglorious slaves of the belly. And although we do not deny that, with a somewhat more excitable and vehement disposition, he may have let fall something which disturbed feelings dictated, we must not doubt that he had sufficient and most just grounds for complaint, and grounds which brought the clergy into the utmost contempt. Hence the same man whom we have just cited, in his book On the freedom of the Church, says that priests and clerics had become contemptible, especially while their learning, life and morals were wavering. This complaint about the morals and ignorance of that age meets us everywhere. Let certain more recent, over-clever little fellows therefore stop seeking support for an old error in the multitude of books. For if the presidents of the Church and School of Zurich had wished to use this argument two hundred years ago, how foolishly would they have cut their own throats with their own sword! Most of them grew stiff with idle inactivity, living from day to day, and left to others the handling or the publishing of books. Indeed, that slothful life of the leaders of the College, the Church and the School was harmful to the diocese of Zurich in many ways. For since even the teachers often did not know their letters or could not swim, what could they demand from their pupils, and from future colleagues? Men were not bound, for admission to the cure of souls, to a strict examination in Greek dialects, Latin elegances, the monstrous characters of the Orientals, the variety of theological commonplaces, the reading of sources, or other specimens worthy of a candidate in theology. Those who had passed all the marks were those who (to keep their technical little flowers) could read well, expound competently, judge, practise in calculation, sing, and whatever other things there are, not to call them the mockeries of Priscian, but rather exercises of the elementary school and the market place rather than of the learned. I would hardly say whether these things seem more ridiculous or worthy of tears! This much is certain: such things would hardly deserve belief from posterity, unless the history of the deeds done removed every doubt and difficulty. Let me set before your eyes, by one example, the practice of this manly but idle and sluggish age. Leonhard Brun, of Ulm or Eckingen, (his times fell in the provostship of Nidhart, and thus in those of Malleolus), was examined for the cure of souls (that is, for the ministry, for they used to call their ministers curati, as I find that in 1443 this Leonhard was the curate of the church of Horgen on the Lake of Zurich) and was examined: he reads well, expounds competently and judges, does not know the reckoning, sings badly, and answers competently on other matters concerning the cure: let him be admitted. Such were the rigid examinations of our forefathers, which were imposed even on those who aspired to the ecclesiastical ministry. O blind night! O shameless ignorance! But why do we linger so long in these shadows? Let us hasten to the light, and to the Sun which, at the last period of the elementary school, sends its rays from afar. For just as, when the untimely night has reached its midday, as I may say with Plautus, the dawn soon follows with its rising star, so the experience has shown that the darker the shadows of the earlier age, the nearer to the Reformation of the Churches and the Schools lived our predecessors. This last age, which follows the Zurich School from the fifteenth century, had indeed to struggle with various monsters of ignorance; yet it surpassed by many parasangs the strength of the preceding centuries. For now our school had risen to the point where it gradually pressed on to more serious studies; it nourished learned men at home, attracted foreigners, sent its own abroad, and stimulated them with rich stipends, and adorned them with rewards too, which is enough to mention. And first, in this age Zurich had not a few learned men, chiefly patricians and nobles, who had such authority among others that through them the name and fame of the homeland could be won. Do you doubt it? Consider our Malleolus, who became so well known through his books that his memory was to be venerated even by posterity. For the Frenchman, the Jesuit Gaultherius, included him in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, and a German, not long after his death, published his life in the German language in such a panegyric style that it commended not less his studies than his morals, especially his generosity to the poor, though not to the able-bodied beggars, who were not even bound by a vow. He treated theology, law, history and natural philosophy in such a way that, although he could have said many things more accurately and better, he was nonetheless a scourge against the barbarism then raging. A rather full catalogue of his works exists in our Gesner. But also Felix Schmid, a Zurich man by birth, a monk by profession, of the see of Ulm, commended himself with great zeal to posterity, with his Swabian Annals, and with the description of the eastern journey of Bernhard Breydenbach, dean of the Church of Mainz.

units.la: Si qui deinde foris erant viri supra vulgus docti, Tigurum illi non modo salutarunt; verum etiam lares ibidem suos fixerunt. Qua occasione suum Tigurini fecerunt Nicolaum VVile Poetam, Rodolphum Arzet, sive Physicum, cujus de Cometa anni 1472. tractatum antehac in agro vidi Tigurino; Henricum Nidhartum, Martinum de Bartenstein, Petrum Numagem, Trevirensem &c. quorum omnium scripta Mathematica, Theologica, & Historica vel publicæ sunt exposita luci, vel in Bibliothecarum delitescunt scriniis. Atque hi omnes Tiguri, hac Scholæ nostræ ætate, vixerunt & scripserunt.
units.tr: If any learned men of note came from abroad, they not only greeted Zurich, but also set up their household gods there. On this account the Zurichers made their own Nicolaus Wile, a poet, Rudolf Arzet, or Physicus, whose treatise on the comet of 1472 I saw earlier in the Zurich countryside, Heinrich Nidhart, Martin von Bartenstein, Peter Numagen of Trier, and others. The mathematical, theological and historical writings of all of them have either been brought out publicly into the light or lie hidden in library cabinets. And all of these lived and wrote at Zurich in the age of this our School.

units.la: Insuper, ut cultiores Ecclesia & Schola Tigurina haberet Doctores, ad emporia literarum exteriora, Academias, ablegari suos, (eò tamen in Schola patria, ut non planè absque fructu ad lectiones admitti potuerint publicas, perductos) & magno quidem numero, operæ pretium duxerunt. Aliis in Germania, Basilea placuit; aliis Vienna, Heidelberga aliis, in Gallia, Lutetia; in Italia prae caeteris Mediolanum, Pisae, &c. Et Heidelbergam quidem sedem Academicam ex Tigurinis non paucos elegisse, vel matricula Antiquissimae Universitatis testis est. Initium literariae illius peregrinationis, an. Ch. 1420. fecerat, Johannes Schwanenflugel, de Hottingen (quis enim Nicolaus ille de Turego, cujus an. Ch. 1406. fit mentio, fuerit, cum ignarissimis juxta ignoramus) quem frequentiori postea numero ad Reformationem secuti sunt 42. ex quibus Johannes Higgvvaus, Canonicus ejusdem seculi, an. Ch. 1422. Burkhardus Frey, 1432. Conradus Keller, 1438. Casparus Studler, 1452. qui adhuc an. Ch. 1495. Canonicus fuit, & Cantor Ecclesiae Constantiensis, S. Johannis; Johannes Schwarzmurer, itidem Canonicus, 1452. Johannes Stuki, 1488. Henricus Schwend, 1484. qui etiam postea 1488. Magisterii titulum obtinuit; quos honores, vel primam saltem lauream, eodem anno Heidelbergae impetrarunt alii nonnulli Tigurini, Henricus Engelhard, Henricus Engel, Jacobus VVyss, Henricus Psittacus, quibus viam undecennio ante straverat Conradus Hofmannus, Bremogartensis, Plebanus postea Tigurinus, Zwinglii antecessor, Vir animosus, audax tamen magis, quam fortis, superstitiosus, quam religiosus. Unde & ad monitionis suae, Capitulo Ecclesiae Tigurinae contra Reformatorem Zuinglium traditae, argumentum primum, ab authoritate Theologi Heidelbergensis, Viri eruditi & gravis, cui non Ecclesiastica tantum, sed & Academica commissa erat Cathedra, accersit. Hac semel feliciter jacta alea, strenue nostrates, quibus de meliori luto praecordia erant fi&ta, pede, quo laudabiliter coeperunt, opportunitate in vicina, nobisque confoederata, Basilea magis blandiente, perrexerant. Et ut vel quaedam eorum, qui ab an. 1464. ad Reformationem usque literis in inclyta Basileensium Academia dederunt operam, referam nomina, ecce praesto sunt, Jacobus de Cham 1464 L. L. Doctor, Præpositus & Protonotarius an. Ch. 1471. Nicolaus Monachi, Johannes Nieslin, Canonicus postea, D. Decretorum, & ultimus, ante Reformationem, Scholasticus 1479. Rolandus Goldlin. Eod. Bernhardus Blarer 1482. Henricus Schwvarzmurer 1484. Canonicus; Felix Mejer, Johannes Pfisser, 1486. Reinhardus Goldlin 1488. Conradus Fabri, Johannes Amman, Caspar Reust, idem ille, nisi fallor, qui cohortis Pontificiæ Dux, in expugnatione urbis, occubuit; Henricus Brenwald, insignis Historicus, & Collegiatæ Ecclesiæ Imbriacensis Præpositus, ante Reformationem postremus, 1495. Felix Manz, I. V. D. Collegij Carolini Præpositus, Cathedralis Sedunensis Canonicus, Curatus & Rector Parochialis Ecclesiæ Sallioniæ, Judex, & Commissarius nomine Pontificis, Cardinalis Matthæi, Episcopi Constantiensis, ordinarie, suo tempore constitutus, 1496. Henricus Goldlin, 1497. Jacobus Edlibach, Felix Funck 1500. 1501. Udalricus Zuingli Glaronæ primum, postea in Eremo Plebanus, Pontificis Sacellanus, & Acolytus, Canonicus Collegii Carolini, tandemque auspicatissimus Reformator, 1506. Bernhardus Clauser, Johannes Clarer, postea Sacellanus Badensis 1504. Jacobus Goldlin 1506. Joh. Wilhelmus Keller, qui & Italicas, eo tempore, quo frater ejus Nicolaus an. Ch. 1513. pro obsessis amicis & Confœderatis ad Novariam arma gestavit, adivit Academias, Clericali postea privilegio à Philonardo impetrato, ad solitos sibi aditum patefecit gradus, 1508. Ludovicus Myller, Nicolaus Wyss, Canonicus, Diethelmus Papa, Henricus Wolf, Nicolaus & Johannes Engelhart, Conradus Grebel, Caspar Grosman; Jacob. Meys, Andreas Wirz, Jacobus de Cham; Leonhardus Hofman, Joachimus Gaachlinger, Beatus Faber, ab an. Chr. 1508. ad 1523. Et qui periculum istis fecerunt peregrinationibus, vel stipendiis juvabantur liberalissimis, vel privilegiis muniebantur compendiosissimis, adeo ut illis, qui in Canonicorum numerum recepti jam erant, & conscripti, portio. tio sua Papæ & Episcoporum authoritate confirmata fuerit, totoque peregrinationis literariæ tempore concessa. Hæc postea consuetudo ad ipsa usque Reformationis tempora fuit in usu: unde non potuit non fieri, ut Ecclesia posthac non tantùm, sed & Schola digniores haberet Antistites, per quos, Deo fidem vitamque ad Scripturæ Canonem, reformare, placuit. Hinc Gymnasii Tigurini famâ alii ex cæteris Cantonibus, & Sociis acciti, prima studiorum suorum fundamenta ponere duxerunt honori: & illi quidem, quorum summa deinceps & domi fuit potestas, & foris authoritas. Quorum consiliis res fere florentissimæ & potentissimæ tum Reipublicæ Helveticæ fuerunt. Vel unum nominâsse sufficiat Scholæ nostræ alumnum, Episcopum Vallesiæ & Cardinalem, Matthæum Schinerum, virum in annalibus Helveticis decantatum, Papæ, Regum, Principum commendationibus & promotionibus, ad invidiam clarum, ipsius quin etiam, ut multis placet, Sedis Pontificiæ candidatum. Hic primam fermè fortunæ suæ officinam in Schola quæsivit Tigurina. Cum enim, pro more eorum, quibus res angusta domi, hymnos ad victum comparandum, in multorum præsentia decantâsset, senecio quidam, aspectu venerabilis, vocatum ad se puerum attentius intuetur, cujus esset? quo veniret nomine? studiose inquirit, cui, cum præsenti animo, Matthæus respondisset, memorabile adstantibus reliquit augurium: Hic puer, inquit, aliquando Episcopus & Princeps noster erit; quæ quidem vox calcaria Schinero addidit, ad eluctandum, studiaque impigrè excolenda, cumque nec Pater ab iis abhorreret, Sedunum primùm ab illo missus fuit, illinc Tigurum, ubi prima literaturæ rudimenta imbibit, indeque demum uberioris capessendæ culturæ ergò in Italiam concessit.
units.tr: Moreover, so that the Church and School of Zurich might have more cultivated teachers, they thought it worth the effort to send their men in large numbers to the outside marketplaces of learning, the universities. (They were brought up in the home school so that they could be admitted to public lectures not entirely without profit.) Some preferred Basel in Germany, others Vienna and Heidelberg; others in France chose Paris, and in Italy above the rest Milan, Pisa and so on. That not a few Zurichers chose Heidelberg as their academic seat is attested by the register of that very ancient university. Johannes Schwanenflugel of Hottingen made a start on this literary journey in the year of Christ 1420. (For who that Nicolaus of Turego was, whose mention is made in the year of Christ 1406, we know no more than the most ignorant men do.) He was followed, in larger numbers later on, by 42 at the time of the Reformation, among whom were Johannes Higgwaus, a canon of the same century, in the year of Christ 1422, Burkhard Frey, 1432; Konrad Keller, 1438; Kaspar Studler, 1452, who was still a canon and cantor of the Church of Constance, St John, in the year of Christ 1495; Johannes Schwarzmurer, likewise a canon, 1452; Johannes Stuki, 1488; Heinrich Schwend, 1484, who afterwards, in 1488, also obtained the title of Master; and several other Zurichers who obtained these honours, or at least the first laurel, in Heidelberg in the same year: Heinrich Engelhard, Heinrich Engel, Jakob Wyss, Heinrich Psittacus. A way had been paved for them eleven years earlier by Konrad Hofmann of Bremgarten, later parish priest of Zurich, the predecessor of Zwingli, a spirited man, bolder than brave, more superstitious than religious. Hence also, when he drafted his admonition to the Chapter of the Church of Zurich against the Reformer Zwingli, he summoned as his chief argument the authority of a Heidelberg theologian, a learned and serious man who held not only an ecclesiastical but also an academic chair. Once this die had been successfully cast, our countrymen, whose hearts had been fashioned from better clay, pressed on with the step they had so commendably begun, and were carried further by the opportunity offered by Basel, a neighbouring city allied with us, which was even more inviting. And, so that I may mention the names of some of those who studied at the famous Academy of Basel from 1464 down to the Reformation: here they are. Jakob von Cham, Doctor of Both Laws, 1464, provost and protonotary in the year of Christ 1471; Nikolaus Monachi; Johannes Nieslin, afterwards canon and Doctor of Decrees; and Rolandus Goldlin, the last scholasticus before the Reformation, in 1479. In the same year Bernhard Blarer, 1482; Heinrich Schwarzmurer, 1484, canon; Felix Meyer; Johannes Pfisser, 1486; Reinhard Goldlin, 1488; Konrad Fabri; Johannes Amman; Kaspar Reust, that same man, unless I am mistaken, who fell as commander of the papal cohort in the storming of the city; Heinrich Brennwald, an outstanding historian and provost of the collegiate church of Embrach, the last before the Reformation, 1495; Felix Manz, Doctor of Both Laws, provost of the Carolinum, canon of the cathedral of Sion, curate and parish rector of the church of Sallioniae, judge, and commissary in the name of the Pontiff, Cardinal Matthäus, Bishop of Constance, appointed in his time in the ordinary way, 1496; Heinrich Goldlin, 1497; Jakob Edlibach; Felix Funck, 1500, 1501; Ulrich Zwingli, first at Glarus, afterwards parish priest in the hermitage, chaplain and acolyte of the Pontiff, canon of the Carolinum, and at last the most fortunate Reformer, 1506; Bernhard Clauser; Johannes Clarer, afterwards chaplain of Baden, 1504; Jakob Goldlin, 1506; Johannes Wilhelm Keller, who also visited the Italian academies at the time when his brother Nikolaus bore arms for our besieged friends and allies at Novara in the year of Christ 1513; he afterwards, by a clerical privilege obtained from Philonardus, opened for himself the usual steps to advancement; Ludwig Müller; Nikolaus Wyss, canon; Diethelm Papa; Heinrich Wolf; Nikolaus and Johannes Engelhart; Konrad Grebel; Kaspar Grossmann; Jakob Meyer; Andreas Wirz; Jakob von Cham; Leonhard Hofmann; Joachim Gächlinger; Beat Faber, from the year of Christ 1508 to 1523. Those who risked these journeys were either helped by very generous stipends or protected by the most convenient privileges, so that for those who had already been received and enrolled among the canons, their share was confirmed by the authority of the Pope and the bishops and was granted for the whole time of their literary journey. This custom remained in use right up to the times of the Reformation. Hence it could not fail to happen that the Church and School thereafter had worthier leaders, through whom it pleased God to reform faith and life according to the canon of Scripture. Hence other young men, from the other cantons and allies, invited by the fame of the Zurich gymnasium, thought it an honour to lay the first foundations of their studies there; and those whose supreme power thenceforth lay at home and whose authority abroad was great, by whose counsels the Helvetic commonwealth was then almost at its most flourishing and powerful. It will suffice to name one alumnus of our School: Matthäus Schiner, Bishop of Sion and Cardinal, a man celebrated in the Helvetic annals, renowned for envy, for the commendations and promotions bestowed on him by popes, kings and princes, and, as many think, even a candidate for the papal see. He sought his first workshop of fortune in the Zurich school. For when, as was the custom of those whose households were poor, he had sung hymns in the presence of many to earn his living, a certain elderly man of venerable appearance called the boy to him and looked at him closely, asking whose son he was and what his name was. When Matthäus answered him readily, he left a memorable prophecy for those standing by: "This boy," he said, "will one day be our bishop and prince." That word indeed spurred Schiner on to strive and to cultivate his studies with unflagging diligence. Since his father did not object to this, he was first sent by him to Sion, and from there to Zurich, where he drank in the first rudiments of learning, and then at last went to Italy to pursue a richer culture.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem exterorum paulatim adventus Gymnasii magis magisque florentis fuit indicium; ita & qui Reformationis tempore ejus rexerunt habenas, vel solo nomine,& fama majorem pollicebantur eruditionem, quàm qui anterioribus duobus præcesserunt seculis. Et de Antecessoribus quidem, Scholæ Trivialis Moderatoribus, retrò ultimis, vix supersunt ἐξίηλα ἴχνη. In antiquissimo Ecclesiæ Carolinæ Libro vitæ (ita Catalogum eorum defunctorum, pro quorum liberatione ex Purgatorio solitæ redimi consueverunt inferiæ, amabant appellare) unum reperi, M. Albertum de Roiwvila, quondam Rectorem Scholarum hujus Ecclesiæ, & Adelheid uxorem ejus, cum quinque pueris, qui parvi hic sunt sepulti; proximè verò ante Reformationem in quibusdam Ludi Moderatorum Catalogis præmittuntur Johannes Kaltschmid 1486. M. Felix Frey, Collegii postea Præpositus, M. Henricus Utingerus, Vir diligentissimus, & de universa patria præclarè meritus, Paraftates Zuinglij fidelissimus, Balthasar Sprostius 1514. quem biennio post idem ille excepit, qui, cùm Scholæ prius Abbatissanæ parallelæ Tiguri auspicatum fecisset initium, in Ecclesia & Academia Basileensi Reformata Oecolampadio, sive Haussschyn (quem Hussschyn per allusionem Eccius, Ingolstadiensis Theologus nuncupare solebat) Theologo incomparabili, successit. Erat is vir pius, eruditus, & pacis studiosissimus Osvvaldus Myconius, Lucernensis, qui, postquam Scholæ Tigurinæ aliquamdiu præfuisset, sedem mutavit, Basileam abiit, ibique magno cum applausu optimorum quorumvis, cavillantibus interea & ringentibus aliis, ad Cathedram Theologicam promotus fuit.
units.tr: Just as the arrival of foreigners was a sign of the gymnasium's growing prosperity, so too those who held its reins at the time of the Reformation promised, by their name and reputation alone, a greater learning than those who went before them in the two previous centuries. Of the earlier masters of the Trivial School, the last of them, scarcely any traces remain [ἐξίηλα ἴχνη]. In the most ancient Book of Life of the Church of the Carolinum (for so they liked to call the catalogue of the dead, for whose release from purgatory the customary funeral offerings were wont to be redeemed), I found one entry: Master Albert von Roiwila, formerly rector of the schools of this church, and Adelheid his wife, with five children, who are buried here while small. But shortly before the Reformation, in some catalogues of the masters of the school, there are placed in front Johannes Kaltschmid, 1486; Master Felix Frey, afterwards provost of the college; Master Heinrich Utinger, a most diligent man, who deserved very well of the whole fatherland, a most faithful paraphrast of Zwingli; Balthasar Sprost, 1514, whom two years later that same man succeeded, who, having first made a start at Zurich in the parallel school of the Abbess, succeeded, in the Church and Academy of Basel, which had been reformed, Oecolampadius, or Hausschein (whom Eck, the Ingolstadt theologian, used to call Husschein by way of a pun), an incomparable theologian. This was the pious, learned man, and most devoted to peace, Oswald Myconius of Lucerne, who, after he had presided over the Zurich school for some time, changed his seat, went to Basel, and there, with great applause from all good men, while others mocked and sneered, was promoted to the theological chair.

units.la: Disputationes publicæ coronidem huic ætati imponunt. Cùm enim, ex quo tempore Pontifices Romani Helvetios sibi fœdere devinxerunt, devinctos magna solicitudine retinuerunt, Legati Pontificii sedem Tiguri ut plurimùm fixissent, ad literarum etiam paulò ante Reformationem incrementa, iidem aliquid contulerunt. Stipendium enim, L. Florenorum Rhenensium, annuum, quatuor Tigurinis Pisæ literis operam daturis, nomine Ducis Urbinatis & Florentini
units.tr: Public disputations crown this period. For when the Roman pontiffs bound the Swiss to themselves by treaty and kept them bound with great care, the papal legates, who for the most part had fixed their seat at Zurich, also contributed something to the growth of learning shortly before the Reformation. They offered a yearly stipend of fifty Rhenish florins to four Zurich students who were to study at Pisa, in the name of the Duke of Urbino and of Florence.

units.la: {Myc} Myconius. offerunt; Disputationes publicas, in Collegio habitas, praesentia sua cohonestant, nihilque adeo reliqui faciunt, quo vel authoritatem Scholae nostrae augerent, vel nomen conciliarent. En specimen publicae disputationis, aegre ab interitu & oblivione vindicatum, habitae Tiguri proxime ante Reformationem, ipso praesente & judicante Pontificis Legato, quod αὐτολεξεὶ ita sonat: Dubium Theologicum, disputandum in praesentia Reverendissimi Domini, Antonij Puccij, Legati ad Helvetiam, die 14. mensis Septembris, hora XII. in Ecclesia Collegiata, in Thurrego, est tale:
units.tr: Myconius. They also lent their presence to the public disputations held in the College, and they left nothing undone that might either increase the authority of our School or win it a reputation. Here is a specimen of a public disputation, barely rescued from destruction and oblivion, held at Zurich just before the Reformation, with the papal legate present and presiding. Word for word it reads: A theological question, to be disputed in the presence of the Most Reverend Lord Antonius Puccius, legate to Helvetia, on the 14th day of September, at the twelfth hour, in the Collegiate Church at Thurrego, is as follows:

units.la: Cum Paulus Apostolus dicat; Deum patrem in Christo nos elegisse ante Mundi constitutionem; quaeritur non inmerito, An Deus Optimus Maximus aliquam creaturam ad supernaturalem beatitudinem praedestinaverit?
units.tr: Since the Apostle Paul says that God the Father chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, it is not unreasonably asked: Has God, the best and greatest, predestined some creature to supernatural blessedness?

units.la: Decuit Deum, cunctarum rerum providorem, ad ultimam felicitatem, homines pariter & Angelos (licet nunquam misertos) sua ineffabili bonitate praedestinare.
units.tr: It was fitting that God, the provider of all things, should predestine men and angels alike (though the angels never needed mercy) to ultimate happiness, by his ineffable goodness.

units.la: Praedestinatio, a Providentia & Libro vita ratione differens, sicut hominem non necesitat; ita nec in praedestinato aliquid ponit.
units.tr: Predestination, differing from providence and from the reckoning of the Book of Life, does not necessitate man; and so it does not place anything in the one predestined.

units.la: Praedestinatio tam Entium, quam non Entium, unica existens, secundum legem communem, hominibus passim revelari non debuit, ne omnis boni fons, Deus optimus, malitiae & desperationis causa existat.
units.tr: Predestination, of beings and of non-beings alike, being single and existing according to a common law, ought not to have been revealed to men generally, lest God, the good fountain of all good, become the cause of malice and despair.

units.la: Praedestinationis causa totalis, (licet partialis) praeter meram Dei liberam voluntatem, ex parte praedestinatorum, nulla (teste Apostolo) assignari potest.
units.tr: The whole cause of predestination (though it is only a partial cause), apart from God's mere free will, can be assigned on the part of the predestined, as the Apostle testifies, in no way.

units.la: Praedestinationis infallibilis numerus, & certitudo ex hoc dignoscitur, quia omnipotens Deus in suo opere minime impeditur.
units.tr: The infallible number and certainty of predestination are known from this, that almighty God is in no way hindered in his work.

units.la: Praedestinatis suae electionis quandoque effectus sanctorum precibus donatur, pro quibus tantummodo Ecclesiae communia suffragia summo Deo offerri intelliguntur. Ad ultimum ergo felicitatis finem Deus optimus maximus aliquos homines misericorditer Prædestinavit; Reliquos vero non injustè reprobavit.
units.tr: The effect of his election is sometimes granted to the predestined through the prayers of the saints, for whom only the common suffrages of the Church are understood to be offered to the highest God. Therefore, to the final end of happiness, God the best and greatest has mercifully predestined some men; but the rest he has not unjustly reprobated.

units.la: Impertinentia Theologica.
units.tr: Miscellaneous Theological Theses.

units.la: Gratia in statu naturæ lapsæ homini sicut necessaria, ut, ea absente, nec Dei observare præcepta, aut bonum velle, & facere, aut à peccatis resurgere aliquo modo valeat.
units.tr: Grace is necessary for man in the state of fallen nature, so that without it he cannot in any way observe God's precepts, or will and do the good, or rise again from sins.

units.la: Gratia, quæ à Deo datur, in Essentia animæ subjectivè ponitur, ut virtus ipsa minimè censeatur.
units.tr: The grace which is given by God is placed subjectively in the essence of the soul, so that it is not regarded as virtue itself.

units.la: Gratiæ auxilio potest homo sibi mereri vitam æternam de condigno; sed nullus sibi primam gratiam (licet alteri) dempto Salvatore Christo, de congruo.
units.tr: By the help of grace man can merit eternal life de condigno; but no one can merit for himself the first grace, though he can for another, de congruo, apart from the Saviour Christ.

units.la: Lex vetus, præcepta Decalogi continens, aptissimè, tempore Moisi, fuit mortalibus data: quæ omnes obligabant, tanti sunt roboris, ut indispensabilia ipsa perseverent.
units.tr: The Old Law, containing the precepts of the Decalogue, was most aptly given to mortals in the time of Moses; it bound all, and is of such strength that the precepts themselves remain indispensable.

units.la: Lex nova, veteri levior, in finem mundi usque duratura, per Christi fideles præcones in cunctis terræ plagis fuit promulgata.
units.tr: The New Law, lighter than the old, to last until the end of the world, has been published by Christ's faithful heralds in every corner of the earth.

units.la: Adam, in statu innocentiæ, peccare venialiter non potuit; sed, illo in statu, opera magis meritoria elicuisset.
units.tr: Adam, in the state of innocence, could not sin venially; but in that state he would have elicited works more meritorious.

units.la: Sancti, Felix & Regula incomprehensibilem divinam essentiam clara & intuitiva visione (absque similitudine aliqua) cernunt: sic tamen, ut resumptis corporibus eorum beatitudo major fiat.
units.tr: The saints, Felix and Regula, see the incomprehensible divine essence by a clear and intuitive vision (without any likeness); yet so that when their bodies are taken up again, their blessedness becomes greater.

units.la: Lumen gloriæ, in hac patria pernecessarium, diversi diversimodè sunt accepturi, omnes tamen de sua felicitate perpetuò erunt securi.
units.tr: The light of glory, most necessary in this fatherland, will be received by different people in different ways; yet all will be perpetually secure about their happiness.

units.la: Impertinentia Philosophica.
units.tr: Miscellaneous Philosophical Theses.

units.la: Infinitum in rebus creatis, nullum est dabile, eo nihilominus dato, à nobis minimè esset cognoscibile.
units.tr: An infinite in created things cannot be given; and even if it were given, it would by no means be knowable by us.

units.la: Vacuo positio, quod natura abhorret, motus per illud non subitò; sed in tempore fieret. Locus, conservativus locati, est superficies corporis continentis semper immobilis.
units.tr: The positing of a vacuum, which nature abhors, would make motion through it not instantaneous but occur in time. Place, which preserves what is placed, is the surface of the containing body, which is always immobile.

units.la: Ad argumenta, in contrarium fienda, respondebit Frater Vuendelinus Ofualdi, Ordinis Prædicator. Sacræ Theologiæ Baccalaureus formatus.
units.tr: Brother Vuendelinus Ofualdi, of the Order of Preachers, a formed Bachelor of Sacred Theology, will reply to the arguments to be made on the other side.

units.la: Ego Mauritius Bretini, ipsius Legati Notarius, de illius mandato subscripsi.
units.tr: I, Mauritius Bretini, notary of the same legate, have subscribed by his command.

units.la: Sed quò delabor? Abunde de Schola mihi ante Reformationem triviali, dixisse videor, ejusque statum informem, formatum, deformatum, & reformatum enarrasse; ad eandem nunc, qualis post Reformationem fuit, accedendum esset; Academicam; quando vero nec temporis ratio, nec brevitatis data fides, nec attenta vestra expectatio longius me excurrere sinunt, ipsa vero messis tum ubertas, tum pretium, fuliorem requirit termonem, vel alii lampadem tradam, vel ipse, ubi salvum me præstiterit & incolumem supremum Numen, quod restare videtur, suo tempore expediam. Colophonem ergo Orationi nostræ imposituri, ad Deum nos convertamus. Tibi itaque, Clementissime Deus, Pater benignissime, gratias, quas mentes nostræ capere, oraque exprimere possunt agimus maximas, tum pro infinitis tuis beneficiis, tum vero & cumprimis, quod urbem hanc nostram Tigurinam non justitiæ tantum Tuæ, sed & misericordiæ speculum extare voluisti. Placuit Tibi, Majoribus nostris ex Gentilismi tenebris ereptis, lucem accendere Evangelii Tui, eamque, cum suas nonnunquam pateretur Eclipses, subinde restituere. Merebamur equidem, ut eodem nobiscum, quo contra alios ingratos, ageres rigore, sed aliter gratiæ tuæ visum fuit, atque paternæ clementiæ. Imperatorum, Regum, Principum, Rerum publicarum flexisti animos, qui munifica sua liberalitate Scholas in his etiam Europæ angulis erigerent, atque sustentarent. stentarent. Et quanquam læva multorum acciderit mente, ut, quæ pio Zelo ad Dei gloriam, animarumque salutem magnis impensis erant instituta, superstitioni paulatim, privato commodo, otio, libidini, ignorantiæ inservierint, noluisti tamen, pro merito, in nos animadvertere nostro. Quin potius, majores nostros, jugo Ecclesiasticæ tyrannidis presios, mancipiis insciti æ oneratos potenter liberasti, Scholæ idoneos Magistros & Doctores clementer concessisti, superstitionem, cultum Idololatricum penitus evertisti, subsidia, Te verum Deum, & quem misisti Jesum Christum, ex ipsis limpidissimis verbi Tui fontibus cognoscendi, subministrasti, novaq; adeo Pentecoste nos beasti. Da, quæsumus, ut Te tanti beneficij animo grato agnoscamus authorem, dignisque laudibus & encomijs, celebremus. Ne permittas, rogamus, ut turpi ingratitudine procaciter in Te peccemus, ansamq; adeo Scholas iterum nostras veræ pietatis & eruditionis Gymnasia, in squalidos insciti æ carceres convertendi, præbeamus. Prævidemus facile, nisi aliorum, & Majorum quidem nostrorum, exemplo sapiamus domestico, fore, ut graviores nos maneant poenæ, eorumque, quæ gratia Tua singulari, cum admiratione multorum, habuimus bonitatis tuæ monumenta, justissimo Tuo judicio, sed & magno nostro merito, faciamus jacturam. Id ut ne fiat, rogamus Te supplici voce & mente, per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum.
units.tr: But whither am I drifting? I seem to have said enough about the School before the Reformation, when it was merely trivial, and to have described its state as unformed, formed, deformed, and reformed. Now I should turn to the same School as it was after the Reformation, as an academy. But since the nature of the time, the limits I promised for brevity, and your attentive expectation do not allow me to run on longer, and since the harvest itself, both its abundance and its worth, calls for a fuller discourse, I will either hand the torch to another or, when the supreme Deity, who seems to remain, has kept me safe and sound, take it up myself in its own time. So, about to set the seal on our oration, let us turn to God. To you, therefore, most merciful God, most kind Father, we give the greatest thanks that our minds can grasp and our mouths express, both for your infinite benefits and above all because you have willed that this our city of Zurich should stand as a mirror not only of your justice but also of your mercy. It pleased you, when our forefathers had been snatched from the darkness of heathenism, to kindle the light of your Gospel, and, though it sometimes suffered eclipses, to restore it again and again. We certainly deserved to be treated with the same severity with which you treated others who were ungrateful; but your grace and your fatherly clemency thought otherwise. You bent the minds of emperors, kings, princes and commonwealths, who by their generous liberality set up and maintained schools even in these corners of Europe. And although it has happened, through the perverse minds of many, that what had been founded with great expense for the glory of God and the salvation of souls was gradually put to the service of superstition, private advantage, idleness, lust and ignorance, you nevertheless were unwilling to punish us as we deserved. Rather, you powerfully freed our forefathers, who were oppressed and burdened under the yoke of ecclesiastical tyranny, and you mercifully granted to the School fit masters and teachers; you utterly overthrew superstition and idolatrous worship, and you supplied the means of knowing you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent, from the very clearest fountains of your Word; and so you have blessed us with a new Pentecost. Grant, we beg, that we may acknowledge you as the author of so great a benefit with a grateful mind, and celebrate you with worthy praises and eulogies. Do not permit, we pray, that we sin against you with shameless ingratitude, and so give occasion for turning our schools, the gymnasia of true piety and learning, back into squalid prisons of ignorance. We easily foresee that, unless we are wise by the domestic example of others, and of our forefathers in particular, heavier punishments will await us, and that by your most just judgment, and by our great desert, we shall suffer the loss of those monuments of your goodness which, by your singular grace, we have held, to the wonder of many. That this may not happen, we ask you with suppliant voice and mind, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: Pater noster, &c.
units.tr: Our Father, etc.
