units.la: Pictoribus atque Poëtis
units.tr: To Painters and Poets

units.la: Quidlibet audendi semper fuit aqua potestas.
units.tr: Whatever one dares to do has always been an equal right.

units.la: Nobis, Poëtarum Principis tritum de Poëtis & Pictoribus judicium, sensu paulò moderatiori ita nostrum facere liceat:
units.tr: Let us, with a somewhat more moderate sense, make our own the well-worn judgment of the Prince of Poets on poets and painters:

units.la: Pictoribus atque Poëtis
units.tr: To Painters and Poets

units.la: Quidlibet augendi semper fuit ampla facultas.
units.tr: Whatever one wishes to exaggerate has always been an ample licence.

units.la: Nam, ut Poëtas Poëtarum foro relinquamus, quàm artificiosè Pictores & suos extollere possunt manuum levissimos ductus, & aliorum molestissimos, callosæ dextræ, labores extenuare? Quàm facilè muscas suas Elephantos faciunt, Elephantos aliorum muscas? Carbone notatam chartam, quibus jactant ampullis & sesquipedalibus verbis? Cùm Rhodum Apelles annavigâsset (verba sunt Plinij II. Veronensis, solertissimi rerum naturalium Scrutatoris, & Scriptoris) avidus cognoscendi opera Protogenis, famâ tantum sibi cogniti, officinam continuò petiit. Aber at ipse, sed tabulam magna amplitudinis in machina, aptatam pictura, anus una custodiebat. Hac Protogenem foris esse respondit, interrogavitque, à quo quaesitum diceret. Ab hoc, inquit Apelles, arreptóque peniculo lineam ex colore duxit summa tenuitatis per tabulam. Reversò Protogeni, quæ gesta erant, anus indicavit. Ferunt, artificem, protinus, contemplatum subtilitatem, dixisse: Apellem venisse. Non enim cadere in alium tam absolutum opus. Ipsum tum alio colore tenuiorem lineam, in ipsa illa duxisse, præcepisseque abeuntem, si rediisset ille, ostenderet, adjiceréque, hunc esse quem quæreret, atque ita evenit. Revertitur enim Apelles; sed vinci erubescens, tertio colore lineas secuit, nullum relinquens amplius subtilitati locum. At Protogenes victum se confessus, in portum devolavit, hospitem quærens; placuitque si ea am tabulam posteris tradi, omnium quidem, sed artificum præcipuè miraculo. Non instituti jam nostri est, exactius rimari, quid artis periti in hoc lineolæ unius ductu, festivo Dædalæ manus lusu, ita suspiciant, ut miraculum esse possit. Scilicet!
units.tr: For, to leave the poets to their own court, how skilfully painters can make their own lightest strokes seem great, and reduce the most laborious work of others, done by hardened hands, to nothing! How easily they make their flies into elephants, and others' elephants into flies! Paper marked with charcoal, which they puff up with bombastic and foot-long words! When Apelles had sailed to Rhodes (these are the words of Pliny, the most diligent investigator and writer of natural things), eager to see the works of Protogenes, whom he knew only by reputation, he went straight to the workshop. He did not find Protogenes there, but a large panel fixed to the easel, and only an old woman guarding it. She replied that Protogenes was out, and asked whom she should say had asked for him. "Tell him it was this man," said Apelles, and taking a brush he drew with paint a line of the finest thinness across the panel. When Protogenes came back, the old woman told him what had happened. The artist, they say, at once studied the fineness of the line and said: Apelles has been here. No other could produce so perfect a work. Then, with another colour, he drew a finer line over that very line, and told her, when he left, to show it to him if he came back, adding that this was the man he was looking for. And so it happened. For Apelles returned, but ashamed to be beaten, he cut lines with a third colour, leaving no room at all for finer work. Protogenes, confessing himself beaten, flew down to the harbour looking for his guest. And it was resolved that this panel should be handed down to posterity, admired by all, but especially by artists. It is not now our purpose to examine more closely what skilled artists admire in this single stroke of a line, a playful sport of the Daedalian hand, so that it could be a marvel. Indeed!

units.la: Pictoribus atque Poëtis Quidlibet audendi semper fuit ampla facultas.
units.tr: To Painters and Poets: Whatever one dares to do has always been an ample licence.

units.la: Suum cuique pulcrum, trahitque sua quemque voluptas: Satis sit, vel verbo monuisse, artificiosum potius Apellis & Protogenis, quàm vel ingeniosum, vel judiciosum fuisse certamen. Et, ut illud Pictoribus non invidemus; ita ampliorem longè ἱερῶν ἀγώνων, splendidéque pro palma disputationis ijs superesse campum, qui fusa, & per vasta scriptorum volumina diffusa, arctis Rhetorum cancellis includere, compendiosáque in charta exhibere didicerunt, cur diffiteamur? Illud enim manuum; hoc mentis opus est. Illud visum obiter, & quasi per transennam perstringit; hoc & aures suaviter demulcet, & animum solidè oblectat. Illud vel stillicidio leviter tactum, vel cultro erasum, vel teredine erosum, vel quolibet alio nævo labefactatum, gratiam amittit omnem; hoc verò semel præmeditatè conceptum, & in chartas providè relatum, quævis alia æternitatis monumenta facilè provocat, nullàque amplius deleri, aut obliterari potest oblivione. Illud hiantes duntaxat spectatores, quibus præter transitorium oculorum pabulum, pictura nihil pollicetur, admittit; hoc virtute quādam flexanimā & vorticordia rupes trahit & saxa, planéque adamantina in obsequium cogit pectora. Quanquam verò Rhetorum palæstra longè latéque pateat, nusquam tamen ingenij vires, dicendíque copia se exerunt luculentius, quàm si enarrandis & decantandis Dei beneficiis gnaviter serioque illæ impenduntur. Ego certè, ad quem pro rostris differendi vices, publicā iterum authoritate, sunt devolutæ, neque de lana caprina verba facere constitui, neque de fumo disceptare; Sed Schola mihi Vestra Schola Reformata, Publica, aurem mihi vellicat. Illustre argumentum! Divinum & immortale beneficium, ad cujus pleniorem enarrationem, non Tullianum jam mihi flumen, aut Demosthenéum fulmen, non Nestoream eloquentiam, aut mella Poëtica; nec tam gravem, politam, aut nitidam, quàm fecundam, vibrantem & nervosam à Deo immortali optārim Orationem. Et quia iniquis horulæ arctamur spatiis, ita aptabimus lacertos, ut quam à pictoribus mutuare non possumus augendi & dilatandi artem, veniam tamen cum ijs, quod assequi non datur, vel silentii supparo involvendi, vel primis tantùm lineamentis adumbrandi, vel in contractas tabellas referendi, impetraturos nos confidamus. Nolo esse pollicitis dives; nec Vos, quod vix de quoquam sperari potest, à me, quasi dignum haberet Schola hodie Tigurina laudis praeconem, expectabitis. Conatum tamen receptæ consuetudini satisfaciendi, luculentámque pro tam liberali & munifico dono, debita Deo labiorum sacrificia offerendi, ostendemus, atque occasionem.
units.tr: Each thing is beautiful to its own, and each man is drawn by his own pleasure. Let it suffice to remark, in a word, that the contest of Apelles and Protogenes was one of craft rather than of wit or judgment. And just as we do not begrudge painters that prize, why should we deny that a far wider field, and a brighter one for the palm of disputation, lies open to those who have learned to take things that are spread out and diffused through vast volumes of writings, to enclose them within the narrow bars of the rhetoricians, and to present them compendiously on a page? For the one is the work of the hands, the other of the mind. The one glances at the eye in passing, as though through a window; the other both sweetly soothes the ears and solidly delights the mind. The one, if touched lightly by a drip of water, scraped by a knife, eaten by a worm, or weakened by some other blemish, loses all its charm; but the other, once conceived with deliberate thought and carefully committed to paper, easily rivals any other monument of eternity, and can no longer be erased or blotted out by oblivion. The one admits only gaping spectators, to whom a picture promises nothing beyond a fleeting feast for the eyes; the other, by a certain moving power, draws rocks and stones, and compels even hearts of adamant to obey. Although the arena of the rhetoricians stretches wide and far, nowhere do the powers of talent and the abundance of speech show themselves more brilliantly than when they are spent diligently and seriously on recounting and celebrating the benefits of God. I, to whom by public authority the duty of speaking from the rostrum has once again fallen, have resolved neither to talk about goat's wool nor to dispute about smoke. But School, your Reformed, Public School, tugs at my ear. An illustrious subject! A divine and immortal benefit, for whose fuller telling I would wish for an oration not of Tullian flow, nor of Demosthenic thunder, nor of Nestorian eloquence, nor of poetic honey, but one not so much grave, polished or bright as fruitful, vibrant and sinewy, from the immortal God. And since we are confined by the unfair limits of a single hour, we shall so prepare our arms that, although we cannot borrow from the painters the art of enlarging and expanding, we may nonetheless obtain your pardon for what cannot be achieved: by wrapping it in the scant covering of silence, by sketching only its first outlines, or by setting it down on small contracted tablets. I do not wish to be rich in promises, nor, since it can hardly be hoped of anyone, shall you expect from me that the Tigurine School today deserves a herald of praise as if from me. Nevertheless, we shall show an endeavour to satisfy the accepted custom, and an occasion to offer, for so generous and munificent a gift, the due sacrifices of lips to God in a splendid manner.

units.la: Benevolentiam solicitè ambirem vestram, nisi audiendi gratiâ convenisse Vos, mihi constaret, & ipsum causæ, quam acturus sum, momentum, attentas mihi sponderet aures. Id verò, quia non injussa canam, nec mea authoritate hanc confcendi cathedram,ut quicquid à me, homine, quod ignorare non potestis,utcunque occupato,proficiscitur,æqui boníque consulatis, rogo, obsecro ,obtestor. Quod & tantò facilius vos mihi daturos spero, quantò,tractatio nostra operosa,difficilis, invidiæ etiam plena,& liberalius requirit otium, & æquius Auditorum postulat judicium. Ut verò suis decurrat Oratio limitibus, telam, quam ante annum , de Schola Carolina (sic enim hanc nostram jure appellari, haud obscuris tum condocefecimus documentis) vestro arbitrio suscepi, jam, οὐν Θεῷ ἐ λόγῳ, pertexam. Et quemadmodum trivialem illam ante Reformationem, & Grammaticam, adeoque humi jacentem,per aliquot Secula mecum percurristis; ita publicam,post Reformationem, sive Academicam (quod ei axioma ne exteri quidem denegant) non inferiorum tantum difciplinarum Organicarum,& Philologiæ Sacræ nutricem almam ; sed & superiorum Facultatum, Scientiarum cumprimis Reginæ, Sacro-Sancta Theologia, felicissimam cultricem, mecum intuemini. Sistere quidem ex conceptis jam meditationibus vobis possem (quod nec livor aliorum obscurare,nec malitia adversariorum inficiari audet,) Scholam Tigurinam ordine inter Reformatas primam ; insigni Doctorum corona splendidam ; Professorum unanimi concordia beatam ; indigenarum,ut plurimum,imo civium, raro exemplo, industria,& administratam,& auctam,subsidiorum robore suffultam, Legibus prudenter adstrictam,ab exteris non minus , quam domesticis frequentatam ,omnibus bonis, ipsis etiam adversariis,honoratam , imo, nisi modestia me hæc alijs relinquere juberet , adderem , constantissimam,semel recepta orthodoxia nutricem,multarum Ecclesiarum Reformatarum promtuarium, dulce eruditorum gremium. Sed quando & præfiniti temporis , & augusti habenda est ratio Auditorij,ibimus quò poterimus,triplici potissimùm Scholæ nostræ encomio contenti,quòd ordine fuerit prima, famâ celeberrima
units.tr: I would anxiously seek your goodwill, were it not clear to me that you have come together to listen, and were the weight of the cause I am about to plead not promising me attentive ears. But since I sing things not unbidden, and do not mount this chair on my own authority, I ask, beg and entreat that you accept kindly and fairly whatever proceeds from me, a man, as you know, however busy. I hope you will grant this all the more easily, as our task is laborious, difficult, full of ill will, and demands a more generous leisure and a fairer judgment from the audience. So that my speech may run within its proper bounds, I shall now carry on, with God's help, the web I undertook at your decision a year ago, concerning the Carolinian School (for so, by right, we call this school of ours, as we then taught with clear proofs). And just as you went through with me the old trivial school before the Reformation, a grammar school lying low on the ground, so now look with me at the public school after the Reformation, or the Academic one (which not even outsiders deny as an axiom): the kindly nurse not only of the lower Organic disciplines and of Sacred Philology, but also of the higher Faculties, above all of the most sacred Theology, the queen of the sciences, and her most fortunate cultivator. I could indeed set before you, from the meditations already conceived, what neither the envy of others dares to obscure nor the malice of adversaries dares to deny: the Tigurine School, first in rank among the Reformed; brilliant with a notable crown of teachers; blessed with the united harmony of its professors; managed and enlarged by the industry, for the most part of natives, indeed of citizens, a rare example; supported by the strength of resources; prudently bound by laws; frequented by outsiders no less than by natives; honoured by all good men, even by its adversaries; and, were modesty not bidding me leave these things to others, I would add: most constant in nourishing orthodoxy once received, a storehouse of many Reformed churches, and a sweet bosom for the learned. But since both the fixed time and the dignity of the audience must be considered, we shall go where we can, content mainly with a threefold praise of our school: that it was first in rank, most famous in reputation

units.la: Varie quidem posset tractari.
units.tr: It could be treated in various ways.

units.la: Sed ad tria revocatur.
units.tr: But it is reduced to three heads.

units.la: I. Oridine prima. rrima,& docentium concordia beatissima. Fuit ergo, ut vela entis committamus, non Schola minùs, quàm Ecclesia Tigurina inter Reformatas prima. Dignum πρωτείων certamen! De patria Homeri acerbè Græci olim disceptárunt. Pergunt Leipsanolatræ pro suppositicia reliquiarum merce etiamnum armis infestis, animísque pugnare infensis. Nobis in tam vili & abjecto mustaceo laureolam quærere volupe non est. Id verò primis merito Patriæ nostræ annumeramus honorum ornamentis, quòd inter Scholas à sece & fermento Papistico purgatas, Tigurina nostra primum ordine obtineat locum. Quemadmodum enim Zuinglius Reformator literis non ita leviter fuit tinctus, ut antecessorum more vel Homiliarios exscriberet serviliter, vel horas Canonicas insulsè deblateraret, vel Missam confusè & imperitè demugiret; sed ita planè plenéque imbutus, ut ipsos fontes, tum Scripturæ Sacræ, tum venerandæ antiquitatis, consuleret; sobriæ Philosophiæ rivulos & ipse sectaretur, & aliis ostenderet; Eloquentiæ cum primis, cujus torrens ille fuit, Helvetiæ proinde Cicero à Viris magnis nuncupatus, studia excoleret; Linguarum Originalium situ & squalore obsitarum pretium revocaret; ita prima hæc ejus, potissimáque fuit cura, ut non modò Gymnasio, sive Scholæ Triviali de Moderatore erudito, & Sparta tam luculenta digno, prospiceretur; sed & Scholæ publicæ doctissimis Professoribus Tigurum nostrum statim illustrius redderetur. Prima Gymnasij Reformati fundamenta jecit Vir doctrinâ, pietate, integritate cumprimis morum, probatissimus, Osvvaldus Myconius, Lucernensis, fidelissimus Zuinglii Achates, qui tamen paulò post Scholæ Abbatissanæ præfectus, successorem reliquit M. Georgium Binderum, Tigurinum, virum & doctum, & didacticum, cujus industria jam ante Vienæ Joachimo Vadiano, nō uno fuit nomine probata. Dati fuère deinceps Scholis etiam Classicis tum Moderatores, tum Collaboratores, Viri pij, eruditi, qui, ut ut ad majora nati, in sancto tamen hoc ergasterio tempus tanto majori transegerunt animo, quanto copiosius & luculentius inde ad universam Patriam redundare animad verterunt emolumentum. Inter Scholae certe classicae Rectores reperimus Binderos, Frisios, Ochsneros, Huldricos, Zelleros; Collaboratores vero Guldibekios, Gualtheros, Pontisellas, Fabricios, Hospinianos, Collinos, Evandros, quorum nonnulli ad alia transierunt studia, caeteri, tanquam felicissimi ingeniorum cultores, juventutisq; formatores non tantum probatissimi, sed & celeberrimi; Ecclesiae se, suosque labores consecrarunt. Publica vero Schola adeo felicibus instituta fuit auspiciis, ut plantari simul & florere coeperit. Insigne profecto decoris compendium; quod aliis vix postea concessum fuit sive Scholis, sive Academiis. Quemadmodum enim notorium satis, inter Doctores eruditos & celebres, est discrimen; Illi vel in abjecto saepe delitescunt angulo, & Diogeniano rotantur dolio; hi vero in publica constituti luce omnium judicio expositi, ubi tela invidiae semel utcunque everberarunt, albis famae quadrigis triumphant; & tanquam Arbitri rei literariae, ex specula futuras eruditorum tempestates prospectant; ita certum est, publicorum Phrontisteriorum, Scholarum & Academiarum, famam eundo crescere, virésque annis acquirere. Non ita feliciter hic nascitur foetus, ut virilem protinus induat togam. Quae tamen praerogativa Scholae Tigurinae, singulari Dei beneficio, contigisse videtur. Postquam enim An. Chr. 1525. Capitulum Carolinum in mandatis Zuinglio dedisset, ut Viros magnos undiquaque conquireret, conquisitos blande invitaret, munificisque stipendijs alliceret, mox fama Zuinglij, ejusque studiorum amore, literas, exulantes ubique, in Helvetia praesertim (gloriosissima aliquot seculorum belli non altrice modo, sed & pene moderatrice) Tigurum
units.tr: I. First in rank, and most blessed in the harmony of its teachers. Let us then, as the saying goes, commit our sails to the wind: the Tigurine school, no less than the Tigurine church, was first among the Reformed. A worthy contest for primacy [πρωτείων]! The Greeks once disputed fiercely over the homeland of Homer. The relic-worshippers still fight with hostile arms and bitter spirits over the spurious merchandise of relics. We have no wish to seek a little laurel in such a cheap and worthless cake. Rather, we rightly count it among the chief ornaments of honour for our homeland that, among the schools purged from the leaven and dregs of Popery, our Tigurine school holds the first place. For just as Zwingli, the Reformer, was not so lightly tinged with letters that, like his predecessors, he either copied out homiliaries slavishly, or babbled the canonical hours foolishly, or bellowed out the Mass in confusion and ignorance; but was so thoroughly and fully steeped in them that he consulted the very sources, both of Holy Scripture and of venerable antiquity; and himself followed, and showed to others, the streams of a sober philosophy; and cultivated eloquence above all, of which he was a torrent, and hence was called by great men the Cicero of Helvetia; and restored the value of the original languages, buried in dirt and neglect; so this was his first and chief care: that not only should there be provision for a grammar school under an erudite headmaster, worthy of so splendid a Sparta, but that the public school should also be made more illustrious for Tigurum by the most learned professors. The first foundations of the Reformed gymnasium were laid by the man most approved for learning, piety and above all integrity of character, Oswald Myconius of Lucerne, the most faithful comrade of Zwingli; who, however, shortly afterwards, being placed over the school of the Abbey, left as his successor Master Georg Binder of Zurich, a man both learned and gifted in teaching, whose industry had already been proved in Vienna under Joachim Vadianus, not in one respect alone. Thereafter, both headmasters and assistants were given to the classical schools, pious and learned men, who, although born for greater things, spent their time in this holy workshop with the greater spirit, the more they saw the benefit that flowed from it, more abundantly and brightly, to the whole fatherland. Among the rectors of the classical school we find the Binders, Frisius, Ochsner, Huldrich and Zeller; among the assistants Guldibeck, Gualther, Pontisella, Fabricius, Hospinian, Collin and Evander, some of whom passed over to other studies, while the rest, as most fortunate cultivators of minds and formers of youth, not only most approved but also most famous, dedicated themselves and their labours to the Church. The public school was founded under such happy auspices that it began at once to be planted and to flourish. This was truly a remarkable shortcut to honour, which was hardly granted afterwards to other schools or academies. For just as the difference between learned and celebrated teachers is well known, since the former often lie hidden in some obscure corner and roll about in a Diogenes-style tub, while the latter, placed in public light and exposed to the judgment of all, triumph on white chariots of fame once they have somehow beaten back the darts of envy, and look down from their watchtower, as arbiters of letters, on the coming storms of the learned; so it is certain that the reputation of public seminaries, schools and academies grows as they go, and gains strength with the years. Such a foetus is not born so fortunately that it at once puts on the manly toga. Yet this prerogative seems to have come to the Tigurine school by the singular benefit of God. For after, in the year of Christ 1525, the Carolinian Chapter had given Zwingli the commission to search out great men everywhere, to invite them kindly once found, and to attract them with generous stipends, soon the fame of Zwingli and his love of learning drew letters, wandering everywhere, especially in Helvetia (which, for some centuries of glorious war, was not only its nurse but almost its moderator), to Tigurum; so that, with a zeal for transplanting, it came about that all the most learned flocked to the dedication of the new school. And so that Zwingli might provoke others by example, the first Rector of the Reformed school (whom our people preferred to call Scholarch, a sufficiently august term) was proclaimed on the 14th of April 1525, after the death of Dr. Nicolinus,…

units.la: rum num transferendi Zelo, effectum est, ut doctissimi quique ad novæ Scholæ confluerent encœnia. Et ut exemplo cæteros Zuinglius provocaret, primus Reformatæ Scholæ Rector (quem Scholarcham, satis augusto axiomate appellare nostri maluerunt) defuncto Dr. Nicolino die 14. Aprilis 1525. proclamatur, ipsasque (quas Vestro jam beneficio, Patres Conscripti, Fratres honorandi incolo,) Scholastici ab annis quadringentis, ædes, occupare jubetur; cui ordine postea in Scholarchatu successerunt Bullingerus, Anwianus, Johannes VVolfius, Gualtherus, Lavaterus, Hallerus Wolfgangus II. Simlerus, Kellerus Georgius, Medicus; II. VVolfius Casparus, Medicus II. Funckius, Leemanus, H. Stuckius Wilhelmus II. Frisius, Jacobus; Trubius, Hosspinianus II. Cornerus, Beumlerus II. Lavaterus, Henricus, Medicus, VVaserus II. Ernius, Murerus, Huldricus Jacobus, Lavaterus, Johannes Rodolphus, Holzhalbius, Irmingerus, Kellerus, Osvvaldus, Huldricus, Joh. Henricus, à Kusen, Schwarzenbachius, Lavaterus Joh. Casparus, Stuckius Joh. Rodolfus, VVisfius: Ille Præceptor meus, postea etiam Collega honoratissimus, hic Antecessor Venerandus. Majusne ab initio imperantium fuerit desiderium, an exsequentis studium, merito dubitemus. Vix enim Collegium jubere definit; Zuinglius imperata facere incipit: omnemque, ut viros Scholæ nostræ conciliaret, qui non minus celebritate nominis, quam institutionis methodo toti orbi literario erant noti, movit lapidem. Recte Medicorum Filij observant, medicamina tum demum prodesse recuperandis viribus, cum maligna prius, valetudinis repagulum, sublata fuerit materia. Zuinglius certe noster, cum animadvertisset, a morbis paulatim quidem adnatis, totum vero, successu temporis, corpus Ecclesiasticum & Scholasticum infestantibus, nullam sperandam salutem, nisi barbariei, & ignorantiæ Linguarum Originalium, tolleretur gangræna, ab eorum vocatione initium illi placuit facere, re ,qui in Linguis excellerent,hàncq; felicissimè fundi Theologici calamitatem removerent. Non obscuro vel indicio,vel monito,ut ne posthac ad eandem, superciliosò Linguarum contemptu , captivitatem Ægyptiacam,repedaremus. Succeßit consilium fortissimi Reformatoris, Heroi magno, respondítque conatibus eventus : Scholæ enim Reformatæ, præviâ vocatione, operam suam primùm consecrat Jacobus Ceporinus, Dinharto-Tigurinus, Vir quidem juvenis, sed Linguarum , Græcæ & Hebraicæ callentissimus, publicis etiam scriptis clarus ; cuj paulò post è vivis sublato, Conradus Pellicanus, Rubeaquensis; literaturæ Hebraicæ non modò studiosissimus, sed ad stuporem penè peritus ; Rectoris Zuinglij suasu & consilio ; surrogatur. Duo præterea alij ijs fuerunt asciti Collegæ, Johannes Jacobus Ammianus, Tigurinus, & Rodolphus Collinus, alias Clivanus, Lucernensis, contubernales antea,& studiorum socij Mediolani conjunctissimi; quorum ille Latina ;hic, de cannabi (restis enim erat, qui torquendi funes squalorem Homeri lectione abstergere subinde solebat) ad cathedram publicam protractus, Græca magno cum applausu tractavit. Hæc Scholæ nostræ Reformatæ fuerunt primordia,hæ primitiæ. Et ut ne Zuinglius Capitulo novæ Scholæ Professorum numero majori crearet molestiam,ipse quoque,scenæ prudenter inserviens,partem Scholasticorum,non communium tantum Rectoris, sed & singularium Professoris Theologiæ,suis passus est humeris imponi,laborum. Retrimenta & quisquiliæ Sententiariorum, Summistarum, Quodlibeticorum, &c. omnia penè occupárunt Scholarum & Templorum subsellia ; muscus traditionum arborem vitæ,Evangelij doctrinam,ita obduxit & involvit, ut læta præconij incrementa impediret; Vinum denique Verbi divini pannosam superstitionum contraxit fæcem,quam tamen avidè nimis, illi etiam , qui ad gubernacula sederant, hauserunt; ut ergo omnem, quantum poterat Zuinglius invidiam declinaret, neque probaret ipsâ, neque de Ecclesia subvertenda, neque de Scholis abolendis, sed repurgandis tantum ijs, emuscandis, defœcandis, esse se solicitum; modestâ moderatâque συγκαταβάσει, quicquid in Veteri disciplina & institutione vel tolerabile fuit, retinuit; eo duntaxat sive repurgato, quod detrimentosum erat; sive refecto, quod superfluum. Hinc in Agendis Ecclesiasticis (ita Liturgiam appellare nostri amant) quicquid, ex Papismi Ægypto, Templi novi structuræ inservire poterat, pomoerijs nostris proscriptum ille noluit. Cùmque horis Canonicis longo usu, Lingua peregrina decantandis, Capitulum assuevisset; Zuinglius, ut quod penso horario Methodo proximè accederet, commodis verò illud longè superaret; substitueretur, haud ægrè obtinuit. Sic itaque horarum Canonicarum boatui potius, quàm devotæ recitationi, lectio successit Scholastica, ut, matutina Concione dimissa, precibus peractis publicis, Studiosus Textum ex translatione Vulgata, quæ Hieronymo vulgò tribui solebat, prælegeret, quem Professor deinde Hebraicos ad sontes examinavit; Versionem hinc LXX. Viralem alter Theologus, quam Provinciam ipse, inter sexcentas occupationes, Zuinglius sustinuit, cum veritate Hebraica contulit; Textúmque in Capita sua distinctum, ordine ad Auditorum captum accomodavit. Ad has audiendas lectiones Canonici obstricti erant omnes, Sacellani, Sacerdotes, Monachi; universus imò Clerus, & quicunque aliquam saltem Linguæ Latinæ habebant notitiam. Quæ consuetudo longius deinde processit, & ab ijs etiam religiosè fuit observata, qui non modò sine cortice jam poterant natare; sed & ipsi Oceanum Theologicum cum admiratione potius, quàm laude, enavigârunt. Reperimus certè Pellicanum, Bullingerum, quanta nomina & lumina! Bibliandri, qui Zuinglium in Professionis munere, ut Bullingerus, in Scholarchatu An. Chr. 1532. excepit, lectiones Theologicas & diligenter frequentasse, & meditationes illius studiose consignasse. Finita tandem lectione, Ministri Ecclesiae, quae Lingua peregrina inter Doctos erant ventilata, plebi vernaculè exponebant. Haec prima Theologiae tradendae in nova Schola Theologica erat Methodus. Prudentissimo utique instituto! Adeo enim Scriptura Sacra superioribus Seculis, non ex limpidis fontibus, sed turbidis rivulis, jejunè, frigidè, & ineptè fuit tractata; vel verius, modo dilaniata atque lacerata, modo, quod Polydorus Vergilius de Canonistis queritur, corij instar didućta, ut vel referre pigeat. Alij in propudiosas omnia transformabant allegorias; alij uni capiti viginti continuos annos impendebant, (certè, Thomas Haselbach, Ænea Sylvio teste, ne 22. annorum fluxu primum Jesajae Caput absolvit) non ut Spiritus Sancti mentem aut religiosius scrutarentur, aut penitius eruerent, sed ut vel Aristotelis, vel Platonis placita Scripturae Sacrario sacrilegè inferrent. Obtinuit haec Sacras Literas conferendi & explicandi Methodus ad Petri Martyris adventum, qui, inducta paulatim horarum Canonicarum oblivione, lectiones, alternis Septimanis, magis Scholastica, id est, artificiosas, Scholisque aptas, instituit, fontium interim, cum Versione Graeca continuata, collatione. In ea quid praestiterit Collega, Bibliander, exemplar ejus, quod in manibus nostris adhuc est, notis ubique illustratum, abundè fidem facit. Molestia autem quotidie legendi ideo Theologi erant liberati, ut publicis commodius navare possent, quae Tiguro tum maximè expectabantur, lucubrationibus. Ne verò literatura interea humanior prorsus jaceret, ejusque cultura pertinaciorem ostracismi rigorem experiretur, reliqui duo Professores, Jacobus Ammianus Latina, Collinus verò Graeca, praelegerunt. units.tr: Out of zeal to transfer ... it came about that all the most learned men flocked to the dedication of the new school. And so that Zuinglius might challenge the others by example, the first Rector of the Reformed School (whom our people preferred to call the Scholarch, a rather grand title) was proclaimed on 14 April 1525, after Dr. Nicolinus died. He was ordered to occupy the buildings of the Scholastici, which have stood for four hundred years and which, thanks to your kindness, Conscript Fathers and honoured brothers, I now inhabit. In the office of Scholarch he was afterwards succeeded in order by Bullingerus, Anwianus, John Wolfius, Gualtherus, Lavaterus, Hallerus, Wolfgang II. Simlerus, Kellerus, George, physician; II. Wolfius, Caspar, physician II; Funckius, Leemanus, H. Stuckius, William II; Frisius, James; Trubius, Hosspinianus, II. Cornerus, Beumlerus, II. Lavaterus, Henry, physician; Wascerus, II. Ernius, Murerus, Huldricus, James; Lavaterus, John Rudolph; Holzhalbius, Irmingerus, Kellerus, Oswald; Huldricus, John Henry; à Kusen, Schwarzenbachius, Lavaterus, John Caspar; Stuckius, John Rudolph; Wisfius. The first of these was my teacher, later also my most honoured colleague; this one is my venerable predecessor. We may reasonably doubt whether the desire of the rulers at the start was greater than the zeal of the man who carried it out. For the Council had scarcely finished giving its order when Zuinglius began to do what was commanded, and he moved every stone to win over men for our school who were known throughout the whole learned world no less for the fame of their names than for their method of teaching. The sons of physicians rightly observe that medicines help to restore strength only once the malignant obstacle of ill health, the matter causing it, has been removed. Our Zuinglius, at any rate, saw that the Ecclesiastical and Scholastic body, which was being attacked by diseases that at first crept in gradually but in time afflicted the whole body, could expect no cure unless the gangrene of barbarism and ignorance of the original languages were removed. He therefore chose to begin by calling men who excelled in the languages, and so most happily to remove the calamity that had befallen theology. This was no obscure hint or warning, lest we should return to the same Egyptian captivity through a haughty contempt for languages. The plan of this most courageous Reformer succeeded, and the outcome matched his efforts. For the first to dedicate his labour to the Reformed School, after a formal call, was Jacobus Ceporinus of Dinhard near Zurich, a young man but very skilled in Greek and Hebrew and already known for his published writings. After he was taken from the living a little later, Conradus Pellicanus of Rufach was substituted, at the persuasion and advice of Rector Zuinglius; he was not only most devoted to Hebrew literature but nearly astonishingly expert in it. Besides these, two other colleagues were admitted: Johannes Jacobus Ammianus, a Zurich man, and Rodolphus Collinus, otherwise called Clivanus, of Lucerne, who had earlier been fellow lodgers and very close companions in study at Milan. Of these, the former taught Latin, while the latter, who was drawn from hemp (for he was a rope-maker, and used at times to wipe the grime of twisting cords off with the reading of Homer), was brought to the public chair and taught Greek to great applause. These were the beginnings and first fruits of our Reformed School. And so that Zuinglius would not trouble the Council by creating a larger number of professors for the new school, he himself, prudently serving the stage, allowed part of the scholastic burden to be placed on his shoulders: not only the common duties of Rector but also the particular work of Professor of Theology. The dregs and rubbish of the Sentences, Summists, Quodlibetarians, etc. had almost taken over the benches of the schools and the churches. The moss of traditions had so covered and entangled the tree of life, the doctrine of the Gospel, that it hindered the happy growth of the proclamation. Finally, the wine of the divine Word had taken on the ragged lees of superstitions, which those who sat at the helm also drank down all too eagerly. So, to avoid as much odium as he could, Zuinglius declared that he was concerned neither to approve these things nor to overthrow the Church or abolish the schools, but only to cleanse them, scour them, and strain them clear. With a modest and moderate accommodation [συγκατάβασις], he kept whatever in the old discipline and instruction was at least tolerable, removing only what was harmful and trimming what was superfluous. Hence, in the Ecclesiastical Agenda (our people like to call the Liturgy by that name), he would not banish from our precincts whatever out of the Egypt of Papism could serve for building the new temple. When the Chapter had grown accustomed, through long practice, to chanting the canonical hours in a foreign tongue, Zuinglius obtained without great difficulty that a reading be substituted, since it came closer to the scheme of the hours and far surpassed them in usefulness. So for the mere noise of the canonical hours, rather than their devout recitation, a scholastic reading took over. After the morning sermon was over and the public prayers were finished, a student read the text from the Vulgate translation, which was commonly attributed to Jerome. The Professor then examined it against the Hebrew sources. Next, another theologian compared the Septuagint with the Hebrew truth. Zuinglius himself, among six hundred other duties, undertook this task and divided the text into chapters, arranged to suit the understanding of the hearers. All canons, chaplains, priests and monks were bound to attend these readings, indeed the whole clergy and anyone who had at least some knowledge of Latin. This custom went on for a long time afterwards and was devoutly kept even by those who could now swim without a float, and who themselves sailed the theological ocean with wonder rather than praise. We certainly find Pellicanus, Bullingerum, what great names and what lights! Bibliander, who succeeded Zuinglius in the Professorship in 1532, as Bullinger did in the Scholarchate, both attended the theological lectures diligently and carefully recorded his meditations on them. When the reading was finished, the ministers of the Church explained in the vernacular to the people what had been discussed among the learned in a foreign tongue. This was the first method of teaching theology in the new Theological School. A most prudent arrangement indeed! For before this, Holy Scripture had been handled in earlier centuries not from clear springs but from muddy streams, dryly, coldly and foolishly; or rather, it was now torn and mangled, and now, as Polydore Vergil complains of the canonists, stretched like leather, so that it is shameful even to report. Others turned everything into shameful allegories; others spent twenty continuous years on a single chapter (certainly Thomas Haselbach, according to Aeneas Sylvius, finished the first chapter of Isaiah only after a span of twenty-two years), not in order to search out or draw out more devoutly the mind of the Holy Spirit, but to bring the opinions of Aristotle or Plato sacrilegiously into the sanctuary of Scripture. This method of comparing and explaining the sacred writings prevailed with the coming of Peter Martyr, who, as the memory of the canonical hours gradually faded, set up lectures on alternate weeks that were more scholastic, that is, artful and suited to the schools, while in the meantime the sources were compared with the continued Greek version. What Bibliander, his colleague, achieved in this is amply shown by his copy, which is still in our hands and illustrated with notes everywhere. Meanwhile the theologians were freed from the daily burden of lecturing so that they could more conveniently devote themselves to the scholarly work that Zurich was then looking forward to most eagerly. Lest polite literature meanwhile lie utterly prostrate and experience the harsher rigour of banishment, the two remaining Professors, Jacobus Ammianus in Latin and Collinus in Greek, gave lectures. The former, at twelve noon, first chose Quintilian for the arts and languages; then, by turns, he polished the precepts of dialectic and rhetoric, sometimes adding some speech or a book of Cicero in which he showed the dialectical and rhetorical art and transferred the precepts to the practice of speaking and writing. The latter, at four in the afternoon, began with various Greek authors...

units.la: Artium & Linguarum primò delegit ;alternis postea Dialecticæ & Rhetoricæ præcepta expoluit ; addita interdum oratione aliqua vel Libro Ciceronis, in quo artificium Dialectico-Rhetoricum ostendit, præceptaque ad dicendi scribendíque usum transtulit: Hic vero, horâ quartâ, varios Græcos Authores, initio facto ab Homero, tam soluta, quàm ligatâ Oratione interpretatus est. Hæc Scholæ nostræ publicæ, cum ipsa dogmatum Reformatione natæ, sunt incunabula, hæc prima facies. Nam, quo minùs plures cum in Professorum recipi potuerint Senatum, temporum obstitit difficultas. Aluit sub Papatu Collegium Carolinum Canonicos nonnunquam 24. sæpe etiam 26. absentes plerumque, donec Bulla Martiniana præsentes eos esse coegit; quòd si quibus de meliori luto ficta erant præcordia, ut sanioribus Zuinglij consilijs aures substringerent, doctrinæque repurgationem admitterent, loco illi non movebantur. Quibus vero nec publica concionandi aut profitendi, nec privata, Oeconomiæ Capitularis administrandæ, cura poterat committi; illis rude donatis metam vitæ tranquillè decurrere permittebatur. Inglorium enim erat, ne dicam iniquum, ea vitæ subsidia per Reformationem, quæ suum cuiq; asserebat, subtrahere; quæ Papatus superstitiosus non denegavit. Defunctis verò paulatim, ex præscripto Naturæ ordine ijs, qui per Capituli juramentum, & receptas Leges repelli non poterant; magna Scholæ nostræ ex reditibus illorum facta est accessio, adeò quidem, ut non longè post, duabus iterum illustrior illa evaserit Professionibus, Academiis valde necessarijs, Theologicâ N. T. & Physica, quarum illa Josiæ Simlero, hæc Conrado Gesnero, Tigurinis primùm fuit demandata, magnóq; cum Scholæ ornamento pariter atque emolumento hucusque retenta. Et ut nihil piæ eruditionis Candidatis deesset, quo omnibus veræ Sapientiæ dotibus redderentur cumulatiores; ijs deinceps aucta est Schola nostra progressibus, ut nullum literaturæ vel Theologicæ, vel humanioris nectar alibi in celeberrimis instillaretur Academijs, cujus πρόγυμα nostrum non etiam propinaret Tigurum. Habuit enim dehinc, habet etiamnum, Theologiæ Professores duos, quorum alter Novi, alter Veteris Testam. Pandectas, præter Locorum Communium tractationem, explanat & explicat. Habet, qui Cursum ἐγκυκλοπαιδείας absolvunt, partibus omnibus absolutissimum, Metaphysicam, Physicam, Ethicam, Logicam, Rhetoricam. Si cui Mathematica placeant deliciæ eas degustandi occasio nunquam fuit negata. In Linguis desijmus ab aliquo tempore acquiescere in Græca & Hebraica; cæteras etiam, quod ne extranei quidem ignorant, Orientales, non infelicissimè omnium tractavimus. Historia, Sacra potissimum & Ecclesiastica, non diligenter minus à Professoribus fuit tradita & proposita, quàm à Studiosis avidè excepta & hausta. Et quemadmodum vel præcipitati, vel nimis diducti Viatorum gressus citius iter abrumpunt; ita qui in studiorum cursu rapido prosiliunt gradu, diu non durant. Circumspectè igitur institutum à nostris fuit Majoribus, ut ne, quod alibi fieri solet, ex Schola statim triviali sive Grammatica, ad Lectiones, illotis, quod ajunt, manibus, publicas provolarent. Unde de commodo cogitârunt loco, ubi & respirare non nihil possent Musarum Castarum alumni à molesto pulvere Scholastico, & ad graviora superiorum Facultatum studia se præparare. Novum ergo, medium inter Scholas Classicas, & Auditorium publicum, erectum est Collegium, congruo, quòd humaniores potissimum in eo tractarentur Literæ, Humanitatis Collegij nomine, insignitum. Huic etiam quatuor destinati erant Professores, Græco-Latinus, Rhetoro-Logicus, Catecheticus, & Hebræus. Quo quidem excusso & explorato consilio illud maximè urgebatur, ut in Latinis, non quod Scholæ flagitant Classicæ, puritas tantum & castimonia Linguæ, jam ante comparata, conservaretur illibata; sed & florum leporumque elegantia aucta vernaret: In Graecis, praeter continuam N.T. repetitionem tum Grammaticam, tum etiam Criticam, ex Ecclesiasticis & profanis authoribus tantum accederet, ut à Musis quisque publicis avulsus, suo deinceps pergere posset Marte. Et quia haec jam aetas matura videbatur, quae praeceptis Rhetoro-Logicis paulatim imbueretur, ad palaestram disputatoriam & oratoriam excitaretur, futurisque insuper audiendis lectionibus apta idoneaque redderetur, Logicus etiam Collegio isti assignatus fuit Professor. Catecheticus vero abesse non poterat, tum ut, qui operam aliquando suam locaturi essent Ministerio, Theologiae, per uberiorem institutionem Catecheticam sive ex ipso Catechismo, sive ex Confessione Helvetica, depromptam, prima solide ponerent fundamenta; tum ut reliqui, qui in Politia, Reipublicae prodesse studerent, mature fidei rationem illis, qui per ossicij eam Authoritatem poscere audent, discerent reddere. Et ut ne ea Lingua, qua solâ Deus sine Interprete adhuc nobiscum loquitur, turpiter hic relinqueretur, aut ad provectioris aetatis hyemem rejiceretur, consultum visum est, ab hoc etiam Collegio, in ipso adolescentiae vere, Hebraismi exigere tyrocinia. Haec Origo, hi progressus, haec ipsa ἀρχή Scholae Tigurina, eo, procul dubio, nomine non prorsus obscurae, quod & reliquis omnibus per Europam purius Reformatis ordine praecedat; & ipsi statim dogmatum restaurationi inservire jussa, Cimmerias Papatus, & Scholasticae barbariei depulerit tenebras. Quod si ergo ordinis privilegium gratiam conciliet & authoritatem, apud eos praesertim, qui annis omnia metiuntur & duratione, quo colore aut praetextu Scholae illa nostrae abjudicari posset aut, negari, non video.
units.tr: They first taught the arts and languages. Then, in alternate courses, they went through the precepts of dialectic and rhetoric, sometimes adding a speech or a book of Cicero in which he shows the dialectical and rhetorical art and applies its precepts to speaking and writing. The latter, at four in the afternoon, expounded various Greek authors, beginning with Homer, in both prose and verse. These public lectures of our school, born together with the Reformation of doctrine itself, were its cradle and its first appearance. For the difficulty of the times stood in the way of admitting more professors to the Senate. Under the Papacy the Carolinum college supported canons, sometimes twenty-four and often twenty-six, mostly absent, until the Bull of Martin compelled them to be present. But if some had hearts formed of better clay, so that they stopped their ears to the wiser counsels of Zwingli and did not admit a purging of doctrine, they were not moved from their place. Those to whom neither the public duty of preaching or teaching nor the private administration of the chapter's economy could be entrusted were allowed to finish the course of their life quietly, with their benefices granted to them. For it was inglorious, not to say unjust, to take away through the Reformation those livelihoods which gave each man his own; the superstitious Papacy had not denied them. As they gradually died, in the order prescribed by nature, those who could not be removed by the chapter's oath and the accepted laws, a large addition came to our school from their revenues. So much so that not long afterwards it became more illustrious again through two professorships, very necessary academies: theology of the New Testament, and physics. Of these, the former was first entrusted to Josiah Simler, the latter to Conrad Gesner, both Zurichers, and has been kept to this day to the equal ornament and profit of the school. And so that nothing of pious learning should be lacking to the candidates, so that they might be made richer in all the gifts of true wisdom, our school then advanced to such a degree that nowhere else in the most celebrated academies was the nectar of literature, whether theological or humane, poured out without our Zurich also offering its sample. For then it had, and still has, two professors of theology, one of whom expounds and explains the whole New Testament and the other the whole Old Testament, besides the treatment of the Commonplaces. It has men who complete the course of encyclopaedic learning, most thoroughly in all its parts: metaphysics, physics, ethics, logic, rhetoric. If anyone is pleased by mathematics, the opportunity to taste those delights has never been refused. In languages, we have for some time not been content with Greek and Hebrew alone, but have also dealt, not unsuccessfully, with the other Oriental tongues, as even outsiders know. Sacred and especially ecclesiastical history has been taught and set forth by the professors no less diligently than it has been eagerly received and absorbed by the students. And just as travellers who hurry or wander too far break off their journey sooner, so those who leap forward with too rapid a stride in their studies do not last long. Our forefathers therefore wisely arranged that students should not, as happens elsewhere, rush straight from the elementary or grammar school to public lectures, with unwashed hands, as they say. Hence they considered a place where the pupils of the chaste Muses could breathe a little from the troublesome dust of the school and prepare themselves for the weightier studies of the higher faculties. So a new college was set up between the classical schools and the public auditorium, and it was named the College of Humanity, a fitting name, since it was chiefly the more humane letters that were taught there. Four professors were appointed to it: the Greco-Latin, the Rhetorico-Logical, the Catechetical, and the Hebrew. Indeed, once this plan had been thoroughly considered and tested, the chief aim was this: in Latin, not only should the purity and chastity of the language, already acquired beforehand, which the classical schools demand, be preserved unimpaired, but it should also flourish, increased by the elegance of flowers and charms. In Greek, besides the continual repetition of the New Testament, there should be added both grammar and criticism, drawn from ecclesiastical and profane authors, so that each student, once torn away from the public Muses, might thereafter be able to proceed by his own strength. And since this age seemed ripe, it should be gradually steeped in the precepts of rhetorico-logical learning, trained for disputation and oratory, and made fit and suitable for the lectures to be heard in the future; for this reason a professor of logic was also assigned to that college. The catechetical professor could not be absent, so that those who would one day offer their labour to the ministry might lay solid foundations of theology by means of a fuller catechetical instruction, drawn either from the Catechism itself or from the Helvetic Confession; and so that the rest, who wished to serve the commonwealth in civil life, might learn early to give an account of the faith to those who dare to demand it by virtue of their office. And so that the language by which God alone, without an interpreter, still speaks with us should not be shamefully neglected here, nor deferred to the winter of more advanced age, it was thought good that this college should also require the rudiments of Hebrew in the very spring of youth. This is the origin, this the progress, this the very beginning of the Zurich school, which surely is not at all obscure under that title, since it precedes in order all the other more purely reformed churches throughout Europe; and since it was at once commanded to serve the restoration of doctrine, it has driven away the Cimmerian darkness of Papacy and of scholastic barbarism. If therefore the privilege of its order wins favour and authority, especially among those who measure everything by years and duration, I do not see by what colour or pretext that school of ours could be denied or refused this.

units.la: Sed majus est & gravius longè, quod ex doctorum Corona Virorum ei assurgit pondus, & encomium. Plura, quod praefulcinè fiscinè dixerim, Scholæ nostræ patriæ intra Seculi, & quod excedit, spatium omnigenæ literaturæ lumina & columina cœlitus, larga Dei manu, fuerunt concessa, quàm quæ in vastissimis alibi regionibus quæri potuerint, aut inveniri. Vidit & admiratus est orbis, multos simul Orientes Soles in extimo Helvetiæ angulo, quorum singuli latissimum illustrare potuissent horizontem. Vidit, Tiguri ipsas quasi Musas sacras tum sedem fixisse, quando Bullingerum, Bibliandrum, Gualtherum, Collinum, Martyrem, Lavaterum, Johannem Wolfium, Simlerum, Frisium, Gessnerum, plurésque alios arcta Tigurinorum eodem tempore, concluserunt moenia. Vidit, per alteram quasi Novi Testamenti Pentecosten, damnatum antea, & proscriptum Linguarum studium, cum triumpho esse restitutum. Et utut multi æruginis & livoris æstro perciti (majori patientis damno, quàm potentis incommodo: Codro enim iliarum puntur; & invidus alterius macrescit rebus opimis) nihil quod ipsi non possederint, ament; nihil, quod ipsi non fecerint, probent, hoc tamen virtutem Altissimi, digitum Potentissimi in dubium vocare nemo sustinuisset, nisi cui aversus plane à Deo & religione fuisset animus. Et revera, rideat Ignatij familia lacustres nostras Synodos; adoret Magistros suos Sorbona, eminenti quadam ratione, Tertulliani non merito, sed exemplo, sic vocitatos. Doctores suos (ut tutulis & titulis suis hoc hominum genus libenter titillatur) miretur irrefragabiles, invincibiles, singulares, Seraphicos, Angelicos. Jactent Magistros sententiarum Lombardos, Subtiles Scotos, contentiosos Durandos, & Occamos. Nobis domi nostræ vel nati, vel alti, nec foris minori in pretio habiti sunt; Divinus & magnanimus Zuinglius, Moderatus & solidus Bullingerus, fortis & prudens Freyus, cordatus & indefessus Leo-Judæ; Pellicanus Hebraismi restaurator felicissimus; ὁ αὐτομαθής Biblianderr, communis Theologiæ exegeticæ parens; facundus & artificiosus, uficiosus Gualtherus, officiosus Hallerus, Vir acceptus omnibus bonis, ἡ χαρίεσσα; Scholasticus Reformatus Werdmyllerus, gravis & tersus Wolfius, laboriosus & festivus Frisius, subtilis & acutus Martyr, perspicuus & eruditus Simlerus, diffusæ scientiæ Gesnerus, locupletissimum rerum naturalium cornucopiæ, idemq; φιλογλώττας. Quibus ex ordine succenturiati sunt, Polyhistor Hofpinianus, πολύγραφος Stuckius, ingeniosus Eglinus, πολύγλωττος & celebris Waserus, dexter & Methodicus Beumlerus, judiciosus & Felix Breitingerus, disertus Ernius, industrius & masculus Huldricus, moderatus Stuckius, promptus & expeditus Wirzius, Tomanii Philologiæ Græcæ cum primis & Latinæ cultores industrij, plurésque alij, quorum nomina apud seram posteritatem erunt in benedictione.
units.tr: But what lends it weight and praise is far greater: the crown of learned men who have risen up from it. Our country's schools have been given, within a century and more, by the large hand of God from heaven, more lights and pillars of every kind of learning than could have been sought or found in the vastest regions elsewhere, if I may say so with a little exaggeration. The world has seen, and marvelled, that many rising suns shone at once in the farthest corner of Helvetia, each of whom could have lit up a very wide horizon. It has seen that Zurich then became, as it were, the seat of the sacred Muses themselves, when Bullinger, Bibliander, Gwalther, Collin, Martyr, Lavater, Johann Wolf, Simler, Frisius, Gesner, and many other men, were enclosed within the walls of the Zurichers at the same time. It has seen that, through a second Pentecost of the New Testament, the study of languages, once condemned and proscribed, was restored in triumph. And although many men, stung by the gadfly of envy and spite (to the greater harm of the one who is patient than the inconvenience of the one who is powerful, for the Codrus is stung by his own spleen, and the envious man wastes away amid the rich goods of another), love nothing that they themselves do not possess and approve nothing that they themselves have not done, yet no one would have dared to call into doubt the power of the Most High and the finger of the Most Mighty in this, unless his mind had been utterly turned away from God and religion. And indeed, let the family of Ignatius laugh at our lake Synods; let the Sorbonne worship its Masters, called so in a special way, not on merit but by example, after Tertullian; let them admire their Doctors, irrefutable, invincible, singular, Seraphic, Angelic, as this kind of men is gladly tickled by its tufts and titles. Let them boast of the Lombards, Masters of the Sentences, the Subtle Scots, the contentious Durands and Occams. Ours, born or raised in our own house, were held in no less esteem abroad: the divine and great-souled Zwingli, the moderate and solid Bullinger, the strong and prudent Frey, the wise and tireless Leo Judae, Pellican the most fortunate restorer of Hebrew studies, the self-taught Bibliander, the parent of common exegetical theology; the eloquent and skilful Gwalther, the obliging Haller, a man acceptable to all good men, the gracious one [ἡ χαρίεσσα]; the Reformed scholastic Werdmüller, the grave and polished Wolf, the laborious and merry Frisius, the subtle and sharp Martyr, the clear and learned Simler, Gesner of wide learning, the most abundant cornucopia of natural things, and at the same time a lover of tongues [φιλογλώττας]. To these, in order, were added as reserves: Polyhistor Hottinger, the prolific writer [πολύγραφος] Stuckius, the ingenious Eglin, the polyglot [πολύγλωττος] and renowned Waser, the dexterous and methodical Beumler, the judicious and fortunate Breitinger, the eloquent Ernius, the diligent and manly Huldrich, the moderate Stuckius, the ready and quick Wirz, the diligent cultivators of Greek and Latin philology, Tomann foremost among them, and many others, whose names will be in blessing among the distant posterity.

units.la: Extollit Ecclesia Romana claustralium suorum labores, æternitatis crebra nobis objicit monumenta, scriptorum publicorum signa & tabulas ad ravim ubique inculcat; sed ne hanc quidem Schola Tigurina certaminis olim detrectâsset aleam. Habeant Ordines Ecclesiæ Romanæ, studia excolendi, subsidia liberalia, nova præsertim Ignatij Lojolæ familiæ; id, contra reliquos fidei consecraneos superbè obtineat, non fucos plane esse, aut ἄχθος ἀργής, quos Societas nuper nata admittit Collegas; nondum tamen animum abjicimus, nec existimamus, nostros inter tot curas, labores, occupationes, publicas & privatas, vel numero librorum, vel æstimatione etiam laborum, esse inferiores. Anullus unquam (ne Tostatum quidem, Lapideum, Bellarminum, Baronium, Azorium aut alium aliquem χαλκέντερον Romanum exceperim) vel ad Bullingeri nostri accessit industriam & sedulitatem, vel Calvini elegantiam, vel Petri Martyris acumen? Gesneri scientiam Naturalem, Hospiniani Polyhistoriam? Et, ut Majorum nostrorum exemplo posteritatem, si non ad imitationem; quam sperare non licet; saltem ad conatum & admirationem stimulemus; quem, quæso, Facultatum, Scientiarum, Linguarum cursum magna cum laude, illi non sunt emensi? Theologos desideras Exegeticos? Nemo, opinor, Tigurum, tempore Reformationis, primariam eorum fuisse sedem, ibit inficias. Tigurina enim Schola Exegeticis potissimùm studiis, reliquis ad tempus, si non sepositis, paulò saltem moderatiùs tractatis, initiari voluit. Hæ dapes erant ambrosiæ, non Ecclesiæ tantùm Pastorum Bullingeri, Gualtheri, Lavateri; sed & Scholæ Professorum Pellicani, Bibliandri, Martyris, Simleri, Violphij. His lubentiùs meditationibus, quàm quibuscunque aliis inorari & inori sacrata Deo pectora voluerunt. Eorundem studiorum Principes æquè ac Theologi exteri illecti, animum semper nostris, ut quod cepissent feliciter, felicissimè absolverent, addiderunt; sententiámque eorum, de ratione & modo sacras Literas compendiosis illustrandi observationibus, rogârunt. Et Bibliander quidem, acris judicij, raràque Linguarum Orientalium notitiâ præditus, Theologus, primam fregit glaciem: Gualtherus remos, transtra, vela, suppeditavit; Petrus Martyr tandem; absit vanitas & jactantia verbo; Cynosuram, utpote qui non res tantùm; sed & verba phrasésque suggerit Theologicas, subministravit. Quanquam verò, ut inventis facile est addere, aliorum, successu temporis, industriâ fuerit factum & solertiâ, ut novo induta populóque proposita scheмaтe μελετήματα nostratium prima, magis placerent, extra contradictionis tamen aleam optimi quique ponunt. Majorum nostrorum fontibus prata sua plerosque Theologos Practicos, Anglos cumprimis & Belgas, irrigâsse.
units.tr: The Roman Church boasts of the labours of its monks, constantly sets before us the monuments of their immortality, the public records and tablets, and hammers them home everywhere in abundance. But the Zurich school would not have shrunk from that contest either, had it ever been waged. Let the orders of the Roman Church have their zeal for learning and their liberal resources, especially the new family of Ignatius Loyola. Let them proudly claim, against the rest of the faithful, that they are not mere drones or a burden of idleness [ἄχθος ἀργής], the men whom the newly born Society admits as colleagues. Yet we have not lost heart, nor do we think that ours, amid so many cares, labours and occupations, public and private, are inferior either in the number of their books or in the reckoning of their labours. Has anyone ever (not excepting Tostatus, Lapide, Bellarmine, Baronius, Azorius, or any other brazen-bowelled [χαλκέντερον] Roman) come near the industry and diligence of our Bullinger, the elegance of Calvin, or the acumen of Peter Martyr? Or the natural learning of Gesner, or the polymathy of Hospinian? And, if we are to stir posterity by the example of our forefathers, not to imitation, which we may not hope for, but at least to effort and admiration, who, I ask, has run the course of the faculties, sciences and languages with greater praise than they did? Do you want exegetical theologians? No one, I think, will deny that Zurich, in the time of the Reformation, was their chief seat. For the Zurich school wished above all to be initiated into exegetical studies, the rest being treated, if not set aside, at least somewhat more moderately for the time. These were the ambrosial feasts, not only for the ministers of the Church, Bullinger, Gwalther, Lavater, but also for the professors of the school, Pellican, Bibliander, Martyr, Simler and Wolphius. They preferred that hearts consecrated to God be occupied with these meditations more gladly than with any others. The leaders of these studies, and the foreign theologians drawn to them, always added spirit to ours, so that they might bring to a most happy end what they had begun well, and they asked for our opinion on the method and manner of illuminating Holy Scripture by brief observations. Bibliander, a theologian of keen judgement and rare knowledge of the Oriental languages, broke the first ice. Gwalther supplied the oars, the thwarts and the sails. Peter Martyr at last (let there be no vanity or boasting in saying so) supplied the Cynosure, since he furnished not only the matter but also the theological words and phrases. Yet, as it is easy to add to discoveries, the work was done by the industry and skill of others over time, so that our first exercises, clothed in a new form and set before the people, pleased more. Still, all the best men place them beyond the reach of dispute. Most of our practical theologians, the English and the Dutch especially, have watered their meadows from the springs of our forefathers.

units.la: Ubi ad Topicam deventum fuerit, quanta hic, Optime Maxime Deus, bonorum & donorum tuorum in Scholam nostram seges! Et ut ab Elenctica ordiamur, quot Doctorum nostrorum clara atq; exornata sunt trophæa & epinicia? Quis luxuriantem Anabaptistarum messem in herba, magnam partem, felicius suffocavit, quàm, ex Tigurina Schola Theologica, Zuinglius, Bullingerus, Huldricus? Quis Papùmo jugulum fortius & certius petiit, quàm idem ille Romani stabuli eversor Zuinglius? Quis Socinianorum, Arianorum, Servetanorum impietates, eo tempore, majori ausu & conatu aggressus est, quàm Wolfius & Simlerus? Quis abstrusa de Prædestinatione, Providentia Dei, Cœna Domini, mysteria apertius reseravit, adversariorum Sophismata clarius detexit, quàm malleus ille Heterodoxorum, ipsis Venerabilis Pontificijs, Martyr? Ad errorum investigandas Origines, an ullus unquam tanto cum successu & applausu animum appulit, quanto Hospinianus, & ante ipsum Bullingerus, cujus de hoc Themate scriptum omnium propemodum eruditorum puncta tulit? Quibus verborum elegantijs, quo argumentorum robore, & phalange, Scripturæ Sacræ authoritatem, contra temerarias & impias Cochlæi offucias, cum adversarij stupore, asseruit Bullingerus? Quanta Δεινότης & Ciceroniano plane eloquio de Ecclesia disseruit Wolfius? Non obscuro de Schola Pædotribæ, sed Dudithio, Episcopo Quinquecclefiensi (quanto prius in castris Philistæis Goliatho! vix nominetenus ad tempus nostro, turpissimo verò tandem defertori, Antitrinitario) scopuli & scrupuli erant eximendi. Et cùm infelices Osiandri de justitia, Brentij & Andreæ de Ubiquitate & Prædestinatione, Illyrici de peccato Originali, aliæque plures Ecclesiam vexâssent controversiæ, quâ demonstrationum evidentiâ, figmenta illa per Ecclesiæ & Scholæ Tigurinæ Ministros fuerunt elusa & elisa, absurditâsque eorum in apricum producta? Huberus caput vix effert, Theologorum Tetrapolitanorum, quos inter erat Stuckius, judicio cadit. Doctrina Sacramentaria plus forte ex Schola Tigurina accepit lucis, quàm à me, absque suspicione tenerioris in patriam amoris, possit commemorari. Sed quid singulas Theologiæ enarrem partes, aut distincta proferam capita? Universam Topicam, sive Locorum Communium tractationem ita Scholæ Tigurinæ Professores percurrerunt, ut perspicuitatis non minorem, quàm soliditatis deportárint famam. Zacharias Ursinus, noster aliquando, in Collegio Sapientiæ Heidelbergensi, Antecessor meritissimus, de studiorum Theologicorum Methodo solicitè quærentibus respondere solebat: Philippus ocreas mihi induit, Calvinus me equo imposuit, Martyr calcaria addidit. Habent studiosi nostri suam etiam trigam, quâ ad bella Domini gerenda commodissimè possunt instrui. Tyronibus vel Bullingeri nostri Compendium viam sternet, vel Hypotypofis Beumleriana, per γνῶσιν ejus discipulum Venerabilem Breitingerum nostrum, Auditorum captui accommodata, vel Catechesis Senioris, nostræ Ecclesiæ, Venerandi; currentibus calcar addent vel Decades à Bullingero quoque adornatæ, vel Commentarius, in Beumleri hypotypofin, Stuckianus. Veteranis verò Loci Communes, quos ex Petri Martyris scriptis exegeticis collegit & publicavit Robertus Massonius, satisfacient. Plura quidem cum Systemata à nostris, Simlero præsertim, cùm vicinarum Academiarum Lutheranarum studia Topica ferverent, flagitabantur; satis tamen intercedentibus, aliis provincia illa fuit relicta, quam egregiè, procul dubio, multi exornâssent (quod vel ex Wolfij affecto Schematismo probatu est facile) nisi aliæ magis tum necessariæ occupationes ab instituto eos revocâssent.
units.tr: When we come to Topics, O Best and Greatest God, what a harvest of your good gifts and blessings there is in our school! And to begin with Elenctics, how many glorious trophies and victory songs of our teachers are there? Who, from the Zurich theological school, suffocated the rank harvest of the Anabaptists while it was still in the blade, and for the most part more successfully than Zwingli, Bullinger and Huldrych? Who attacked the throat of Papism more boldly and surely than that same Zwingli, overthrower of the Roman stable? Who tackled the impieties of the Socinians, Arians and Servetians at that time with greater daring and effort than Wolf and Simler? Who unveiled the mysteries of predestination, the providence of God and the Lord's Supper more plainly, and exposed the sophisms of the adversaries more clearly, than that hammer of the heterodox, Martyr, venerable even to the Papists themselves? Has anyone ever turned his mind to investigating the origins of errors with such success and applause as Hospinian, and before him Bullinger, whose writing on this theme has won the approval of almost all the learned? With what elegance of words, what strength of arguments and what battle array did Bullinger assert the authority of Holy Scripture against the rash and impious tricks of Cochlaeus, to the astonishment of his opponent? With what eloquence and a truly Ciceronian style did Wolf discourse on the Church? It was not without difficulty that the rocks and stumbling-blocks had to be removed, not for the schoolmaster Pædotribe, but for Dudith, Bishop of Pécs (how much earlier, a Goliath in the Philistine camp, scarcely named in our time, and at last a most shameful deserter, an Antitrinitarian). And when the unhappy controversies of Osiander on justification, of Brenz and Andreae on ubiquity and predestination, of Illyricus on original sin, and several others had troubled the Church, by what evidence of demonstration were those fictions mocked and refuted by the ministers of the Church and the Zurich school, and their absurdity brought into the light? Huber scarcely raises his head before he is condemned by the judgement of the Theologians of Strasbourg, among whom was Stuckius. The sacramentarian doctrine received perhaps more light from the Zurich school than I, without any suspicion of too tender a love for my country, could mention. But why should I recount the individual parts of theology, or set out its distinct heads? The professors of the Zurich school ran through the whole of Topics, or the treatment of the common places, in such a way that they carried away no less a reputation for clarity than for solidity. Zacharias Ursinus, once our own man in the College of Wisdom at Heidelberg, a most deserving teacher, used to answer those anxiously asking about the method of theological study: "Philip put greaves on me, Calvin set me on a horse, Martyr added the spurs." Our students also have their own chariot, by which they can most conveniently be equipped for waging the Lord's wars. For beginners, either the Compendium of our Bullinger will pave the way, or the Beumlerian Hypotyposis, adapted to the grasp of the hearers, by way of the knowledge of its disciple, our venerable Breitinger; or the Catechism of our senior, our venerable Church. For those already running, the Decades likewise adorned by Bullinger will add spurs, or the Commentary of Stuckius on Beumler's Hypotyposis. For veterans, however, the Common Places which Robert Masson gathered and published from the exegetical writings of Peter Martyr will suffice. Indeed more systems were demanded of our men, especially of Simler, when the Lutheran studies of the neighbouring academies were flourishing in theology; yet, other men intervening, that field was left to others, which, without doubt, many would have adorned excellently (as may easily be proved from Wolf's well-known schematism), had not other, more pressing occupations called them away from their purpose.

units.la: Ad reliqua properandum esset studia, publicè in Schola Tigurina culta & exculta; sed video diem citiùs defecturum, quàm dicendorum copiam defuturam. Abundè nobis sit, paria Majores nostros in literario stadio, cum quibusvis aliis facere, curæ habuisse cordíque. Venditet Plinium suum, Naturæ sagacissimum indagatorem Verona primum; Tiguro non invidebit secundum, Conradum Gesnerum, quem θαυμάζων alij, PræPræceptorem suum, illi etiam, qui in aulis Imperatorum, Regum, Principum magna pollebant authoritate, appellare non sunt dedignati. Placeat eruditis Ramus vel propter Mathematica studia, placuit illi vel eo nomine Simlerus. Bodinum toties, brevi tempore, typis excusum de Republica plurimi mirentur: Scio, non inferiori à multis loco haberi, quæ de Helvetiorum Republica scripsit Simlerus. Baronio Φιλοπονίας laudem nolumus detractam aut obfuscatam; utrum verò non pro meliori causa, vel eadem, vel majora indefessi laboris Hoffpinianus noster mereatur præconia, æquis relinquo judicibus. Ut enim non tam colligendi molestiam, quàm disponendi limam ille sibi voluit reservatam; ita hic Atlas utramque sustinuit molem. De Linguarum studio ne Soli vi-deamur mutuare lucem, nolumus esse prolixi. Ne tamen vel præteritæ invideamus ætati felicitatem, vel præsentem imitationis exemplo defraudemus, hoc potissimum charactere Scholam nostram, ab ipsis incunabulis, fuisse commendatam, cur dissimulemus? Namque madmodum Zuinglius Reformator trium Linguarum Cardinalium solidam, eòque Seculo raram, consecutus fuit notitiam; ita & Schola nostra odorem deinceps, quo semel fuit imbuta, constanter retinuit. Pellicanum ne ipse quidem Munsterus erubuit suum vocare Præceptorem. Plura ex abditis & abstrusis Rabbinorum Commentariis, Talmudicis, Allegoricis, Historicis sua manu tractata reliquit monumenta, quàm subsecuta ætas facilè crederet. Bibliandrum, propter apparatum Linguarum Orientalium exquisitissimum, Arabicæ etiam, cæteri tanquam Oraculum venerabantur. Postello persuasum fuit, vix alibi reperiri, cui, defuncti lampas in his studijs meliori jure, pluribusque competeret nominibus, quàm nostro Φεργωνύμως Bibliandro. Ipse Gesnerus, quam vis ad alia natus & vocatus, non Ennium τεϊγλωτλον, sed Mithridatem πολύγλωσσον posteritati reliquit. Inter tot, quod miremur, curas & negotia, ita fuit Linguarum amore accensus, ut nulla occurreret, de qua non & commodè loqueretur, & erudite scriberet. Mitto successores, qui propius nostram attingunt ætatem, quíque publico ὧν πλυγλωσσῶν encomio fuerunt insigniti. Verbo, quam eminentiæ laudem Patavium quæsivit in Medicina, Bononia in Jurisprudentia, Lutetia in Scholastica, ea Scholæ Tigurinæ ex continuo felicíque tum Theologiæ, tum Linguarum Orientalium, eóque Philologiæ Sacræ cultu, magnorum Virorum judicio, accessisse videtur. Eccur aliter sentiant illi etiam, qui Linguas sacras colunt potiùs, quàm callent? Omnia, & merito quidem, Pentecostes festo personant Christianorum pulpita, de miraculosa charismatum Spiritûs Sancti, Linguarum præsertim, communicatione: Stupemus, quoties Apostolos, qui natalibus suis nec Prophetæ erant, nec Prophetarum filij, non Philosophi, non Linguarum exoticarum, imò ne Hebraeæ quidem purioris, Galilæam ægrè balbutientes, gnari, derepente hospites undique concurrentes, in admirationem rapuisse, erectis comis, & arrectis auribus percipimus! Cur nos, ubi idem Spiritus, eadem charismata, tot barbaris nationibus immaniores & inferiores, vel minori reverentia illa jam colamus, vel prorsus extinguamus? Sed nihil hic periculi: Cave enim credas, illos, qui Linguarum studia vel clam, vel palàm suggillant, serió agere; Sardonius eorum risus est, qui quod non libenter ignorant, in alijs ægrè ferunt. Certè, quo quis, ubi ex Originalibus aliquid eruderandum est monumentis, minùs se præbet aptum, eò Pentecostes miraculum firmioribus ebuccinare, plebíque Ecclesiasticæ comendare annititur lateribus. Sed mitto Linguarum studium, ubi hoc præmisero: Zuinglium, ceu prudentem Architectum pensa distribuisse, Pellicanum fundamentum solidè jecisse, Billiandrum commodè superstruxisse, VVaserum tectum ornatè impositisse.
units.tr: Hurrying on to the remaining studies, which have been cultivated and refined publicly in the Zurich school, I see that the day will run out sooner than the material for speaking will run short. It is enough for us to say that our forefathers were equally concerned, and cared in their hearts, to match any others in the literary arena. Let Verona sell its Pliny, the most keen investigator of Nature, as its first; Zurich will not begrudge it the second, Conrad Gesner, whom others, marvelling at him, call their Preceptor, and whom even those who wielded great authority in the courts of emperors, kings and princes did not disdain to name. Let Ramus please the learned, partly for his mathematical studies; Simler pleased him for that reason too. Many marvel that Bodin, printed so often in a short time, wrote on the Commonwealth. I know that what Simler wrote on the Commonwealth of the Helvetians is held by many in no lesser esteem. We do not wish the praise of Baronius for his industry to be taken away or dimmed; but whether our Hospinian does not deserve, for the same or a better cause, the praise of tireless labour, I leave to fair judges. For as Baronius wished to keep for himself the labour of arranging rather than the trouble of gathering, so Hospinian bore both burdens like Atlas. As for the study of languages, lest we seem to borrow light from others alone, we do not wish to be prolix. Yet, lest we envy the past age its happiness or deprive the present of an example to imitate, why should we conceal that this above all was the mark by which our school was commended from its very cradle? For just as Zwingli the Reformer attained a sound knowledge of the three cardinal languages, and a rare one for that century, so our school has constantly retained the flavour with which it was once imbued. Munster himself was not ashamed to call Pellican his teacher. Many monuments, handled by his own hand, from the hidden and abstruse commentaries of the rabbis, Talmudic, allegorical and historical, he left behind, more than the following age would readily believe. Bibliander, on account of his most exquisite equipment in the Oriental languages, including Arabic, was revered by others as an oracle. Postel was persuaded that there was hardly anywhere else to be found one who, with better right and by more titles, could take up the torch of the departed in these studies than our Bibliander, rightly called Pheryngonymus. Gesner himself, though born and called to other things, left to posterity not an Ennius of three tongues, but a Mithridates of many tongues. Amid so many cares and business, which is a wonder, he was so fired with love of languages that there was no subject on which he did not speak fittingly and write learnedly. I pass over successors who come closer to our own age, and who have been distinguished by public praise as men of many tongues. In a word, the eminence which Padua sought in medicine, Bologna in jurisprudence and Paris in scholasticism, seems, in the judgement of great men, to have been added to the Zurich school by its continuous and happy cultivation of theology and of the Oriental languages, and so of sacred philology. Why should even those who cultivate the sacred languages rather than know them think otherwise? Every pulpit of the Christians, and rightly so, resounds on the feast of Pentecost with the miraculous communication of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, above all of tongues. We marvel, whenever we perceive that the Apostles, who were neither prophets by birth nor sons of prophets, neither philosophers nor learned in foreign tongues, nor even in purer Hebrew, stammering with difficulty in their Galilean speech, suddenly, as strangers ran together from every side, carried them into admiration, with hair on end and ears pricked up! Why should we, where the same Spirit and the same gifts are at work, honour them with less reverence, or extinguish them altogether, now that we are far more civilised and superior to those barbarous nations? But there is no danger here. Do not believe that those who openly or secretly disparage the study of languages are in earnest; their sardonic laughter belongs to men who take it ill in others that they do not willingly know what they are ignorant of. Certainly, whenever someone is less fit to draw something out of the original monuments, he strives all the more to trumpet the miracle of Pentecost with firmer lungs, and to commend it to the ecclesiastical populace. But I will set aside the study of languages once I have premised this: that Zwingli, like a prudent architect, distributed the work; that Pellican firmly laid the foundation; that Bibliander built upon it appropriately; and that Waser set the roof on with ornament.

units.la: Philosophiam sobriam nunquam nostri neglexerunt; ut ne vero carceres suos transiret, aut honesti famulitij jugum excuteret, adeóque pari passu cum Theologia, quod ante factum erat, ambularet, vel etiam ambitiosè præcurreret, seduló illi caverunt. Logica pretium non in quæstionum sutilium, & tricarum inutilium quæsiverunt senticeto, sed in florentissimo jucundissimæ πραξεως roseto; revocatis ad usum Theologicum, analyticum & geneticum feliciter; quæcunque antea perspicuis & Methodicis præceptis inculcata erant fideliter. In Rhetoricis crebrarum potiùs exercitationum, sacrarum & profanarum nucleo, quàm otioso terminorum involucris se delectárunt. Physica denique & Metaphysica tantum est datum, quantum & Ecclesiæ requirebat necessitas, & adversariorum argutæ postulabant strophæ.
units.tr: As for philosophy, our people never neglected sober philosophy. They took care never to let it step beyond its bounds, or shake off the yoke of its proper service, or run ahead of theology when it ought to keep pace with it. Logic they did not seek the value of in the thorny thickets of subtle questions and useless tangles, but in the flowering rose-garden of most pleasant practice [πραξεως].
