Its rules, which had earlier been set out in clear and methodical precepts, were happily and faithfully turned to theological use, to analysis and to the genesis of doctrine. In rhetoric they delighted less in the empty wrappings of technical terms than in the kernel of frequent exercises, sacred and secular. Finally, physics and metaphysics were allowed only as much as the needs of the Church required and the sharp challenges of its opponents demanded.

units.la: Hæc studia, ubique ante eliminata, cùm Tigurum ab ipso statim Reformationis jubare & ambabus ulnis exceperit, & benignè foverit, & constanter deinceps promoverit, cur non Scholæ celebritas nominis, Doctoribus verò præclara, imò sanctissima nata fuerit existimatio? De Zuinglio nihil dicam, qui ceu aquila ex alto prospiciens, omnium suffragio Orthodoxorum, Vindex, Reformator Ecclesiarum & Scholarum fuit habitus; Bullingerus ob vitæ sanctimoniam, absolutam eruditionis, Theologicæ cumprimis, peritiam, prudentiam Regiminis Ecclesiastici insignem, à maximis Theologis, Patris semper loco cultus; Gualtherus, Theologiæ Practicæ antésignanus; Petrus Martyr, communis Ecclesiæ Reformatæ ingeniosissimus Scripturæ & Locorum Communium Tractator, VVolfius os sæpe cæterorum & Interpres, ubi limata opus fuit & exasciata oratione; Gessnerus, Medicorum oraculum, Simlerus omnis; sacræ, Ecclesiasticæ, & Scholasticæ; literaturæ penu, &c. tot exterorum (non loquor obscura, Auditores, vel incerta, sed quotidiana propemodum lectione mihi trita) condecorantur encomijs, tot votis Deo commendantur, tot mandatis ad publicos suscipiendos labores onerantur dicam, an honorantur? ut, nisi & ingratitudinis erga Deum, & manifestæ in patriam injuriæ rei esse velimus, non possimus non datis & elatis manibus cum Davide exclamare: Non nobis Domine, non nobis; sed Nomini tuo dedisti honorem, propter benignitatem tuam, propter fidem tuam. Et quanquam publicis Scriptis Theologi Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ, Scholæque (neque enim, quia Deus hos duos ordines arctissimè inde à Reformatione conjunxit, ambitio hominum separare debet) pariter inclaruerint omnes, prudenter tamen observo, ita eos partitos inter se operas, ut, post Zuinglium, Bullingerus, omnes ex æquo amplecteretur & juvaret Ecclesias; Italicas sibi deligeret Pellicanus; Polonicas, Hungaricas & Transylvanicas Wolfius & Simlerus; Anglicas Petrus Martyr, & Gualtherus; Germanicas, Rhæticas, Helveticas Gualtherus, Wolfius, Simlerus & Stuckius. Summâ, amicum erat, pro publico bono, certamen: nemo sefibi tantum natum vel fingebat; sed Patriæ, sed Ecclesiæ. Habuerunt primis, post Christum in Cœlos sublatum, periodis, Ecclesiæ Doctores eximios, Patrum nomine & dignos, & appellatos, mellifluum Chrysostomum, eruditum Basilium, facundum & Hieronymum, Adamantinum Origenem, Augustinum disputatorem, Lactantium Oratorem: verùm, veniam date, si, absque tantorum Virorum injuria, & ego nostros nobis fuisse Patres, libere fuero fassus. Non ut vel blandiamur nobis propterea, vel cristis erectis supercilium tollamus, sed humiliter potiùs Deo & demisse, pro tam liberali munificentia gratias agamus. Latino eloquio, vernaculo tamen, Latinam destruxit superstitionem Lactantius, & Augustinus; destruxit illo, sed pertinaci industria acquisito, eandem, præter Calvinum, Zuinglius. Profligavit feliciter, memoratus modò Hipponensium Episcopus, horrendam pelagianismi excætram; Profligavit
units.tr: These studies, which had been driven out everywhere else, were received by Tiguri from the very first light of the Reformation, embraced with both arms, fostered kindly and promoted steadily from then on. Why, then, should the fame of the school not have grown, and a splendid and indeed most holy reputation arisen for its teachers? I will say nothing of Zwingli, who, looking down like an eagle from on high, was held by the agreed judgment of all the orthodox to be the defender and reformer of the Churches and schools. Bullinger, distinguished for the holiness of his life, his complete learning, especially in theology, and his prudence in governing the Church, was always honoured by the greatest theologians as a father. Gualter was the forerunner of practical theology. Peter Martyr, the most gifted writer on Scripture and the common places of the Reformed Church, Wolf, often the voice and interpreter of the others when polished and finished speech was needed, Gesner, the oracle of physicians, Simler, the storehouse of all sacred, ecclesiastical and scholastic learning, and so many others: I will not speak of obscure or doubtful names, hearers, but of men I have read almost daily. So many foreigners have been adorned with their praises, so many prayers have commended them to God, so many commissions have burdened them with public labours. Shall I say they were burdened, or honoured? Unless we wish to be guilty of ingratitude toward God and of plain injury to our country, we cannot help but cry out with David, hands lifted and raised: Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy and for thy truth's sake. And although the theologians of the Church of Tigurum and of the school (for since God joined these two orders most closely together from the Reformation onward, human ambition ought not to separate them) all shone equally in their public writings, I observe that they divided their labours among themselves so that, after Zwingli, Bullinger embraced and helped all the Churches equally; Pellican chose the Italian Churches for himself; Wolf and Simler the Polish, Hungarian and Transylvanian; Peter Martyr and Gualter the English; Gualter, Wolf, Simler and Stuck the German, Rhaetian and Helvetian. In short, there was a friendly contest for the common good: no one imagined that he was born for himself alone, but for his country and for the Church. In the first periods after Christ was taken up into heaven, the Church had outstanding teachers, worthy of and called by the name of Fathers: the honey-tongued Chrysostom, the learned Basil, the eloquent Jerome, Origen the adamantine, Augustine the disputant, Lactantius the orator. But forgive me if, without injury to such great men, I freely confess that our own men were also Fathers for us. I say this not to flatter ourselves or to lift our crests in pride, but rather to give thanks humbly and modestly to God for so generous a gift. Lactantius and Augustine overthrew the Latin superstition in Latin, though in the vernacular; Zwingli, besides Calvin, overthrew the same superstition in a language he had acquired by stubborn industry. The bishop of Hippo, just mentioned, happily crushed the dreadful monster of Pelagianism; Martyr

units.la: {y} Distincti Theologorum Tigurinorum labores. gavit & Martyr. Donatistas ad ἐχεμυθίαν redegit Optatus, Milevitanus & Augustinus; Redegit etiam Zuinglius & Bullingerus. Blasphemam Arianorum impietatem coërcuit Athanasius; Coërcuit & Simlerus. Magno, pro Cathedra, zelo fulminavit Chrysostomus; fulminârunt & nostri, non contra mores seculi tantùm corruptos; sed & contra dogmata superstitione & magia infecta. Eruditio, & Linguarum peritia, Bibliorum cumprimis translatio, Hieronymum reddit venerabilem; reddidit & Leonem Judæ, atque Bibliandrum. Φιλοπονία Adamantini & Chalcenteri nomen conciliavit Origeni; Adamantinus verè fuit ὁ Συντακτής Gesnerus. Sed
units.tr: {y} The distinct labours of the Tigurine theologians. also overthrew it. Optatus of Milevis and Augustine reduced the Donatists to silence [ἐχεμυθίαν]; Zwingli and Bullinger also reduced them. Athanasius restrained the blasphemous impiety of the Arians; Simler restrained it too. Chrysostom thundered with great zeal for his see; our men also thundered, not only against the corrupt morals of the age but also against doctrines tainted by superstition and magic. Learning and skill in languages, and above all the translation of the Bible, made Jerome venerable; they also made Leo of Judah and Bibliander venerable. The industry [Φιλοπονία] of the adamantine man and of the Chalcenterus won Origen his reputation; Gesner was truly the compiler [ὁ Συντακτής] of his age. But

units.la: Sit modus in rebus, sint certi denique fines,
units.tr: There must be a measure in things; there must be fixed limits, after all,

units.la: Laudandi nostros.
units.tr: Let us praise our own.

units.la: Alterum audivistis Scholæ nostræ ornamentum, nominis longè latéque sparsam famam & celebritatem: Tertium succedit, unicum laborum condimentum, jucundum occupationum vehiculum, certissimum molestiarum præmium, Concordia fratrum, quæ tanta inter primos illos fuit Heroës, ut major in militante Ecclesia sperari vix, aut optari potuerit. Locum certatim dederunt μακαρίζω Regio: Ecce quàm bonum, quamǫ jucundum fratres habitare simul! Neque verò, quibus vel sancitus fuerit Legibus, vel sustentatus fulcris tam constans animorum consensus, obscurum est. Non urgebo; quod alendæ inter fratres Concordiæ, omnium Gentium calculo ποππν afferre poterat, & momentum; arctum, quo sibi longa serie devinciebantur conjugij, indéque ortæ consanguineitatis & affinitatis nexum; quo factum, ut Socer generum non diligeret modò; sed & amaret tanquam filium; Gener Socerum coleret ut Patrem: quod tantò ardentiori cordis affectu quisque eorum præstitit, quantò plura amandi & redamandi, in tam generosis erant argumenta pectoribus. Ne quaso contentio sit inter me & te inter pastores meos & pastores tuos, quia Viri fratres sumus, verba sunt Abrahami ad Lothum nepotem; & nostros, qui inde penè à Reformatione, hoc etiam retinendæ concordiæ delegerant ferrumen, vim secis-se Naturæ legibus, omniúmque Gentium consuetudini, vel mentem nostram subeat? Gualtherus Gener fuit Zuinglij; Lavaterus & Simlerus, Generi Gualtheri: Lavateri gener Hofpinianus, Hofpiniani Stuckius. Ita Bullingerus Generum habuit Simlerum, Simlerus Waserum, &c. Omnes amorem merebantur & honorem, extranei etiam, & nullo Coniubij sanguinis aut & affinitatis vinculo constricti; eo vero accedente, cur mutua officiorum studia (quandoquidem Theologia nec Oeconomiam tollit, nec Politiam labefactat) ejusmodi ἐμπυρεύματα non fuerint accensa? Quando vero non carnis & sanguinis, sed Spiritûs & Evangelij hæc Fratrum fuit concordia; Agite, firmiores, quibus illa nitatur, quæramus ei proceres, solidioráque fulcimenta. Et primum quidem serium caulæ Christi promovendæ erat studium. Non sua quisque quærebat; sed quæ Christi erant; Luminis instar, publico inserviendo absumi maluerunt, quàm privati commodi studio Evangelij cursum sufflaminare. Abfuit deinde omnis vanæ gloriolæ κραυγαλιασμός. Quisque suum cuique tribuit. Quisque Dei dona in Collega & socio vel amare, vel admirari, laudi; pernicioso verò invidiæ malleo contundere, aut dissipare, religioni duxit. Studuit quisque amore & honore Fratrem antevertere. Inferiores Superioribus libenter honorem, Inferioribus Superiores promtè amorem detulerunt. Bullingerum omnes ut Patrem & Antistitem suspiciebant; Bullingerum non puduit & Bibliandrum agnoscere Præceptorem, ejusque conscribere lectiones, & in melioribus cedere Petro Martyri. Communis Ecclesiæ & Scholæ causa, communiter semper à constituto Collegio fuit deliberata; executio verò illi, qui & per otium, & vires par mamaximè esset, demandata. Nullus hic livor, vel atræ loliginis succus, qui halcyonia illa turbaret; sincerè & apertè non susceptà minùs, quàm perac̈ta omnia fuerunt. Sunt adhuc in manibus nostratium scripta, quæ, ut germanam fidem Antecessorum, priscámque Gentis Helveticæ redolent integritatem; ita aurei illius seculi vegistia & exemplum nobis merito commendant. Quòd si verò, ut homines sumus, aliquid sunt passi humani, si inter amicissimos & conjunctissimos levia oborta fuerunt friguscula, non erant ἀζπνσ sed amantium iras in amoris converterunt redintegrationem. Unde, quod albo rarius corvo, nunquam legimus, Theologos nostros, inde à Reformatione, publicis scriptis inter se commissos, in mutua Collegij sæviisse viscera. Quod quàm sit miraculo vicinum, illi non ignorant, qui raram fratrum gratiam, raram, quæ non dissensùs patiatur ἡπήμαπ esse Academiam, exploratè habent perspectum. Et quemadmodum perniciosum discordiæ seminarium est, ubi Scholæ & Ecclesiæ Ministri nimis à se invicem remotis abeunt passibus; ita Majores nostri Scholæ ab Ecclesia, & Ministrorum utriusque, eodem ordinis charaćtere notatorum divortium, nunquam voluerunt introdućtum, memores, utrorumque operam ad commune causæ Christi concurrere incrementum. Et ut in Veteri Testamento Prophetæ atque Sacerdotes, ita distinćtas in Synagoga habuerunt provincias, ut mutuas tamen sibi porrigerent dexteras; Eadem ratione Doćtores Ecclesiæ & Scholæ Tigurinæ ςυμφεξη αξεῖη contulerunt, quicquid ad utriusque faceret authoritatem, honorem, & emolumentum. Ad Scholafticos labores nemo facile fuit admissus, nisi qui priùs ordinariam pro Ministerio examinis subijset aleam. Ministerio sacro in urbe initiatus, Scholasticis ut plurimùm laboribus ad tempus erat explorandus. Falcem quidem in alienam mittere messem cuique nec libuit, nec licuit; amico tamen, plaplanéque fraterno consensu, & Pastores primarij ad Scholæ gubernacula admittebantur, & Professores publici causis Ecclesiasticis cognoscendis, dijudicandis & decidendis in Venerando D.D. Examinatorum Collegio adhibebantur. Ut ergo DoctoresScholæ,sic & ProfessoresEcclefiæ,omnes ad eandem ædificationis publicæ tendentes metam, Ministri, fuerunt, recepti declarati & habiti. Et revera periculosum est, præter modum & decorum heic velle,non dico, ἀφιςτάσθαι δὲ ἵνα μὴ ἔχον ἐμμένειν ἄλλων, sed,quod Apostolus graviter taxat, καταξιώσειν τ᾽ ἁλήσων. Nolumus confusionem aut ἀταξίαν Independentismi in Ecclesiam introductam. Scimus, Christum dedisse alios quidem Apostolos, alios Prophetas, alios Evangelistas, alios Pastores & Doctores; non ad destructionem, sed ad consummationem sanctorum, ad opus Ministerij, ad ædificationem Corporis Christi. Spartam ergo, quam quisque nactus est, strenuè exornet. Minister es? Ministerij tui, quo omnibus fieri debes omnis,ut aliquos lucreris,cum humilitate memineris,& gratia, ab omni fastu, & thrasonico Fratrum contemtu alienus. Professor es? caveas, ne,dum moderationem, mansuetudinem commendas alijs, ipse cursu contrario brabeo excidas. Nam,
units.tr: You have heard the second ornament of our school: a fame and renown spread far and wide. The third follows, the one seasoning of our labours, the pleasant vehicle of our duties, the surest reward for our troubles: the harmony of the brethren. Among those first heroes it was so great that one could scarcely hope for or wish for a greater in the militant Church. They eagerly gave place to one another: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! Nor is it obscure how this constant agreement of minds was either enacted by laws or sustained by supports. I will not press the point that concord among brethren, which could bring weight and influence in the reckoning of all nations, was also nurtured by the close bond of marriages linked across a long series, and of the kinship and affinity that arose from them. The result was that a father-in-law not only loved his sons-in-law but loved them as sons, and a son-in-law revered his father-in-law as a father. Each of them showed this with a warmer affection of heart, the more reasons there were, in such generous breasts, for loving and being loved in return. "Let there be no strife, I pray you, between me and you, between my herdsmen and yours, for we are brethren," are Abraham's words to his nephew Lot. And could it enter our minds that our men, who from almost the very time of the Reformation chose this iron bond for keeping concord, did violence to the laws of nature and to the custom of all nations? Gualter was son-in-law of Zwingli; Lavater and Simler were sons-in-law of Gualter; Hospinian was Lavater's son-in-law, and Stuck Hospinian's. So Bullinger had Simler as son-in-law, Simler had Waser, and so on. All of them earned love and honour, even outsiders who were bound by no bond of marriage, blood or affinity. Since that bond was added, why should mutual zeal in duties (since theology neither abolishes household economy nor undermines the state) not have been kindled into such sparks of warmth? And when this brotherly concord was of the Spirit and the Gospel, not of flesh and blood, let us seek the pillars on which it rests, and firmer props. And first of all there was a serious zeal for advancing the cause of Christ. "They sought not their own, but the things of Christ." Like light, they preferred to be spent in serving the public rather than to hinder the course of the Gospel for the sake of private advantage. Then all empty vainglory was absent. Each gave each his due. Each thought it right to love or admire his colleague and partner's gifts from God in praise, but to crush or scatter them with the destructive hammer of envy would be sacrilege. Each strove to outdo his brother in love and honour. The lesser willingly gave honour to the greater, and the greater readily gave love to the lesser. All looked up to Bullinger as father and chief; Bullinger was not ashamed to acknowledge Bibliander as his teacher, to take his lectures, and to yield to Peter Martyr in some matters. The common cause of the Church and the school was always deliberated in common by the appointed college, and its execution was entrusted to the man who had most leisure and strength for it. There was no spite here, no black ink of the cuttlefish to trouble that halcyon calm; everything was undertaken and carried out sincerely and openly. Writings are still in the hands of our countrymen which, as they smell of the genuine faith of our forebears and the old integrity of the Helvetian people, rightly commend to us the traces and example of that golden age. But if, being men, they did suffer some human frailties, and if slight coolnesses arose between the closest friends and relatives, these were not irreconcilable [ἄσπονδα] quarrels; they turned the anger of lovers into a renewal of love. Hence we have never read, what is rarer than a white crow, that our theologians, since the Reformation, though engaged with one another in public writings, raged against each other's vitals within the college. How close this comes to a miracle those know who have well and truly observed that the Academy has a rare fellowship of brethren, one that suffers no dissension, and that it is free from harm [ἡπήμαπ]. As a school of discord is one in which the ministers of the school and of the Church walk too far apart from one another, so our forebears never wished the school to be separated from the Church, nor the divorce of ministers of either body, both marked with the same character of order, to be introduced, mindful that the work of both must converge on the common increase of the cause of Christ. And just as in the Old Testament the prophets and priests had distinct provinces in the synagogue, yet still gave each other their right hands, so by the same method the teachers of the Church and of the Tigurine school contributed [ςυμφεξη αξεῖη] whatever would serve the authority, honour and advantage of each. Hardly anyone was admitted to scholastic labours unless he had first undergone the ordinary examination for the ministry. Once initiated into the sacred ministry in the city, he was usually to be tested for a time in scholastic labours. No one was pleased or permitted to thrust his sickle into another's harvest; yet by friendly and truly brotherly agreement, leading ministers were admitted to the government of the school, and public professors were called into the venerable college of examiners, to know, judge and decide ecclesiastical causes. Thus the teachers of the school and the professors of the Church were all received, declared and regarded as ministers, all heading toward the same goal of public edification. And indeed it is dangerous to want, here, beyond measure and propriety, not, I say, "to stand apart, lest one hold fast to others," but what the Apostle sharply censures, "to make light of" [καταξιώσειν τ᾽ ἁλήσων]. We do not want confusion or disorder [ἀταξίαν] of Independency introduced into the Church. We know that Christ "gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ." Therefore let each adorn the post he has obtained with vigour. Are you a minister? Remember, in the humility and grace of your ministry, by which you must become all things to all men, that you may gain some, to be free from all arrogance and boastful contempt of your brethren. Are you a professor? Take care that, while you commend moderation and gentleness to others, you do not, by running the opposite course, fall from the prize [brabeo]. For

units.la: Turpe est Doctori,si culpa redarguit ipsum.
units.tr: It is shameful for a teacher when his own fault condemns him.

units.la: Id verò, meo judicio, conferruminatam & stabilitam Fratrum concordiam constantissimè aluit,quòd turbulentorum ingeniorum,& novaturientium conatibus,publicaSynodi semestris authoritate,frænum fuerit in edtum. Etenim,ne pro libidine chartas quilibet comaculare, & emitteret dentatas, vel latentem sub cinere doloso ignem fodicaret, ad arma Theologica in altissima pace conclamaret, cautum providè fuit, ut ne à recepta doctrina vel atum unguem Ecclesiæ Scholæque Tigurinæ Minister, quisquis esset, recederet, ullum dogma, quod Confessioni Helveticæ repugnaret, nisi Venerandæ illud prius Synodi arbitrio exposuisset & communicaffet, spargeret. Hoc Concordiæ sepimentum inde à seculo, & quod excurrit, felicissimè nostris cessit: Adeò, ut nemo hactenus vel ita perfricuerit fronte, qui se novatorem Synodo incautè prodere; vel etiam, Synodi neglecta authoritate, saluberrimo statuto pertinaciter voluerit contrahiscere. Sed quo me Patriæ, vel Ecclesiæ verius & Scholæ nostræ abripit amor? Ægrè nempe à jucundissimo tot Heroum, Concordiæ jam nomine ad exemplum & imitationem positorum, amplexu divellor, divellor tamen; ne vestra in audiendo patientia abuti videar. Libenter pergerem, si & Vos attentionem probaturos vel sperare auderem; sed quia temporis præscripti limites metam & Vobis & mihi ponunt; paucis, Coronidis loco, adumbrare facilius, quàm exprimere, quartum Scholæ nostræ publicæ κεφαλαῖον, bona Vestra cum venia, mihi liceat; Indigenarum scilicet, ut plurimùm, Civiúmque industria Scholam nostram natam esse, administratam & auctam. Insigne bonum, quod domi nobis nostræ nascitur! Non omnis fert omnia tellus. Literarij præsertim proventus raro sunt αὐτόχθονες. Florentisimas Germania & Belgium habet Academias; sed quarum maxima lumina aliunde sæpe sunt mutuata. Aluit Leida Scaligerū, Lipsium, Salmasium, non Leidenses tamen, sed Gallos, & Brabantinum. Triumphavit Theologis; Francisco junio, Francisco Gomaro, Antonio Walæo, Antonio Thysio, Johanne Polyandro, Andrea Riveto, Jacobo Triglandio, nullo tamen Leidensi: Gallis, Flandris, Brabantinis omnibus. Groninga, ex quo Academia esse coepit, virorum eruditorum numero & corona nulli cessit; sed quàm ex illis pauci fuerunt, quibus ortum natalem dedit urbs Provincialis? Admiramur in ea labores Altingi, sed Emdani; Gomari, sed Brugensis; Marefij, sed Picardi; Paforis, sed Herbornensis. Marpurgum Hyperio suo ὑπερέχον vix habuit, & tamen Flander erat. Nostrae vero Scholae Senatus inde a prima Origine vel ex civibus, vel subditis, vel municipibus Tigurinis erat constitutus. Tigurini erant Gualtherus, Halleri, VVerdmyllerus, Lavaterus, Gesnerus, Frisius, VVolfius, Simlerus, Hospinianus, Stuckius, Huldricus, Leemannus, Breitingerus, Bullingerus ex Liberarum provinciarum Bremogarto, Bibliander ex Landgraviatu Durgaeo, Zuinglius ex Doggio ortum suum traxerunt. Ille & iste ut aliis Helvetiae Cantonibus primis, ita & Tiguro parent; hoc jam olim Civitatis nostrae jure gaudere voluit. Ex his autem omnibus, quos honoris causa nominavi, num vel unus fuerit, qui non omnium eruditorum suffragio aestimetur munere, quod in Schola vel Ecclesia Tigurina sustinuit, dignissimus? Patriae alias amore non ita Majores nostri erant fascinati, ut Naturam praeferrent gratiae, aut ineptos; propterea, quod Cives essent, vel indigenae; obtruderent. Nôrant utique, eam eligendi rationem esse tutissimam, qua & virtuti suus constaret honos, & Scholae sua utilitas, per Doctores, qui vel celebritate nominis studiosos allicere, vel praeclara eruditione eosdem retinere possent. Unde de ijs semper Majores nostri soliciti fuerunt Professoribus publicis, quos necessaria ad obeundum munus commendarunt dona. Theologica cum primis Professio non ambitu quaesita, sed oblata saepe a doctissimis Viris modeste fuit rejecta. Et ut ex primis Scholae nostrae Theologis nullus fuit, qui non toto inclaruerit orbe literato, scriptisque Rempublicam literariam feliciter juverit; ita certum est, successionis onus, quantum fieri potuit, nostros, ubi extraneorum, vel quorumcunque aliorum, praecesserunt merita, serio fuisse deprecatos. Certe, cum defuncti Petri Martyris lacuna fuisset explenda, & de Zanchio plerique (qui jam & tentatus suam pene condixerat operam, modo liti, quae cum Marpachio tum Argentorati ei inrercesserat, Amplissimus Magistratus Colophonem imposuisset,) cogitarent, alij de Hyperio, alij, ex Polonia etiam, Ursinum prolixè commendarent; Lavaterus noster, Theologus Veteranus, scriptis, publicis non obscurè notus, Patritius Tigurinus, Consulis filius, Antistitis generis meritis in patriam maximis, ac penè immortalibus probatus, dubiæ facilè optioni finem imponere potuisset. Hic verò Venerandi Antecessoris vestigia veneratus, ne solicitatus quidem obsequitur; sed oblatam ultrò successionem adeò gravibus amolitus est argumentis, ut Proceres in ijs quiescentes ad aliam executiendam quercum animum applicuerint. Eâdem modestiâ excelsi ingenij, subtilis & acris judicij Theologus Breitingarus (quem quanti Patres Dordraceni fecerint, ego, testis αυτηκο, non ignoro) Professionem Theologicam, cujus potiundæ spem Mæcenates fecerunt; quod ingenuè fateretur, nulli hos cothurnos, nisi Herculi aptandos; suscipere noluit; sed Casparo VVasero de literatura cumprimis Orientali præclarè merito, locum cessit. Cui mortalibus exemto, & ad superas sedes translato Joh: Jacobus Huldricus, Collegij Carolini Præpositus ægerrimè (quod explorate mihi perspectum est) etsi solidè doctus, & Ecclesiasticæ Antiquitatis peritissimus, successit. Neque verò abs re: Non enim, quæ vulgi opinio est, Theologus publicis lectionibus Scholasticis, quamquam & illæ liberale Ministerij Ecclesiastici subsidium, imò alimentum, elaboratæ esse debeant, officium suis absolvit partibus. Longè plura, vasta hæc, & illustris provincia, habet in recessu, quàm rudis plebeculæ assequatur judicium: quod qui pertinaciter ignorare velint, suo periculo ignorare pergant; æqui nunquam tam luculentæ Spartæ dederunt æstimatores. Quæ quidem propterea, Auditores Honoratissimi, monere operæ erat pretium, ne quis vel prensatorum impudentiâ, vel Curatorum imprudentiâ coeteros, patriæ tantùm amore, à publicis in Schola Tigurina honoribus, exclusos suspicetur. Non ita sibi erant suffeni, ut glebæ suæ eruditionem adscriberent omnem, nec adeò hospites in Mundo, ut, quid distarent æra lupinis, aut quid ageretura libi,nescirent. At quoniam extraneorum etiam sententiâ & judicio, Tigurum nostrum inclyta fuit Kiriath-Sepher, Bibliopolis celeberrima, quando ex hac Schola & Ecclesia, ceu Equo Trojano, tot prodierunt Viri, omnigenâ eruditione ornati, ingenuâ probitate candidi, variâ denique rerum cognitione instructi, ut Præceptores potiùs, quàm discipulos pleræque hinc Ecclesiæ exspectârint, extremæ utique sive dementiæ fuisset, sive ingratitudinis, aut Dei donum, quod in nobis, & inter nos erat, non satis æstimare, incultum relinquere, contemptui planè habere, aut aliunde accersitum, ideo tantùm, quòd peregrinum esset, domestico præferre.
units.tr: In my judgment, what most constantly nourished the firmly cemented and stable concord of our brethren was this: the attempts of turbulent and restless minds were checked by the bridle of the public authority of the semi-annual Synod. For, so that no one might at his pleasure stain the pages and put out biting pamphlets, or stir up a treacherous fire smouldering under the ashes, or shout to arms in theology in the deepest peace, it was wisely provided that no minister of the Zurich Church and School, whoever he might be, should depart even a hair's breadth from the received doctrine, or spread any dogma that conflicts with the Helvetic Confession, unless he had first set it out and communicated it for the judgment of the Venerable Synod. This hedge of concord, from that century onward and beyond, has turned out most happily for us. So much so that no one until now has been so brazen-faced as to rashly betray himself to the Synod as an innovator, or, neglecting the authority of the Synod, has stubbornly wished to resist that most salutary statute. But where does the love of my country, or rather of the Church and of our School, carry me? I am reluctantly torn from the most delightful embrace of so many heroes, who by now have been set up as examples and models of concord. Yet torn away I am, lest I seem to abuse your patience in listening. I would gladly continue, if I dared hope that you would also approve of the attention. But since the limits of the prescribed time set a boundary for both you and me, I may, with your kind permission, sketch briefly, as a crown to the discourse, rather than set out in full, the fourth head [κεφαλαῖον] of our public School: that it was founded, administered and enlarged, for the most part, through the industry of native-born citizens. What a remarkable good it is that such a benefit is born for us at home! Not every land bears every thing. Literary produce in particular is seldom autochthonous [αὐτόχθονες]. Germany and the Low Countries have flourishing academies, but their greatest lights have often been borrowed from elsewhere. Leiden nourished Scaliger, Lipsius and Salmasius, yet they were not Leideners but Frenchmen and a Brabanter. It has triumphed in theologians: Franciscus Junius, Franciscus Gomarus, Antonius Walaeus, Antonius Thysius, Johannes Polyander, Andreas Rivetus and Jacobus Triglandius, none of them from Leiden, but all Frenchmen, Flemings and Brabanters. Groningen, since the Academy began there, has yielded to none in the number and splendour of learned men; but how few of them were born in that provincial city? We admire the labours of Altingius, but he was from Emden; of Gomarus, but he was from Bruges; of Maresius, but he was a Picard; of Paforus, but he was from Herborn. Marburg hardly had its own Hyperius, outstanding [ὑπερέχον], and yet he was a Fleming. But in our School, from its very origin, the Senate was composed of citizens, subjects or townsmen of Zurich. The Zurich men were Gualtherus, Halleri, Werdmüller, Lavater, Gesner, Frisius, Wolf, Simler, Hospinian, Stuck, Huldrich, Leemann, Breitinger, Bullinger; from the free province of Bremgarten came Bibliander, from the landgraviate of Thurgau came Zwingli, who drew their origin from Toggenburg. The one and the other, as they obey the first of the other Swiss cantons, so also obey Zurich; and Zurich has long wished to enjoy this right of our city. Yet of all those whom I have named for the sake of honour, is there even one who is not judged, by the agreement of all learned men, most worthy of the office which he held in the School or Church of Zurich? Our forefathers were not so bewitched by love of country as to prefer nature to grace, or to thrust upon the School men who were unfit merely because they were citizens or natives. They surely knew that the safest method of choosing was that by which the honour of virtue and the usefulness of the School would both be maintained, through teachers who could either attract students by the fame of their name or keep them by outstanding learning. Hence our forefathers were always anxious about public professors, whom the gifts necessary for discharging the office recommended. The theological professorship in particular was often offered by very learned men, but it was modestly declined, not sought by ambition. And just as among the first theologians of our School there was none who did not become famous throughout the whole literary world and help the republic of letters by his writings, so it is certain that our men, wherever the merits of foreigners or of any others went before them, earnestly begged to be spared the burden of succession, as far as it could be done. Certainly, when the gap left by the death of Peter Martyr had to be filled, and most people were thinking of Zanchius (who had already been tempted and had nearly promised his services, only waiting for the lawsuit which had arisen between him and Marbach, and then at Strasbourg, to be brought to a close by the most distinguished Magistrate), while others thought of Hyperius, and others, even from Poland, commended Ursinus at length, our Lavater, a veteran theologian, not obscurely known by his writings, a Zurich patrician, son of a Burgomaster, and proved by the great and almost immortal services of his ancestor to the fatherland, could easily have put an end to the doubtful choice. But he, venerating the footsteps of the honoured predecessor, did not even obey when solicited; and so he pushed aside the succession, offered to him unasked, with such weighty arguments that the leaders, quieting down on those grounds, turned their minds to another oak to be felled. With the same modesty of a lofty mind and a keen, subtle judgment, the theologian Breitinger (how highly the Fathers of Dort valued him, I, a witness by hearing, am not unaware) refused the theological professorship, whose possession the patrons had held out as a hope; for, as he frankly confessed, these buskins were fit only for Hercules. Instead he yielded the place to Caspar Waser, who has been rightly praised above all for his learning in Oriental literature. When he had been taken from mortals and translated to the heavenly seats, Johann Jakob Huldrich, Provost of the Collegium Carolinum, succeeded him, very reluctantly (as I have clearly perceived), although he was solidly learned and most skilled in ecclesiastical antiquity. Nor without reason: for a theologian does not discharge his duty by the public scholastic lectures, as the common opinion holds, although these too, which ought to be carefully prepared, are a liberal aid, indeed a nourishment, of the ecclesiastical ministry. This vast and illustrious province has far more hidden in its depths than the untrained judgment of the common crowd can grasp. Whoever stubbornly wishes to ignore this may continue to ignore it at his own risk; fair judges have never given such a splendid Sparta to such estimators. And this, most honourable hearers, was worth mentioning, lest anyone suspect that the others were excluded from public honours in the Zurich School, either through the impudence of the self-promoters or the imprudence of the curators, merely from love of country. They were not so self-satisfied as to ascribe all their learning to their native clod, nor so much strangers in the world as not to know how far bronze differs from lupine beans, or what they were doing. But since Zurich was also famous, by the judgment of outsiders too, as a Kiriath-Sepher, a most celebrated book-city, since from this School and Church, as from the Trojan horse, so many men have come forth, adorned with learning of every kind, candid in genuine uprightness, and finally instructed in a varied knowledge of things, so that most people have expected from here teachers rather than disciples for the Church, it would surely have been either the extreme of madness or of ingratitude not to value enough the gift of God which was among us and among ourselves, to leave it uncultivated, to hold it in plain contempt, or to prefer what was summoned from elsewhere merely because it was foreign to what was at home.

units.la: Atque hæc quidem de Vestra; de Vestra, Patres & Fratres; de Schola Tigurina, verba facere, animum induxi.
units.tr: So much, then, I have resolved to say about your concord, fathers and brethren, and about the Zurich School.

units.la: Ita nos fuimus Troes; & hæc Ilij nostri gloria!
units.tr: So we were Trojans, and this is the glory of our Ilium!

units.la: Quando verò
units.tr: But when

units.la: Non minor est virtus, quàm quærere, parta tueri; Agite, vires intendamus omnes, ut quod magnâ Prædecessorum curâ paratum atque partum est, posterorum non pereat aut flaccescat incuriâ. Concordiâ res nostræ parvæ, imò penè desperatæ, præter votum multorum & expectationem, creverunt; ut ne discordiâ dilabantur, velis remisque nitamur. Labor & amor literarum, Tigurum reddidit venerabile; ut ne otium & odium eas pessum det, vigilemus. Valeant simultates omnes, & quicquid studiorum cursui moram injicit periculosam. Livorem præsertim & invidiam pestem studiorum, infensum gratitudinis Deo debitæ hostem, abesse procul jubeamus. Etsi enim æruginem vir fortis
units.tr: Not less is the virtue to keep what has been won than to seek it. Come, let us all strain our powers, so that what has been prepared and won with great care by our predecessors may not perish or wither through the neglect of posterity. Through concord our affairs, small and almost despaired of, have grown beyond the wish and expectation of many; let us strive with sails and oars, lest they slip away through discord. The labour and love of letters have made Zurich venerable; let us take care lest idleness and hatred destroy them. Let all quarrels be farewell, and whatever puts a dangerous delay in the course of studies. Above all, let us bid envy and jealousy, the plague of studies and the hostile enemy of the gratitude owed to God, to keep far away. For although a brave man may easily devour the rust...

units.la: Epilogus tum ... (Greek note) κος. tis facile devoret, certò persuasus, superiorem felicitatis gradum, quàm qui invidia premitur, non dari; spreta enim & contemta nec Zoilus mordet, nec Momus allatrat; indignus tamen Viro erudito, nedum Christiano, est naevus, in invidiae illud argumentum convertere, quod Dei laudem excitare in nobis deberet. Integritas & ingenuitas, quae & in Majoribus nostris emicuit, & remotissimas allexit nationes, nobiscum etiam habitet, pernoctet, peregrinetur, rusticetur φιλο-ξενίαν suam, non ex sumptuoso apparatu, sed liberali vultu aestimatam, ita Majores probârunt, ut non laudem tantùm illa meruerit, sed & vota pro salute & incolumitate nostra multis extorserit. Hunc τέχνων γνησίων characterem si gradu assequi cominus non possumus, conatu saltem exprimere eminus allaboremus. Privata nostra ita curemus, ut publica semper praeeant.
units.tr: Epilogue ... Though a brave man can easily swallow the bitter taste of envy, he is fully persuaded that there is no higher step of happiness than to be free of envy's pressure. For Zoilus does not bite, nor Momus bark, at what is despised and scorned. Yet it is unworthy of a learned man, let alone a Christian, to turn a blemish into a reason for envy, when it ought to stir up in us the praise of God. Integrity and candour, which shone forth in our ancestors and drew even the most distant nations to them, should also dwell, lodge, travel and live in the country among us. Our ancestors so proved their hospitality [φιλοξενία], valued not for lavish display but for a generous countenance, that it earned not only praise but also prayers for our safety and well-being from many people. If we cannot reach this mark of true children [τέχνων γνησίων] up close, let us at least strive to express it from afar. Let us so care for our private affairs that public ones always come first.

units.la: Tu verò, ô Deus, qui fons es & Scaturigo omnis gratiae & Sapientiae perennis, hanc nobis, quaesumus, largire gratiam, ut gratiam tuam rectè agnoscamus, agnitámque digne celebremus. Gratia tua est, non vel volentis cujusquam meritum, vel currentis brabeum, quòd Tigurum hactenus nostrum Schola fuerit & solidae (subtilem libenter alijs relinquimus) Theologiae, & bonarum Literarum Gymnasium. Potentiae tuae est infinitae, & gratiae paternae, quòd densissimis barbariei & ignorantiae tenebris, quae superiora aliquot Secula obruerunt, discussis, & Sole Evangelij Tui, & bonarum Artium Linguarúmque stellis fulgentissimis, nostrum etiam hemisphaerium colluströsti. Gratia tua est, quòd nobis iterum in Scholis nostris earum traduntur mysteria Linguarum, quae adintimum nos admittunt, sine Interprete, Colloquium, non carnis & sanguinis, Regis aut Principis terreni; sed Regis Regum, & Domini Dominantium. Gratia tua est, quòd, qui in extremo latemus Germaniae angulo, hinc tamen, velut ex Zione
units.tr: But you, O God, who are the fountain and spring of all grace and of perennial wisdom, grant us, we pray, this grace: that we may rightly acknowledge your grace and, having acknowledged it, celebrate it worthily. Your grace is not the merit of any man who wills or runs for the prize, that Zurich has so far been our school and gymnasium of sound theology (we gladly leave the subtle kind to others) and of good letters. It is the grace of your infinite power and fatherly kindness that, when the thickest shadows of barbarism and ignorance, which overwhelmed several earlier centuries, were dispelled, you lit up our hemisphere too with the Sun of your Gospel and the most brilliant stars of the good arts and languages. Your grace is that in our schools again the mysteries of those languages are handed down to us, which admit us into intimate fellowship, without an interpreter, a conversation not of flesh and blood, nor of some earthly king or prince, but of the King of kings and Lord of lords. Your grace is that, though we lie in the farthest corner of Germany, you have been pleased to bring forth your law from Zion, as it were, from Zion

units.la: tum λόγος. Zione Legem tuam prodire volueris. Bonitas Tua est, quòd cùm alij horâ demum nonâ aut undecimâ in Vineam Tuam sunt vocati, nobis sancta hæc cultura ab ipso diluculo fuerit commissa. Hanc rogamus, per Jesum Christum, Cœlestem illum Doctorem, Magistrum nostrum ἀνυπόδῠτον, gratiam in nobis conserva, auge, & si nostris aliquid, addere audeamus votis, ad seros propagare, nepotes clementer perge: Donec ex hac Schola crucis in Lucis Scholam promoti, æternis fruamur gaudijs. Hanc nobis concede gratiam ad Sanctissimi Nominis Tui gloriam, Reipub. Christianæ emolumentum, bonarum Literarum incrementum, Ecclesiæ augmentum, sempiternam denique animarum salutem:
units.tr: ... your law. Your goodness is that, while others were called into your vineyard only at the ninth or eleventh hour, this holy labour was committed to us from the very dawn. We beg you, through Jesus Christ, that heavenly Teacher, our unshod Master [ἀνυπόδητον], keep and increase this grace in us; and if we dare to add anything to our prayers, graciously extend it to our late descendants and grandchildren, until, raised from this school of the cross to the school of light, we may enjoy eternal joys. Grant us this grace, for the glory of your most holy Name, for the benefit of the Christian commonwealth, for the increase of good letters, for the growth of the Church, and finally for the eternal salvation of souls.

units.la: ô Pater noster, &c.
units.tr: O Our Father, etc.

units.la: APPENDIX I. BIBLIOTHECAM EXHIBENS TIGURINAM.
units.tr: APPENDIX I. CONTAINING THE LIBRARY OF ZURICH.

units.la: Adamus Michaël, ex Judæo Christianus reformatus, Civis postea (quanquam observo, Imperatorio quodam privilegio aliquot retro seculis S. P.Q. Tigurino permissum fuisse, ut certum etiam Iudæorum numerum Civitatis jure donarent) Tigurinus. Sex libros de bellis judaicis, Capitibus 97. distinctos, Germanicè vertit, & edidit, sed Characteribus HebræoGermanicis. Ita & Pentateuchum & libros V.T. Historicos, excusos Constantiæ 1545. Vixit adhuc 1550.
units.tr: Adam Michael, a Jew turned reformed Christian, afterwards a citizen of Zurich. (I note that by an imperial privilege granted some centuries ago, the Senate and People of Zurich were permitted to confer the rights of citizenship on a certain number of Jews as well.) He translated into German, and published in Hebrew-German characters, six books on the Jewish War, divided into 97 chapters. He also published in the same way the Pentateuch and the historical books of the Old Testament, printed at Constance in 1545. He was still alive in 1550.

units.la: Agricola Laurentius, V. toduranus, Pastor Stamheimensis, in agro Tigurino, scripsit libros aliquot de re militari, quos tamen hactenus, videre nunquam contigit. Aliquid etiam in Poësi fuit conatus. Habeo opera Zuinglii an. Chr. 1547. ab ipso Augustæ Vindelicorum emta, ubi & Eteosticho mortem ejus indicat, & Conclusiones ejusdem egregio ornat Epigrammate.
units.tr: Laurence Agricola, of Toggenburg, minister at Stammheim in the Zurich countryside, wrote several books on military affairs, which I have never yet had the chance to see. He also made some attempt at poetry. I have the works of Zwingli, from the year of Christ 1547, which I bought at Augsburg from him, where he announces Zwingli's death in an acrostic poem and adorns Zwingli's Conclusions with an excellent epigram.

units.la: Nec indigna, quæ hic inseratur, observatio, quæ ad ejusdem exemplaris T. II pag. 559. b. margini est adscripta, ad vexatum illum in Fidei christ. expositione locum: Hic Herculem, Theseum, Socratem, Aristidem &c. Synecdoche, inquit, potest esse speciei allegorica, qua certus numerus personarum insignium pro incerto ponitur. Ac sensus est: Hic Herculem, Theseum, Socratem, &c. id est, fortes, sapientes &c. Videbis, Quæ vero sit sententia Zuinglii vide sol. 119. ubi de medio salutis agit 2. Hanc Synecdochen ipse explicat verbis: Et summatim: Non fuit vir bonus, non erit mens sancta, non fidelis anima, ab ipso Mundi exordio, usque ad ejus consummationem, quam non sis isthic visurus. De hujus loci vindiciis à nobis alibi est actum.
units.tr: The following observation, written in the margin of page 559 b of volume II of the same copy, is not unworthy of being inserted here. It concerns that much-disputed passage in Zwingli's Exposition of the Christian Faith: "Here Hercules, Theseus, Socrates, Aristides, etc." This, he says, may be a synecdoche, an allegorical kind of figure in which a fixed number of famous persons stands for an indefinite number: the sense is "Here Hercules, Theseus, Socrates, etc.," that is, the brave, the wise, and so on. You will see what Zwingli's own view is at page 119, where he treats of the means of salvation, at No. 2. He explains this synecdoche himself in these words: "And in short: there has not been a good man, there will not be a holy mind or a faithful soul, from the very beginning of the world to its end, whom you will not see there." I have dealt elsewhere with the defence of this passage.

units.la: Amandus, alijs Henricus Suso, quibusdam etiam Amandus Sifus: Bellarminus simpliciter Germanum; Labbeus Suevum, Murerus Constantiensem vocat. Magnum ei sanctitatis nomen tribuit Bellarminus, Labbæus, præsertim Murerus, qui, post Felicem Malleolum nostrum, ejus vitam prolixè descripsit in Helvet. sanct. pag. 346. Sed si alia non est, quam quæ à Murero refertur, judicent alii, quo loco haberi illa debeat. Eum huc refero, quia Conventualis fuit Tigurinus, Cœnobii Ottenbacensis in urbe, & Tossensis propè Vitodurum frequens, ut ex Murero patet, visitator. Meminit scriptorum generaliter Murerus. Opuscula quædam ejus Germanica in Linguam Latinam transtulisse refert Senensis, Laurentium Surium. Eià Labbæo & Bellarmino tribuuntur 1. Centum meditationes Passionis Domini, cum totidem petitionibus. 2. Liber de novem rupibus. 3. Herologium sapientiæ. 4. Officium quotidianum de æterna sapientia; quod valde devotum vocat Labbæus, ac sæpe commissum typis.
units.tr: Amandus, otherwise called Henry Suso, and by some also Amandus Sifus. Bellarmine simply calls him a German; Labbe calls him a Swabian; Murer calls him a man of Constance. Bellarmine and Labbe, and especially Murer, ascribe to him a great reputation for holiness. Murer, after our Felix Malleolus, described his life at length in the Helvetic Saints, page 346. But let others judge what place should be given to him, if his life is no other than what Murer reports. I refer him here because he was a Conventual of Zurich, and frequently, as Murer shows, a visitor of the monastery of Ottenbach in the city and of Tossa near Winterthur. Murer mentions his writings only in general terms. The Senensis reports that Laurence Surius translated some of his German pamphlets into Latin. The following are attributed to him by Labbe and Bellarmine: (1) One hundred meditations on the Passion of the Lord, with as many prayers. (2) A book on the nine rocks. (3) The Horologium of Wisdom. (4) The daily office of Eternal Wisdom, which Labbe calls very devout and which has often been printed.

units.la: Albertus, D. Theol. prædicat. Ordinis. Huic scriptum tribuitur, quo sontem miraculosum, qui sub porticu ad templum Aquaticum, aliquando scaturierit, quóque morbi pertinacissimi fuerint curati, commendárit. Meminit Martinus de Biberstein p. m. 17.
units.tr: Albertus, Doctor of Theology of the Order of Preachers. To him is ascribed a writing in which he commends a miraculous spring that once welled up under the portico at the Aquatic Temple, and by which the most stubborn diseases were cured. Martin of Biberstein mentions it on page 17.

units.la: Ammianus, Iohannes Iacobus, Patritius Tigurinus, Mediolani operam dedit literis & Parisiis, vir doctus, primus Scholæ Tigurinæ Reformatæ Professor Latinus, & perpetuus Scholarcha ab an. Chr. 1534. ad 1573. (ætatis 73.) quo obiit. Scripsit elementa artium dicendi, libellum phrasium Rhetoricarum. Interfuit etiam colloquio Ilantino in Rhætia an. Chr. 1526. habito, & per Sebastianum Hofmeisterum Schafhusianum, Tigurī, eo ipso anno, edito. Ammani nostri in ipsa præfatione honorifica fit mentio.
units.tr: Ammian, John James, a patrician of Zurich, studied at Milan and at Paris. He was a learned man, the first Latin professor of the Reformed School of Zurich, and perpetual scholarch from the year of Christ 1534 until 1573, when he died at the age of 73. He wrote the Elements of the Arts of Speaking, a little book of rhetorical phrases. He was also present at the Ilanz colloquy in Rhaetia, held in the year of Christ 1526, which was published at Zurich that same year by Sebastian Hofmeister of Schaffhausen. Our Ammian is mentioned with honour in the preface itself.

units.la: Est & alius, ei (Συνωνυμος), chirurgus, Civis itidem Tigurinus, cujus prodiit Itinerarium terræ sanctæ, Germanicè 1618. De Turcarum statutis, moribus, Orientis statu & situ satis loquitur perspicuè.
units.tr: There is also another, a surgeon of the same name (Synonymus), likewise a citizen of Zurich, whose Itinerary of the Holy Land appeared in German in 1618. It speaks quite clearly of the customs, morals, and the condition and situation of the Turks in the East.

units.la: Ammianus iudocus, Iacobi Professoris filius pictûræ peritissimus, dedit 1. Libellum de arte pingendi, Germanicè Francofurti 1578. 2. Figuras Biblicas cum explicatione rhythmica Henrici Petri Rebenstock; Ib. 1571. 3. Figuras in Dominicales textus, & Passionem, addita præfatione, in qua Ammianus luculenter commendatur; Sigismundi Feyrabend Bibliopolæ, & explicatione Germanico Latina. 4. Quinque corpora Platonica, ex optica disciplina depicta. 5. Figuras novas omnis generis venationes repræsentantes. Floruit Norimbergæ 1583.
units.tr: Ammian, Jodocus, son of Professor James, a most skilled painter, produced: (1) A little book on the art of painting, in German, at Frankfurt in 1578. (2) Biblical figures with a rhythmic explanation by Henry Peter Rebenstock, Frankfurt 1571. (3) Figures for the Sunday texts and the Passion, with a preface added, in which Ammian is splendidly commended, published by the bookseller Sigismund Feyerabend, with explanations in German and Latin. (4) The five Platonic solids, drawn according to the science of optics. (5) New figures representing hunts of every kind. He flourished at Nuremberg in 1583.

units.la: Antmianus Ludovicus, inagro primum Tigurino, Glaronæ postea Minister scripsit conciones anniversarias de processione illa famosa, ad Navalia. Prodiit opus posthumum an Chr. 1661. Obijt 1660.
units.tr: Ammian, Louis, first at Zurich in the countryside, afterwards minister at Glarus, wrote annual sermons on that famous procession ad Navalia. The posthumous work appeared in the year of Christ 1661; he died in 1660.

units.la: Anenstetter Henricus, Collegiatæ Ecclesiæ apud Tigurinos Præpositus ab an Chr. 1427. ad 1439. Decretorum Licentiatus. Id memoratu dignum ejus habet electio, quòd contra Pontificis intentionem, qui Felici Malleolo provinciam illam tradi voluit, successerit. Multa ejus in actis Collegij sunt documenta.
units.tr: Anenstetter, Henry, provost of the collegiate church among the Zurich people from the year of Christ 1427 to 1439, Licentiate in Decrees. What is worth recording about him is his election, for he succeeded, contrary to the intention of the Pope, who wished that office to be given to Felix Malleolus. Many records of his are found in the acts of the college.

units.la: Arnoldus Brixiensis. Hujus Arnoldi in Bibliotheca Gesneriana Edit. postrema, his verbis fit mentio. Arnoldus Brixiensis sua ætate (hoc est, Conrado Imp.) Papa & Ecclesiasticorum tyrannidem & luxum graviter reprehendit, & alios quoque abusus: docuit Brixiæ, inde Italiâ pulsus Tigurum venit, & post obitum Papæ Romam rediit, & tandem propter parrhesiam suam combustus est. Otto Frisingensis & Guntherus Ligurinus, ejus meminere. Ita est. Docuit Arnoldus Brixiensis Tiguri seculo duodecimo, inter alia, omnem animam subesse potestatibus eminentibus sive Magistratibus, ipsos etiam, quo ad temporalia, Sacerdotes, pluràque alia; Imò, si Francisco Guillim. de reb. Helvet, lib. 3. pag. 353. habenda fides, pleraque, quæ Zuinglius docuit, iis, quæ Arnoldus Brixiensis quadringentis annis ante docuerat, fuerunt affinia. Unde & nuperrimus Scriptor Sforzia Palavicinus, Hist. Concil. Tridentini l. 1. c. 19 circa finem monet: parum fideliter agere hoc loco Suavem dum ab accessu Frat. Sampsonis, ac proinde à Romana libidine pecuniæ emungendi, novam Zuinglii hæresin educit: Viguisse jam, antequam Frater Sampson accessisset; neque initium fecisse occasione Indulgentiarum Zuinglium; sed longè graviorum & difficilimorum articulorum. Lutheri verò hinc natam Reformationem. Insigne hominis nobis adversi, pro Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ antiquissimo, erroribus Pontificiis resistendi, studio, testimonium! Huc, dubio procul, Iesuita & ad alia capita (de quibus consuli potest nostra legendi Historias Helveticas Methodus) alludit. Et certè, subjectionem Cleri in temporalibus strenuè Tigurinos jam olim ursisse, non modo ex Guntheri Poëtæ, qui Friderici I. aulam sectabatur, aperta manifestum est Confessione (quam prolixè inseruit Guillim. l. c. nos compendiosè, Hist. Eccles. sec. XII. pag. 170.) sed & actis Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ nostræ. Hæc enim ubi primùm semel hæsit sententia, ægrè majoribus amplius nostris evelli potuit. Unde factum, ut credibrioribus se contra onera civilia, & fori mutationem, etiam Canonici, munire debuerint Imperatorum privilegiis, immunitatem concedentibus. Primum, quod sciam, est Henrici V. circa an. Chr. 1128. eòque adeò seculo, quo Arnoldus suam Tigurì spargere cœpit doctrinam, quo inter alia Collegiatam Ecclesiam reddidit immunem & penitus absolvit, à vigiliis nominatim & ab omnibus exactionibus, quæ vel Legibus vel Canonibus videntur aliquo modo obviare, non obstante aliqua consuetudine, vel statuto Consulum, vel cujuscunque potestatis secularis. Eodem planè tempore, an. Chr. 1280. inhibitorium etiam misit Episcopus Constantiensis super juramentis, quibus se mutuo obligarunt Cives Tigurini, super expulsis & expellendis quibusdam mulierculis in confusionem cleri quo relaxavit, cassavit, tanquam juri rationi & consuetudini contraria. Sed redisse videntur cives, vel perstitisse potius in recepta consuetudine, unde nova, non longè post Rodolphi 1. superioris privilegii confirmatio, in qua diserta verba: Ipsa enim advocatia sic nobis & imperio attinebit, ut à nobis & ab ipso alienari non possit. Item à civilibus oneribus, & expressè à vigiliis & ab aliis omnibus actionibus, Ecclesiasticis, libertatibus, legibus & canonibus contrariis & obviantibus, ipsos immunes decernimus & penitus absolvimus, non obstante statuto irrationali Consulum, vel cujuscunque seculuris potestatis violentia introducta. Sed ne sic quidem Clero satis fuisse cautum, ex alio patet ejusdem Rodolphi diplomate, quod intercesionem miscet authoritate, & ex ipso autographo, Advocato & universis Civibus, inscripto, ita habet: Rodolphus, Dei gratia, Romanorum Rex, semper Augustus, Prudentibus viris, Advocato, & universis Civibus de Turego, dilectis fidelibus suis, gratiam suam & omne bonum. Honorabilis vir, Praepositus Thuricensis, Capellanus noster dilectus, graviter nobis conquerendo monstravit, quod vos, in praejudicium honoris & privilegii Clericalis, ipsum & Ecclesiam suam gravibus lacessitis injuriis, & libertates & jura ipsorum, ad Ecclesiasticum Forum pertinentia, praesumptione nephatia vobis temere usurpatis. Quod cum multis ex causis singulari quadam affectione nos moveat & conturbat, cumque ipsa Ecclesia nostra protectioni immediate noscitur esse subjecta, cumque dictus Praepositus, inter caeteros nostros devotos, singularis nobis favoris & dilectionis privilegio est astrictus; Prudentiam vestram seriosa precum nostrarum instantia requirimus, & rogamus, Regia vobis nihilominus auctoritate mandantes, quatenus ab his violentis injuriis vos inantea cohibentes, memoratum Praepositum & Ecclesiam ipsam, juribus & libertatibus ipsorum gaudere sinatis, inantea pacifice & quiete. Jura hujus, cum ad vos non pertineant ullo jure, vobis de cetero nullatenus vendicantes. Inpraemissis igitur, & in iis maximè, quae ipsius Prepositi jura, libertates, commoda respiciant & honores, vos adeo reverenter, adeoque benevole tenere, de cetero studeatis, quod in cunctis vestris agendis, idem Praepositus in conspectu Regio, diligentis semper procuratoris officium, debeat, cum valeat exercere. Datum Vienne, XIII. Kalend. Febr. Indictione V. Regni nostri anno quarto.
units.tr: Arnold of Brescia. Arnold is mentioned in the last edition of Gesner's Bibliotheca in these words: Arnold of Brescia, in his own age (that is, under the Emperor Conrad), sharply censured the tyranny and luxury of the Pope and the clergy, and other abuses too. He taught at Brescia, and driven from Italy from there he came to Zurich, and after the death of the Pope returned to Rome, and at last, because of his outspokenness, was burned. Otto of Freising and Gunther the Ligurian both mention him. This is true. Arnold of Brescia taught at Zurich in the twelfth century, among other things, that every soul is subject to the higher powers or magistrates, and that the clergy themselves are subject to them in temporal matters, and much else besides. Indeed, if Francis Guillimann (On the Affairs of Helvetia, book 3, page 353) is to be believed, most of what Zwingli taught was akin to what Arnold of Brescia had taught four hundred years before. Hence also the most recent writer, Sforza Pallavicino (History of the Council of Trent, book 1, chapter 19), warns near the end: Suave acts rather unfaithfully here, when from the arrival of Brother Sampson, and so from the Roman lust for squeezing out money, he derives Zwingli's new heresy. The heresy was already flourishing before Brother Sampson arrived, and Zwingli did not begin from the occasion of the indulgences, but from far graver and more difficult articles. It was from Luther that the Reformation was born. What a remarkable testimony from an adversary of ours, to the most ancient zeal of the Church of Zurich in resisting Papist errors! No doubt the Jesuit also alludes here to other heads (on which one may consult our Helvetic Methodus for Reading Histories). And certainly it is plainly shown that the Zurich people had long ago vigorously upheld the subjection of the clergy in temporal matters, not only by the open Confession of Gunther the poet, who attended the court of Frederick I (which Guillimann inserts at length in the place cited; we give it briefly in the Ecclesiastical History, 12th century, page 170), but also by the acts of our Church and Commonwealth. For once this opinion had taken root, it could hardly be uprooted by our ancestors. Hence it came about that even the canons were obliged to protect themselves, against civil burdens and a change of court, with privileges of the emperors granting immunity. The first, as far as I know, is that of Henry V, around the year of Christ 1128, that is, in the very century when Arnold began to spread his teaching at Zurich. In it, among other things, he made the collegiate church immune and completely released it, specifically from night watches and from all exactions which seem in any way to conflict with the laws or the canons, notwithstanding any custom, or any statute of the consuls, or the authority of any secular power. At just that time, in the year of Christ 1280, the Bishop of Constance also sent an injunction concerning the oaths by which the citizens of Zurich bound themselves to each other, about certain women expelled and to be expelled, to the confusion of the clergy, which he relaxed and annulled as contrary to law, reason and custom. But the citizens seem to have returned to their former ways, or rather to have persisted in the custom they had received. Hence, not long after, came a new confirmation of the earlier privilege by Rudolf I, in which are the explicit words: For the advocacy itself shall so belong to us and to the empire that it cannot be alienated from us and from it. Likewise we decree them immune from civil burdens, and expressly absolve them and wholly release them from night watches and from all other ecclesiastical actions, liberties, laws and canons that conflict with or stand in the way, notwithstanding any irrational statute of the consuls or the violence introduced by any secular power. Yet even this does not seem to have been enough caution for the clergy, as is clear from another diploma of the same Rudolf, which mixes in his authority, and from the autograph itself, addressed To the Advocate and all the Citizens, which reads as follows: Rudolf, by the grace of God, King of the Romans, ever Augustus, to the prudent men, the Advocate, and all the citizens of Zurich, his beloved faithful subjects, his grace and every good. The honourable man, the Provost of Zurich, our beloved chaplain, has shown us with grave complaint that you, to the prejudice of the honour and privilege of the clergy, have grievously assailed him and his Church with wrongs, and have rashly usurped for yourselves, by a presumption that is wicked, liberties and rights of theirs which belong to the ecclesiastical court. Since this moves and troubles us in many ways with a certain special affection, and since our Church itself is known to be directly under our protection, and since the said Provost, among our other devoted men, is bound to us by the privilege of our special favour and love; we require your prudence by the earnest urgency of our prayers, and we request, and nonetheless command you with royal authority, that you restrain yourselves from these violent injuries henceforth, and allow the said Provost and the Church itself to enjoy their rights and liberties peacefully and quietly henceforth. Since these rights do not belong to you by any right, do not henceforth claim them for yourselves in any way. Therefore, in all the matters set forth, and especially in those that concern the rights, liberties, advantages and honours of the same Provost, take care to hold him in such reverence and such goodwill, that in all your affairs the same Provost may be able to exercise before the royal presence the office of a diligent agent. Given at Vienna, on the 13th day before the Kalends of February, in the fifth indiction, the fourth year of our reign.

units.la: Sed, quod de Tigurinis Carmine dixit, Guntherus poëta: Servat adhuc uva gustum gensi stapaterna.
units.tr: But as the poet Gunther said of the Zurichers in his verse: The grape still keeps the taste of its noble stock.

units.la: adipsam usque obtinuisse reformationem observo. Primè enim, foederi Helvetico Vrbs innexa, leges statim cum caeteris Cantonibus sancivit; quae saluti publicae consulerent: non laicis tantum; sed & Clericis. Observanda hinc fundamentalis illa lex, Der Pfaffenbrief vulgo, an. Chr. 1370. data, cujus sensum & apographum habet Method. legendi Hist. Helvet. pag. 456. Illi proxime accedit aliud inter Helvetios, Landgravium Durgæi Dominos, & Constantiensem Episcopum Conventionis Instrumentum an. Chr. 1493. decretum & confirmatum, ubi litem inter Clerum Helvetiæ, Abbates Sangallensem, & Murensem, Præpositum Tigurinum, Capitulum Lucernense & Zofingense, ortâ ipsi Helvetiæ ordines, & ita quidem amicè composuerunt, ut in causis matrimonialibus, subsidiis charitativis, taxa, pœnis Cleri, ejusque subordinatis tribunalibus sive foris, non admittendis quæstionarijs (quæstuarii vocantur alias: de quibus Angel. de clavas. Clav. Conscient.) leges præscripserint. Quin & expresse statuerunt, ut casuum reservatorum absolutio cuilibet permitteretur ordinario; neque Mendicantes, Sacerdotes laicos (Die Pfaffheit) quoquomodo, pro cathedra, laderent; sed ut Clementinam diligenter observarent; neque Pœnitentiarii Plebanorum subditos ludibrio haberent. De excommunicatione insuper, aliisque clara & distincta data & in chartas conjecta sunt capita. Reperio deinceps Catalogum gravaminum, quæ passa sit Ecclesia Collegiata sub regimine VValdmanni (ita inscriptio habet) ubi conqueritur Clerus, de privilegiis diminutis, libertate faciendi Testamenta, ad emta, mandato publico, ne quid deinceps Clericis legaretur, vel legatum concederetur; nihil etiam emtione illi acquirerent, aut acquisitum obtinerent; pœnis Canonicis & Sacellanis, tum irrogatis, tum per publicos Ministros collectis: tributis extraordinariis (de illa gravissima erat querela, qua Collegium Carolinum 1800 pendere debuit florenos: reliqui etiam, ad structuram duarum Templi Majoris turrium, Clerici omnes, qui ex ditione Tigurina proventus aliquos exspectabant) novarum legum impositione, aliisque, quæ obiter attingere placuit. Vix longè post Amplissimus Magistratus, jus suum longa defensum consuetudine, ipsi Pontifici tradidit confirmandum, cum commendatione sive Nuncii, sive alterius, id quod manifestum est ex articulis illis, de quibus in nostris Anal. P. I. p. 73. Sed & Hugonis Episcopi programma, quo omnibus ditioni suæ Clericis significat, ut pro excommunicatis habeant Bartholomæum Mejer de Hagenavv, Iohannem Griesium, eorumque asseclas, quòd sacrilegas ac violentas manus injecerint in sacerdotes varios, non obscurè indicat, non semper Cleri libidinem ferre Majores fuisse paratos. Reformationis tempore controversia hæc initio gliscere iterum cœpit: Privatim tamen Zuinglius eam ita componere studuit, ut ne Reformationi illa poneret obicem. Erat Præpositus illius temporis Vir magnæ æstimationis, & eo apud Zuinglium loco, ut cum ei an. Chr. 1518. Præpositura committeretur, literis ex Eremo scriptis, per Myconium illi fuerit gratulatus, utpote sub quo futurum speraret, ut literæ bonæ promoverentur: quia vero Hofmannus Plebanus, juxta cæteros, vestigiorum avitorum, & Collegii privilegiorum erat observantissimus, cæteri etiam Collegæ metuebant, ne veteribus paulatim migrandum esset colonis, suam de immunitate cleri, & competentia fori Episcopalis serió defendit hypothesin. Sed atnicè Zuinglius Præpositum an Chr.1520.monuit, & ita quidem, ut non modestiæ hic minorem erga Magistratum, quàm fidei & diligentiæ in Collegium probârit fidem. Et in hujus quidem gratiam privilegiorum Imperatoriorum, Rodolphi cumprimis Habspurgici &c. revifionem, quæ ad manus est, instituit; in illius vero honorem contulit, quicquid μετρiόητα, commendare poterat, qua & Ecclesiæ necessariis proventibus erat prospectum, & Magistratus authoritati confultum. Hæc paulò accuratius examinare placuit, ut quæ de Arnoldo Brixiensi, ejusque apud Tigurinos sparso semine dicuntur, lucem aliquam haberent.
units.tr: I observe that the Reformation was carried through to that very point. First, when the city was joined to the Swiss confederation, it at once enacted laws, together with the other cantons, that would serve the public welfare, not only for laymen but also for clergy. From this comes that fundamental law to be observed, commonly called the Pfaffenbrief, given in the year of Christ 1370, whose content and copy are in the Method of Reading Swiss History, p. 456. Closely following it is another instrument of agreement among the Swiss, the Landgraves of Thurgau, and the Bishop of Constance, dated in the year of Christ 1493, decreed and confirmed, in which the estates of Helvetia themselves composed in so friendly a way the dispute that had arisen between the clergy of Helvetia, the abbots of St Gall and Mur, the provost of Zurich, and the chapters of Lucerne and Zofingen, that they laid down rules concerning matrimonial cases, charitable subsidies, fees, penalties of the clergy, and their subordinate tribunals, whether outside or inside the courts, and the exclusion of quaestionarii (otherwise called quaestuarii; on whom see Angelus de Clavasio, Summa Confessorum). They also expressly decreed that the absolution of reserved cases should be granted to any ordinary priest; that the mendicant friars should in no way injure the lay priests (die Pfaffheit) in regard to their pulpit; that they should diligently observe the Clementine decree; and that the penitentiaries should not make a mockery of the subjects of the parish priests. Besides, clear and distinct chapters concerning excommunication were also given and written down. Next I find a catalogue of the grievances suffered by the collegiate church under the rule of Waldmann (so the inscription reads), in which the clergy complain of diminished privileges: the freedom to make wills; the purchase of property by public order, so that nothing further might be left or bequeathed to the clergy; that they could acquire nothing by purchase or hold what they had acquired; the canonical penalties imposed on canons and chaplains, and collected by public officials; extraordinary taxes (the most serious complaint concerned the Carolinum, which was obliged to pay 1800 florins; the rest of the clergy too, all who expected some income from the Zurich district, were asked to contribute to the building of the two towers of the Great Minster); the imposition of new laws; and other matters which I was pleased to touch on in passing. Shortly afterwards the most distinguished magistracy handed over to the Pontiff himself, to be confirmed, its right, long defended by custom, with a recommendation either from the nuncio or from someone else; this is clear from those articles discussed in our Analecta, part I, p. 73. But the programme of Bishop Hugo, by which he tells all the clergy in his jurisdiction to regard Bartholomew Meyer of Hagenau, John Grieß, and their followers as excommunicated, because they had laid sacrilegious and violent hands on various priests, plainly shows that the bishops were not always ready to tolerate the lust of the clergy. At the time of the Reformation this controversy began to flare up again. Privately, however, Zwingli tried to settle it in such a way that it would not block the Reformation. The provost of that time was a man of great esteem, and stood so high with Zwingli that when the provostship was entrusted to him in the year of Christ 1518, Myconius congratulated him in a letter written from the hermitage, since he hoped that under him good letters would be advanced. But because Hofmann, the parish priest, like the others, was most careful to keep the traditions of the ancestors and the privileges of the college, and the other colleagues too feared that the old tenants would gradually have to move out, he firmly defended his thesis about the immunity of the clergy and the competence of the episcopal court. Yet Zwingli admonished the provost in a friendly way in the year of Christ 1520, in such a manner that he showed as much faith to the magistracy in modesty as he had shown faith and diligence toward the college. And for his sake he undertook a revision of the imperial privileges, of Rudolph of Habsburg especially, etc., which is at hand; and in his honour he bestowed whatever moderation [μετριότητα] could recommend, by which provision was made for the necessary income of the Church and the authority of the magistracy was consulted. I have thought it fit to examine these matters somewhat more carefully, so that what is said about Arnold of Brescia and the seed sown by him among the Zurichers might gain some light.

units.la: Arzet Rodolphus, Physicus. Meminit ejus Anniversarium Ecclesiæ Cathedralis Tigurinæ, m. Aprili: Magister Rodolphus Physicus; Et Lupoldus Arzet, armiger, filius Magistri Rudolphi Physici prædictâ. Edidit librum de Comera 1472. quem habet Reverendus Ecclesiæ Bulacensis Minister, D. Ioh. Iacobus Engelerus.
units.tr: Rudolph Arzet, physician. The anniversary of the cathedral church of Zurich, for April 4 [m. Aprili], mentions him: "Master Rudolph, physician"; and "Lupold Arzet, esquire, son of the aforesaid Master Rudolph the physician." He published a book on the comet in 1472, which the reverend minister of the church of Bülach, Mr. Johann Jakob Engeler, possesses.

units.la: Bartenstein Martinus, Franco natione, postea, an. Chr. 1480 & deinceps, ad Reformationem, Augustinianus Regularis, in monte Thuricensi. Scripsit Legendam, quam vocat, sanctorum Martyrum, Felicis, Regulæ, Exuperantii, Germanicè, ubi de antiquitate urbis Tigurinæ, Legione Thebæa, Prot Evangelistarum Martyrio: Indulgentiis, miraculis, in templo præsertim Aquatico, Tempore belli septennalis Tigurini, quod vocant, refert, an Chr. 1444 ab omnibus Cantonibus, apertis diu noctúque portis, urbem fuisse obsessam, sed miraculosè liberatam. Ex eo tempore, diem Caroli toti Civitati Cantea enim minor, sive antiquior urbs non feriabatur; Neque mirum, deprehendo enim, crebras inter Præposituram Carolinam, & Abbatiam Tigurinam à Ludovico Germanico fundatam, fuisse liteans; Illa hæc quovis modo vellicávit, ejúsque donationibus & privilegiis insidias struxit) fuisse festum. Habeo tractatum ἀνέκδοτον, cum judicio & censura D. Breitingeri. Videtur adhuc superfuisse an. Chr. 1519 quo cœnobio montis Martinus quidam præerat.
units.tr: Martin Bartenstein, by nationality a Frank, afterwards, in the year of Christ 1480 and following, up to the Reformation, a regular Augustinian on the Zurich mountain. He wrote a so-called Legend of the holy martyrs Felix, Regula and Exuperantius, in German, in which he relates the antiquity of the city of Zurich, the Theban Legion, the martyrdom of the Protector and Evangelists, indulgences, miracles, especially in the Aquatic church, and the time of the so-called Seven Years' War of Zurich, when, in the year of Christ 1444, all the cantons had besieged the city for a long time, with the gates open day and night, but it was miraculously delivered. From that time the day of Charles was a feast for the whole city. (For the smaller or older town was not kept as a holiday. Nor is this surprising, for I find that there were frequent lawsuits between the Carolinian provostry and the abbey of Zurich founded by Louis the German; the former in every way harassed the latter and plotted against its gifts and privileges.) I have an unpublished treatise, with the judgement and criticism of Mr. Breitinger. He seems still to have been alive in the year of Christ 1519, when a certain Martin was in charge of the monastery on the mountain.

units.la: Baldungus Hieronymus, Medicus olim fuit Tigurinus, ejus quædam scripta extare audio, inquit Gesnerus in Bibliotheca.
units.tr: Hieronymus Baldung, once a physician of Zurich; I hear that some of his writings exist, says Gesner in the Bibliotheca.

units.la: Beumlerus Marcus, Tigurinus, Volcxensuila in Comitatu Kirburgico an. Chr. 1555 natus Minister verbi primum Alzeæ in Archi Palatinatu, postea Tiguri in Templo Cathedrali Archi Diaconus; Tandem Professor publicus tam Linguæ Græcæ, quàm Theologiæ ad an. Chr. 1611. quo obiit. Scripsit A. philosophica & philologica, ut sunt 1. Analysis Dialectica Ciceronis Catonis Majoris, sive Dialogi de senectute tum Lulij, sive de amicitia, ad Methodum P. Rami accommodata, Spirae 1583. Pro Sexto Roscio, Spir. 1595. Plutarchi de liberorum educatione cum commentario, lb. 1593. & Arnheim. 1606. Grammatica Latina, Tig. 1595. Analyses in Demosthenis Orationes, Olynthiacas tres, Tig. & Francof. 1585. Elocutionis Rhetoricae libri 2. Tigur. 1598 Theologis in Praxi Ecclesiastica sive concionandi arte valde commendati. B. Theologica 1. Antichristus Romanus, sive vindicatio disputationis D. Georgii Sohnij (quam Theologi Germani magni semper fecerunt) contra Iohannis cujusdam Aquiportani Sacerdotis cavillationes Herborn. 1599 2. Hypotyposis Theologiae Methodice & Scholastice exarata, & tribus libris distincta, Tiguri 1607. Hanc deinceps γνώριος ejus discipulus, D. Breitingerus recensuit, commentariis vero perspicuis illustravit Iob. Rodolphus Stuckius de quo postea. 3. Disputationes variae; duae, una de persona christi, altera de phrasibus Scripturae, cum de Christo loquitur. Tig 1596. b. de libro Naturae, & Scripturae ex Psalmo 19. Tig. 1597. c. Disputationes tres de scripturarum 1. Authoritate, 2. Perspicuitate 1605. 3. Perfectione, oppositae Pontificiorum Sophismatis, Tig. 1600. 4. Confessionis Helveticae compendium ad disputandum propositum Tigur. 1606. 5. An Paulus, ad Romanos 7.v.7. ad finem, loquatur de se ut converso. 6. De Scripturae Natura, Proprietatibus, Effectis. 7. De Deo Creatore & Conservatore 8. De Cognitione hominis lapsi & instaurati 9. De peccato in Sp. S. 10. De christi munere prophetico. 11. De Ecclesia Catholica 12. Anne Ecclesia complectens & profitens puram Propheticam & Apostolicam doctrinam, destituta successione visibili & & personali, continuata jam inde a temporibus Apostolorum fit vera Ecclesia. Oralis cum Iacobo Andreae Tubingae de communicatione Idiomatum disputatio 1582. habetur in Hospin. Hist. Sacrament. P. pag. 370. &c. 4. Apologia brevis & necessaria in qua primo exponuntur rationes cur Iacobi Andreae manus & Lingua instar Ismaelis sit contra omnes. Deinde diluuntur ejus falsae criminationes adversus Grynaeum, Marcum Beumlerum & Zuinglium confictae, Tig. 1585. 5. De duabus quaestionibus, conjunctione nempe Sacramentali & vera communione Corporis & Sanguinis Christi adversus Synusiastas, & sutilem Consensus orthodoxi refutationem, duo tractatus. 1584. b. Vera fides Filiorum Dei, sive de Origine, proprietatibus & effectis verae fidei. 1595. Germ. 7. Analysis disputationis Iacobi Andreae, de religiosa carnis Christi adoratione Tig. 1584. 8. Contra Iacobum Heilbrunnerum: Verum & solidum antididagma, contra falsam assertionem de doctrina Calviniistarum & Zuinglianorum, quam an. Chr. 1590. publicavit, Tig. 1593. Solida refutatio prolixae falsaeque narrationis Iacobi Heilbrunneri, sparsae 1595. de Calvini & Zuinglii erroribus, Tigur. 1598. Addi potest ejusdem judicium Msc. ad quaestiones Casuisticas an.
