Deinde, post obitum patris, qui labore assiduo in vita nos aluerat, angusto multis liberis patrimonio relicto, ego aliquandiu aqua inter cutem afflictus, mox inpristinam, ope divina, restitutus valetudinem, cum in patria Maecenates studiorum mihi deessent, Argentoratum descendi, ubi aliquot menses optimo felicis memoriae Viro, V Volfgango Captoni, non sine fructu in bonis literis inservij: Inde reversus in patriam, & publico stipendio auctus, cum Johanne Frisio meo, tanquam Fratre, Galliam ingressus per anni spatium Biturigibus paedagogum egi (stipendium enim sumptibus in liberalia studia faciendis non respondebat) ibi docendo alios, ipse plurimum profecisse mihi videor; quippe nullum fere tempus vacabat, quo non Latinis aut Graecis authoribus legendis astrictus essem. Insequente anno Lutetiam Parisiorum accessi, ut liberius operam literis navarem, urbis illius & Academiae celebritate impulsus: sed nescio, quomodo partim inopia necessaria, partim negligentia voluntaria culpa (vix dum enim decimum octavum annum attigeram: quae aetas maxime sui negligens est, si desit consiliarius aut hortator) amanitates studiorum secutus, ut a puero consueveram, Philosophiam, Artesque severiores minime colens, varios authores sine certo fine pervolitabam, Graecos & Latinos, Historicos, Poetas, Medicos, Philologos, quandoque etiam Dialecticos & Rhetores, multa interim transiliens, paucos libros integre perlegebam, ut sola vicissitudine, varietateque lectionis ingenium demulcerem, quod plurimis hodie impedimentum accidit, quo minus proficiant. Quamobrem ego etiam curiosius hæc de me scribo, ut meo exemplo admoneam, quàm noxium sit adolescentes sibi suòque arbitrio permittere, citra Phænicem aliquem, qui subinde hortetur ac doceat, ut ille suum Achillem: μύθων τε ῥητῆρ ἑμεναι πεπρακτῆρα τε ἔργων. Vehementer illi prosecto reprehendendi sunt, qui, ut pecuniæ precant, adolescentibus, quos excolendi ingenij gratiâ alio mittunt, Pædagogos non conducunt: quæ noxa major est, quàm ut brevi sermone dici queat. Vos autem o boni juvenes, quorum conatibus obstat res angusta domi, moneo & hortor, Viros eruditos sæpe accedite, nihil absque consilijs eorum agite, proficientes audite, nihil ingenio vestro confidite, lectiones domesticas Professoribus non ante ferte: Omnino enim hæc studiorum vestrorum damna insignia sunt, quæ vestra ætas nondum vidit. Gravis parænesis, cui qui locum non dederit, irreparabili suo tempore discent damno, quid sit temnere magnos. Redeo ad Gessnerari. Ex Gallia, pergit, reversus Argentoratum, evocabar in patriam; pari, & paulo post intempestivius uxore ducta in publica Schola angulum detrusus, aliquandiu bona diei parte pueros Grammaticæ rudimenta docebam: minimo interim stipendio, unde nisi me esuritum satis, spes nulla affulgeret: Itaque successivis horis libros Medicorum inspexi, deinde quo potui modo molesta conditione extricatus, Basileam me contuli, ut amplius proficerem, idem stipendium, quo prius fruebar, concedentibus Ecclesiæ nostræ præfectis; quod tamen illic etiam in rei medicæ studijs liberum me sustinere non potuit; quare coactus Dictionarium Græco-Latinum ex Phavorini Camerinis Lexico apud Græcos omnium locupletissimo ita auxi, ut nihil in eo extaret, quod non singulari fide ac diligentia adjicerem, quam Typographus exiguam duntaxat accessionis nostræ partem adjecit, quod me inscio factum est, donec totum fere opus exivisset, an. D. 1537. An autem typographus vel judicij tantum acerudition is sibi usurpaverit, ut quaedam de industria seligeret, vel in aliud tempus reservare voluerit, ne voluminis prætextu aliàs locupletati careret, haud facile dixerim: Et ipse haud multò post impressum librum fato concessit. Na istud mihi plurimum dolet, tantum laborem nostrum tam negligenter tractatum esse. Fuerunt etiam, qui postea, viri, ut sibi videbantur, eruditi, multa tanquam superflua flua Græcas præsertim Interpretationes deleverant: Forte, quia suspicabantur aliquid meum esse, & ideòque non prolabant, cùm omnia prorsus ex Phavorino Camerte, vel quod idem est, Suida, & varijs Græcorum Commentarijs adjuncta essent, quod tamen Typographus in Præfatione Lectorem non admonuit, ne quid illis incommodaturus videretur, qui Phavorini magnum Lexicon eodem tempore Basileæ excudebant. Jam annus Basileæ mihi abiverat, & statim obtulit se mihi conditio Græcas literas profitendi Lausannæ ad lacum Leemannum, liberale stipendium largiente Magnifico Senatu Bernensi. Triennium igitur illic docui; & in familiaribus doctorum, piorumque hominum Petri Vireti, Beati Comitis, Himberti Professoris Hebraici, Johannis Ribitti, qui mihi successit, & aliorum amicitiis jucundissimè vixi. Sed cum à puero ingenium meum in Medicina studium proclive ferretur (ab infantia enim educavit me avunculus meus magnus, sacerdos etiam Tigurî, ac in re Medica, præsertim herbaria non imperitus) & semper succesivis horis libenter in Medicorum libris divertissem, & Patroni studiorum, qui stipendijs Tigurî præsunt, me ultrò currentem instigassent, visum est Montempessulanum, Medicinæ nomine celeberrimum adire. Eò cùm venissem, relictâ Lausanna, nec ullum ex doctioribus Medicis reperirem, qui me domo hospitem susciperet: minus enim ex publicis lectionibus, quàm domestica consuetudine doctrinæ mihi accessuorum speraram) non diu moratus, nonnihil in anatomicis & stirpium Historia peritior factus, Germaniam repetij, & Basileæ insignibus Medici donatus in patriam redij, ubi nunc Philosophiam, quo ad ejus possum; adolescentes doceo. Hæc D. Gesnerus de studiorum suorum cursu.
units.tr: Gesnerus Conradus, of Zürich, was born at Zürich in 1516. A most distinguished physician and philosopher, he was Professor of the Collegium Carolinum and its physician from 1558 until 1565, when he died of plague on 13 December, in his forty-ninth year. Two things in this author deserve notice, both more to be wondered at than imitated. First, as a young man he did not follow a method that would lay the way to solid learning, but a wandering and haphazard one; second, that among the writers of his age he was extremely prolific (polygraphotatos), although he scarcely reached the average span of life. On the first point it is pleasant to hear him speak himself, in the first edition of the Bibliotheca: "Distinguished men were my teachers in boyhood and youth in my homeland: Osvaldus Myconius, Theodorus Bibliander, Petrus Dasypodius, Johannes Jacobus Ammianus, Scholarch of our Gymnasium, and Rodolphus Collinus. Under these teachers I was trained from the first rudiments to a knowledge of both languages of physicians, chiefly under Ammianus, a most learned man, who for three full years, with remarkable generosity, kept me at his home free of charge and taught me as one of the family. Then, after the death of my father, who by constant labour had supported us during his life and left a narrow inheritance to his many children, I was for some time afflicted with dropsy under the skin; soon, by divine help, I was restored to my former health. Since in my homeland there were no patrons of learning for me, I went down to Strasbourg, where for some months I served the good letters, not without profit, under the excellent man of blessed memory Volfgangus Capito. Returning from there to my homeland, and with a public stipend increased, I entered France with Johannes Frisius, my friend as a brother, and for a year I acted as tutor at Bourges (the stipend, indeed, did not match the expense of pursuing liberal studies). There, by teaching others, I seem to myself to have profited greatly, for there was hardly any time free in which I was not bound to read Latin or Greek authors. The following year I came to Paris, to devote myself more freely to letters, drawn by the fame of that city and its Academy. But I know not how, partly through necessary want and partly through the fault of voluntary negligence (for I had scarcely reached my eighteenth year, an age that is most careless of itself when it lacks an adviser or encourager), I followed the pleasures of study, as I had been accustomed from boyhood, and, not cultivating philosophy and the sterner arts at all, I flitted about through various authors without any fixed aim, Greek and Latin, historians, poets, physicians, philologists, and sometimes also dialecticians and rhetoricians; skipping over much in the meantime, I read through few books entire, so that I might soothe my mind by variety and change of reading alone, which is an obstacle that today hinders very many from making progress. Therefore I write these things about myself more carefully, so that by my example I may warn how harmful it is to let young men be left to themselves and their own judgment, without some Phoenix who from time to time urges and teaches them, as he did his Achilles: 'to be a speaker of words and a doer of deeds.' Those surely are to be severely reproved who, to save money, do not hire tutors for young men whom they send elsewhere for the sake of cultivating their talents; this harm is greater than can be told in a few words. But you, good young men, whose efforts are hindered by straitened circumstances at home, I advise and exhort you: often seek out learned men, do nothing without their counsel, listen to those who make progress, trust nothing to your own wit, and do not bring your private readings before your professors. For these losses of your studies are indeed remarkable, such as your age has not yet seen." This is a weighty exhortation, and whoever does not heed it will, in time, suffer irreparable loss, learning what it is to despise great things. I return to Gesner. He goes on: "Returning from France to Strasbourg, I was called to my homeland; soon after, equally and rather untimely, having married, I was pushed into a corner of the public school, and for some part of the day I taught boys the rudiments of grammar, on a very small stipend, from which, unless I was starving, no hope shone forth. Therefore in the hours I could spare I looked into the books of the physicians; then, extricating myself from that troublesome position as best I could, I went to Basel to make further progress, the same stipend I had before being granted by the leaders of our Church; yet even there it could not sustain me free for the study of medicine. Hence, compelled, I enlarged the Greek-Latin Dictionary, from the Lexicon of Phavorinus of Camerino, the most copious of all Greek lexica, so that nothing in it remained that I did not add with singular fidelity and diligence. The printer, without my knowledge, added only a small part of my addition, and this was done when almost the whole work had already come out, in the year 1537." Whether the printer presumed so much on his learning that he selected certain things deliberately, or wished to keep them for another time, lest the book, enriched in some other way under the pretext of a volume, should lack them, I could hardly say. He himself died not long after the book was printed. This grieves me very much, that so great a labour of ours was treated so carelessly. There were also later men, who thought themselves learned, who deleted many things as superfluous, especially the Greek interpretations, perhaps because they suspected that something was mine and therefore did not approve it, although everything had been taken entirely from Phavorinus of Camerino, or what is the same, Suidas, and from various Greek commentaries; yet the printer did not warn the reader of this in the Preface, so as not to seem to harm those who were printing Phavorinus's great Lexicon at Basel at the same time. By now the year at Basel had passed for me, and at once an offer came to me to profess Greek letters at Lausanne on Lake Leman, the Magnificent Senate of Bern granting a generous stipend. I taught there for three years, and I lived most pleasantly in the familiar friendship of learned and pious men: Peter Viret, Beatus Comes, Himbert, professor of Hebrew, John Ribit, who succeeded me, and others. But since from boyhood my mind was naturally inclined to the study of medicine (for my great-uncle, a priest also at Zürich and not unskilled in medicine, especially herbal medicine, brought me up from infancy), and since I had always gladly turned aside to the books of physicians in spare hours, and since the patrons of studies who preside over stipends at Zürich, seeing me run eagerly to it, urged me on, it seemed right to go to Montpellier, famous for medicine. When I had come there, having left Lausanne, and found no one among the more learned physicians who would receive me as a guest in his house (for I had hoped for more from private intercourse than from public lectures), I did not stay long; having become somewhat more skilled in anatomy and the history of plants, I returned to Germany, and having been honoured with the insignia of a physician at Basel, I came back to my homeland, where now, so far as I am able, I teach philosophy to young men." Thus Dr Gesner on the course of his studies.

units.la: Domum ergo reversus animum ad scribendum publicè appulit initio magis, quàm docendum. Doluit, sibi ob rem angustam domi multa effundenda citius fuisse, quàm bene formata edenda. Quæ tamen ingenua potius, quàm necessaria erat Confessio. Extant verba in Bibliothecæ Editione prima: nobis properandum est ad lucubrationum ejus Catalogum, prout ipse nobis eum reliquit.
units.tr: Returning home, therefore, he turned his mind to writing for the public, at first more than to teaching. He regretted that, because of his narrow circumstances at home, many things had been poured out more quickly than they were well formed and published. Yet this was a frank confession rather than a necessary one. The words stand in the first edition of the Bibliotheca: we must now hasten to his catalogue of works, as he himself left it to us.

units.la: Primum igitur circa annum D. 1537. (ita ipse Gesnerus) Lexicon Græcolatinum, quod jam ante à diversis & innominatis nescio quibus miserè satis confarcinatum erat, ex Phauorini Camertis Lexico Græco ita auxi, ut nihil in eo extaret, quod non ut singulari fide ac diligentia, ita labore maximo adjicerem: sed Typographus me inscio, & præter omnem expectationem meam, exiguam duntaxat accesionis meæ partem adjecit, reservans sibi forte auctuarium ad sequentes etiam editiones. Eodem paulo post defuncto, meum exemplar recuperare non potui. Ab eo etiam tempore in gratiam Henrici Petri, Basilien&is Typographi, ter aut quater ex diversis lectionibus meis, idem volumen insigni accessione auxi, ita ut semper nominarem authores, à quibus singula excepissem, ut & authoritas major esset, & Orthographia, minus corrumperetur: quod si alij etiam multi Lexicorum corruptores potius quam authores observàssent, non usque adeò aliquot millibus locorum corrupta hæc volumina hactenus in publicum prodijssent, non solùm Typographicis erratis passim innumeris absurdissimè referta, propter imperitiam illorum, qui ad præla corrigunt: sed ipsorum etiam authorum, quorum plurimos idcirco nomina sua profiteri puduit. Ultima quidem editio à me locupletata Basileæ nuper prodijt, ex officina Hieronymi Curionis anno D. 1560. Septembri, in folio, chartis trecentis octoginta quatuor. Cæterùm, hoc anno, quo hæc scribo 1562. Genevæ prodijsse audio longè copiosissimum emendatissimúmque Græcæ linguæ Thesaurum, à Rob. Constantino, incomparabilis doctrinæ viro, ex Ioan. Crispini officina. Medicaminum su ciduorum (quæ ἀντιβαλλόμενα Græci vocant) Galeno ad scriptorum tabula Latinitate donata, adjectis etiam Græcis multò castigatioribus, & annotationibus in quosdam locos. Eadem ex libris Dioscoridis, Ætij, & Pauli Æginetæ passim excerpta, & in unum diligenter conscripta subjecimus. Chartæ sunt quinque cum dimidia, excusæ Basileæ in octavo cum Actuarij opere de compositione medicamentorum, apud Robertum VVinter, anno D. 1540. Enchiridion historiæ plantarum, ordine alphabetico, ex Dioscoride sumtis descriptionibus, & multis ex Theophrasto, Plinio ac recentioribus Græcis additis: facultatibus autem ex Paulo Ægineta plerunque quàm brevissimè adscriptis, &c. in gratiam Medicinæ candidatorum, qui cognitionis stirpium causà rusticari interdum solent; Robertus VVinter imprimebat in 8. Basileæ anno 1541. Chartis novendecim, & eodem anno Melchior Sessa, Venetijs in 16. Huic similem alium de cæteris simplicibus medicamentis libellum nondum edidi. Compendium ex Actuarij Zachariæ libris, de differentijs urinarum, judicijs, causis & prævidentijs. Universalis doctrina Galeni Pergameni de compositione pharmacorum, secundum locos affectos à capite ad calcem, particularibus medicamentis omissis. Symbola Galeni experimentorum ex lib. ejus collecta, & aliorum quorundam. Hôsce tres libros, Christophorus Froschoverus Tigurinus Typographus uno volumine conjunxit. Tiguri 1541. in 8. Chartis 24. Apparatus & delectus simplicium medicamentorum, ex Dioscoride & Mesuæo præcipuè, Alphabeti ordine, pharmacopolis maximè utilis liber.
units.tr: First, then, about the year 1537 (so Gesner himself): "I enlarged the Greek-Latin Lexicon, which had already been wretchedly patched together by various unnamed persons, from the Greek Lexicon of Phavorinus of Camerino, so that nothing remained in it that I did not add with singular fidelity and diligence, and with the greatest labour. But the printer, without my knowledge and beyond all my expectation, added only a small part of my addition, perhaps reserving the supplement for later editions as well. When the printer soon afterwards died, I could not recover my copy. From that time also, for the sake of Henricus Petrus, printer of Basel, I enlarged the same volume three or four times with a remarkable addition from my various readings, always naming the authors from whom I had taken each item, so that the authority would be greater and the spelling less corrupted. If many other corrupters of lexica had observed this, rather than authors, these volumes would not have been published so corrupted, in some thousands of places, until now, filled not only with countless typographical errors, absurdly scattered throughout, through the ignorance of those who correct at the press, but also with errors of the authors themselves, many of whom were ashamed to profess their names. The latest edition, enriched by me, came out recently at Basel from the workshop of Hieronymus Curio, in the year 1560, in September, in folio, with three hundred and eighty-four sheets. Moreover, this year in which I write, 1562, I hear that a far fuller and more correct Thesaurus of the Greek language has appeared at Geneva, by Robert Constantine, a man of incomparable learning, from the workshop of John Crispin. Of the medicines that are called 'counterpoised' by the Greeks, from Galen, arranged in tables, translated into Latin, with the Greek texts added, much more correct, and with notes on certain passages. Likewise I have added things excerpted here and there from the books of Dioscorides, Aëtius, and Paul of Aegina, diligently written together in one place. The sheets are five and a half, printed at Basel in octavo, with the work of Actuarius on the composition of medicines, by Robert Winter, in the year 1540. A Handbook of the History of Plants, in alphabetical order, with descriptions taken from Dioscorides, and many additions from Theophrastus, Pliny and recent Greeks, with the faculties mostly added from Paul of Aegina as briefly as possible, etc., for the benefit of candidates in medicine, who sometimes go into the country for the sake of knowing plants: Robert Winter printed it in octavo at Basel in 1541, in nineteen sheets; and in the same year Melchior Sessa printed it at Venice in sixteen. I have not yet published another similar little book on the other simple medicines. A Compendium from the books of Zacharias Actuarius, on the differences of urines, judgments, causes and prognoses. The Universal Teaching of Galen of Pergamum on the composition of drugs, according to the affected parts from head to foot, with particular medicines omitted. Symbols of Galen, the experiments collected from his books, and of certain others. Christophorus Froschover, Zürich printer, joined these three books in one volume; Zürich, 1541, in octavo, twenty-four sheets. Apparatus and selection of simple medicines, chiefly from Dioscorides and Mesue, in alphabetical order, a book most useful to apothecaries." The same volume contains also the universal precepts of Paul of Aegina on the composition of medicines according to kinds, and all that is found in the books of Galen on the composition of medicines according to kinds, with many things said superfluously and most particular compositions removed, etc.; the brothers Frellon printed it.

units.la: Continentur autem eodem volumine universalia Pauli Æginetæ præcepta, de medicamentorum, secundum genera, compositione: & ejusdem argumenti, omnia quæ in libris Galeni de compositione med. κατὰ γένη præcepta extant: multis superfluè dictis, & articularibus plerisque compositionibus, remotis &c: Frellonij fratres excudebant Lugduni 1542. in 8. Chartis 18 & dimid. & Venetijs fratres de Nicolinis in 16. Catalogus plantarum nomina, Latinè, Græcè, Germanicè & Gallicè e regione proponens, secundum ordinem Alphabethi, Latinis præeuntibus, una cum vulgaribus pharmacopolarum nomenclaturis &c. His accedunt in calce operis Nomenclatura stirpum secundum varias gentes, Dioscoridi adscriptæ, in ordinem literarum digestæ. Liber impressus est Tiguri apud Froschou. 1542. in 4, chartis 4. & dimidio. De syllogismis compendium, authoris incerti e Græco translatum, excusum, Basileæ in 8. Chartis duabus & dimid. apud Oporin. cum Ioachim Perionij lucubrationibus quibusdam in ganum Aristotelis: 1542. Moralis interpretatio errorum Vlysis Homerici, authoris incerti. Commentatio Porphyrij Philosophi de Nympharum antro in 1 libro Odysseæ Homericæ, Apologiæ quædam pro Homero & arte poetica, fabularumque aliquot enarrationes, ex commentarijs Procli Lucij, Diadochi, Philosophi Platonici in lib. Platonis de Republica: in quibus plurimæ de Diis fabulæ, non juxta Grammaticorum vulgus, historicè, physicè autem thicè tractantur; sed Theologicis, (ut Gentiles loquuntur) exprima Philosophia rationibus explanantur, omnia per nos è Græco sermone conversa, & evulgata Tiguri 1542. in 8. chartis 12. ex officina Frosckoueriana. Porphyrij philosophi quæstiones Homericæ, Pauli Selenciarij hemiambia, dethermis, & alia quædam ex Græcis eodem tempore, aut etiam posteà à me conversa, nondum in lucem exiverunt. De Latte & operibus lactariis libellus, philologus pariter ac Medicus, cum Epistola ad Iacobum Avienum Glaronensem, de montium admiratione, excusus Tiguri 1543. in 8. chartis 6. & dimid. Ian. Stobæi collectanea sive loci communes CXXIII. ex genere authorum vetustissimorum Græcorum, CL. redacti, ex nostra interpretatione Latina &c. His accesserunt opuscula tria, à nobis etiam primùm Latinè edita: nempe Cyri Theodori Dialogus de amicitiæ exilio, Senarijs Iambicis. Opuscula duo Platoni adscripta, unum de justo, alterum, an virtus doceri possit. Omnia Græcè & Latinè, è regione Tiguri apud Frosckoueram cum duplici indice, uno rerum, altero authorum, anno D. 1543. infolio, chartis 210. & iterum Stobæi locis, cum ex manuscriptis exemplaribus, tum aliunde, auctis atque recognitis anno 1550. & tertio 1559. Eosdem locos Oporinus Basileæ edidit Germanicè, Ge Læto interprete. Audio & Antuerpiæ Latina nostra seorsim excusa esse, absque Græcis. Nova editio valde aucta parata prælo apud me est. Heraclidis Ponticj allegoriæ in Homeri fabulas de dijs, & sermo Dionis de Homero Latini facti, excusi Basileæ apud Ioan. Oporinum, adjectis etiam eisdem Græcis, ex aliis quibusdam raris ac elegantibus opusculis,
units.tr: The same volume contains the universal precepts of Paul of Aegina on the composition of medicines according to their kinds, and all the precepts on the same subject found in Galen's books On the Composition of Medicines according to Genera [κατὰ γένη], with many superfluous points omitted and most of the particular compositions removed, etc. The brothers Frellonius printed it at Lyon in 1542, octavo, 18 and a half sheets; and the brothers de Nicolinis at Venice, in sixteenmo. A Catalogue of plants giving their names in Latin, Greek, German and French, arranged alphabetically with the Latin names first, together with the common names used by apothecaries, etc. At the end of the work are added a Nomenclature of herbs according to the various peoples cited by Dioscorides, arranged in alphabetical order. The book was printed at Zurich by Froschauer, 1542, quarto, 4 and a half sheets. A short treatise On syllogisms, of unknown authorship, translated from the Greek, printed at Basel in octavo, two and a half sheets, by Oporinus, with certain lucubrations of Joachim Périon on the Organon of Aristotle, 1542. A Moral interpretation of the errors of Homer's Ulysses, by an unknown author. The Commentary of Porphyry the philosopher On the Cave of the Nymphs in the first book of Homer's Odyssey; some Defences of Homer and of poetic art, and several explanations of fables, drawn from the commentaries of Proclus the Lycian, and Diadochus, the Platonic philosopher, on Plato's Republic. In these many fables about the gods, which the crowd of grammarians does not treat as they should, are handled historically and physically, but are explained by theological reasons (as the Gentiles put it) of exalted philosophy. All of them have been translated by me from Greek and published at Zurich in 1542, octavo, 12 sheets, from the workshop of Froschauer. The Homeric Questions of Porphyry the philosopher, the Hemiambics of Paul the Silentiary, On Thermae, and certain other works from the Greek of the same period, or translated by me afterwards, have not yet come to light. A little book On Milk and Dairy Products, philological as well as medical, with an Epistle to Jacob Avienus of Glarus On the Wonder of Mountains, was published at Zurich in 1543, octavo, 6 and a half sheets. The Anthology of John Stobaeus, or common-place passages, 123 chapters drawn from the most ancient Greek authors, reduced to 150, from my Latin translation, etc. To these were added three short works, which I also first published in Latin: namely, the Dialogue on the Exile of Friendship by Cyrus Theodorus, in iambic senarii; and two short works ascribed to Plato, one On the Just, the other on whether virtue can be taught. All in Greek and Latin, printed opposite one another at Zurich by Froschauer, with a double index, one of things and one of authors, in the year of our Lord 1543, folio, 210 sheets. And again the Stobaeus passages, enlarged and revised both from manuscript copies and from other sources, in 1550, and a third time in 1559. Oporinus at Basel has published the same passages in German, with Gelaius as translator. I hear that our Latin version has also been printed separately at Antwerp, without the Greek. A new and greatly enlarged edition is ready for the press in my hands. The Allegories of Heraclides of Pontus on the fables of Homer about the gods, and the Discourse of Dio on Homer, rendered into Latin and printed at Basel by John Oporinus, with the same Greek texts added, together with certain other rare and elegant little works,

units.la: 1542. 7. 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. 13. 1543. 14. 15. sculis, anno D. 1544. in 8. chartis 14 & semef. Michaelis Ephesij Scholia in Aristotelis libellos, nempe De juventute & senectute, vita & morte. De longitudine & brevitate vitae. De divinatione per somnum. Omnia è Graeco translata, & impressa Basileae in 8. anno D. 1541. Chartis 6. & dimid. cum Nicolai Leonici explanatione in primum librum Aristotelis, de partibus animalium, apud Wechelum & Venetiis anno 1543. in folio, cum Alexandri Aphrodis. Commentariis in librum Aristotelis de sensibus, Lucilio Philaltheo interprete.
units.tr: 1542. 7. 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. 13. 1543. 14. 15. little works, in the year of our Lord 1544, octavo, 14 and a half sheets. The Scholia of Michael of Ephesus on Aristotle's little books: On Youth and Old Age, on Life and Death, on Length and Brevity of Life, and On Divination in Sleep. All translated from the Greek and printed at Basel in octavo in the year of our Lord 1541, 6 and a half sheets; with the explanation of Nicolaus Leonicus on the first book of Aristotle's On the Parts of Animals, at Wechel's, and at Venice in 1543, folio; with the Commentaries of Alexander of Aphrodisias on Aristotle's book On the Senses, translated by Lucilius Philalthaeus.

units.la: M.V. Martialis Poetae epigrammata (ad Linguae Latinae copiam & varias rerum nomenclaturas utilissima) ab omni verborum obscoenitate, in adolescentium praecipue Scholarumque usum, expurgati, & in locos circiter 86. digesti. His adjeci Dialogos tres, quibus ratio hujus instituti redditur, & multa de puerilibus studiis commemorantur. Et in fine annotationes Iac. Mycilli, Froschouerus cudebat Tiguri 1544. in 8. chartis 28. Ambrosij Calepini Dictionarium Linguae Latinae, quod anno 1544. mense Septembri impressum est Basileae apud Leonhardum Hospinianum, innumeris locis castigavimus: & ex postrema editione Venetiis publicata, ad insigne Sirenis, quae supra quatuor millia vocabulorum accessisse gloriatur, ex probatissimis authoribus, omnia in nostrum exemplar transtulimus; & Prosodiae, id est, quantitatis syllabarum notas (plerunque etiam versus Poetarum, quibus ea confirmetur) novo labore singulis dictionibus, quae ordine alphabeti explicantur, inscripsimus. Caeterum nomina propria, ex quibus maxima pars Venetae accessionis constabat, seorsim a Latinis vocabulis in peculiare alphabetum, partim proprio labore, partim juvantibus amicis, digesta sunt, additis omnibus illis, quae in postremis dictionarijs Poeticis continebantur. Huic volumini titulum fecimus, Onomasticon nominum propriorum; quod tertio jam auctum &c. emendatum a nobis prodijt, Basileae, ex Hieronymi Curionis officina. In secunda quidem editione, quaecunque Stephanus Regius Grammaticus Graecus, propria locorum nomina habebat, Latinè interpretatus adjeci, & loca castigavi innumera. Graeca etiam nomina passim addita sunt. Ultima editio publicata est Basileae, anno, 1560. in folio; sunt autem Latinarum dictionum chartae 312. cùm aliàs, tum ex Pauli Manutij observationibus plurimùm auctae. Onomasticici verò nostri privatim chartae 61. in Lexicon Graeco Latinum anno 1544. Basileae excusum in 4. de utilitate ac dignitate Linguae Graecae praefati sumus. Antonij Tilesij, Itali, Confentini opuscula aliquot, partim jam prius diversis in locis, partim nunquam prius edita, tum styli Romanâ puritate, tum editione, varietate & lepore argumentorum, magno studiosorum applausu, excipienda, Ioan. Oporino Basilienfi Typographo dedi: quiea publicavit anno 1545. in 8. chartis 11. Ex his ligato sermone conditus est Imber aureus Tragoedia; & poemata 7. soluto autem, Commentarij duo, unus de coloribus, alter de coronarum generibus. Ab eo quidem tempore etiam alia quaedam huius authoris poemata in Italia typis impressa, nactus sum.
units.tr: The Epigrams of the poet M. Valerius Martialis, most useful for the copia of the Latin language and for the various names of things, purged of all obscenity of words, chiefly for the use of young people and schools, and arranged under about 86 headings. To these I have added three dialogues, which explain the purpose of this undertaking and recall many things about boyish studies; and at the end, notes by Jacob Micyllus. Froschauer printed it at Zurich in 1544, octavo, 28 sheets. The Latin Dictionary of Ambrose Calepinus, which was printed at Basel by Leonhard Hospinianus in September 1544, we have corrected in innumerable places; and from the latest edition published at Venice, at the sign of the Siren, which boasts of having added more than four thousand words drawn from the most approved authors, we have transferred everything into our copy; and by fresh labour we have marked the prosody of each word, that is, the notes of the quantity of syllables (often also with verses of the poets to confirm them), against each entry explained in alphabetical order. Moreover, the proper names, of which the greater part of the Venetian addition consisted, have been arranged separately from the Latin words in a special alphabet, partly by my own labour, partly with the help of friends, with all those things added that were contained in the latest poetic dictionaries. We gave this volume the title Onomasticon of Proper Names; it has come out a third time, enlarged, etc., and corrected by us, at Basel, from the workshop of Jerome Curio. In the second edition I added in Latin whatever proper names of places Stephanus Regius, the Greek grammarian, had, and corrected innumerable passages. Greek names too have been added here and there. The last edition was published at Basel in 1560, folio; it has 312 sheets of Latin words, greatly enlarged both otherwise and from the observations of Paul Manutius. Our own Onomasticon separately has 61 sheets. I have prefaced with a treatise on the usefulness and dignity of the Greek language the Greek-Latin Lexicon printed at Basel in 1544, quarto. I gave to Johann Oporinus, the Basel printer, some short works of Antonius Telesius, an Italian of Cosenza, partly previously published in various places, partly never before published, which deserve to be welcomed by students with great applause, both for the Roman purity of style and for the variety and charm of their subjects. He published them in 1545, octavo, 11 sheets. Of these, in bound verse, there is the tragedy The Golden Rain; and seven poems in free verse, and two commentaries, one on colours, the other on kinds of garlands. Since that time I have also obtained certain other poems of this author printed in Italy.

units.la: 1544. 16. 17. 18. 19. sum: quæ cum præcedentibus conjuncta denuò excudi optârim, ut tam elegantis scriptoris, quæ extant omnia, uno volumine haberentur. Bibliotheca universalis, sive Catalogus omnium scriptorum locupletissimus, in tribus linguis, Latina, Græca & Hebraica: extantium, & non extantium: veterum & recentiorum, usque ad annum Domini 1565. doctorum & indoctorum, excusorum & in Bibliothecis latentium; Opus novum, & non Bibliothecis tantum publicis, privatisq; instituendu necessarium, sed studiosis omnibus cujuscunq; artis aut scientiæ, ad studia melius formanda utilissimum. Tig. apud Froschouerum 1545. in sol.: chartis 325 adjecto ad finem indice nominum universorum, ut ea, quorum præNomina forte Lector ignorat, invenire posset: Non solum autem singula authorum scripta hoc volumine enumerantur: sed singulorum etiam librorum argumenta sæpius adscribuntur, sive ex ipsorum authorum præfationibus, ut simul etiam styli aliquod specimen præbeatur Lectori, sive aliter; & super multis Censuræ doctorum hominum, & alia quædam, quæ in compendijs postea excusis, non meo quidem consilio omissa sunt: poterant enim breviùs quidem exponi; non tamen prorsus omitti. Sed suum plerunque lucrum spectant Typographi, potiùs quàm vel authorum voluntatem, vel utilitatem Lectorum solidam. In compendium quidem illis postea impresis, permulta authorum nomina nova, recentiora præsertim, acceperunt: sed omnis illa accesio etiam seorsim à Froschouero nostro excusa est, ut qui primam editionem emerunt, aut deinceps etiam emturi sunt, fructu illo non frustrentur.
units.tr: Which I would wish to be printed again together with the preceding, so that the works of so elegant a writer, all that survive, might be had in one volume. The Universal Library, or the most complete catalogue of all writers, in three languages, Latin, Greek and Hebrew: extant and non-extant, ancient and recent, up to the year of the Lord 1565, learned and unlearned, printed and lying hidden in libraries; a new work, and not only necessary to be set up in public and private libraries, but most useful to all students of any art or science for shaping their studies better. Zurich, by Froschauer, 1545, folio, 325 sheets, with an index of all names added at the end, so that the reader might find those whose names he perhaps does not know. Not only are the individual writings of authors listed in this volume, but the arguments of individual books are often ascribed to them, either from the authors' own prefaces, so that a specimen of their style may also be offered to the reader, or otherwise; and on many works there are judgments of learned men, and certain other things, which, in the epitomes printed afterwards, were omitted, not indeed by my design: for they could have been set out more briefly, but not wholly omitted. But printers for the most part look to their own profit, rather than either the wishes of authors or the solid usefulness of readers. In the epitomes printed afterwards, they acquired many new names of authors, more recent ones especially; but all that addition was also printed separately by our Froschauer, so that those who bought the first edition, or will buy afterwards, may not be deprived of that advantage.

units.la: Sententiarum sive capitum Theologicorum, præcipuè ex sacris & prophanis libris Græcis collectorum digestorúmque in locos communes, per Antonium & Maximum Monachos, Tomi tres. Antonij loci, Melissa scripti, inque duos Tomos divisi, numero sunt 175. in Maximi verò 71. uno Tomo comprehensi. Abbæ Maximi, Philosophi, confessoris & Martyris aphorismorum seu capitum de perfecta charitate & aliis virtutibus Christianis, centuriæ quatuor, Theophili, sexti Antiochensis Episcopi, de Deo & fide Christianorum, contra gentes institutionum libri tres ad Autolycum. Tatiani Assyrij, Iustini Martyris discipuli, Oratio contra Græcos. Hæc omnia quinque diversorum authorum volumina meâ curâ ex codicibus manuscriptis, & meo labore emendata, ante transcripta & ad præsum (præter Maximi centurias prius excusas, nunc quidem castigatiores) Froschouerus Græcè excudit Tiguri 1546. in sol. chartis 73. Et rursus eadem omnia in Latinum sermonem conversa, eodem anno in sol. chartis 99. Ex his primam partem Melissæ Antonij ego interpretatus sum; & Tatiani orationem, cui & annotationes adjeci. Secundam verò Melissæ partem, & Maximi locos Iohannes Ribittus, Sabaudus, Latina fecit. Maximi Centurias, Vincentius Obsopoeus; Theophili institutiones, Conradus Clauserus. Enumeratio medicamentorum purgantium, vomitoriorum, & alvum bonam facientium, ordine alphabeti, excusa in 4. Basileæ in officina Frobeniana, anno Domini 1546. cum Antonij Musæ libello de catapotijs. Naturalis scientiæ totius compendium, ex Aristotelis aliisque libris ab Hermolao Barbaro, Patricio Veneto, confectum, & in Italia impressum mendosissimè, quoad ejus potui, repurgatum Oporino tradidi, è cujus officina prodijt, chartis octo in 8. anno 1548, quibus ille adjecit Hieronymi Vildenbergij. Auri montani, in plerosque Aristotelis Physicorum libros epitomen, chartis 11. Pandectarum sive partitionum universalium, qui secundus Tomus Bibliothecæ nostræ est, libri 19. excusi Tiguri apud Frosch oueru m, in sol. 1548. chartis 191. In his libris omnium, qui in primo Bibliothecæ Tomo nominantur, authorum, & plurimorum insuper aliorum scripta, non alphabetico ordine, ut in primo Tomo, sed secundum artium & scientiarum genera per certas classes & locos communes annumerantur, non titulis modo librorum commemoratis, sed capitum etiam inscriptionibus, & particularibus, plurimorum librorum argumentis. Librorum inscriptiones hæ sunt. 1. De Grammatica & Philologia. 2. De Dialectica. 3. De Rhetorica. 4. De Poetica. 5. De Arithmetica. 6. De Geometria, Optices & Catoptrices 7. De Musica. 8. De Astronomia 9. De Astrologia. 10. De divinatione tum licita, tum illicita & magia. 11. De Geographia. 12. De historiis. 13. De diversis artibus illiteratis. 14. De naturali philosophia & Theologia Gentium. 15. De prima philosophia seu Metaphysicis. 16. De morali philosophia. 17. De Oeconomica philosophia. 18. De re politica, id est, civili & militari. 19. De jurisprudentia. His liber vicesimus subjungendus erat, de re medica, quem certas ob causas reliqui, & ne hactenus quidem absolvi, quamvis materia satis copiosa mihi sit congesta. Pandectarum hoc est, Secundi Tomi Bibliothecæ liber 21. sive ultimus, De Theologia christiana, seorsim cujus ibidem infol. 1549. chartis 90. Est autem liber veluti index per locos digestus, in plerosque veterum & recentiorum Theologorum libros, hoc est, librorum titulos & capita fere, &c. Ex chartis 90 quibus constat, postremæ septem continent indicem Alphabeticum, huic de Theologia libro & superioribus 19. communem. Cl. Galeni librorum editioni Latinæ, quæ est publicata Basileæ in officina Frobeniana ex Iani Cornarij recognitione, anno 1549. capitum distinctionem & argumenta in plerosque libros, ab initijs singulorum, adjeci: quæ in multis (ijs præsertim, qui rei Medicæ tyronibus præcipuè necessarij lectu sunt) ita copiosè ac methodicè tractantur, ut vel Epitomes aphoristicæ instar haberi possint. Historiæ animalium liber 1. qui est de quadrupedibus viviparis, cum figuris ad vivum expressis, opus Philosophis, Medicis, Grammaticis, Philologis, Poëtis, & omnibus rerum, linguarumque variarum studiosis, utilissimum simul, jucundissimumque futurum: in quo non modò simplex animalium historia continetur, sed etiam veluti commentarij locupletissimi, & castigationes plurimæ in veterum ac recentiorum ejusdem argumenti, quæ videre nobis licuit omnia, ex authoribus ferè ducentis quinquaginta &c. ita digestis, commodo perpetuoque ordine omnibus,ut quicquid de uno quoque animali cognoscere libuerit, nullo negotio statim inveniatur. Neque enim ad continuam lectionem à nobis hæc condita sunt, sed ut eorum qui Dictionariorum esse solet,ad inquirendum maximè,usus fit: quod non intellexerunt, qui prolixitatis in hoc opere nos accusárunt. In sequentibus quidem animalium libris, minùs prolixus fui, hoc est, in Philologia parcior. Hoc volumen in Epitomen contraxit, philologiâ omni omissâ, excellens doctrina & virtute Medicus Laurentius Hiel, in illustri Academia Ienensi hoc tempore Professor : idem forte facturus in reliquis etiam nostris de animalibus libris, ut aliquando conjuncti publicentur. In Germanicum verò sermonem simili compendio transtulit hunc & secundum, de quadrupedibus oviparis, Conradus Forer Vitoduranus Medicus, nunc etiam Ecclesiæ Minister, & similiter de aquatilibus volumen. Avium verò historiam Germanicam fecit Rod. Huslinus, quæ jam excusa est, anno 1548. chartis 87. Thesaurus Euonymi philiatri de remedijs secretis (voco autem secreta in quibus pars purior & tenuior,ab impuriore crasioreque secernitur) liber physicus, medicus & partim etiam Chymicus, & oeconomicus in vinorum diversi saporis apparatu. Medicis & Pharmacopolis omnibus præcipuè necessarius, impressus Tiguri apud Andream Gessnerum Fin 8. chartis 38. anno 1558. Agit autem præcipuè de artificiosis aquarum & oleorum destillationibus,sive extractionibus,ex herbis aliisque simplicibus medicamentis. Secunda ejus editio prodiit anno 1558. adjectis quibusdam instrumentorum destillatoriorum figuris, & novo Iacobi Bessoni libello, de absoluta ratione extrahendi olea & aquas è medicamentis simplicibus. Hunc librum cum in gratiam Andreæ Gessneri patruelis mei, novitum Typographi, immaturum ederem, nomen meum addere nolui. Nunc quoniam & magno studiosorum rei medicæ applausu eum exceptum video, & aliquando absolutiorem dare cogito, si Deus vitam dederit: me ejus authorem esse dissimulare amplius nolui, præsertim cum jam viri quidam eruditi id deprehenderint. Ex eadem officina Germanicus etiam evulgatus est, Rodolpho Landebergero nostro (Ecclesiæ Bulaci Diacono, in agro Tigurino) interprete. Et Latinè in 16. Lugduni: ibidémque, nî fallor, Gallicè. Veterum aliquot Theologorum Græcorum Orthodoxorum libri Græci, & ijdem Latinitate donati eregi ne: quorum plerique partim Latinè, partim Græcè antehac non sunt editi, nostrâ plerique curâ excusi,Tiguri apud Andream patruelem anno 1552. in sol. chartis 104 Sunt autem hi, Canones Apostolorum, & veterum tredecim sanctorum Conciliorum decreta, à Clemente Romano, ut quidam putant, versi & collecti. Ignatij Martyris, & Archiepiscopi Antiocheni Epistolæ 12. Ioanne Brunnero Tigurino interprete. Athenagoræ Atheniensis Philosophi Christiani Apologia, vel vel legatio pro Christianis, ex nostra interpretatione, cum annotationibus nostris. Ejusdem de mortuorum resurrectione liber, Petro Nannio interprete, cum Hen. Stephani Typographi doctissimi (qui hos duos Athenagoræ libellos seorsim prius excudit Genevæ) in Græcum simul contextum, & Nannij versionem Annotationibus. Æneæ Gazæi Platonici Theophrastus, sive de animarum immortalitate & corporum resurrectione Dialogus, Ioan: Wolphio Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ ministro, interprete. Cidonij de contemnenda morte oratio, Raphaele Seilero I.C. Augustano interprete. Hermeæ Philosophi irrisio Gentilium Philosophorum, eodem interprete. Expositio capitum admonitoriorum Agapeti, Diaconi, ad Iustinianum Imperatorem, innominato interprete. Ex his ego suppeditavi Æneæ Gazæi, Platonici Theophrastum ex nobili Bibliotheca Augustanæ Reip. nactus: & Ignatij Epistolas, quæ Lutetiæ paulo ante Græcè excusas ignorabam. In Hieronymi Tragi deStirpibus commentarios Argentinæ excusos apud Rihelium Anno 1552. præfationem adjeci in gratiam Typographi, quæ continet Catalogum rei herbariæ scriptorum, qui ad illud usque tempus aliquid ediderunt, extantium & non extantium, &c. satis copiosum, chartis 3. De thermis & fontibus Helvetiæ & Germaniæ libri duo, excusi Venetijs in officina Iuntarum anno 1553. in sol. chartis 5. cum quadrante, cum permultis aliorum libris, qui thermas Italiæ descripserunt. Ab eo autem tempore, quoniam plurima observavi, quibus hoc argumentum pleniùs illustrem, spero me brevi eundem librum auctum & recognitum seorsim editurum. Tabulæ collectionum, quibus per singulos anni menses, quæ stirpes in singulis per Germaniam flores fructúsque, ut plurimum proferant, ordine recensetur. Argentinæ à Rihelio impressæ 1553. in 8. chartis quinque cum quadrante, cum Davidis Kyberi, summi amici mei, herbariæ rei Lexico: quod dum sub prælo esset eodem anno, mense Ianuario, optimus & doctissimus vir peste sublatus obiit, mihi verò jam morti proximus quæ excudenda supererant, ut ante prælum inspicerem, atque emendarem commendari voluit &c. itaque & præfationem in illum librum, & in Authoris mortem Idyllium lugubre Græcum condidi. Icones animalium quad rupedum vivi parorum, & oviparorum, quæ primo & secundo Historiæ animalium libris à nobis describuntur, cum Nomenclaturis singulorum Latinis, Italicis, Gallicis & Germanicis, plerunque per certos ordines digestæ, Tiguri procudebat Froschouerus 1553. in sol. chartis 32. Ligari autem debent cum sequentibus animalium iconibus. Historiæ quadrupedum oviparorum liber, id est, secundus de animalibus, cum appendice ad quadrupedes viviparas, anno 1554. ibidem excusos in sol. chartis 37. Et quia parvus est, commodè uno volumine cum Historia avium, id est, tertio de animalibus libro ligabitur. Historiæ avium liber (qui est tertius de animalibus), cum figuris ex eadem officina anno 1555. chartis quatuor supra ducentas. In fine adduntur paralipomena. Icones avium omnium, quæ in nostra avium Historia describuntur, cum Nomenclaturis singularum in linguis diversis Europæ: Ibidem evulgatæ, anno 1555. in sol. chartis 32. Et rursus anno 1560. novis aliquot iconibus ac descriptoribus auctæ atque recognitæ, chartis 37. In eam editionem emendationes, & additiones aliquot conjeci ad finem iconum quadrupedum secundæ editionis. De Medicinæ chirurgicæ præstantia & antiquitate scriptum nostrum, & enumerationem alphabeticam virorum illustrium, qui rem chirurgicam, vel scriptis, vel artis usu excoluerunt, Gesneri fratres duo (Patrueles mei) Tiguri publicárunt, chartis septem & dimidia ferè, in volumine satis magno, quo diversos chirurgiæ scriptores, mea ferè cura complexi sunt. De raris & admirandis herbis, quæ sive quòd noctu luceant, sive alias ob causas, Lunariæ nominantur, Commentariolus: & obiter de alijs etiam rebus, quæ in tenebris lucent. Inferuntur & novæ quædam herbarum icones. De scriptio montis Fratti, sive Pilati vulgò dicti, juxta Lucernam in Helvetia: Patrueles mei imprimebant Tiguri anno 1555. in 4. una cum Iohan. du Choill. G. F. Lugdunensis Pilati montis in Gallia, descriptione, & Iohann. Rhellicani Idyllio, quo Stocchorum montem altissimum, in Bernensium Helvetiorum agro, versibus heroicis describit. Chartæ sunt omnium duodecim cum dimidia. Epitome Bibliothecæ nostræ tomi primi, à Conrado Lycosthene Rubeaquensi, edita primùm Basileæ, per Iofiam Simlerum, Tigurinum, recognita & auctâ, plusquam bis mille authorum accessione, excusa Tiguri apud Froschquerum in sol. 1555. chart: 105. Adeam quidem augendam nos quoque collectanea nostra contulimus &c. Hujus epitomes accessio. Appendix primi tomi futura, seorsim etiam impressa est, ut supra diximus. Rob. Constantinus Gallus, etiam Lutetiæ edidit Nomenclatorem scriptorum insignium, qui veluti epitome brevisima utilisimaque Bibliothecæ nostræ est; ubi optimos quosque Veteres & recentiores scriptores nominat, extantes) duntaxat manuscriptos vel impressos, secundum genera artium & scientiarum digesto libro &c. Eum Andreas VVechelus Parisijs excudit 1555. in 8. chartis 12. Mithridates, sive de differentijs linguarum, tum quæ hodie apud diversas nationes in toto orbe terrarum in usu sunt, observationes, typis Froschoueri excusæ Tiguri 1555. in 8. chartis 10. cum tabula, quæ orationem Dominicam in plurimis linguis scriptam proponit. Libelli 3. medicinales: Vnus de sanitate tuenda: Alter contra luxum conviviorum. Tertius, contra notas Astrologicas Ephemeridum de secandis venis. Sesqui charta, à Patruelibus impressi 1556. in 8. CL. Aeliani, Prænestini Pontificis & Sophistæ, qui Romæ sub Imperatore Antonio Pio vixit, Meliglofsus aut Meliphthongus ab orationis suavitate cognominatus, monumenta, quæ extant omnia Græcè, Latinèque è regione, curâ & operâ nostra in lucem edita. Sunt autem hæc De animalium natura lib. 17. ex Petri Gillij, Galli & nostra interpretatione, ad Græcos codices Manuscriptos recogniti, & tertia ferè parte ex ijsdem per nos auctì, Græ-
units.tr: Sentences, or chapters of theology, chiefly gathered from sacred and profane Greek books and arranged under common headings, by Antonius and Maximus the Monks, three volumes. Antonius's loci, written as the Melissa and divided into two volumes, number 175; Maximus's 71, contained in one volume. The aphorisms or chapters on perfect charity and other Christian virtues by Abbot Maximus, philosopher, confessor and martyr, in four centuries. Theophilus, sixth bishop of Antioch, three books of institutes on God and the faith of Christians, against the Gentiles, addressed to Autolycus. Tatian the Assyrian, disciple of Justin Martyr, an Oration against the Greeks. I have corrected all five of these volumes of different authors from manuscript codices by my own care and labour, and had them transcribed beforehand and prepared for the press. Froschauer printed them in Greek at Zurich in 1546, in folio, 73 leaves (apart from the centuries of Maximus, printed earlier and now more correctly). The same works were again translated into Latin and printed in folio, 99 leaves, in the same year. Of these I translated the first part of Antonius's Melissa and the oration of Tatian, to which I also added notes. The second part of the Melissa and the loci of Maximus were rendered into Latin by Johannes Ribittus of Savoy. The Centuries of Maximus were done by Vincentius Obsopoeus; the institutes of Theophilus by Conradus Clauserus. An Enumeration of purgative, emetic and laxative medicines, arranged in alphabetical order, was printed in quarto at Basel in the Frobenius workshop in 1546, together with Antonius Musa's little book on lozenges. I handed over to Oporinus an Compendium of all natural science, compiled by Hermolaus Barbarus, a Venetian patrician, from Aristotle and other books, printed in Italy very full of errors, which I cleansed as far as I could; it came from his workshop in eight leaves in octavo in 1548, to which he added Hieronymus Vildenbergius's epitome of most of the books of Aristotle's Physics by Auri Montanus, 11 leaves. The Pandects, or universal divisions, which is the second volume of our Library, 19 books, printed at Zurich at the Froschauer press, in folio, 1548, 191 leaves. In these books the writings of all the authors named in the first volume of the Library, and moreover of many others, are listed not in alphabetical order, as in the first volume, but according to the kinds of arts and sciences, by certain classes and common headings, with the titles of the books mentioned and also the headings of chapters and particular summaries of many books. The titles of the books are these: 1. On Grammar and Philology. 2. On Dialectic. 3. On Rhetoric. 4. On Poetry. 5. On Arithmetic. 6. On Geometry, Optics and Catoptrics. 7. On Music. 8. On Astronomy. 9. On Astrology. 10. On divination, both lawful and unlawful, and magic. 11. On Geography. 12. On histories. 13. On various unlettered arts. 14. On natural philosophy and the theology of the Gentiles. 15. On first philosophy, or Metaphysics. 16. On moral philosophy. 17. On economic philosophy. 18. On politics, that is, civil and military affairs. 19. On jurisprudence. A twentieth book on medicine was to be added to these, which I left out for certain reasons and have not yet finished, although I have gathered enough material for it. The twenty-first book, or last, of the Pandects, that is, of the second volume of the Library, is On Christian Theology, printed separately in folio at the same place in 1549, 90 leaves. This book is an index arranged by headings to most of the books of the ancient and recent theologians, that is, to the titles of the books and nearly to their chapters, etc. Of the 90 leaves of which it consists, the last seven contain an alphabetical index, common to this book on Theology and the nineteen preceding ones. To the Latin edition of the works of the illustrious Galen, published at Basel in the Frobenius workshop, revised by Janus Cornarius, in 1549, I added the division into chapters and summaries of most of the books, from their beginnings; these are treated so fully and methodically in many of them (especially those which are most necessary reading for beginners in medicine) that they may be regarded almost as aphoristic epitomes. The first book of the History of Animals, which concerns viviparous quadrupeds, with figures drawn from life, will be most useful and at the same time most pleasant to philosophers, physicians, grammarians, philologists, poets and all students of things and of various languages. It contains not only a plain natural history of animals but also, as it were, very rich commentaries and many corrections of the works of ancient and recent writers on the same subject, all of which I have been able to see, drawn from nearly two hundred and fifty authors, etc., arranged in such a convenient and permanent order that whatever one wishes to know about any single animal can be found at once without any trouble. For these things were not composed by us for continuous reading, but for consultation, as is usual with dictionaries: which those who accused us of prolixity in this work did not understand. In the following books on animals I was briefer, that is, more sparing in philology. The learned and virtuous physician Laurentius Hiel, at present professor at the famous Academy of Jena, reduced this volume to an epitome, omitting all philology; perhaps he will do the same with the rest of our books on animals, so that they may at some time be published together. The second book, on oviparous quadrupeds, was translated into German in a similar abridgement by Conradus Forer of Winterthur, physician, now also a minister of the Church, and likewise the volume on aquatic animals. The German history of birds was made by Rudolf Huslin, and was printed already in 1548, 87 leaves. The Thesaurus of Euonymus Philiater on secret remedies (I call those things secret in which the purer and finer part is separated from the grosser and impurer) is a book of physics, medicine, partly also chemistry, and of household management in the preparation of wines of various flavours. Most necessary to physicians and all apothecaries, it was printed at Zurich by Andreas Gesner, in octavo, 38 leaves, in 1558. It deals chiefly with the artificial distillations, or extractions, of waters and oils from herbs and other simple medicines. A second edition of it came out in 1558, with added figures of distilling instruments and a new little book by Jacques Besson on the complete method of extracting oils and waters from simple medicines. When I published this book too early, at the request of Andreas Gesner, my cousin, and the printer's novice, I did not want to add my name. Now, since I see that it has been received with great applause from students of medicine, and since I intend, if God grants me life, to give it some day in a more complete form, I have not wished to hide any longer that I am its author, especially since certain learned men have already discovered it. A German version was also published from the same workshop, translated by our Rudolf Landsberger (deacon of Bülach, in the Zurich countryside). And a Latin edition in sixteenmo at Lyon, and there too, unless I am mistaken, a French one. Some books in Greek of several orthodox Greek theologians of old, and the same given a Latin dress: most of which had not previously been published, partly in Latin, partly in Greek, most of them printed by our care at Zurich at the house of our cousin Andreas in 1552, in folio, 104 leaves. These are the Canons of the Apostles and the decrees of the thirteen holy councils of the ancients, translated and collected, as some think, by Clement of Rome. Twelve Epistles of Ignatius, martyr and archbishop of Antioch, translated by Johannes Brunner of Zurich. The Apology, or Plea for the Christians, of Athenagoras the Athenian Christian philosopher, from our translation, with our notes. The same author's book on the resurrection of the dead, translated by Petrus Nannius, together with the Greek text of the very learned printer Henri Estienne (who first printed these two little books of Athenagoras separately at Geneva), and Nannius's version with notes. The Theophrastus of Aeneas of Gaza, a Platonist, or a dialogue on the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies, translated by Johannes Wolf, minister of the Church of Zurich. The oration of Cydonius on despising death, translated by Raphael Seiler, jurist of Augsburg. The Mockery of the Gentile philosophers by Hermias the philosopher, with the same translator. The Exposition of the admonitory chapters of Agapetus, deacon, to the Emperor Justinian, by an unnamed translator. Of these I supplied the Theophrastus of Aeneas of Gaza, the Platonist, which I obtained from the noble library of the Free City of Augsburg, and the Epistles of Ignatius, which I did not know had been printed in Greek shortly before at Paris. For the commentaries of Hieronymus Tragus on plants, printed at Strasbourg by Rihel in 1552, I added, for the printer's sake, a preface containing a fairly full catalogue of the writers on herbal matters who had published anything up to that time, both extant and lost, etc., 3 leaves. Two books on the hot springs and fountains of Switzerland and Germany, printed at Venice in the Giunta workshop in 1553, in folio, 5 leaves, with a quadrant, together with many other books by those who described the hot springs of Italy. Since that time, however, because I have observed very many things by which I can illustrate this subject more fully, I hope that I shall soon publish this same book separately, enlarged and revised. The tables of collections, in which the plants that usually bloom and bear fruit in each month of the year throughout Germany are listed in order, printed at Strasbourg by Rihel in 1553, in octavo, five leaves with a quadrant, together with the botanical lexicon of David Kyber, my very dear friend. While it was in the press that same year, in January, that excellent and most learned man was carried off by the plague, and as he was himself close to death he wished to commend to me what remained to be printed, so that I might look over it before it went to press and correct it. Therefore I wrote both the preface to that book and a mournful Greek idyll on the author's death. The pictures of the viviparous and oviparous quadrupeds, which are described by us in the first and second books of the History of Animals, together with Latin, Italian, French and German names for each animal, arranged for the most part in fixed order, were printed by Froschauer at Zurich in 1553, in folio, 32 leaves. They ought to be bound together with the following pictures of animals. The book of the History of Oviparous Quadrupeds, that is, the second book on animals, with an appendix on viviparous quadrupeds, printed at the same place in 1554, in folio, 37 leaves. And since it is small, it will conveniently be bound in one volume with the History of Birds, that is, the third book on animals. The book of the History of Birds (which is the third book on animals), with figures from the same workshop, 1555, more than four hundred leaves. Supplements are added at the end. The pictures of all the birds described in our History of Birds, with the names of each in the various languages of Europe, published at the same place in 1555, in folio, 32 leaves; and again in 1560, enlarged and revised with some new pictures and descriptions, 37 leaves. To that edition I added some corrections and additions at the end of the pictures of the quadrupeds of the second edition. Our treatise On the excellence and antiquity of surgical medicine, and an alphabetical list of illustrious men who cultivated surgery either by their writings or by practice, were published at Zurich by my two cousins, the Gesner brothers, in about seven and a half leaves, in a fairly large volume, in which, largely through my care, they brought together various writers on surgery. A little commentary On the rare and wonderful herbs which are called Lunaria, whether because they shine at night or for other reasons, and incidentally on other things also which shine in the dark. Some new pictures of herbs are inserted. On the Mount Fratt, or as it is commonly called Pilatus, near Lucerne in Switzerland: my cousins printed at Zurich in 1555, in quarto, together with a description of Mount Pilatus in Gaul by Johannes du Choul of Lyon, and an idyll of Johannes Rhellicanus, in which he describes in heroic verse the very high Stockhorn mountain in the territory of the Bernese Swiss. There are twelve and a half leaves in all. An Epitome of our first volume of the Library, first published at Basel by Conrad Lycosthenes of Rappoltsweiler, revised and enlarged by Josias Simler of Zurich, with more than twice a thousand authors added, printed at Zurich by Froschauer in folio, 1555, 105 leaves. We also contributed our own collections to enlarge it, etc. An appendix to this epitome, which is to be an appendix to the first volume, was also printed separately, as I said above. Robert Constantin, a Frenchman, also published at Paris a Nomenclator of notable writers, which is a very brief and useful epitome of our Library, in which he names all the best ancient and recent writers, extant (whether only in manuscript or in print), arranged in a book according to the kinds of arts and sciences, etc. Andreas Wechel printed it at Paris in 1555, in octavo, 12 leaves. Mithridates, or observations on the differences of languages, both those now in use among the various nations of the whole world, printed at Zurich at the Froschauer press in 1555, in octavo, 10 leaves, with a table setting out the Lord's Prayer written in very many languages. Three little medical books: one on preserving health; another against the luxury of banquets; a third, against the astrological notes of almanacs, on letting blood. A sheet and a half, printed by our cousins in 1556, in octavo. Claudius Aelianus of Praeneste, bishop and sophist, who lived at Rome under the Emperor Antoninus Pius, surnamed Meliglossus or Meliphthongus from the sweetness of his speech; his works, all extant in Greek and Latin on facing pages, brought to light by our care and labour. These are his On the Nature of Animals, in 17 books, from the translation of Pierre Gilles of France and of ours, revised from Greek manuscript codices, and about a third part of it enlarged by us from the same, though Greek printed earlier, never before published.

units.la: cè cě quidem prius antehac non excusi. Variæ hist. lib. 14. Iusto Vultejo VVetterano interprete, nunc etiam recogniti. De militaribus ordinibus instituendis more Graecorum, lib. 1 à Fr. Robortello, Utinensi in Latinum sermonem versus, & ab eodem picturis, quàm plurimis illustratus, nunc denuò emendatior. Epistolæ rusticanæ, Sebastiano Guldenbeckio Tigurino interprete. Omnia Tiguri apud patrueles meos anno 1556 in sol. chartis 176. De piscibus & aquatilibus omnibus libelli 7. I. Halieuticon P. Ovidij Nasonis emendatum & Scholijs illustratum. II. Aquatilium animantium enumeratio juxta Plinium, emendata & explicata serie literarum. Eorundem Nomenclator Germanicus longè copiosissimus: Et alia quædam ad piscium Historiam pertinentia Andreas Gesnerus F. excudebat Tiguri. 1556. in 8. De stirpium aliquot nominibus veteribus ac novis, ut sunt Mamirâs, Moly, Oloconitis, Doronicum, Bulbocastanum, Granum alzelin, vel Habbaziz, & alia complura. Epistolæ duæ, una Melchioris Guilandini Borusi, & altera nostra cum novis iconibus tribus. Chartæ sunt tres excusæ Basileæ apud Nicolaum Episcopium F. 1557 in 8. & rursus cum Epistola Matthioli, Senensis. M. Antonini Imperatoris Romani & Philosophi de se ipso, seu vita sua libros 12, unà cum Marini Neapolitani, libro de Procli vita & felicitate, Græcos è Bibliotheca Illustrissimi Principis Otthonis Henrici, cùm vir doctrina excellens Michael Toxites, nobis communicasset, describendos curavi, & ad archetypum contuli, & patrueli Andreæ anno 1558. cudendos dedi, unam cum translationibus Latinis, in Antonini quidem libros Gul. Xylandri Augustani; in Martini verò Proclum, amici cujusdam nostri juvenis eruditi, qui præ modestia nomen suum exprimi noluit. Chartæ sunt 30 in 8. Historiæ animalium liber quartus, quæ est de piscibus & aquatilibus, cum iconibus procusus Tiguri à Froschouero 1558. in sol. chartis 3 15 Ad finem paralipomena quædam accesserunt. Continentur autem eodem volumine Gul. Rondeletij quoque, & Petri Bellonij de Aquatilium singulis scripta. Hannonis, Chartaginensium ducis navigatio, qua maximam Libycæ oræ partem ultra Herculis columnas lustravit, e Græco sermone in Latinum conversa adjectis etiam Scholijs. Seu qui charta impressa Tiguri apud Andream Gesnerum F. anno 1559. cùm Ioan. Leonis Africani Descriptionis Africæ libris novem, in 8. Xenocratis de alimento ex aquatilibus libellus, Græcus nostra operâ editus, idemque Latinus ex nostra interpretatione, unà cum Scholijs. Chartæ sunt quatuor cum dimidia, procusæ Tiguri apud Andream patruelem in 8. unà cum Iani Dubravij Olmucensis Episcopi de piscinis & piscium, qui in eis aluntur, naturis, libris quinque. Icones animalium aquatilium in mari & dulcibus aquis degentium, plus quàm DCC. cum Nomenclaturis singulorum Latinis, Græcis, Italicis, Hispanicis aliisque interdum. Explicantur autem singulorum nomina, ac nominum rationes, præsertim in Latinâ & & Græca Lingua uberrimè, & nominum confirmandorum causa descriptiones quorundam, & alia quædam, præsertim in magno nostro de Aquatilibus volumine non tradita, adduntur: deque singulis Rondeletij, Bellonij, Salviani, & nostræ sententiæ explicantur brevissimè. Frischouerus cudebat Tiguri 1560 in sol. chartis 101. Hoc monendum es, Lector, tres libros, quibus continentur icones quadrupedum, avium & aquatilium, commodè uno volumine ligari. Historia & interpretatio prodigij, quo cælum ardere visum est per plurimas Germaniæ regiones, ineunte anno 1561. die tertio à Natali Dominico, deque aliis quibusdam prodigijs veteribus ac novis. Chartæ sunt tres impressæ apud nos eodem anno in 8. Con. Bolovesi authoris nomine, meum enim non ponere placebat, ne quis sutorem ultra crepidam mihi objiceret. Placuit hæc interpretatio Anglis, qui suâ lingua eam ediderunt.
units.tr: ...Greek, though not previously printed. Varia Historia, book 14, in the Latin version of Justus Vultejus of Wetter, now also revised. On Establishing Military Orders after the Manner of the Greeks, book 1, translated into Latin by Fr. Robortello of Udine and illustrated with very many pictures by the same man, now again more correctly edited. Rustic Letters, translated by Sebastian Guldenbeck of Zurich. All printed at Zurich, at the house of my cousins, in the year 1556, in folio, 176 pages. On Fishes and All Aquatic Animals, in seven little books: I. The Halieutica of P. Ovidius Naso, emended and explained with scholia. II. An enumeration of aquatic animals after Pliny, emended and explained in an alphabetical sequence. A very full German nomenclature of the same. And certain other matters pertaining to the history of fishes, printed at Zurich by Andreas Gesner the younger, 1556, in octavo. On Some Ancient and New Names of Plants, such as mamirâs, moly, oloconitis, doronicum, bulbocastanum, granum alzelin or habbaziz, and many others. Two letters, one by Melchior Guilandinus of Prussia and the other by me, with three new illustrations. The sheets were printed at Basel by Nicolaus Episcopius the younger, 1557, in octavo, and again together with a letter of Matthiolus of Siena. The Twelve Books of Marcus Antoninus, Roman Emperor and Philosopher, concerning Himself, or His Life, together with the book of Marinus of Naples on the life and happiness of Proclus, in Greek. When the learned man Michael Toxites had communicated these from the library of the most illustrious prince Otto Henry, I took care to have them copied out, collated them with the archetype, and gave them to my cousin Andreas to be printed in 1558, along with Latin translations: for the books of Antoninus, that of Gul. Xylander of Augsburg; for Marinus's Proclus, that of a young friend of mine, a learned man, who out of modesty did not want his name given. The sheets number 30 in octavo. The fourth book of the History of Animals, which concerns fishes and aquatic animals, with pictures, was printed at Zurich by Froschauer in 1558, in folio, 315 sheets. At the end some supplementary material has been added. The same volume also contains writings on each aquatic animal by Guillaume Rondelet and Pierre Belon. The Voyage of Hanno, General of the Carthaginians, by which he explored the greater part of the Libyan coast beyond the Pillars of Hercules, converted from Greek into Latin with scholia added. Printed on paper at Zurich by Andreas Gesner the younger in 1559, together with the nine books of the Description of Africa by Johannes Leo Africanus, in octavo. The little book of Xenocrates On Food from Aquatic Animals, published by us in Greek, and the same in Latin from our translation, together with scholia. The sheets are four and a half, printed at Zurich by my cousin Andreas, in octavo, together with the five books of Jan Dubravius, Bishop of Olomouc, On Fishponds and the Natures of the Fish That Live in Them. Pictures of aquatic animals living in the sea and in fresh waters, more than 700, with the Latin, Greek, Italian, Spanish and sometimes other names of each. The names of each are explained, and the reasons for the names, especially in the Latin and Greek languages, very fully; and to confirm the names, descriptions of certain animals and certain other matters are added, especially those not treated in my large volume on aquatic animals; and the opinions of Rondelet, Belon, Salviani and my own on each are explained very briefly. Froschauer printed it at Zurich in 1560, in folio, 101 sheets. It must be noted, reader, that the three books containing the pictures of quadrupeds, birds and aquatic animals can conveniently be bound in one volume. The History and Interpretation of the Portent, in which the sky was seen to burn over very many regions of Germany at the beginning of the year 1561, on the third day after Christmas, and of certain other portents, ancient and new. Three sheets, printed by us in the same year in octavo, under the name of author Con. Bolovesus, for I did not wish to put my own name, lest anyone object to me that the shoemaker should stick to his last. This interpretation pleased the English, who have published it in their own language.

units.la: Amicus quidam hic Germanicè reddidit, sed nondum edidit. Dictionarium Germanico Latinum; nostra ad hortatione, copiosissimum tosua Pictorius noster confecit, ex cusum Tiguri à Frischouero in 4. 1561. cum nostra præfatione, in qua de lingua Germanica in universum, ejusque dialectis, & quàm latè patcat, quid ei cum Gothica & Gallica commune, deque antiquis & recentibus in ea scriptis & illustrandæ ejus ratione differimus, per sesquichartam ferè. Valerij Cordi Simesusij Annotationes in Pedacij Dioscoridis Anazarbæi de medica materia libros quinque longè aliæ, quàm antehac sunt evulgatæ. Ejusdem historia stirpium libri quatuor, nunc primum in lucem editi; adjectis etiam stirpium iconibus & brevissimis annotatiunculis. Ejusdem sylva, quæ rerum fossilium plurimarum in Germania, Metallorum Lapidum & stirpium aliquot rariorum notitiam brevissimè sequitur. Ejusdem de artificiosis extractionibus liber. Ejusdem compositiones medicinales aliquot, non vulgares. His accedunt Stocchornij & Nesti in Bernatium Helvetiorum ditione montium, & nascentium in eis stirpium descriptio, Benedicti Aretij, Professoris in Schola Bernensi. Descriptiones quædam & icones plantarum nostrae, & de hortis Germaniæ liber à me tum recens conscriptus. Hæc omnia Typographo Argentinensi Iosiæ Rihelio suppeditavi Anno 1562. qui ea publicavit in sol. chart. 303. Hortorum Germaniæ privatim chartæ sunt 22. Prolegomena in opera Galeni Latina, quæ hoc anno 1562. Basileæ prodierunt, ex ultima doctissimorum hominum recognitione &c. chartæ sunt sedecim cum quadrante in magno folio. Cassij iatrosophistæ Naturales & medicinales quæstiones 48. circa hominis naturam & morbos aliquot, ex nostra interpretatione Latina. Eadem, Græcè longè, quàm antehac, castigatiores, cum Scholijs nostris, Iacobus Gesnerus imprimebat Tiguri 1562. in 8. chartis 9. cum dimidia: Vnà cum Antonij Snebergeri, Medici Catalogo medicamentorum simplicium, pestilentiæ veneno adversantium Santis Ardoyni, Pisaurensis Medici de Venenis libri S. cum tribus ejusdem argumenti Ferdinandi Ponzetti, Cardinalis, excusi Basileae apud Henricum Petri, & P. Pernam anno 1562. in sol. Utriusque authoris codicem ante annos quadraginta, aut amplius retro excusum, Typographis ego suppeditavi; cum in nullis amplius bibliopolijs prostarent. Aristotelis libellum de virtutibus, a me translatum, passim Stobaei collectaneis Graece & Latine inserui, sicut & Theophrasti characteres, Graeco contextu & Politiani translatione, quoad ejus potui emendatis. His ultimus, hoc tempore, annumeretur praesens hic de scriptis, tum proprijs tum aliorum a me editis. Ex his haftenus impressis lucubrationibus nostris, pleraque olim, si vixero, & iterum edi contingat, aucta & emendata dabo. Ita Gesnerus de scriptis suis editis:
units.tr: A certain friend has translated it into German here, but has not yet published it. A German-Latin Dictionary, very full, compiled at my urging by our Tosua Pictorius, printed at Zurich by Froschauer in quarto, 1561, with my preface, in which I discuss the German language in general, its dialects, how widely it extends, what it has in common with Gothic and French, and the ancient and recent writings in it and the method of illustrating it, over about a sheet and a half. The Annotations of Valerius Cordus of Simshausen on the five books of Pedanius Dioscorides of Anazarbus, On Medical Matter, quite different from those previously published. The same author's History of Plants, four books, now first brought to light, also with pictures of plants and very brief little notes. The same author's Sylva, which very briefly follows the knowledge of many fossils in Germany, metals, stones and some rarer plants. The same author's book On Artful Extractions. The same author's several medicinal compounds, not commonplace. To these are added the description by Stockhorn and Nestius of the plants growing in the mountains of the Bernese territory of the Helvetians, and the description by Benedict Aretius, professor in the school at Bern. Certain descriptions and pictures of our plants, and a book on the gardens of Germany, which I had then recently written. I supplied all these to Josias Rihel, printer at Strasbourg, in 1562, who published them in folio, 303 sheets. The Gardens of Germany, printed separately, are 22 sheets. Prolegomena to the Latin works of Galen, which appeared at Basel this year, 1562, from the latest recension of the most learned men, etc., sixteen and a quarter sheets in large folio. The Natural and Medical Questions, 48 in number, of Cassius the iatrosophist, concerning the nature of man and certain diseases, from our Latin translation. The same, far more correct than before in Greek, with our scholia, was printed by Jacob Gesner at Zurich, 1562, in octavo, nine and a half sheets; together with the Catalogue of Simple Medicines Opposing the Poison of Plague by Antonius Sneberger, physician; the Five Books on Poisons by Santes Ardoynus, physician of Pesaro, with three of the same subject by Ferdinand Ponzetti, Cardinal, printed at Basel by Henricus Petri and P. Perna, 1562, in folio. I supplied the printers with the text of each author, printed some forty or more years ago, since they were no longer on sale in any bookshop. I inserted in various places in the Stobaean collections, in Greek and Latin, the little book of Aristotle On Virtues, translated by me, and likewise the Characters of Theophrastus, with the Greek text and the translation of Politian, emended as far as I could. Let this last, at this time, be counted among the present list of writings, both my own and those edited by me of others. Of these works of mine printed so far, most, if I live and it is my chance to print them again, I shall give augmented and corrected. Thus Gesner on his published writings:

units.la: De nondum editis, partim perfectis, partim imperfectis adhuc ita idem ille: Versabar hoc tempore in adornanda nostra Stirpium Historia, cujus materiam & picturas, quàm plurimas, permultis retro annis congerere caepi. Ab ea vero multae subinde occupationes necessariae, multa etiam ex improviso impedimenta me avocant. Nuper quidem doctissimo Typographorum, Henrico Stephano, Xenophontis de venatione libellum ab Omnibono Leoniceno minimè bene conversum, in ejus gratiam, ut emendarem, roganti, obsecundare volui: & spero translationem illam cum Scholijs forte nostris, inter caetera Xenophontis opera Latina ex ejus officina propediem apparituram, una cum nostris, in eundem librum, observationibus & emendationibus Graeci contextus. Alterum impedimentum immatura doctissimi Augustani Medici, Iohannis Moibani mors mihi attulit: qui nuper suo fato fungens amicis mandavit, ut conversionem suam & annotationes in Euporiston Dioscoridis Anarzabaei libros duos, nusquam antehac editos, imperfectos ad me mitterent: quos ego propter amicitiam, quae nobis viventibus intercesit, ipsius nomine perficerem ederemque: id quod eo, facilius iuscepi, quoniam & illum amavi plurimum, & libros Graecos Senatus Augustani liberalitate jam dudum transcriptos habui, inque ijs interdum animi gratiâ me exercui.
