Nuper etiam Valerij Cordi descriptiones Stirpium librum quintum sum nactus, quem in Italia confecit, eumque perlectum Argentinam ad Rihelium Typographum, ut maturè excuderet, mihi. Oppiani de Aucupio librorum Paraphrasin, quam Venetijs olim mihi describendam curavi, Graecam Latinitate donavi, & nostrae animalium Historiae passim inserui, editurus etiam seorsim, si occasio fuerit, cum alijs quibusdam Graecis de animalibus scriptis &c. Procopij Gazaei in Octoteuchum (id est, priores octo Veteris Testamenti libros) commentarios Graecos, copiosos sane & eruditos, ex eadem Bibliotheca nactus, ante annos aliquot transcribendos curavi, & Con. Clauséro convertendos dedi, ubi primum Typographus contigerit, Graecè etiam editurus. De canibus, Ioan. Caij Angli, Medici & Philosophi
units.tr: Concerning those not yet published, some complete and some still incomplete, the same man again: At this time I was occupied in preparing my History of Plants, the material and very many pictures of which I began to collect many years ago. But many necessary occupations and many unforeseen hindrances frequently call me away from it. Recently, indeed, I was willing to oblige the most learned printer Henry Estienne, who asked me, for his sake, to correct the little book of Xenophon On Hunting*, very badly translated by Omnibonus Leonicenus; and I hope that translation, perhaps with our scholia, will shortly appear from his workshop among the other Latin works of Xenophon, together with our observations and corrections on that book of the Greek text. A second hindrance was brought to me by the untimely death of the most learned physician of Augsburg, Johann Moiban: who, while still performing his duties, ordered his friends to send me his translation and annotations on the two books of Dioscorides' Euporiston of Anazarbus, never published before, unfinished; these I, out of the friendship that existed between us while he lived, undertook to complete and publish in his name; which I took up the more easily, since I loved him very much and had long since obtained transcriptions of the Greek books through the generosity of the Senate of Augsburg, and at times I have exercised myself in them for my own pleasure. Recently I also obtained the fifth book of Valerius Cordus's Descriptions of Plants, which he composed in Italy, and which, once read through, he sent to me at Strasbourg to Rihel the printer, so that he might print it promptly. I have rendered into Latin the Greek Paraphrase of the Books of Oppian On Fowling, which I once had copied out for me at Venice, and have inserted it in various places in our History of Animals, intending also to publish it separately, if an opportunity arises, together with certain other Greek writings on animals etc. Having obtained from the same library the Greek commentaries of Procopius of Gaza on the Octateuch (that is, the first eight books of the Old Testament), which are indeed copious and learned, I had them transcribed some years ago and gave them to Conrad Clauser to be translated, and I shall publish them in Greek too as soon as a printer is available. The little book of John Caius, English physician and philosopher, On Dogs, with some additions of ours, is kept by me, to be published either by itself or together with some other book pertaining to animals. I have gathered a copious material for the history of serpents and insects. Of observations on gems, stones and every kind of fossil...

units.la: P phi summi libellus, cum nostris quibusdam additionibus, vel per fe, vel cum alio quopiam ad animalia pertinente libro edendus, apud me asservatur. Ser. pentium & in fectiorum Historiæ materiam copiosam congessi. De lapidibus gemmis & omni fossilium genere observationum fylvam collegi. Remediorum fecundum genera & locos digestorum maximum numerum in schedis reposui. Aristotelis quosdam libros physici argumenti, Paraphrases aut Scholia, in alios Græcè, in alios Latinè, ex Græcorum interpretum commentariis concinnavi. Admirandas Aristotelis narrationes emendavi, & meliori ordine digessi, Græcè. Latina quædam, & Græca carmina, Epigrammata, Idyllia conscripsi. Germanicorum nominum proprietorum, virorum & mulierum (quibus usa est Germania antequam Sanctorum nomina ex Linguis peregrinis reciperet) aliquot millia secundum terminationes disposita habeo. Apparet autem in singulis pene certa aliqua significatio, ut vel ominis gratia, vel saltem non temere, sed certam ob causam imposita, videantur, sicut & apud Græcos fere. Nihil autem antiquum in nostra Lingua, & unde qualis ante multa secula fuerit, magis appareat, extare puto. Hunc librum Marcus Widlerus Tigurinus, à Geßnero inchoatum, sese auxisse, & absolvisse professus, ejus editionem pollicebatur. Vix puto tamen, non utile minus, quàm curiosum scriptum unquam prodijsse. Germanicorum vocabulorum, quàm plurimorum ex Hebraica, Græca & Latina, origines meditor, & alia quædam, fi Deus concesserit: sed ut res humanæ sunt, πολλὰ μετὰξὺ πηλὸς κυλικος καὶ χείλεος ἄκρα. Volui tamen nondum editas & imperfectas lucubrationes meas commemorare, partim ut viri boni & eruditi, me, dum vixero nunquam otiosum futurum, neque & mea omnia Reipublicæ literariæ promovendæ perpetuò devotissima, fore, intelligant: partim, ut qui ætate ac valetudine firmiores, & otio magis abundantes homines literati, similiter erga bona studia, atque ego, affecti reperiantur, ij de rudibus atque inchoatis quibusdam meis materiam sibi expoliendam, perfacilè impetraturi, postulare à me posint. Habeo & ego Epistolas adhuc quasdam, & miscellanea ejusdem, quæ hominis stupendam tum πολυμαθίαν demonstrant, tum φιλοπονίαν.
units.tr: The little book of P., the greatest philosopher, is kept by me, to be published either by itself or together with some other book on animals, with some additions of my own. I have gathered a copious store of material for a history of serpents and insects. I have collected observations on precious stones and every kind of fossil. I have put in my papers a very large number of remedies, arranged by kind and by place. From the commentaries of the Greek interpreters I have put together, in Greek for some and in Latin for others, paraphrases or scholia on certain books of Aristotle on natural philosophy. I have corrected Aristotle's admirable narrations and arranged them in better order, in Greek. I have written some Latin and Greek poems, epigrams and idylls. I have several thousand proper names of German men and women, the names Germany used before it received the names of saints from foreign languages, arranged according to their endings. In nearly every one of them some definite meaning appears, so that they seem to have been imposed either as omens or at least not carelessly but for a definite reason, as was almost the case among the Greeks too. I think there is nothing older in our language, and nothing from which it is clearer what sort of language it was many centuries ago. Marcus Widler of Zurich professed that he had added to and completed this book, which Gesner had begun, and he promised its edition. Yet I hardly think anything has ever appeared that is less useful than it is curious. I am meditating on the origins of very many German words from Hebrew, Greek and Latin, and certain other things, if God grants it; but as human affairs go, "many things lie between the cup and the lip." I wished, however, to mention my studies, not yet published and unfinished, partly so that good and learned men may understand that I shall never be idle as long as I live, and that all my efforts will always be devoted to advancing the republic of letters; and partly so that those learned men who are stronger in age and health and more abundant in leisure, and who are found to be similarly inclined toward good studies as I am, may be able to ask me for these rough and unfinished materials of mine, which they will very easily obtain, so that they may polish them for themselves. I also still have some letters and miscellanea of the same man, which show both the amazing range of his learning and his tireless diligence.

units.la: Goldlius Henricus, Tigurinus, medicus passivus, Germanica Lingua scripsit Regimen pestilentiæ. Itemque medicamentum approbatum in pleuritide, quæ pestis quasi species quædam est. Tum præterea formam medicamenti edidit; ac in super pretiosæ aquæ descriptionem contra ingentes capitis dolores, vertiginem, maniam & apoplexiam. Quin etiam modus quo morbus Gallicus curari potest citra unctiones, fuffumigia aut lotiones ullas, gummata nasci prohibentem, si morbus recens, nec prius àquoquam unctionibus aut suffumigijs alijsque modis vexatus fuerit. Omnia hæc in uno libello continentur, in 4. sine notatione, loci & temporis, excusa.
units.tr: Henricus Goldlius, of Zurich, a physician in practice, wrote in the German language a regimen against plague. Likewise he published an approved remedy for pleurisy, which is a sort of plague. Besides this he published a form of medicine, and in addition a description of a precious water against severe headaches, vertigo, mania and apoplexy. Indeed there is also a method by which the French disease can be cured without anointings, fumigations or any washings, and which prevents gummata from forming, if the disease is recent and has not previously been troubled by anointings, fumigations or other means. All these things are contained in one little book, in quarto, printed without any indication of place or time.

units.la: Grebelius Conradus, juvenis in utraque lingua eruditissimus, patria Tigurinus, præfationem scripsit in Pomponium Melam: Parisijs excusam, cum Vadiani commentarijs, item Epigrammata quædam nondum edita.
units.tr: Conrad Grebel, a very learned young man in both languages, a native of Zurich, wrote a preface to Pomponius Mela, printed at Paris together with the commentaries of Vadianus; also some epigrams not yet published.

units.la: Gualtherus Rodolphus, natus 1519. Tiguri, Zuinglij Reformatoris gener, Ecclesiæ & Scholæ Tigurinæ Minister, juvenis admodum publicis inclaruit scriptis. Ex Pastore, ab ann. Chr. 1542. Petrino Antistes, & Bullingeri successor, 1575. Viribus exhaustus rude donatur 1585. obijt 1586. Vehementissimi & eloquentissimi Concionatoris axioma habet. Scripsit in secundam & tertiam Ciceronis de lege Agraria, contra Rullum, orationem, & in Verrinas annotationes, sub nomine Eubuli Dynasteri, Basileæ impressas primum apud Robertum VVinter, & postea apud Ioan. Oporinum. Anno D. 1553. cum alijs diversorum annotationibus in omnes Ciceronis orationes, Iulij Pollucis onomasticon, Latinitate ab eo donatum, excudit Robertus VVinter Basileæ 1541. item Monomachia Davidis & Goliæ, & allegorica ejusdem expositio, Heroico carmine descripta cum Epicedijs Eobani Hessi, Henrici Lavateri, Nicolai Patrigij Angli, Friderichi Pistorij Niddani 1541. ibidem excus. & Apotheosis Simonis Grynæi versibus elegis in tabula. Epicedium in mortem Margaritæ Blaurerae, Virginis lectissimæ & eruditæ, ut ex Epistolis quibusdam Blaurerianis colligo, ad Ambrosium & Thomam Blaureros, fratres. Epicedia plura in variorum Clarissimorum virorum obitus: ut Pet. Martyris, Bullingeri, Parkhurst, Episcopi Nordwicensis in Anglia, Simleri generi, Gualtheri F. & aliorum excusa Tiguri. Varia item carmina venusta & erudita ad Ioannem Frisium, Tigurinum, sibi amicitiæ jure conjunctissimum. De ratione syllabarum & carminis libri duo. Et de Germanicæ nobilitatis studijs Elegia, ad nobilem juvenem Eberhardum à Bruch, anno Domini 1542. Argumenta omnium tam Veteris, quàm Novi Testamenti capitum, Elegiaco carmine conscripta, anno D. 1543. excusa Tiguri apud Frosch-ouerum, Ioannis Cantacuzeni, Constantinopolitani, contra Mahometicam fidem apologias quatuor, & orationes totidem, è Græco in Latinum translulit, anno Domini 1543. Basileæ apud Oporinum. Ejusdem extat etiam collatio novi Testamenti ad Græcam veritatem. Eleganti satis & tersö stylo Germanico, quæ & separatim in 8. profitat, & in folio cum Translatione Tigurinorum Theologorum Veteris Testamenti. Huldrici Zwinglij libros circiter 34. è Germanico in Latinum translulit. Item ad Catholicam Ecclesiam, omnémque fidelium posteritatem, pro Huldricho Zwinglio & operum ejusdem editione Apologiam, quæ & Zwinglij operibus præfixa, & seorsim excusa exstat, anno D. 1545. Orthodoxa fidei doctrina confessio, per Tigurina Ecclesiæ ministros, contra Lutheri calumnias & convitia, Germanicè scripta, eodem interprete Latinitate donata est, anno D. 1545. Scripsit etiam Homilias quinque de novissumis Iimi t. poribus & Antichristo, in locum Matth.24. Germanicè & Latinè apud Frolchouerum excusa. Idem scripsit in Ioannis Apostoli & Evangelistæ Epistolam Canonicam Homilias 37. & in ejusdem Apostoli duas posteriores Epistolas Homiliarum sylvam. Tiguri excudit Frofchouerus, anno D. 1553. in 8. chartis 36. Quæ omnia etiam in Germanicam Linguam transtulit. Orationem de officio ministri Ecclesiastici, ibidem excusam in 4. anno D. 1548 Homilias aliquot Germanicas, nempe in Canticum Zachariæ, Homilias duas, ibidem impressas anno 1552. in 8. Denativitate Domini nostri Jesu Christi, Homilias tres anno 1553. De pueritia & educatione Domini nostri Iesu Christi Homilias duas, anno 1553. De servitute peccati & libertate fidelium, homil. è 6. capite Epistolæ D.Pauli ad Romanos anno 1552. De origine, præstantia, & dignitate seu authoritate sacræ Scripturæ, ex 15. Epistolæ ad Romanos 1553. De adventu Domini nostri Jesu Christi, & quomodo nos ad eum præparare debeamus, ex 4. capite 1. Epist. D. Petri. In psalmum 113. qui in actione cœnæ Domini in Ecclesia Tigurina recitatur. Theodoreti de Providentia sermones X. Latinitate donavit. Excudit Tiguri Frofchouerus. Nabal, comœdia sacra, ex 1. Samuel 25. Frofchouerus excudit. Scripsit, & ibidem edidit Homilias tres de ascensione Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & missione Spiritus Sancti speculum Christianorum, sive Homilias duas de Christiani hominis nomine & officio. Præterea scripsit Homiliam de circumcisione. In orationem Dominicam Homilias 10. De constantia & perseverantia in fide ex 1. Iohan.2. In passionis Dominicæ Historiam, Homilias 2. de resurrectione Christi, item de nostrorum corporum Resurrectione, & Paschate Christianorum Homilias 3. de afflictionibus & eorundem consolatione, ex 2.Corinth 1 Homiliam 1. Homiliam in testimonium Iohannis Baptistæ de Christo: Homiliæ istæ omnes Germanicæ editæ sunt in 8. De in carnatione Filij Dei, Homilias 6. Latinè & Germanicè editas. Psalterium in Germanicam transtulit Linguam, argumentis & annotationibus illustravit. Postremò sequentes libros sacros Homiliis integras explicavit. Duodecim Prophetas minores, Evangelium Sancti Marci, Evangelium Sancti Lucæ, Evangelium Sancti Iohannis. Acta Apostolorum, Epistolam D.Pauli ad Romanos, ejusdem utramque Epistolam ad Corinthios. Singula hæc diversis temporibus à Frofchouero excusa sunt Tiguri, in folio. Scripsit etiam Homilias 61. in Epistolam ad Galatas, cum Præfatione ad Scotiæ Regem, Iacobum VI de officio Regum & Principum in constituenda Ecclesia. Tiguri apud Frofchouerum sol. 1576. Homilias in Matthæum. Præterea scripsit de tentationibus Conciones IX. Germanicas in Matth.c 4. Item de vero pane vitæ, Domino nostro Christo, & quomodo manducetur, Homilias 10. in c 6. Iohannis, Tiguri apud Frosch. 1548. Germanicè. Ad hæc Latino stylo vulgavit in Ies-jam Prophetam sermones 327. quos Lingua vernacula habuit ad populum
units.tr: Rudolph Gwalther, born in 1519 at Zurich, son-in-law of the reformer Zwingli, minister of the Church and school of Zurich, became very famous for his writings while still quite young. From minister he became, in the year of Christ 1542, Petrinus antistes, and successor to Bullinger in 1575. Worn out by his labours, he was granted his release in 1585, and died in 1586. He has the reputation of a most vehement and eloquent preacher. He wrote, under the name Eubulus Dynasterus, a speech against Rullus in the second and third of Cicero's speeches on the agrarian law, and annotations on the Verrines, first printed at Basel by Robert Winter and afterwards by Johann Oporinus. In the year of the Lord 1553 he published, with other men's annotations on all Cicero's orations, the Onomasticon of Julius Pollux, which he rendered into Latin; Robert Winter printed it at Basel in 1541. Also the Monomachy of David and Goliath, with an allegorical exposition of it, described in heroic verse, together with the funeral poems of Eobanus Hessus, Henry Lavater, Nicholas Patrigius of England, and Friedrich Pistorius of Nidda, printed at the same place in 1541; and the Apotheosis of Simon Grynaeus in elegiac verses on a tablet. An elegy on the death of Margaret Blaurer, a most select and learned virgin, as I gather from some Blaurer letters to Ambrose and Thomas Blaurer, her brothers. Several elegies on the deaths of various most distinguished men, such as Peter Martyr, Bullinger, Parkhurst, bishop of Norwich in England, the son-in-law of Simler, Gwalther's son, and others, printed at Zurich. Also various graceful and learned poems addressed to John Frisius of Zurich, bound to him by the closest bond of friendship. Two books on the principles of syllables and of verse. And an elegy on the study of German nobility, addressed to the noble young man Eberhard von Bruch, in the year of the Lord 1542. Arguments of all the chapters of both the Old and the New Testament, written in elegiac verse, in the year of the Lord 1543, printed at Zurich by Froschauer. He translated from Greek into Latin four apologies of John Cantacuzenus of Constantinople against the Mahometan faith, and as many orations, in the year of the Lord 1543, at Basel by Oporinus. There also exists by the same author a comparison of the New Testament with the Greek truth, written in a fairly elegant and polished German style; it has been issued separately in octavo, and in folio together with the translation of the Old Testament by the Zurich theologians. He translated about thirty-four books of Huldrych Zwingli from German into Latin. Likewise, an apology addressed to the Catholic Church and to all the posterity of the faithful, on behalf of Huldrych Zwingli and the edition of his works; it stands both prefixed to Zwingli's works and printed separately, in the year of the Lord 1545. The Orthodox confession of the doctrine of the faith, written in German by the ministers of the Zurich Church against Luther's calumnies and reproaches, was rendered into Latin by the same translator in the year of the Lord 1545. He also wrote five homilies on the last times and Antichrist, on Matthew 24, printed in German and Latin by Froschauer. He wrote thirty-seven homilies on the canonical Epistle of John the Apostle and Evangelist, and a collection of homilies on the two later Epistles of the same Apostle. Froschauer printed them at Zurich in the year of the Lord 1553, in octavo, thirty-six sheets. He translated all these into the German language too. An oration on the office of the ecclesiastical minister, printed there in quarto in the year of the Lord 1548. Several German homilies: namely two homilies on the Canticle of Zechariah, printed there in octavo in 1552; three homilies on the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, in 1553; two homilies on the childhood and education of our Lord Jesus Christ, in 1553; homilies on the servitude of sin and the freedom of believers, from the sixth chapter of St Paul's Epistle to the Romans, in 1552; on the origin, excellence and dignity or authority of holy Scripture, from the fifteenth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, in 1553; on the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and how we ought to prepare ourselves for him, from the fourth chapter of the first Epistle of St Peter. On Psalm 113, which is recited at the celebration of the Lord's Supper in the Zurich Church. He translated into Latin ten sermons of Theodoret on Providence. Froschauer printed them at Zurich. Nabal, a sacred comedy, from 1 Samuel 25. Froschauer printed it. He wrote and published there three homilies on the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ and the sending of the Holy Spirit, the mirror of Christians, or two homilies on the name and office of a Christian man. He also wrote a homily on circumcision. Ten homilies on the Lord's Prayer. On constancy and perseverance in the faith, from 1 John 2. On the history of the Lord's Passion, two homilies; on the resurrection of Christ, likewise on the resurrection of our bodies, and on the Christian Passover, three homilies; on afflictions and their consolation, from 2 Corinthians 1, one homily; one homily on the testimony of John the Baptist concerning Christ. All these homilies were published in German in octavo. On the incarnation of the Son of God, six homilies, published in Latin and German. He translated the Psalter into the German language and illustrated it with arguments and annotations. Finally, he explained the following sacred books in full in homilies: the twelve minor Prophets, the Gospel of St Mark, the Gospel of St Luke, the Gospel of St John, the Acts of the Apostles, St Paul's Epistle to the Romans, and both of his Epistles to the Corinthians. Each of these was printed at Zurich at different times by Froschauer, in folio. He also wrote sixty-one homilies on the Epistle to the Galatians, with a preface to James VI, King of Scotland, on the office of kings and princes in establishing the Church. Printed at Zurich by Froschauer, in folio, 1576. Homilies on Matthew. Besides this he wrote nine German sermons on the temptations in Matthew 4. Likewise ten homilies on the true bread of life, our Lord Christ, and how it is to be eaten, on John 6; at Zurich, by Froschauer, 1548, in German. In addition, in Latin style he published three hundred and twenty-seven sermons on Isaiah the Prophet, which he had delivered to the people in the vernacular.

units.la: Jum lum Tigurinum Tiguri 1583. cum Praefatione ad Cl. V. Michaelem Sailerum, de Scholarum antiquissimo usu & laude fundatorum. Ejusdem extat in Pentateuchum Mosis translatio Germanica cum singulorum librorum & capitum argumentis, dispositionibus, explicationibus perspicuis. Quae in lesajam ineditatus est eadem Methodo & ordine, ἀνεκδότως adhuc sunt, ejusdem manu exarata; Optârim profecto, hunc laborem potuisse absolvi, & propter purae versionis Germanicae tum Emphasin, tum elegantiam, & propter notarum solidam brevitatem. Autographum habet Reverendus Collegij Parthenij veteris Inspector, D. Iob. Guilelmus Simlerus, Gualtheri abnepos. Praeter haec, Epistolas ejusdem quasdam habeo, & consilia de variis thematibus, multis mihi nominibus gratissima.
units.tr: Jum lum Tigurinum, Zurich 1583, with a preface to the distinguished Michael Sailer, on the very ancient use and value of schools and their founders. There also exists his German translation of the Pentateuch of Moses, with arguments, outlines and clear explanations for each book and chapter. His work on Isaiah, arranged in the same method and order, remains unpublished and is still in his own hand. I would certainly have wished that this labour could have been completed, both for the force and elegance of the pure German version and for the solid brevity of the notes. The autograph is held by the Reverend D. Johann Wilhelm Simler, great-grandson of Gualther, the former Inspector of the Parthenian College. Besides these, I have certain letters of his and counsels on various subjects, which are very welcome to me for many reasons.

units.la: Gualtherus Rodolphus, Fil. ore & ingenio Patrem referens, juvenis admodum Ecclesiae Petrinae Diaconatum administravit. In ipso aetatis flore, anno 25. qui a Christo nato erat 1577, magno cum dolore bonorum obijt. Non Germaniae tantum, sed & Angliae Academias salutavit. Extat ejus Elegia de militia Christiana in his terris adversus Satanam, carnem & mundum militantium, 1575. Epitaphium Graecum in ejusdem Bullingeri obitum, Tiguri etiam excusum. Scripsit quoque Epicedium in obitum D. Iohannis Parckhurfti, Episcopi Nordovicensis in Anglia. Item carmen in Tigurinorum navigationem, Tiguro Argentoratum usque uno die confectam, quod Argos Helvetica inscripsit. Ejusdem sunt carmina in imagines doctorum superioris seculi virorum, quae in Typographia Frosthoueriana in parietibus depicta extabant. Habeo ejusdem quasdam Epistolas.
units.tr: Gualther Rudolf, son who in speech and talent resembled his father, served as deacon of the church of St Peter while still very young. In the flower of his age, in the year 1577 after the birth of Christ, in his twenty-fifth year, he died to the great grief of good men. He paid his respects not only to the universities of Germany but also to those of England. There is extant his elegy on the Christian warfare waged on this earth against Satan, the flesh and the world, 1575. There is also a Greek epitaph on the death of Bullinger, likewise printed at Zurich. He also wrote a funeral poem on the death of Dr John Parkhurst, Bishop of Norwich in England, and a poem on the voyage of the Zurich men, composed in a single day from Zurich as far as Strasbourg, which he entitled "Helvetic Argos". His verses on the portraits of learned men of the previous century, which were painted on the walls of the Froschauer printing house, are also his. I have some of his letters.

units.la: Grobius, Iob: Huldricus Ecclesiae Lithopolitanae Minister, Poeta felix, Cygnum Evangelicum edidit Tiguri. Vitas virorum apud Tigurinos, ante & post Reformationem clarorum, carmine descripsit; pluraque & typis & calamo descripta ejus extant Poematia, quorum magnam authoris manu exaratorum habeo partem. Floruit adhuc hoc seculo, 1606.
units.tr: Grob, Johann Huldrych, minister of the church at Lithopolis, a fortunate poet, published "The Evangelical Swan" at Zurich. He described in verse the lives of men famous among the Zurich people before and after the Reformation; several of his poems, both printed and written out by hand, survive, and I possess a large part of those written in the author's own hand. He flourished in this century, in 1606.

units.la: Guldebeck Sebastianus, Scholae primum Abbatiffanae 1535. Provisor; postea Collegij Parthenij Inspector 1541. Graecae & Latinae Linguae peritissimus. Vertit Hesiodi Theogoniam ad verbum. Prodijt Basileae, quamvis non adjecto Interpretis nomine, cum caeteris Hesiodi Graecis & Latine redditis operibus. Item Aristophanis Comoedias omnes, adjectis etiam annotationibus. Item Tragaediam Gregorij Nazianzeni, de Christi passione, & quaedam alia. Electram item Euripidis Latine dedit: Scripsit etiam marginales annotationes in 1. & 2. librum Iliados Homeri impressas. Praeterea in Chrysostomo multa ad Graecum exemplum castigavit. Aelianum Graecum ex vetustissimo exemplari descripsit, & quaedam in illo transtulit.
units.tr: Gull(er)beck, Sebastian, first provisor of the school at Abbatissa in 1535, afterwards inspector of the Parthenian College in 1541, was most skilled in Greek and Latin. He translated Hesiod's Theogony word for word. It was published at Basel, though without the translator's name, together with the other works of Hesiod rendered into Greek and Latin. He also gave all the comedies of Aristophanes, with notes added, and the tragedy of Gregory Nazianzen on the Passion of Christ, and certain other things. He likewise gave a Latin version of Euripides' Electra. He also wrote marginal notes on the first and second books of Homer's Iliad, which were printed. Moreover, he corrected many passages in Chrysostom by the Greek exemplar. He copied out the Greek Aelian from a very old manuscript and translated some things in it.

units.la: H.
units.tr: H.

units.la: Hallerus, Iohannes (Iohannis Ansoltingensis primum in ditione Bernensi, Bulaci postea 1528. in agro Tigurino ad an. Chr. 1531. pastoris filius) in Synodum receptus Tigurinam 1542. Pastor in monte Hirzelano, 1543. Ilnaviensis, eodem: Archidiaconus Templi Carolini 1547. Ecclesiae postea Augustanae ad fatalem periodum interimisticam, mutuo datur. Paulo post Beram, ad tempus primum, postea ad vitae dies concessus, obijt 1575. d. 1. Septemb. Psalmos Davidis omnes in precum certas formulas redegit. Henrici Bullingeri primum & secundum sermonem Decadis tertiae in Linguam Germanicam transtulit. Idem integrum Decadum opus Germanicè reddidit. Collegit etiam ex decretis Canonicis sententias, quibus quid de plerisque in Ecclesia hodie controversis capitibus sit sentiendum, ostendit. Plurimas ejus Epistolas habeo, & compendium rerum suo tempore gestarum.
units.tr: Haller, Johann (son of the minister Johann of Ansoltingen first in the Bernese territory, afterwards at Bülach in 1528, and in the Zurich country by the year of Christ 1531), was received into the Zurich synod in 1542. He was minister at Hirzel hill in 1543, and in the same year at Wülflingen; archdeacon of the Carolinum in 1547. Afterwards he was lent to the church of Augsburg for the fateful interim period. Shortly after he was granted Bern, first for a time and later for the rest of his life; he died on 1 September 1575. He reduced all the Psalms of David to certain fixed forms of prayer. He translated the first and second sermons of the third Decade of Henry Bullinger into German. He also rendered the whole work of the Decades into German. He gathered from the canonical decrees opinions which showed what is to be thought on most of the controverted heads in the Church today. I have a great many of his letters, and an abstract of the events of his own time.

units.la: Hallerus, Iohannes Iacobus, VVolfgangi filius, A. L. M. Ecclesiae Zolikonensis Pastor 1586. Patris in Archidiaconatu successor ab an. Chr. 1596. ad 1624. Mathematicus insignis, author est Globi terrestris & coelestis sua magnitudine & justa proportione admirandi. In Theologicis Lexicon Biblicum conscripsit Lingua vernaculâ, Methodo satis concinna, & verbi Ministris accommodata, Sant loci communes Biblici, ordine Alphabetico disposit. Αυτόγραφον adhuc in Ecclesiae nostrae Archivo asservatur.
units.tr: Haller, Johann Jakob, son of Wolfgang, A. L. M., pastor of the church at Zollikon from 1586, successor of his father in the archdeaconate from the year of Christ 1596 until 1624. He was an outstanding mathematician and the author of a terrestrial and celestial globe, to be admired for its size and exact proportion. In theology he wrote a Biblical lexicon in the vernacular, in a fairly neat method and suited to ministers of the Word, and he arranged the Biblical commonplaces in alphabetical order. His autograph is still preserved in the archive of our church.

units.la: Hallerus Iohannes, Iacobi Filius, Tigurinus, Ordinis Politici, sed Historiarum diligens collector. Annales de rebus Tigurinis Bullingeri aliquot tomis continuavit, qui in Bibliotheca nostra Civica extant.
units.tr: Haller, Johann, son of Jakob, citizen of Zurich, of the political order, but a diligent collector of histories. He continued Bullinger's Annals concerning the affairs of Zurich in several volumes, which are extant in our civic library.

units.la: Hallerus Wolfgangus, superioris Iohannis, Anfoltingensium & Bulacensium Pastoris filius; Bernensis frater, Verbi Dei in agro primum Tigurinorum, Hufae prope Capellam, 1545. deinde Meilae ad lacum Tigurinum 1547. postea in ipsa urbe Archidiaconus, & Collegij Carolini Praepositus ab a. 1552. ad 1601. Libros sex Iacobi Rueff, de conceptione & Generatione hominis, & ijs, quae circa haec potissimum considerantur, ex Germanica Lingua in Latinam transtulit, 1554. Carmina etiam scripsit in obitum Petri Martyris, Gesneri, Bullingeri, Simleri. In colligendis & conscribendis juribus privilegijs, consuetudinibus, Actis, Ecclesiae Tigurinae fuit solertissimus. Vidi, quae conscripsit de origine Collegij Carolini, fundatione Ecclesiae Tigurinae, tempore Clodovei, sub Ruperto; Confirmatione Imperatorum & Regum, Catalogum Plebanorum, Praepositorum, Scholasticorum, caeterorumque usque ad Reformationem & deinceps Canonicorum, Sacellorum & Sacellanorum Templi Carolini Alio Tomo consignata ab ipso vidi Acta Concordiae VVittebergensis, Reformationem Sangallensem, Abbatis cellanam, Anabaptistarum praesertim ibidem tum erumpentium doctrinam, tumultus, Schismata; Reipublicae Tigurinae curam pro confervanda libertate, & amore in confaederatos, plurâque alia.
units.tr: Haller, Wolfgang, son of the above Johann, minister of the Anselting and Bülach people, brother of the Bernese; he preached the Word of God first in the Zurich countryside, at Hausen near Kappel, in 1545, then at Meilen on Lake Zurich in 1547, and afterwards in the city itself as archdeacon and provost of the Carolinum from 1552 until 1601. He translated from German into Latin six books of Jakob Ruf on the conception and generation of man, and on the matters which are chiefly considered in connection with these, in 1554. He also wrote poems on the death of Peter Martyr, Gesner, Bullinger and Simler. He was most skilful in collecting and writing out the rights, privileges, customs and records of the Zurich church. I have seen what he wrote on the origin of the Carolinum, the foundation of the Zurich church in the time of Clovis under Rupert; the confirmation by emperors and kings; a catalogue of the parish priests, provosts, scholasticus and the others, down to the Reformation and afterwards of the canons, chapels and chaplains of the Carolinum church. In another volume, written by his own hand, I have seen the acts of the Wittenberg Concord, the Reformation of St Gall, the monk's cell, and especially the teaching, tumults and schisms of the Anabaptists who then broke out there; the care of the Zurich commonwealth for preserving liberty and its love for its confederates, and many other things.

units.la: Hambergerus Hartmannus, Tigurinus, Graecae Hebraicaeque Linguae eruditissimus, Decanus Ecclesiarum superioris Capituli VVezikonensis meritissimus mus ab anno 1561. ad 1608 quo obijt. Transtulit Procopij Gazæi Sophistæ commentarios Græcos in libros Mosis, Numerorum, Deuteronomium: Item librum Josuæ, judicum, secundum Paraleipomenon: Prodierunt Tiguri apud Gessneros 1551. cum reliquis Procopij commentarijs. Ejusdem aliquot habeo Epistolas Græcas & Latinas.
units.tr: Hamberger, Hartmann, Zurich man, most learned in Greek and Hebrew, deservedly dean of the churches of the upper chapter of Wetzikon from 1561 until 1608, when he died. He translated the Greek commentaries of the sophist Procopius of Gaza on the books of Moses, Numbers and Deuteronomy; also the book of Joshua, Judges, and the second book of Chronicles. They were published at Zurich at the Gesner press in 1551, together with the rest of Procopius' commentaries. I have some of his letters, in Greek and Latin.

units.la: Hambergerus, Tobias, Hartmanni filius, Berneggæ primùm apud Rhegulcos, postea Glaronensium, tum denique Kilchbergæ ad lacum Tigurinum Pastor, Vicinarùmque Inspector ab an. Chr. 1627. ad 1632. quo fatis cessit. Edidit anniversariam Concionem ad Navalia Glaronensium habitam, de justificatione hominis coram Deo, ex c. 5 ad Gal. Tig. 1606.
units.tr: Hamberger, Tobias, son of Hartmann, first pastor at Berneck among the Rheintal people, afterwards at Glarus, and finally at Kilchberg on Lake Zurich, and inspector of the neighbouring parishes from the year of Christ 1627 until 1632, when he met his fate. He published the annual sermon delivered at the shipyards of Glarus, on the justification of man before God, from chapter 5 of Galatians. Zurich, 1606.

units.la: Heideggerus, Johannes Henricus, SS. Theologiæ Doctor in illustri Arnoldino quod Steinfurti est, dignissimus, publicis suis scriptis indies & orbem literatum juvare, & eruditionem suam probare pergit. Scripta quæ & Heidelbergæ, ubi Collegij Sapientiæ ad tempus Præceptor fuit ordinarius, & Steinfurti prodierunt, sunt tum variæ disputationes Philologicæ, Philosophicæ, Theologicæ, in quædam veteris & N. T. loca: in Genesin præsertim, & 1. Samuelis c. 38. de apparitione Samuelis; in Matthæi quosdam textus controversos. De vera & falsa religione; de Consilijs Evangelicis. Demonstratio vicariæ potestatis Pontificis falsò usurpatæ, de justificatione; de fine Mundi, de Paschate emortuali, de justitia legali; tum etiam integri tractatus, ut sunt elaboratum scriptum de lege cibaria, suffocato & sanguine, ex Act. 15. adversus Curcellæum, & compendiosa Synodi Tridentinæ refutatio. Deus pijs & sanctis ejus laboribus porrò benedicat.
units.tr: Heidegger, Johann Heinrich, Doctor of Sacred Theology, most worthy in the distinguished Arnoldinum at Steinfurt, continues daily to help the literary world by his public writings and to prove his learning. The works which were published both at Heidelberg, where he was for a time the regular tutor of the College of Wisdom, and at Steinfurt, are indeed various philological, philosophical and theological disputations on certain passages of the Old and New Testaments: especially on Genesis, and on 1 Samuel chapter 28 concerning the appearance of Samuel; on certain disputed texts of Matthew. On true and false religion; on the evangelical counsels. A demonstration of the vicarious power of the Pope, falsely claimed; on justification; on the end of the world; on the Easter of the dead; on legal righteousness. Indeed there are also complete treatises, such as his worked-out writing on the law of food, on what is strangled and on blood, from Acts 15, against Curcellaeus, and a concise refutation of the Council of Trent. May God further bless his pious and holy labours.

units.la: Hochbholzerus Samuel, L. A. M. Scholæ primum Abbatisanæ Præceptor, Pastor postea Lithopolitanus 1599. Patri surrogatus, Capituli Decanus 1599. ad 1606. quo decessit è vita. Egregium scripsit tractatum de mendicis, Tig. 1591. Vbi contra validos mendicantes ita pugnat, ut digniorum causam præclarè commendet.
units.tr: Hochholzer, Samuel, L. A. M., first teacher of the school at Abbatissa, afterwards minister at Lithopolis in 1599, surrogate for his father, dean of the chapter from 1599 until 1606, when he departed from life. He wrote an outstanding treatise on beggars, Zurich, 1591, in which he so fights against able-bodied beggars that he commends the cause of the more deserving admirably.

units.la: Hofmeisterus, Johannes Rodolphus, Ecclesiæ & Scholæ Tigurinæ Minister, & Professor publicus, multi laboris, fusæque eruditionis edidit tractatum de Nomine Jesu; Tiguri 1653. Alia præterea quædam practica, de Temperantia, &c Suspiria insuper ad pietatem & devotionem feliciter composita. Vivit etiamnum solertissimus Literarum sacrarum scrutator.
units.tr: Hofmeister, Johann Rudolf, minister of the church and of the school of Zurich, and public professor, of great labour and wide learning, published a treatise on the Name of Jesus, Zurich 1653. Besides this, certain other practical works, on temperance and so on, and sighs also, happily composed for piety and devotion. He is still living, a most diligent searcher of the Sacred Letters.

units.la: Hofmannus Conradus A. L. M. Bremogartensis, Plebanus primùm Tigurinus, Antecessor Zuinglij, postea an. Chr. 1524. Canonicus. Extant quædam ejus scripta in Zuinglium & Reformationem.
units.tr: Hofmannus Conradus, Master of Arts, of Bremgarten, first parish priest (plebanus) of Zurich and predecessor of Zwingli; later, in 1524, a canon. Some of his writings against Zwingli and on the Reformation survive.

units.la: Heingartner Conradus, Tigurinus, Medicinæ Doctor, & Caroli VIII. Francorum Regis Physicus, scripsit defensionem Astronomiæ.
units.tr: Heingartner Conradus, of Zurich, Doctor of Medicine and physician to Charles VIII, King of the French, wrote a defence of astronomy.

units.la: Holzhalbius Conradus, scripsit contra Apocalypsin Iohannes Plaustrarij Cæsareo Lutrensis 1621, Germanicè.
units.tr: Holzhalbius Conradus, wrote in German, in 1621, against the Apocalypse of Johannes Plaustrarius of Cæsareo-Lutrensis.

units.la: Hospinianus Christianus, Lithopolitanus, Epistolam scripsit ad Ioannem Fratrem, quae Basileae est edita. Plures ejusdem Epistolas habeo.
units.tr: Christian Hospinian of Lithopolis wrote a letter to his brother John, which was published at Basel. I have several more of his letters.

units.la: Hospinianus Iohannes, superioris Frater, scripsit carmen Panegyricum in D. Magnum ab Emershofen, & aliquot Epithalamia, excusa Basileae 1539. Quaestionum Dialecticarum lib. 6. lb 1543. Vrbani Bellunensis institutionum Grammaticarum lib. 2. redegit in Epitomen, lb. 1546. Librum de Quantitate syllabarum, & Aristotelis librum de Categoriis, quaestionibus explicavit. Libellum de Categorici Syllogismi modis. Epistolas duas ad Christianum Hospinianum Fratrem. Aristoteiis etiam Organum correxit, in capita distinxit, vertit, Graece & Latine edidit duobus Tomis Basil. 1573. Epitomen Quaestionum Dialecticarum, Tractat. de justificatione hominis. In laudem Theob. ab Erlach.
units.tr: John Hospinian, the elder brother, wrote a panegyric poem on D. Magnus ab Emershofen and several wedding songs, printed at Basel in 1539. He published six books of Dialectical Questions (Basel, 1543); he reduced the two books of Urbanus Bellunensis's Grammatical Institutes to an epitome (Basel, 1546); he explained by questions the book on the Quantity of Syllables and Aristotle's book on the Categories; and he wrote a little book on the moods of the categorical syllogism, and two letters to his brother Christian Hospinian. He also corrected Aristotle's Organon, divided it into chapters, translated it, and published it in Greek and Latin in two volumes (Basel, 1573). He wrote an epitome of the Dialectical Questions, a treatise on the justification of man, and a work in praise of Theobald von Erlach.

units.la: Hospinianus Joh. Rodolphus, Tigurinus, natus 1547. Ecclesiae & Scholae Tigurinae Minister ab an. Chr. 1568. ad 1626. quo pie defunctus est, aetatis 78. quem coaetaneus ipsius, D. Rodolphus Goclenius paulo post fuit insecutus. De hoc Ecclesiae Tigur. Polyhistore audire placet Venerandum Ecclesiae nostrae non ita pridem Antistitem, D Ioh. Iacobum Breitingerum Orat. de Eccl. Antiquiss. & Reformatarum nostrarum sensu atque consensu: Cum in Frisia, inquit, Occidentalis Academia Sibrandum Lubbertum, insignem Theologum audirem adolescens, essemque aliquando Conradi Kochii, nunc Ecclesiae Schaphusianae Antistitis longe vigilantissimi, ipsum convenientis Comes, adesset etiam Johannes Dysius Antverpianus, vir eruditione clarus, magnos illos viros, ab affectu liberos, liberalissime profiteri memini, erudito hoc seculo Pontificiorum errores impugnari egregie a multis, sed qui eorum felicius obtinuret ora, praeter Hospinianum Tigurinum, esse neminem. Edita autem ab eo sunt, Oratio de origine & progressu rituum & Ceremoniarum Ecclesiasticarum, Tiguri 1586. Historiae Sacramentariae partes duae. Et prioris libri 5. de Coenae Dominii institutione, ejusque Ceremonijs Tig. 1598. Posterior vero pars anno 1602. prodierunt. Origines errorum, hoc est de origine, progressu usu & abusu Templorum, P. 1, Tiguri 1587. De origine & progressu Monachatus lib. VI. Tig. 1588. De origine Festorum Christianorum Tiguri 1593. De origine, Progressu, ceremonijs, & ritibus Festorum Iudaeorum, Graecorum, Romanorum & Turcarum lib. III. Tig. 1592. Historia Iesuitica, Tig. 1619. Concordia discors, de origine & progressu formulae Concordiae Bergensis, Tiguri 1607. Oratio de animarum immortalitate. Germanice nihil edidit praeter explicationem Hymni Mariae, in 8. In his autem scriptis suis non modo Historice versatur; sed & dogmatice. Elenchum ubique instituit, praesertim contra Bellarminum, Baronium,Gretserum,alios,qui quidem suam ad stabiliendum Papismum,ex antiquitate deprompunt argumenta. Sunt etiam quaedam ejus opuscoli ἀνέκδοτα adhuc, & ab haeredibus asservata 1. de authoritate veterum, Patrum & Conciliorum, hoc ordine. a. Traduntur regulae generales, de vera antiquitate & Lectione Patrum. b. de scriptis Patrum, quorum alia publica sunt alia privata. De utrisque ordine: primo de Canonibus Apostolorum, Epistolis Decretalibus, Constitutionibus Clementinis, Concilijs; postea de scriptis Polycarpi, Ignatij, Irenaei, Iustini Martyris, Clementis Alexandrini, Origenis. Elegantı omnia proponuntur Methodo, notatis ante caetera ijs, quae pie dicuntur, errores postea leviores indicantur. Vindiciae denique locorum ab Adversarijs, impetitorum, subjiciuntur. II. De sepulchris, varijsque variarum Gentium sepeliendi modis, quaedam conscribere caepit, quae etiam digna essent luce publica.
units.tr: John Rudolf Hospinian of Zurich, born 1547, was minister of the Church and school of Zurich from 1568 until 1626, when he died piously at the age of 78. His contemporary, D. Rudolf Goclenius, followed him a short time later. On this Polyhistor of the Zurich Church, I am pleased to quote the venerable leader of our Church, not long ago, D. John James Breitinger, in his oration on the sense and consensus of the most ancient Church and our Reformed churches: "When I was a young man studying at the Western Academy in Friesland under Sibrandus Lubbertus, a notable theologian, and once went with Conrad Koch, now the most vigilant leader of the Church of Schaffhausen, to visit him, and John Dyck of Antwerp, a man distinguished for his learning, was also present, I remember them declaring, with complete freedom from partisanship, that in this learned age the errors of the Papists have been ably attacked by many, but that, apart from Hospinian of Zurich, there is no one who has more successfully won over their minds." Among the works he published are: an oration on the origin and development of ecclesiastical rites and ceremonies (Zurich, 1586); two parts of a History of the Sacramentarians; and the first five books, on the institution of the Lord's Supper and its ceremonies (Zurich, 1598), with the second part following in 1602. Origins of Errors, that is, on the origin, progress, use and abuse of temples, part 1 (Zurich, 1587); On the Origin and Progress of Monasticism, six books (Zurich, 1588); On the Origin of Christian Festivals (Zurich, 1593); On the Origin, Progress, Ceremonies and Rites of the Festivals of the Jews, Greeks, Romans and Turks, three books (Zurich, 1592); a Jesuit History (Zurich, 1619); Discordant Concord, on the origin and development of the Formula of Concord of Bergen (Zurich, 1607); and an oration on the immortality of souls. He published nothing in German except an explanation of the Hymn of Mary, in octavo. In these writings he does not deal only with history but also with doctrine. Everywhere he sets up a refutation, especially against Bellarmine, Baronius, Gretser and others, who draw their arguments for establishing Papism from antiquity. There are also some of his short pieces that are still unpublished [ἀνέκδοτα] and kept by his heirs: 1. On the authority of the Fathers and Councils, arranged in this order: a. general rules are laid down concerning the true antiquity and reading of the Fathers; b. on the writings of the Fathers, some public, some private. Under both headings, he treats first the Canons of the Apostles, the Decretal Letters, the Clementine Constitutions and the Councils; then the writings of Polycarp, Ignatius, Irenaeus, Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria and Origen. Everything is presented in an elegant method, with the passages that are piously said noted first, and the lesser errors pointed out afterwards. Finally, defences of passages attacked by opponents are added. II. On sepulchres and the various burial customs of various nations: he began to write some things on this subject, which would also be worthy of publication.

units.la: Hottingerus, Iob. Henricus, Tigurinus, natus d. 10. Martij 1620. Ab anno 1641. quo, Gallia, Belgio, Anglia peragratis, domum revocatus, publicaeque functioni tum in Patria, tum etiam postea, ultra sexennium Heidelbergae fui admotus, aliquid subinde muginari, & vel invitante officij ratione, vel urgentibus amicis, ad praelum parare studui. Vixi, ante iter Heidelbergense, in patria Professor publicus, Historiae Ecclesiasticae 1642. Theologiae Catecheticae & Linguarum Orientalium 1643. Artium Rhetorologicarum ordinarius, & Theologiae V.T. atque Controversiarum extraordinarie designatus Professor 1653. Heidelbergae vero (quo a Serenissimo Electore Palatino, D. Carolo Ludovico, Domino meo clementissimo, an. Chr. 1655. ad restaurationem Facultatis Theologicae clementissime vocatus concessi,) administravi provinciam Professoris Veteris Testamenti & Linguarum Orientalium; Collegij Sapientiae Inspectoris, Rectoris Academici, Decani Facultatis Theologicae, & Senatus Ecclesiastici Assessoris. Revocatus vero in patriam, ad primariam Profesionem Theologicam, & gratiosissime, a Serenissimo Electore Palatino fui dimissus, & in maximi, nulloque merito expectandi affectus testimonium, Consiliarij Ecclesiastici extraordinarij axiomate honoratus. Toto illo tempore, non potui, quin inter occupationes ordinarias, scriptioni etiam aliquid darem, & meditationibus publicis. Id qua occasione contigerit, breviter primo enarrabo, tum opusculorum meorum Catalogu Alphabeticum dabo; classes deniq; indicabo, in quas digeri illa possent. Scribendi initium feci 1644. ab Exercitationibus Anti-Morinianis, Fervebat eo tempore, & jam ante, controversia de integritate Codicum, tam Veteris Hebraici, quam Graeci Novi Testamenti. Qui ex Pontificijs in Fontes rigidiores erant & iniquiores, omnem inibant rationem, authoritatem eorum labefactandi, & in suspicionem vocandi. Appulerat jam in oras Europaeas Codex Samaritanus, antehac vix de nomine notus. Et quia in Iohannis Morini, Blesensis, hominis
units.tr: Hottingerus, John Henry, of Zurich, born 10 March 1620. From 1641, when I had travelled through France, the Low Countries and England and was called home, I was appointed to a public office, first in my homeland and then, for more than six years, at Heidelberg. Since I was busy with my office, I tried from time to time to put something together and to prepare it for the press, whether urged on by my duties or pressed by friends. Before my journey to Heidelberg I lived in my homeland as a public professor: of Ecclesiastical History from 1642; of Catechetical Theology and the Oriental Languages from 1643; as an ordinary professor of Rhetoric and an extraordinary professor, designated, of Old Testament Theology and Controversies in 1653. At Heidelberg, to which I was graciously called by the most serene Elector Palatine, D. Charles Louis, my most gracious lord, in 1655, for the restoration of the Faculty of Theology, I went and administered the office of professor of the Old Testament and the Oriental Languages; I was Inspector of the College of Wisdom, Academic Rector, Dean of the Faculty of Theology, and assessor of the Ecclesiastical Senate. When I was recalled to my homeland, to the chief theological chair, I was graciously dismissed by the most serene Elector Palatine, and as a testimony of the greatest affection, which I could never have expected or deserved, I was honoured with the title of extraordinary Ecclesiastical Councillor. Throughout that whole time I could not help, amid my ordinary occupations, giving something to writing and to public meditations. I shall briefly relate first how this came about, then give an alphabetical catalogue of my small works, and finally indicate the classes into which they might be arranged. I began writing in 1644 with the Anti-Morinian Exercises. At that time, and already before, the controversy over the integrity of the codices, both of the Hebrew Old Testament and of the Greek New Testament, was raging. Those among the Papists who were more rigid and unfair towards the sources took every means of undermining their authority and bringing it into suspicion. The Samaritan Codex had by then come to the shores of Europe, scarcely known even by name before. And because the novelty of this merchandise first fell into the hands of John Morinus of Blois, a man not unskilled in Oriental literature, but too hostile to the sacred sources, he drew certain arguments against the integrity of the Hebrew text all the more boldly, the more confidently he had presumed that scarcely any of our own men would detect the fraud by a collation of the codices, and would bring the sores of the Samaritan text so openly into the light.

units.la: 1644. 1. minis in literatura Orientali non infeliciter versati, sed in Fontes sacros nimis injurij, primum hæc insolita merx inciderat manus; argumenta quædam contra integritatem Textus Hebraici tanto audacius depromsit, quanto confidentius præsumserat, vix ex nostris quemquam fore, qui Codicum instituta collatione fraudem detegeret, & Contextus Samaritani ulcera adeo aperte protferret in apricum. Nactus ergo & ego Leidæ unum & alterum Codicem, eos inter se & cum textu Hebraico contuli, notavi sphalmata, & malitiâ Samaritanorum, & incuriâ amanuensium intrusa collegi, causæ denique bonæ patrocinium contra Morinum suscepi. Non displicuerunt hæ primitiæ Viris eruditis, qui hinc inde novo Morini conatui finem impositum, publicis testabantur scriptis. Nihil etiam Morinus, diu, post editum tractatum, superstes, repositum.
units.tr: 1644. In literature of the East... [the text continues:] I therefore obtained one or two codices at Leiden myself, compared them with each other and with the Hebrew text, noted the errors, gathered together what had been inserted through the malice of the Samaritans and the carelessness of the scribes, and finally took up the defence of a good cause against Morinus. These first fruits were not displeasing to learned men, who, here and there, testified in published writings that a stop had been put to Morinus's new attempt. Morinus himself, who survived for a long time after his treatise was published, kept nothing in reserve.

units.la: Eodem tempore Guilelmus Gotthardus, Canonicus Solodurensis, Solodurensis scripsit Magnificat (hoc libri nomen est) ubi de Legione Thebæa & Historicè egit, & dogmaticè. Ea, quæ Celeberrimus antehac Ecclesiæ & Scholæ nostræ Theologus, Iohannes Iacobus Huldricus, de religione Felicis & Regulæ (Protevangelistæ illi Tigurinorum habentur, de eadem Legione) piè & solidè collegit, quæque multos post obitum annos inconcussa erant relicta; jam demum Gotthardus allatravit. Erant Viri tum, utriusque ordinis, eruditi, qui modestæ mihi Apologiæ laborem multis nominibus deberi existimârunt, quibus tandem parui, scriptumque vernaculâ Linguâ adornavi, tribus distinctum Tomis, quibus ex Scriptura, & Antiquitate probavi, Ecclesiam Tigurinam, adeóque Reformatam, neque novitatis, neque Apostasiæ accusari posse, utriusque reatum contraxisse Ecclesiam Romanam. Hanc demonstrationem per omnia capita universæ Theologiæ instituì; hactenus tamen ea tantum, quæ de Scriptura agunt, Traditionibus, Deo, cultu Dei, invocatione Sanctorum, cultu imaginum, justificatione hominis coram Deo, & quæ huic sunt affinia, de merito operum, Purgatorio, Indulgentiis, &c. lucem viderunt. Cætera sunt ἀνέκδοτα, ut & altera Apologiæ pars, quæ Gotthardiani scripti refutationem κατὰ πόδα exhibet. Et hoc scriptum bonis viris non displicuit, maximè ob Methodi Historicæ qualemcunque lucem. Ex adversariis Laurentius Forerus, conatui se nostro opponere conatus est. Nunquam vel scopum, vel laborem nostrum aggredi voluit ordine. Quædam hinc inde vellicavit, cui tamen amicis aliquot velitationibus, & Germanicè, in Commercio Epistolico, & in Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ P.I. Latinè abundè responsum fuit. Vellem equidem, universam ea Methodo Theologiam, inter nos & Pontificios controversam, in plebis maximè gratiam absolvi. potuisse. Sed ad alia properandum erat. Et quia Linguæ tum Sanctæ Professio demnadata mihi quoque fuit, de compendio Erotematum cogitavi, quod Grammaticæ nostræ Latinæ, quantum fieri posset, proximè accederet, ne tyronum memoria obrueretur. Duos ergo Erotematum libro
units.tr: At the same time William Gotthard, canon of Solothurn, wrote a book entitled Magnificat (this is the title of the book), in which he dealt with the Theban Legion, both historically and dogmatically. What the most celebrated theologian of our Church and school, John James Ulrich, had previously gathered piously and solidly about the religion of Felix and Regula (who are regarded as the forerunners of the Zurich Church with respect to this same Legion), and which had remained unshaken for many years after his death, Gotthard has now at last barked at. There were then learned men of both orders who judged that the task of a modest apology was owed to me on many grounds; I gave in to them at last, and I wrote in the vernacular, in three volumes, in which I showed from Scripture and antiquity that the Church of Zurich, and therefore the Reformed Church, cannot be accused of novelty or apostasy, and that the Roman Church has incurred the guilt of both. I have carried out this demonstration through all the heads of the whole of theology; so far, however, only those parts have seen the light that deal with Scripture, Traditions, God, the worship of God, the invocation of the saints, the worship of images, the justification of man before God, and what is akin to these, such as merit of works, Purgatory, Indulgences, and so on. The rest remain unpublished [ἀνέκδοτα], as does the second part of the Apology, which gives a refutation of Gotthard's writing at once [κατὰ πόδα]. This writing was also not displeasing to good men, chiefly because of whatever light it shed on the historical method. Among the opponents, Laurence Forer tried to oppose our effort. He never wished to take on either our aim or our labour in an orderly way; here and there he plucked at some points, to which, however, some friends and I replied fully in some skirmishes, in German in our epistolary exchange, and in Latin in part I of the Ecclesiastical History. I would certainly have wished that the whole theology in dispute between us and the Papists could have been set out in this method, especially for the benefit of the common people. But there was haste towards other matters. And because the professorship of the Holy Language had also been entrusted to me, I thought of a compendium of Erotemata, which would come as close as possible to our Latin grammar, so that the memory of beginners would not be overwhelmed. I therefore [composed] two books of Erotemata

units.la: 1647. 4. conscripsi, qui majori eruditorum cum applausu, quàm paucæ illæ pagellæ Grammaticæ merebantur fuerunt excepti. Quoniam verò, quantum in me erat, literarum Hebraicarum culturam revocatam libenter voluissem, de ratione studij illius, ab insigni, quem haberet in omni scientiarum genere, usu commendandi cogitare cæpi. Ordine ergo locorum communium omnia, quæ ad rem faciunt Theologicam, proponere constitui; initio facto à loco de Scriptura, cui proinde Clavis Scripturæ, sive Thesauri Theologici nomen imponere placuit. Eadem serie universam non Theologiam modo, sed Encyclopædiam paulatim congesi: aliis tamen atque aliis subinde distractus occupationibus, indefessæ operæ opus expedire non potui. Compendium tandem Theologiæ Iudaicæ in usum Collegij privati, quo continuationis specimen contractum exhiberem, adornavi & edidi. Accesi anno 1651. ad Editionem Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ. Sceleton initio concepi, paucissimis absolutum foliis, ut Studiosis nostris, quorum in publica Professione Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ erat habenda ratio, sitim nobilissimi studij excitarem. Crevit tamen paulatim opus sub manu, & prælo, ita quidem, ut vix quinque Partibus Historiam N T. ad Reformationem usque deduxerim. Et hunc meum laborem ingenuis (momos, à quibus nec alia, nec meliora facilè expectantur nō curo) non ingratum fuisse, tum ex distracta jam fermè altera Editione, tu ex continuis amicorum, pro pertexenda tela solicitationibus, colligo. Dabo etiam, Cυνδτω operam, ut quam primùm ab aliis, quæ jam me occupant, me expedivero curis, Reformationis Historiam ad manus sumam. Et quia Orientalium, Arabum cumprimis Historiæ, res gestæ, dogmata à nostratibus hactenus vel parcius, vel incertius, ex Itinerarijs ut plurimum de promta, innotuerunt, universali verò Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ pro materiæ ubertate, inseri omnia non potuerunt, novum Historiæ Orientalis opus meditari cæpi. Nec male successisse, iterata brevi temporis intercapedine Editio probavit. Illud dolebam, opus, qua cæptum erat Methodo, absolvi non potuisse. Ne tamen in abstrusiori hac Orientalium Historia, Studiosi quicquam desiderarent, compendiosè in Archæologia Orientali proposui, quod prolixè per commentaria deducere constitueram. Quo cum conjungi potest Heidelbergæ etiam edita Topographia Ecclesiastica Orientalis, brevem omnium Ecclesiarum Orientalium descriptionem exhibens. Id superesse videtur opus ἀπιτωχον, cujus jam antehac prolixius feci mentionem, Alcoranus nempe cum Versione Latina, notis Grammaticis, Historicis, Theologicis, Elencho præsertim absurdisimæ religionis, & Theatrum Muhammedicum πτεράστεγον, quo, quatuor libris, Muhammedanorum persequi volui 1. Ecclesiam. 2. Scholas & Academias 3. politione & militiam. 4. Oeconomiam. Sed neque per operis prolixitatem, neque seculi nostri (quo in mutua malumus fæ vire viscera, & domesticis contabescere contentionibus, quàm de infidelium conversione cogitare, vel eorundem confusione) teporem, multa polliceri vix icebit. Magnatum excitandi sunt animi, quorum aurigante jussu, authoritate mandato, hæcaliquando studia propterea nitori suo & honori restituantur, nediutiùs debitas has officij partes negligamus. Stylo forte feliciùs Muhammedifmus impugnaretur, quàm pilo. Sed antehac publicum hujus conatus dedi Indicem. Perrexi 1652. cùm observarem studij Linguarum Orientalium amore satis jam Studiosos nostros inflammatos, subsidia parare in Dialectos Hebrææ Linguæ usitatissimas, Chaldæam & Syriacam.Grammaticam itaque utriusque adornavi Harmonicam, addita ad calcem appendice philologica, in analysi textuum quorundam Chaldaico-Syriacorum; eorum præsertim, qui vel usu se commendarent, vel Emphasi. Ne vero Auditoribus, pro ratione pensorum diversorum, exercitia deessent disputatoria, Analectorum P.I. conscripsi, quæ varia continet themata Historica, Patristica, Philologica; quam statim anno 1654. excepit Analectorum P.II. dissertationum miscellanearum Pentade absoluta. Utroque hoc scripto ostendi regulas in legendis Patribus observandas: Patrum usum, & abusum, cui, ob ὁμοιοτέλευτον, addidi Confessionem Cyrilli, Scripturæ & Antiquitatis testimonijs vestitam. Ostendi usum Linguæ Hebraicæ contra Pontificios & Anabaptistas: Arabicæ in Theologia, Medicina, juris prudentia, Philosophia & Philologia. Disserui de Heptaplis Parisiensibus, de jubilæo judaico, & Christiano, de terræ motibus, ex mente Hebræorum & Arabum, de necessitate Reformationis superiori seculo institutæ: Addidi Catalogum scriptorum supposititiorum: Specimen Philosophiæ Historicæ: Irenicum Helveticum & Methodum legendi Historias Helveticas. Nihil ferè recensui, quod non sponte natum, & ratio mihi muneris, invitante Auditorum tam publicorum quàm privatorum diligentia, imperaverit. Continuavi studium juvandi literas Orientalas 1655. tantò libentiùs, quantò vidi indies & magis esse Theologicis Scholis necessarium, & minùs tamen illud coli. Aggressus igitur sum Νομοθεσίαν Mosaicam, ad mentem R. Levi Barcelonitæ, qui compendiosè 613. Mosis præcepta explicuit, & ea quidem Methodo, ob quam mihi à Celeb. D. D. Lempereur, Leidæ pridem ille erat commendatus. Præstuli hunc aliis scriptorem, ut non tantùm in Theologia; sed etiam juris prudentia usum Linguæ Hebraicæ monstrarem. Sed, itinere tum Heidelbergensi occupatus, Leges tantùm 261. absolvi. Catalogum verò omnium præceptorum Mosaicorum, juxta locos communes Majmonidis dispositorum, cum notis & observationibus brevissimis Heidelbergæ edidi 1661. Heidelbergam ergò tum ad Theologicam, tum Linguarum Orientalium Professionem vocatus, utriusq; in publicis scriptis, pro virili, rationem habui. Præmissa enim 1656. Oratione secuları de Collegio Sapientiæ, Notis annexis de Heidelbergensis Academiæ origine, progressu, privilegijs, Linguarum culturam propterea negligere nolui, quòd vererer semper (nec dum evanuit justissimus metus) ne, expulso paulatim & ejecto nobilissimo pariter atque utilissimo Linguarum Originalium studio, barbaries & servitus pristina pastina rediret. Quod si alij, in gravioribus me tum occupatum maluissent, nõrint, non defuisset, qui, cum alia magno cum fructu tractarent, ad haec accedere vel nollent, vel non possent. Malui proinde, quantum in me erat, laborantes juvare, quàm triumphantibus suppetias obtrudere. Accesi igitur an. Chr. 1657 ad tractatum de vario Linguarum Orientalium usu, cui Smegmatis indidi nomen (ex Ier. 22.2.) quod sordibus Barbarismi esset oppositus, an. Chr. 1658 ad promtuarium, five Bibliothecam Orientalem; Grammaticam quatuor Linguarum Hebraicae, Chaldaicae, Syriacae & Arabicae Harmonicam. Technologiam Linguae Arabicae Historico-Theologicam: an Chr 1659 addidi Cippos Hebraicos, item duas differtationes, alterum de variis Orientis monumentis, mensuris, & inscriptionibus, alteram de nummis Orientalium, Hebraeorum maximè & Arabum. Tandem & Etymologicum Orientale, five Lexicon Harmonicum Heptaglottum extortum mihi est, opus ad usum magis, quàm speciem accommodatum, cui Apologia accedit contra Abrahamum Ecchellensem: Maronitam. Prodijt Francofurti 1661. In Theologicis, lectiones quasdam evolare in publicum passus sum, tum etiam disputationes, tam ordinarias quàm extraordinarias. Ex illis sunt Hexaemeron Heidelbergae editum, & Doxiμασία Abrahami, specimina Theologiae Exegeticae, diversa Methodo tractata, alterum magis Theoretica, vero alterum magis Practica. Quam posteriorem magnis Viris ita probari animadverti, ut celeberrimi nominis Doctor & suo, & aliorum nomine, non ita pridem hunc in modum ad me scripserit: Vix credis, quantum me tum Abrahami Doximasia caperit; nec me solum, sed & alios, qui legere. Non posse se lectione ejus saturari, scripsit nuper quidam ex primarijs Ecclesiarum Senioribus ad me, eoque magis incendi, quo sapius legisset. Thesaurum auro cariorem habere nos, si pergeres: Veraque haec & accurata Bibliica Historia esset Oeconomia. Per Deum immortalem oro, ne Ecclesiae desis! Credéque vix ex Tetrastego Theatro (quamvis & hoc opus utilissimum est) tantum ad Christianam Ecclesiam perventurum commodi, quantum ex tali sacrorum librorum elucidatione. Sororio hic vinculo sociatà habemus Theoriam & Praxin. Quod de Theatro Vir doctissimus monet, jam nuper, ante caetera, Anti-Muhamedica amici expectarunt. Ego à te expectabam (ita nuperrimè vir amicissimus) Alcorani editionem cum versione & refutatione, quod argumentum hactenus nemo simul occupavit, primam ejus partem nullus unquam. Mallent alij praecurrere Historiam Reformationis, quo nomine paucis ab hinc diebus magnus viraurem denuo vellicavit. Constitui, ubi Deus salvum me voluerit, serio, illi incumbere curae, ut tandem aliquando tot piorum votis, quantum in me est
units.tr: 1647. 4. I wrote these, and they were received with greater applause from the learned than those few little pages of Grammar deserved. Since, however, as far as lay in me, I had gladly wished to revive the cultivation of Hebrew letters, I began to consider how to recommend the study of it by the notable use it has in every kind of learning. I therefore resolved to set out, in the order of the commonplaces, everything that bears on theology, beginning with the topic of Scripture, to which I decided to give the title Key to Scripture, or Theological Treasury. In the same sequence I gradually compiled not only a theology but a whole encyclopedia, yet, drawn away from time to time by other occupations, I could not finish a work that needed unwearied labour. At length I prepared and published a Compendium of Jewish Theology for the use of a private college, to show in an abridged form a specimen of the continuation. In 1651 I turned to the edition of the Ecclesiastical History. I first conceived a skeleton, completed on very few leaves, so that I might stir a thirst for this most noble study in our students, for whom the public lectures on Ecclesiastical History were to be given. Yet the work grew little by little under my hand and in the press, so that I had scarcely brought the history of the New Testament down to the Reformation in five parts. And I gather that this labour of mine has not been unwelcome to honest men (I do not care for the carpers, from whom neither other nor better things are easily to be expected), both from the second edition, now almost sold out, and from the constant urging of friends to go on with the web. I shall also take pains [συντόμως] to take up the history of the Reformation as soon as I have freed myself from the other cares that now occupy me. And since the deeds and doctrines of the Orientals, above all the history of the Arabs, have hitherto become known to our countrymen either sparingly or uncertainly, chiefly from travel accounts, and since they could not all be inserted into the general Ecclesiastical History because of the richness of the material, I began to plan a new work, the Oriental History. That it turned out well, the edition repeated after a short interval proved. I grieved that the work could not be finished on the plan on which it had begun. Yet, so that the students might lack nothing in this rather obscure history of the Orientals, I set out briefly in the Oriental Archaeology what I had intended to develop at length in commentaries. With this may be joined the Oriental Ecclesiastical Topography, also published at Heidelberg, which gives a brief description of all the Eastern Churches. There remains, it seems, the unlucky work [ἀπότυχον], of which I made mention before at greater length: the Alcoran itself, with a Latin version, grammatical, historical and theological notes, and above all a refutation of that most absurd religion; and the Muhammedan Theatre [πτερόστεγον], in which I wished to pursue in four books the Muhammedans as to 1. their Church, 2. their schools and academies, 3. their polity and military affairs, 4. their household economy. But I can hardly promise much, neither because of the length of the work nor because of the coolness of our age (in which we would rather tear at each other's vitals and waste away in domestic quarrels than think about the conversion of unbelievers, or about their confusion). Men of rank must be stirred up, whose command and authority might at some time restore these studies to their lustre and honour, lest we go on neglecting these duties of our office for longer. Perhaps Muhammedanism could be assailed more happily with the pen than with the sword. But I earlier published a public index of this project. In 1652, since I observed that our students were already sufficiently inflamed with love for the study of the Oriental languages, I set about preparing aids in the most common dialects of the Hebrew tongue, Chaldee and Syriac. So I prepared a Grammar of each, combined as a Harmony, with a philological appendix added at the end, in an analysis of certain Chaldee-Syriac texts, especially those which recommended themselves either by use or by emphasis. Lest the hearers lack exercises for disputation, suited to the different kinds of assignments, I wrote the first part of the Analecta, which contains various historical, patristic and philological themes; in 1654 it was followed at once by the second part of the Analecta, a completed pentad of miscellaneous dissertations. In both writings I showed the rules to be observed in reading the Fathers, their use and abuse; to this, on account of the homoeoteleuton, I added Cyril's Confession, clothed with the testimonies of Scripture and antiquity. I showed the use of the Hebrew tongue against the Papists and the Anabaptists; of Arabic in theology, medicine, jurisprudence, philosophy and philology. I discussed the Parisian Heptaplas, the Jewish and the Christian jubilee, the earthquakes according to the mind of the Hebrews and the Arabs, and the necessity of the Reformation instituted in the last century. I added a catalogue of spurious writings, a Specimen of Historical Philosophy, the Swiss Irenicum and a Method of Reading Swiss Histories. I have recounted almost nothing that did not arise of its own accord, and that the duty of my office did not require, prompted by the diligence of my hearers, both public and private. In 1655 I continued the effort to help the Oriental letters, all the more gladly as I saw day by day that it was more and more necessary for the theological schools, and yet was cultivated the less. So I undertook the Mosaic Legislation, according to the mind of R. Levi of Barcelona, who briefly explained the 613 precepts of Moses, and indeed by the method for which the late Celebrated Dr. Lempereur had long ago commended him to me at Leiden. I preferred this writer to others so that I might show the use of the Hebrew tongue not only in theology but also in jurisprudence. But, then occupied with the journey to Heidelberg, I finished only 261 laws. However, I published at Heidelberg in 1661 a Catalogue of all the Mosaic precepts, arranged according to the commonplaces of Maimonides, with brief notes and observations. Therefore, summoned to Heidelberg to the theological and also to the Oriental language professorship, I took account of both, as far as I could, in my public writings. For, after the Secular Oration on the College of Wisdom had been prefaced in 1656, with notes annexed on the origin, progress and privileges of the Heidelberg Academy, I was unwilling to neglect the cultivation of languages, because I always feared (and that most just fear has not yet vanished) that, once this most noble and equally most useful study of the original languages had been gradually driven out and cast away, the former barbarism and slavery might return. If others had preferred that I be occupied then with weightier matters, let them know that there would not have been lacking men who, while they were handling other things with great profit, either would not or could not turn to these. I preferred, therefore, as far as I could, to help those who were labouring, rather than to force aid upon those who were already triumphing. So in the year of Christ 1657 I turned to a treatise on the various use of the Oriental languages, to which I gave the title Smegma (from Jeremiah 22:2), because it was set against the filth of barbarism; in the year of Christ 1658 to a handbook, or Oriental Library, a Harmonic Grammar of the four languages, Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic, and a historical-theological Technology of the Arabic language; in the year of Christ 1659 I added Hebrew Cippi, likewise two dissertations, one on the various Oriental monuments, measures and inscriptions, the other on the coins of the Orientals, chiefly the Hebrews and the Arabs. At last the Oriental Etymologicon, or Harmonic Heptaglot Lexicon, was wrested from me, a work suited more to use than to show, to which an Apology is added against Abraham Ecchellensis, the Maronite. It came out at Frankfurt in 1661. In theological matters I allowed some lectures to fly out into public, and also disputations, both ordinary and extraordinary. Among these are the Hexaemeron published at Heidelberg and the Doximasia of Abraham, specimens of Theological Exegesis treated by different methods, the one more theoretical, the other more practical. I have noticed that the latter was so approved by great men that a doctor of most celebrated name wrote to me not long ago, in his own name and in that of others, in this manner: You can hardly believe how much Abraham's Doximasia captivated me then, and not only me but others who read it. Someone from the foremost seniors of the Churches wrote to me recently that he could not be satisfied with reading it, and was all the more inflamed the more often he had read it. We hold the treasure dearer than gold; if you would go on, and this true and accurate Biblical History would be an economy. I beg you by the immortal God, do not fail the Church! And I believe that from such an elucidation of the sacred books the Christian Church will derive no less advantage than from the Tetrastegon Theatre (although that work too is most useful). Here we have theory and practice joined by a sisterly bond. As the most learned man advises concerning the Theatre, friends have lately been looking forward, before the rest, to the Anti-Muhammedan works. I was expecting from you (so a most friendly man wrote very recently) an edition of the Alcoran with version and refutation, a subject which no one has yet taken up at the same time, and no one ever the first part of it. Others would prefer to run ahead with the History of the Reformation, for which name a great man lately plucked my ear again after a few days. I have resolved, if God will have me safe, to devote myself earnestly to that task, so that at last I may satisfy, as far as I can, the prayers of so many pious people.

units.la: 16. 1657. 17. 1658. 18. 19. 1659. .est satis faciam. Exhis vero dedi & Primitias Heidelbergenses, & fasciculum Disputationum Heidelbergensium: Selectum utrobique instituì thematum, & in illis quidem exhibui disputationes, de medijs explicandis Scripturæ; de Reformationis causa efficiente & materiali; de usu scriptorum Hebraicorum in N. T. Addidi Meletemata Irenica; Sabbathismum, sive dissertationes de Sabbatho Iudaico, Christiano, Mariano, Muhammedico, Gentili, & Idolographiam V. T. In hoc vero de Resurrectione mortuorum; Notis Ecclesiæ visibilis, de Translationibus Bibliorum in varias Linguas Vernaculas, occasione operis Anglicani, de Nominibus Dei Orientalium: Attributis Hebraeorum. Accesserunt duæ quæstionum Philologico-Theologicarum centuriæ de Principiis fidei Christianæ in genere, & verbo Dei in specie: Cursus Theologicus Altingiana Methodo expositus, cum Oratione de requisitis Theologi. Hæc Heidelbergæ ad an. Chr. 1661. exeuntem edita sunt. Reliquas Disputationes domum reversus Enneade fui complexus, adjectis publicis quibusdam Programmatibus Academicis. Habet autem Enneas disputationes sequentes, de libris V. T. suppositiis, Prophetia præfertim Enochi, & Samaritanorum libro Josuæ, indeque deducto compendio Theologiæ Samaritica Ασκιμασια Abrahami; Paradiso; Necessitate Ministerij Ecclesiastici; Baptismo, Melchisedeco, annexa brevi Apologia contra Labbæum Iesuitam, de causis Cœnæ Dominicæ, cui subjungitur specimen analyseos sacræ, de sensu verborum: Hoc est corpus meum; de Leone Allatio nimiæ temeritatis convicio, & perpetuo Ecclesiarum Latina & Græca dissensu: Subjicitur compendium Theologiæ judaicæ, de quo supra. In patria paulatim ad eadem iterum me studia accinxi. Ut Auditores nostros occuparem, non minus utilibus, quàm varijs exercitijs, disputationes instituì Philologicas, & Theologicas, tam Topicas, quàm Textuales, quarum brevi iterum, ut spero, fasciculum habebimus. Synodales nostras, Textuales esse malui, ut haberent non Studiosi tantùm, sed & alij rationem & modum sacram Scripturam Methodicè explicandi, & ad usum Practicum revocandi. Prodierunt autem potissimum disputationes de Theologia, de Virtutibus boni Interpretis de Sophismatis Theologicis, de lectione & interpretatione Scripturæ, de Theologia Catechetica. Addidi specimen Philologiæ Sacræ, ex c. 5. Matthæi propria ejus sede. Amicorum etiam perpetuis solicitationibus impulsus, aggressus sum Bibliothecarium qui jam sub prælo est, sive, Tractatum, tam de Bibliothecis in genere, quàm Theologica in specie, Origines item Scholæ Tigurinorum Carolinæ, sive Historicam demonstrationem, Scholam Reipublicæ Tigurinæ à Carolo Marcellendam, addita Bibliotheca Tigurina, sive Catalogo eorum, qui vel Tigurinæ, vel Tiguri publicis, indeà multis seculis ; inclaruerunt scriptis.
