Crederis in felix scuticae tremefactus habenis. In sinistra manu scalprum. Hic sedet Donatus, Aristarchus, & Apostata Priscianus. Secunda Dialectica, habens in dextra, secundum quosdam florem: In sinistra, scorpium caudae penitus aculeatae. Alij tamen dicunt, quod in una manu habeat scorpium, in altera crucibolum cum lychno ardente. Hic sedet Porphyrius, Aristoteles, Zeno. Tertia Rhetorica, habens in dextera gladium, & in sinistra librum; secundum alios libram seu stateram. Hic sedet Tullius, qui & Marcus vel Cicero. Item Erinodius, seu Crinodius, Quintilianus, Symmachus, Sidonius. Quarta Arithmetica, habens in dextra quasi Indicam, per quam algorisat in cinere, vel arena, & omnia de numero perscribit. Hic sedet Nicomachus, Gilbertus, Pythagoras, Chrysippus. Quinta Musica, habens in sinistra Citharam, in dextra plectrum, quo tangit Chordas. Hic sedet Milesius, Micalus, Gregorius Papa, de quo Anti Claudianus: Navigat in medio, partemque relinquit utramque, Gregorius noster refugitque pericula vocis. Sexta Geometria capite enclitico, & hanc virgam virgo gerit, qua totum circuit orbem; qua spatium terrae metitur, qua mare claudit, limitibus certis, qua circinat ardua cali. Hic sedet Thales, Euclides, & alij quam plurimi. Septima Astronomia, cui non morbo, non maestitia, non mente magistra degenerat caput in terram, sed vultus in astris haeret. Haec in manu habet sphaeram: Hic sedet AlbuMasar, Atlas, & alij quam plures.
units.tr: Finally, let the third example be the word philosophy. Philosophy is the true grasp of the secrets of nature. Or, philosophy is the true comprehension of things which are and are not seen, and of things which are and are seen, and it is set out under various aspects. Under it are the seven liberal arts. The first is Grammar, of childlike form, holding in her right hand a palmer or ferule, or a whip, that is, a scourge made of weals or thongs. Ovid, Epistles: "You are believed happy, trembling under the reins of the whip." In her left hand a penknife. Here sit Donatus, Aristarchus and the apostate Priscian. The second is Dialectic, holding in her right hand, according to some, a flower; in her left, a scorpion with its tail thoroughly armed with a sting. Others, however, say that she holds the scorpion in one hand and in the other a crucible with a burning lamp. Here sit Porphyry, Aristotle and Zeno. The third is Rhetoric, holding a sword in her right hand and a book in her left; according to others, a balance or scales. Here sits Tully, who is also called Marcus or Cicero. Likewise Erinodius, or Crinodius, Quintilian, Symmachus, Sidonius. The fourth is Arithmetic, holding in her right hand what is like an Indian abacus, by which she calculates in ash or sand and writes out everything about number. Here sit Nicomachus, Gilbert, Pythagoras and Chrysippus. The fifth is Music, holding a cithara in her left hand and in her right a plectrum with which she touches the strings. Here sit Milesius, Micalus, Pope Gregory, concerning whom Claudian says: "He sails through the middle, and leaves both sides, and our Gregory flees the dangers of the voice." The sixth is Geometry, with her head bent down, and a maiden carries this rod, by which she measures the whole circle of the globe; by which she measures the extent of the earth, by which she shuts in the sea with fixed limits, by which she measures the lofty heights of heaven. Here sit Thales, Euclid and very many others. The seventh is Astronomy, whose head, not made degenerate by illness, nor by sadness, nor with the mind as teacher, does not sink to the earth, but her face clings to the stars. In her hand she holds a sphere. Here sit Albumasar, Atlas and very many others.

units.la: Item Philosophia subsunt Theorica, Practica, & Logica. Et haec Practica, quam nos possumus dicere actualem, dividitur in Ethicam, qua dicitur moralis, & Oeconomicam, qua dicitur dispensativa, & Politicam, qua dicitur civilis. Similiter Logica dividitur in Dialecticam disputatoriam; in Epidicticam, id est, demonstrativam, in Sophisticam, id est, deceptoriam & fraudulentam.
units.tr: Likewise under philosophy are subsumed the theoretical, the practical and the logical. This practical part, which we may call active, is divided into ethics, which is called moral; economics, which is called domestic; and politics, which is called civil. Similarly, logic is divided into disputatious dialectic; into epideictic, that is, demonstrative; and into sophistic, that is, deceptive and fraudulent.

units.la: Item Philosophia secundum alios, & alio respectu, dividitur in Ethicam, Physicam, Logicam; & ista tres multipliciter subdividuntur. Philosophus est sapientiae amator, naturalium que rerum & secretorum diligens indagator. Nomen autem Philosophorum a Pythagora est inventum. Nam dum antea Graeci Veteres Sophos, id est, sapientes, aut Doctores sapientiae se ipsos jactanter nominarent; ipse Pythagoras interrogatus, quid prositeretur, jactantiam vitans, dixit, se esse Philosophum, id est, amatorem scientiae. Philosophi in tria genera dividuntur. Nam Physici de Naturis, Ethici de moribus, Logici de Naturis & vocibus assignant rationem.
units.tr: Again, philosophy according to others, and in another respect, is divided into ethics, physics and logic; and these three are subdivided in many ways. A philosopher is a lover of wisdom and a diligent searcher into natural things and secrets. The name of philosophers, however, was invented by Pythagoras. For whereas formerly the ancient Greeks called themselves boastfully sophoi, that is, wise men, or teachers of wisdom, Pythagoras himself, when asked what he professed, avoiding boastfulness, said that he was a philosopher, that is, a lover of learning. Philosophers are divided into three kinds. For physicists give an account of natures, ethicists of morals, and logicians of natures and words.

units.la: Et sunt divisi in suis haeresibus, habentes nomina vel ex authore, ut Platonici, Pythagorici; vel a locis conventiculorum, ut Stoici, Academici, vel a modo vivendi, ut Peripatetici, Epicurai, Cynici. Inter Philosophos famosiores sectae videntur Stoici, Epicurai, Peripatetici.
units.tr: And they are divided into their own heresies (sects), having names either from their author, as the Platonists, the Pythagoreans; or from the places of their meetings, as the Stoics, the Academics; or from their way of life, as the Peripatetics, the Epicureans, the Cynics. Among the more famous philosophical sects appear to be the Stoics, the Epicureans and the Peripatetics.

units.la: Ordine tum Alphabethico Philosophos recenseт Graecos, Arabes bes & Latinos: Sententias denique quorumdam acutiores subjicit hac serie. Anacreon: Turpe quid ausurus, te, sine teste, time. Aristoteles: Dubitare de singulis, non erit inutile. Item idem: Servi liberique personam mendacium miscet. Item idem: Adversum inimicos, intra parietes noltros, victoriam stra quaerenda est. Item idem: Injuria injustè irrogata ejus infamia est, qui facit. Viri boni est scire pati, nec facere injuriam. Solum hoc incommodum egestas patitur, quod non possit egentibus subvenire. Bias: Molestius est inter duos amicos, quàm inter duos inimicos judicare. Chilon: Tristia cunctìa exupero, vel animo, vel amico. Demades: Amico mutuam me roganti pecuniam tradens, & ipsum & pecuniam perdo. Democritus: Qui falsò laudat, amico nocet. Idem: Non opto uteos, qui divites sunt, amicos habeam. Demosthenes: Liberi servique personam veritas separat. Item: Optimum est mori, dum juvat vivere. Dionysius: Cuidam eum laudanti dixit: Adulator define utrumque fallere, cùm te intelligam, nihil proficis. Item: Beata Civitas, quae in pace bellum timet. Ennius: Animus aeger neque pati, neque perpeti potest, cupere nunquam desinit. Munus est animi, ratione bene uti. Epimenon: Inimicos meos, praestando beneficium, torqueo. Euclides: Plerique hominum stultisunt, qui servi-les cibos, & servilem fugiunt vestem, serviles mores non fugiunt. Educatio & disciplina mores faciunt. Galenus: Optimae habitudines, cùm in summo sunt, selvuntur. Item: Illi tantum placere stude, cuidisplicet, quod omnibus placet. Hermogenes: Plerique homines in suis domibus saevisimi tyranni, sed in alienis homilimi servi sunt. Julius Caesar: Acceptum beneficium aeternae memoriae est infigendum. Menefres: Occasio non accipi, sed rapi debet; Si rationem non eventum applicas causae. Ovidius: Est virtus placitis abstinuisse bonis. Plato: Amicus diu quaeritur, vix invenitur, difficile observatur. Item: Eadem verisimè est justitia, quae erga inferiores servatur. Item: Triumphus innocentiae est non peccare, ubi liceat. Item: In quem plus potes peccare, define. Pythagoras: Duo genera lachrymarum habentur in oculis faeminarum, unum veri doloris, aliud insidiarum. Phitacus: Loqui ignorabit, qui tacere nescit. Seneca: Secundae res amicos parant, adversae probant. Simonides, cùm interrogaretur, quid inter homines facilè confenescceret, respondit, beneficium. Socrates: Deum reverere, homines ama. Item: Stultum est, ut quis velit aliis imperare, cùm sibi imperare non possit. Soter: Nocere nescit, qui se nocere velle prodiderit. Theophrastus: Expedit jam probatos amicos amare, non amatos probare. Tullius: Vera amicitia est idem velle, & idem nolle. Xenocrates: Absenti loquitur, qui cum ebrio litigat: Item: Locutum me aliquando poenituit, tacuisse nunquam. Xenophon: Maledicenti sibi cuidam, tu, inquit, maledixisti, ego, conscientia teste, didici maledicta contemnere. Xixius: Nihil est, quòd non toleret, qui persectè diligit. Subscriptae verò sententiae dicuntur septem Sapientum. Bias: Quid stulti proprium? Non posse, & velle nocere. Theobulus: Quid prudentis opus? Cùm posit , nolle nocere. Quæ casta est? De qua mentiri fama veretur. Quæ dos matronis pulcherrima? Vita pudica. Pernicies hominis, quæ maxima? Solus homo alter. Quis dives? Qui nulla cupit. Quis pauper? Avarus. Quænam summa boni? Mens semper conscia recti. Hæc paulò prolixiùs de Fabulario Conradi de Mure (quod Lexici Historico-Poetici nomen non immeritò obtineat) tum ut videat Lector, quid illud fit, quod tantopere commendat tum ut constet, quæ in Philologia profana jam ante aliquot secula Scholæ Tigurinæ Præsides tentârint. Pergo jam ad reliqua ejus opera. Idem emendavit novum Græcilmum. Tractatum scripsit carmine de naturis animalium. Libellum de Sacramentis. Felicis & Regulæ Pasionem. Libellum de proprijs nominibus fluviorum & montium. Cathedrale Romanum. Laudes Beatæ Virginis. Clypearium Theutonicorum. Catalogum Romanorum Pontificum & Imperatorum. Commendatitia Rodolphi, Regis Romanorum. Ea, nisi fallor, sunt, quæ Dominicus, Abbas Murensis, non ita pridem edidit. Scripsit etiam Genealogiam & gesta Caroli Magni, excerpta ex plurimis Historijs, & Chronicis compilata. Eidem tribuitur Breviarium Chori Thuricensis an. Chr. 1260. collectum, quod in pergameno scriptum etiamnum in Bibliotheca Carolina asservatur. In usu fuit, etsi hinc inde auctum, mutatum &c. feré usque ad Reformationem, ut supra in Felice monuimus. De hoc scripto alibi plura loquemur. Sed quid si ipsum authorem audiamus, ordine scripta sua enarrantem, causàsque institui sic exponentem: Teste Philosopho (ita ille) quiddam prodire tenus, si non datur ultra. Est enim melius aliquid boni, quàm nihil obtinere. Igitur, cùm ego de Pegaseo fonte potus paulisper ferventer cupidus inter alia mei monumenta, de mea penuria & tenuitate aliquid utile, in Grammaticalium iterum projicere Apothecam istius Fabularij compilatione, ordinatione, non solùm ætate, sed etiam ruditate parvulus, circa Poëtica figmenta, sub spe ad altiora proficiendi, studentibus, non inutiliter sic ut spero, laboravimus. Et tandem, licet difficulter, tamen per Dei gratiam, à quo cuncta bona procedunt, finem laboris utcunque sum assecutus. Non improvidè audituris ipsum opusculum attentè supplico & lectoris, ut dent veniam, si quis in eo, propter insufficientiam compilantis vel festinantiam, sive scriptorum ignorantiam, defectus poterit inveniri. Nam, inter mortalia, nihil omnie ex parte beatum. Præterea exercitium additionis & limam correctionis relinquo posteris & commit- 10, to, quia non dedignor à contemporaneis, seu ipsis posteris bonum Zelum habentibus, in eodem opusculo superfluum eradi, diminutum supplevi, & quocunque modo mendosum emendari. Et si quis rationabilibus ex causis improbat operis imperfectionem, aliem approbet compilantis intentionem, ad quam summè justi judicis examine singula referuntur. Juxta illud: Quicquid agunt homines, intentio judicat omnes. Item: ut desint vires, tamen est laudanda voluntas. Item: Ultra posse meum non me Lex ulla coëgit: Nec reor esse reum, qui totum posse peregit. Item, paupercula in Evangelio pro duobus minutis, quae in Jerusalem devotè projecit in gazophylacium, plus aliis, qui multò majora in re offerebant, à Domino commendatur. Ipse enim Deus non attendit quid, sed ex quanto. Sed licèt in curiis Principum & Magnatum, in regimine Scholarium, in convictu sodalium, plurimos fecerim versiculos, ut taceam de profaice dictatis, de quibus omnibus nihil ad praesens; jam enim extra numerum & memoriam sunt, tamen non ex praesumtuosa de meo ingenio jactantia; sed ad gloriam Dei qui Trinus in personis, unus in essentia, suorum actibus fidelium benignè adspirans bonum principium, melius medium, finem optimum elargitur miseri corditer & affluenter. Hic per stringam meorum numerum & ordinem libellorum, versiculis eorundem supputatis opinabiliter & distinctè:
units.tr: Next, in alphabetical order, he lists the philosophers, Greek, Arabic and Latin, and finally sets out in this sequence some of the sharper sayings of certain of them. Anacreon: About to do something shameful, fear yourself, even with no witness present. Aristotle: It will not be useless to doubt each single thing. Likewise, the same: A lie mixes up the role of slave and free man. Likewise, the same: Against enemies, victory must be sought within our own walls. Likewise, the same: An injury unjustly inflicted brings disgrace on the one who inflicts it. It is the mark of a good man to know how to suffer, and not to do injury. Poverty suffers only this one inconvenience, that it cannot help the needy. Bias: It is more troublesome to judge between two friends than between two enemies. Chilon: I surpass all sorrows, whether of mind or of friend. Demades: When I hand over money to a friend who asks me for a loan, I lose both him and the money. Democritus: Whoever praises falsely harms a friend. Again, the same: I do not wish to have friends who are rich. Demosthenes: Truth separates the role of free man from that of slave. Likewise: It is best to die when living no longer helps. Dionysius: To a certain man who was praising him he said: Flatterer, define both things, since I understand you, you achieve nothing. Likewise: Happy is the state that fears war in time of peace. Ennius: A sick mind can neither bear nor endure, yet it never stops desiring. It is the gift of the mind to use reason well. Epimenides: By conferring a benefit I torment my enemies. Euclid: Most men are foolish: they flee servile food and servile clothing, but they do not flee servile manners. Upbringing and discipline make character. Galen: The best constitutions are the most easily destroyed when they are at their height. Likewise: Strive to please only the one whom what pleases all displeases. Hermogenes: Most men are the cruelest tyrants in their own homes, but the most abject slaves in other people's. Julius Caesar: A benefit received must be fixed in eternal memory. Menander: An opportunity must not be accepted but seized; you apply reason, not chance, to the cause. Ovid: It is virtue to abstain from what is pleasing and good. Plato: A friend is sought for a long time, is scarcely found, and is hard to keep. Likewise: That justice is truly the same which is observed towards inferiors. Likewise: The triumph of innocence is not to sin when one is free to do so. Likewise: Define the one against whom you can sin the most. Pythagoras: There are two kinds of tears found in women's eyes, one of true grief, the other of deceit. Pittacus: He will not know how to speak who does not know how to keep silent. Seneca: Prosperity makes friends, adversity proves them. Simonides, when asked what among men is most easily worn out, replied: a benefit. Socrates: Revere God, love men. Likewise: It is foolish for a man to want to rule others when he cannot rule himself. Soter: He does not know how to harm who has declared that he wishes to harm. Theophrastus: It is now expedient to love friends who have been tested, and to test those who have not been loved. Tullius: True friendship is to will the same things and to refuse the same things. Xenocrates: He who quarrels with a drunkard speaks to one who is absent. Likewise: I have sometimes regretted speaking, but never regretted keeping silent. Xenophon: When a certain man spoke evil of him, he said: You have spoken evil of me, but I, with my conscience as witness, have learned to despise evil speech. Xixius: There is nothing that one who loves perfectly will not bear. The following sayings are said to be those of the Seven Sages. Bias: What is peculiar to a fool? Not to be able to harm, and yet to want to. Theobulus: What is the work of a wise man? When he is able to harm, to be unwilling to do so. Who is chaste? She of whom rumour fears to speak ill. What is the most beautiful dowry for matrons? A modest life. What is the greatest ruin of a man? Another man like himself. Who is rich? He who desires nothing. Who is poor? The covetous man. What is the highest good? A mind always conscious of what is right. I have written this at somewhat greater length about the Fabulary of Conrad of Mure (which may not unfairly claim the name of a historico-poetic lexicon), so that the reader may see what it is that he commends so highly, and so that it may be clear what the Presidents of the Zurich School attempted in profane philology some centuries ago. I now proceed to his other works. He also corrected the New Graecismus. He wrote a treatise in verse on the natures of animals. A little book on the Sacraments. The Passion of Felix and Regula. A little book on the proper names of rivers and mountains. The Cathedral Roman. Praises of the Blessed Virgin. The Shield of the Germans. A catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs and Emperors. The letters of recommendation of Rudolf, King of the Romans. These are, unless I am mistaken, the works which Dominic, Abbot of Mure, published not long ago. He also wrote a genealogy and deeds of Charlemagne, excerpted from very many histories and compiled from chronicles. To him is also attributed the Breviary of the Zurich Choir, collected in the year of Christ 1260, which, written on parchment, is still kept in the Carolingian Library. It was in use, though altered and enlarged here and there, almost until the Reformation, as we noted above in the account of Felix. We shall say more about this writing elsewhere. But what if we hear the author himself, setting out his writings in order and explaining the causes of his undertaking? He says: "As the Philosopher (so he writes) testifies, something is produced as far as it can be, if nothing more is given. For it is better to obtain some good than nothing. Therefore, when I, having drunk for a little while eagerly from the Pegasean spring, among my other records, once again put out into the grammatical storehouse something useful from my poverty and meagreness, I laboured, as I hope, not uselessly, by compiling and arranging this Fabulary, being a child not only in age but also in rawness, over poetic fictions, for the sake of students, in the hope of advancing to higher things. And at last, although with difficulty, yet by the grace of God, from whom all good things proceed, I have in some way reached the end of my labour. I humbly ask the readers who are to hear this little work not to hear it without care, and I ask them to pardon whatever defects may be found in it, on account of the compiler's insufficiency or haste, or his ignorance of the writers. For among mortal things nothing is wholly blessed. Besides, I leave the task of addition and the file of correction to posterity, and I commit it to them, because I do not disdain to have superfluous matter erased, deficiencies supplied, and whatever is faulty corrected in any way in this little work, by those who are my contemporaries or by posterity itself, who have a good zeal. And if anyone for reasonable causes disapproves of the imperfection of the work, let him approve the intention of the compiler, to which, by the examination of the most just Judge, all things are referred. According to that saying: Whatever men do, intention judges all. Likewise: though strength is lacking, the will is still to be praised. Likewise: No law has compelled me beyond my power, nor do I think him guilty who has accomplished all he could. Likewise, the poor widow in the Gospel, who cast two small coins devoutly into the treasury at Jerusalem, is commended by the Lord above others who offered much larger sums. For God does not regard what is given but how much is given from. But although in the courts of princes and magnates, in the governing of scholars, and in the company of comrades, I have written very many little verses, to say nothing of the prose compositions, of all of which nothing is needed for the present, since they are now beyond number and memory, nevertheless I do this not from presumptuous boasting of my talent, but for the glory of God, who is Three in persons and One in essence, who graciously breathes good beginnings into the acts of his faithful, grants a better middle and the best end, lovingly and abundantly to the wretched. Here I set out briefly, by counting the verses, the number and order of my little books, in a clear and distinct estimate:"

units.la: Novus Graecismus, hujus circiter 10. millia quingentos sexaginta versus. Libellus de Sacramentis circiter 4. millia, & fortè paulò minus. Pasio sanctorum nostrorum Felicis & Regulae, & Exuperantij circiter 3. millia, & fortè paulò minus. Libellus de proprijs nominibus fluviorum & montium circiter mille quingentos, Cathedrale Romanum circiter mille centum triginta. Laudes Beatae Virginis, super quinque Ave Maria, circiter trecentos. Clipearium Theutonicorum circiter centum sexaginta. Catalogus Romanorum Paparum, & Imperatorum circiter mille sexcentos, quadraginta. Commendatitia Serenissimi Rodolphi Regis Romanorum semper Augusti, circiter octingentos. Hac autem non pono tanquam arrogans, & inanis gloriae appetitor; sed ut Auditores ad inertis otij detestationem & alicujus boni exercitium sic excitem, traham & inducam. Otia quippe nocent anima: Et alibi: Otia tollas, &c. Apostolo tamen non impingitur, quòd quòd se narrat raptum usque ad tertium calum, & multa in hunc modum. Item hac pono, ut idem Auditores, habita mei notitia, & per consequens, memoria, Deo Patri misericordiarum & consolationis, me suis precibus ita recommendent: ut ipse Deus dare dignetur vitam bonam, & exitum beatum, gratiam in praesenti, & gloriam in futuro. Amen. His alia subjiciuntur manu: Item finito isto Fabulario compositi de vita Martini plusquam mille 700. versus. Item de victoria Regis Rodolphi contra Odoacrum, Regem Romanorum composui plus quam mille octingentos.
units.tr: The New Graecismus, about 10,560 verses. The little book on the Sacraments, about 4,000, perhaps a little fewer. The Passion of our saints Felix and Regula, and of Exuperantius, about 3,000, perhaps a little fewer. The little book on the proper names of rivers and mountains, about 1,500. The Cathedral Roman, about 1,130. Praises of the Blessed Virgin, on the five Ave Marias, about 300. The Shield of the Germans, about 160. The catalogue of the Roman Popes and Emperors, about 1,640. The letters of recommendation of the Most Serene Rudolf, King of the Romans, ever August, about 800. "I do not set these down as one arrogant and seeking empty glory, but in order to rouse and lead the hearers to a detestation of idle leisure and to the practice of some good. For leisure harms the soul; and elsewhere: Take away idleness, etc. Yet it is not charged against the Apostle that he says he was caught up to the third heaven, and many things of this kind. I also set these down so that the same hearers, having learned of me and consequently remembering me, may commend me in their prayers to God the Father of mercies and comfort, so that God himself may deign to grant me a good life and a blessed end, grace in the present and glory in the future. Amen." To these, other things are added in another hand: "Also, after finishing this Fabulary, I composed more than 1,700 verses on the life of Martin. Also, on the victory of King Rudolf against Odoacer, King of the Romans, I composed more than 1,800."

units.la: Myconius Oswaldus, Lucernensis, Ludi apud Tigurinos reformati primus Moderator, Ecclesiae postea Basileensis Pastor, & tandem Antistes. Scripsit commentarios in Poema Henrici Glareani de situ Helvetiae, quo cum impresi sunt Basil. 1519. Ejusdem ad Sacerdotes Helvetiae, qui Tigurinis male loquuntur, suasoria, ut male loqui desinant, 1524. Tiguri. De vita & obitu Huldrici Zuinglij, Basileae 1536. In Evangelium Marci doctam & piam expositionem, Basil. apud Thomam Platerum 1538. Enarrationes in Psalm. 101. Bernae, apud Apiarium 1548. Catechismum Oecolampadij, e Germanico in Latinum translatum, Basil. 1545. Praefatus etiam est in Oecolampadij enarrationes in Matthaeum & Marcum. Aliorum, tum adhuc ἀνεκδότων, mentio fit ejus operum in Bibliotheca Gesneri: ultima, Commentariorum in Ionam, Esajam, Ieremiam: In Psalmum 129 & 142. in Matthaeum, Lucam & Iohannem: Sermonum de poenitentia, de liberis recte educandis, de crapula & ebrietate, de foenore & usura &c. Epistolae Paraeneticae ad Fratres ditionis Basileensis, quomodo se gerere in turbis illis utiliter debeant, 1534. Plurimas ejusdem adhuc habeo Epistolas de variis thematibus, quas magni facio, eam praesertim, qua jam suo tempore docte scripsit contra eam gratiae, morte Christi acquisitae, salutaris universalitatem, quae ad ipsos etiam le reprobos extendit.
units.tr: Oswald Myconius, of Lucerne, first head of the reformed school at Zurich, later pastor of the church at Basel and finally its antistes. He wrote commentaries on Henricus Glareanus's poem on the situation of Helvetia, with which they were printed at Basel in 1519. Also his exhortation to the priests of Helvetia who speak ill of the Zurichers, urging them to stop, Zurich, 1524. On the life and death of Huldrich Zwingli, Basel, 1536. A learned and pious exposition of the Gospel of Mark, Basel, at Thomas Platter's, 1538. Expositions of Psalm 101, Bern, at Apiarius's, 1548. The Catechism of Oecolampadius, translated from German into Latin, Basel, 1545. He also prefaced Oecolampadius's expositions of Matthew and Mark. Mention is made of his other works, some of them still unpublished, in Gesner's Bibliotheca: the last of these are commentaries on Jonah, Isaiah and Jeremiah; on Psalms 129 and 142; on Matthew, Luke and John; sermons on repentance, on bringing up children rightly, on gluttony and drunkenness, on usury and interest, etc. Hortatory letters to the brethren of the Basel territory, on how they should conduct themselves usefully in those troubles, 1534. I still have very many of his letters on various subjects, which I value highly, especially the one in which he wrote learnedly, already in his own day, against that doctrine of the saving universality of the grace acquired by Christ's death which extends even to the reprobate.

units.la: Myllerus, vel Myllnerus Eberhardus, Miles & Scultetus Tigurinus, qui antiquos scripsit Tigurinorum Annales, quos crebro citat Nauclerus, & Gerhardus de Roo, Veteraquinas, de quibus Methodus nostra legendi Histor. Helvet. pag. 213. Vixit, nisi fallor, an. Chr. 1340. & deinceps.
units.tr: Eberhard Myllerus, or Myllnerus, knight and Schultheiss of Zurich, who wrote the old Annals of Zurich, which Naucler often cites, and Gerhard de Roo, Veteraquinas, concerning whom see our Method of Reading the Helvetic History, p. 213. He lived, unless I am mistaken, around the year of Christ 1340 and after.

units.la: Myllerus, Georgius, Ecclesiae Tallvillanae Pastor, & Capituli ad lacum Tigurinum Decanus meritissimus; Poeta felicissimus, non Latino minus quam Germanico carmine jam celebris. Optandum esset, ut dispersa ejus carmina, ea saltem, quae ipsa materiae gravitas commendat, uno volumine exhiberentur. Extant, inter alia, carmina in Conradi Mejeri, Chalcographi peritissimi, Ἰαναπο-χείχω; Ethica explicatio ludorum puerilium, in Helvetia, Tiguri maxime, usitatorum : In librum D. Rodolphi Guerbij de magicis consecrationibus, incantationibus, &c. De officio statuum omnium : Varia Epithalamia, Genethlia; gratulationes publicæ &c. quibus ingenij ubertatem abundè satis expressit. Vix ante hac carmina Germanica nostra patria vidit felicius exasciata.
units.tr: Georg Myllerus, pastor of the church at Tallwil and most deserving dean of the chapter at the Lake of Zurich; a most gifted poet, already celebrated in Latin verse no less than in German. It would be desirable for his scattered poems, at least those which the very seriousness of their subject commends, to be published in one volume. Extant, among other things, are poems: on Conrad Meyer, most skilled engraver, [Ἰαναπο-χείχω] (Ianapocheicho); an ethical explanation of the children's games commonly played in Helvetia, especially at Zurich; on the book of Master Rudolf Gwerb on magical consecrations, incantations, etc.; on the duty of all estates; various wedding songs and birthday poems; public congratulations, etc., by which he has expressed the richness of his talent amply enough. Our homeland has scarcely ever seen German poems polished more happily.

units.la: Myllerus Iohannes, Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ Professor in Schola Patria publicus, Ecclesiæ Petrinæ Diaconus dignisimus, jam aliquot eruditionis singularis, & dexteritatis, publica dedit specimina, cujusmodi sunt disputationes aliquot, Historia Magorum, de Scriptoribus S. Scripturæ, & primario ejus Authore, in specie; de scriptis Matthæi. Conciones miscellaneæ 1661.
units.tr: Johannes Myllerus, public professor of ecclesiastical history in the school of our city, most worthy deacon of the church of St Peter, has already given public specimens of singular learning and dexterity, such as several disputations: on the History of the Magi; on the writers of Holy Scripture, and chiefly on its author in particular; on the writings of Matthew. Miscellaneous sermons, 1661.

units.la: N.
units.tr: N.

units.la: Nidhardus, Henricus, Decretorum Doctor, Ecclesiæ Collegiatæ Carolinæ Canonicus, de duabus confraternitatibus unitis cum Capitulo Ecclesiæ Constantiensis scripsit tractatum. Item de receptaculis animarum. Vixit a.D. 1440. &c. Vtrumque habeo tractatum Msc. Et ille quidem quæstionem tractat: An dicti confratres istius unitæ confraternitatis possent duo, tria, aut quatuor de illis anniversarijs, quæ per octo personas antiquæ, aut decem nova confraternitatum sunt per missa, simul jungere, & una semel peragere, & dicantur obligationibus prioribus satis facere, cum jam quadraginta octo personæ ad minus anniversaria qualibet peragant, & exsolvant? Vbi de valore suffragiorum in genere etiam, & prolixè agitur. Hic vero certis absolvitur quæstionibus, cujusmodi sunt, I. Vtrum ponenda sunt aliqua receptacula corporalia animarum corporibus exutarum? II. Vtrum suffragia per unum facta, possint prodesse aliis? III. Vtrum mortui possint juvari per opera vivorum? IV. Vtrum suffragia per peccatores facta, prosint illis, pro quibus fiunt? V. An suffragia, quæ fiunt pro mortuis, prosint vivis, facientibus ea? VI. Vtrum suffragia prosint existentibus in inferno? VII. Vtrum suffragia prosint existentibus in Purgatorio? VIII. Vtrum solis illis tribus, scil. Orationibus Ecclesiæ, Sacrificio altaris, & Eleemosynis animæ defunctorum juventur? IX. Vtrum cultus exequiarum prosit defunctis? X. Vtrum suffragia, quæ fiunt pro uno defuncto magis proficiant eidem, quàm aliis in Purgatorio existentibus. XI. An suffragium factum pro multis simul tantùm valeat cuilibet eorum, sicut si suisset pro eo solùm factum? XII. Vtrum Sancti in Patria orent pro nobis? XIII. Vtrum Sancti Orationes nostras cognoscant? XIV. Vtrum expediat nobis Sanctos interpellare, ut orent pro nobis? XV. Vtrum Orationes Sanctorum pro nobis suæ semper exaudiantur.
units.tr: Henricus Nidhardus, Doctor of Decretals, canon of the collegiate church of St Charles, wrote a treatise on two confraternities united with the chapter of the church of Constance. Also a treatise on the receptacles of souls. He lived in the year of our Lord 1440, etc. I have both treatises in manuscript. The former treats the question: Whether the said members of this united confraternity could join together two, three or four of those anniversary masses which, by the old confraternity, are said for eight persons, or by the new for ten, and celebrate them once, and so satisfy the earlier obligations, since already at least forty-eight persons each perform and pay their anniversaries? There the value of intercessions in general is also discussed at length. The latter is resolved by certain questions, such as: (1) Whether bodily receptacles are to be posited for souls stripped of their bodies? (2) Whether suffrages performed by one person can profit others? (3) Whether the dead can be helped by the works of the living? (4) Whether suffrages made by sinners profit those for whom they are made? (5) Whether suffrages made for the dead profit the living who make them? (6) Whether suffrages profit those existing in hell? (7) Whether suffrages profit those existing in Purgatory? (8) Whether the souls of the departed are helped only by those three things, namely the prayers of the Church, the sacrifice of the altar and alms? (9) Whether the rites of burial profit the dead? (10) Whether suffrages made for one dead person profit him more than they profit others existing in Purgatory? (11) Whether a suffrage made for many at once is worth to each of them only as much as if it had been made for him alone? (12) Whether the saints in the fatherland pray for us? (13) Whether the saints know our prayers? (14) Whether it is expedient for us to call upon the saints that they may pray for us? (15) Whether the prayers of the saints for us are always heard.

units.la: Numagen, Petrus, Trevirensis, Andreæ Archiepiscopi Craynensis, & Cardinalis in executione Concilij Basileensis Notarius, & Sacellanus S. Leonhardi extra moenia Tigurina, de quo ita Gesnerus in Edit. Bibliothec. prima. Petrus Numagen Trevirensis, Sacerdos in urbe nostra circa an. D. 1483. scripsit de Nicolao subsylvano Helvetio, qui longo tempore sine cibo solitarius vixisse creditur. Item tractatum de Spirituum apparitionibus ac phantasmatibus. Extant in Bibliotheca publica, apud nos authoris manu, nisi fallor, conscripti. Neutrum horum vidi. Extat tamen Passionale Felicis Hemmerlin, manu Petri Numagen, Capellani S. Leonhardi, prope Thuregum scriptum, & finitum Sabbatho 19. Martij 1502. Pro ut reliqua Malleoli opera pleraque ἀνέκδοτα, circa an. D. 1471. Decanus quidam Zurzachensis Hermannus descripsit. Cujus & Apographum extat Disputationis habitae inter Spiritum quendam, & Priorem, Fratrum Dominicanorum. Vt Pater Cottonus non ita pridem; sic & hic Praedicator Spiritui certas propositi quaestiones, ad quas ille respondit. Decima septima (ut vel unico probemus exemplo, quid utilitatis ad Sacrificulos, mortuos, contra expressum Dei mandatum rogantes, redeat) quaestio erat: Num quid Daemones possint videre corpus Christi in altari? Respondit Spiritus: quod sic; & luculentius, quam homines, & illud an velint, an nolint. Negat alias Schola Pontificia, corpus Christi in Eucharistia vel per miraculum esse visibile, ceu monuimus in Apolog. nostra Eucharist. Haec vero tantum ἐν πυρόδῳ. Redimus ad Petrum nostrum. Descripsit idem Fabularium Conradi de Mure, ut supra jam diximus. Notas addidit Actis Archiepiscopi Craynensis, quas, manu ejus descriptas, jam ante hac vulgavimus. Examen etiam & refutatio XXIV. errorum, quos Latini tribuunt Graecis Msc. extat in Bibliotheca nostra Carolina, quod huic etiam adscribitur Petro. Videatur Iob. Iacob. Huldric. de Religione Graecorum p. 64.
units.tr: Peter Numagen, of Trier, notary of Andreas, Archbishop of Crayne and Cardinal, in the execution of the Council of Basel, and chaplain of St Leonhard outside the walls of Zurich, of whom Gesner speaks thus in the first edition of his Bibliotheca: "Peter Numagen of Trier, a priest in our city around the year 1483, wrote on Nicholas of the Forest, a Swiss, who is believed to have lived a solitary life for a long time without food. Also a treatise on the apparitions of spirits and phantasms. They are extant in the public library among us, written, unless I am mistaken, in the author's own hand." I have seen neither. Yet there is extant the Passionale of Felix Hemmerlin, written out by the hand of Peter Numagen, chaplain of St Leonhard near Zurich, and finished on Saturday, 19 March 1502. Likewise most of the other, largely unpublished, works of Malleolus were copied around 1471 by a certain Hermann, dean of Zurzach. There is also extant a copy of a disputation held between a certain spirit and the prior of the Dominican brothers. As Father Cotton did not long ago, so here too the preacher put set questions to the spirit, to which it replied. The seventeenth question (to prove by a single example what use it is to priests who ask the dead, contrary to God's express command) was: "Can demons see the body of Christ on the altar?" The spirit replied: "They can, and more clearly than men, whether they wish to or not." The Papist school otherwise denies that the body of Christ in the Eucharist is visible even by miracle, as we noted in our Apology for the Eucharist. But these things are mentioned only in passing [ἐν πυρόδῳ]. Let us return to our Peter. He copied the Fabularium of Conrad of Mure, as we have said above. He added notes to the Acts of the Archbishop of Crayne, which we published earlier from his copy. An examination and refutation of the twenty-four errors which the Latins attribute to the Greeks, in manuscript, exists in our Carolina library, and this too is ascribed to Peter. See Johann Jakob Ulrich, On the Religion of the Greeks, p. 64.

units.la: Nuschelerus Iohannes Iacobus, Tigurinus, Medicinae Doctor, Euonymi, seu de remedijs Secretis Conradi Gesneri secundam partem e Latino in Germanicum sermonem transtulit: Prodijt Sangalli 1583.
units.tr: Johann Jakob Nuschelerus, of Zurich, Doctor of Medicine, translated the second part of Conrad Gesner's Euonymus, or On Secret Remedies, from Latin into German. It was published at St Gall in 1583.

units.la: O.
units.tr: O.

units.la: Otto Iob. Henricus, Ecclesiae Tigurinae Ministler, Professor Linguarum, Latinae, publicus; Hebraeae in Collegio Humanitatis. Edidit Orationem de causa Iansenitica, Tiguri; De aequalitate Petri & Pauli, Basileae; Et, utrum Petrus fuerit Romae, Genevae.
units.tr: Otto Iob. Henricus, minister of the Church of Zurich, public professor of Latin and of Hebrew at the College of Humanity. He published an Oration on the Jansenist affair (Zurich), On the equality of Peter and Paul (Basel), and Whether Peter was at Rome (Geneva).

units.la: Pellicanus, Conradus, Rubeaquensis, Franciscani primum ordinis, postea religionis reformatae Theologus, Basileae aliquandiu, Tiguri vero ab a. Ch. 1526. ad 1556. Vir probatae pietatis, & Hebraismi restaurator felicissimus, (quem proinde & Munsterus Praeceptorem suum appellare consuevit) unde & plura tranftulit ex spinosis Rabbinorum libris, quàm eo fermè tempore expectari potuerit. Multa habeo ex translationibus ejus descripta. Lectiones praeterea, Conciones & Commentaria, Bibliandri magnam partem & Bullingeri, diligentissime excepta, & manu ejusdem exarata. Possideo & magnum Epistolarum Tomum à maximis superioris saeculi viris ad ipsum scriptum, quem ex nepotibus mihi quidam ejus dono dedit. Indicem laborum ejus, magna cum diligentia, collegit Ioh. Iacobus Frisius, in editione Bibliothecae Gesnerianae postrema. Scripsit, inquit, Grammaticam Hebraicam: Congesit Dictionarium Hebraicum, adjiciens Methodicam proficiendi in ea Lingua rationem, quam postea Groningerus Argentorati unà cum Margarita philosophica publicavit. Scripsit argumenta librorum, D. Augustini, unà cum Augustino impressa, Basileae a. 1540. Hebraicas voces D. Hieronymi operibus, ut Capnion Graecas, adjecit: Psalterium Hebraicum, cum interpretatione Latina; quae Graecis, eorumque versioni apponuntur, è regione posuit, in editione operum D. Hieronymi prima ac secunda, cum indice in editionem secundam Basileensem. In opera Cypriani, Tertulliani, aliorumque multorum Theologorum libros, Elenchos condidit. In omnes V. T. libros commentaria, in tomos, five partes quinque distincta. Excudit Froschouerus Tiguri, Anno 1536. & 1538. Indicem Bibliorum, ibidem impressum, anno 1537. Scripsit collectaneorum in Evangelia Matthaei, Ioannis, Marci & Lucae, duos libros. Annotationes in omnes Paulinas, ac Apostolorum aliorum Epistolas: haec duobus simul tomis excusa Tiguri, anno 1537. In Apocalypsin scripsit Germanicam interpretationem, quae Erasmi Roterodami paraphrasibus Germanicis, coronidis vice accesit. Psalterium ad Hebraicam veritatem transtulit, & brevibus Scholijs illustravit, impressum primùm Argentorati, deinde Tiguri, Anno 1532. Transtulit in Latinum sermonem Syriacis Onkeli, Ionathae, & aliorum Iudaeorum interpretationes omnes, praeter ea quae jam priùs translata erant, in opere Francisci, Cardinalis Toletani, & in opere Augustini Iustiniani in Psalmos, olim excusa. Transtulit praeterea ex Hebraicis Rabbinorum plurium commentaria, ad literam, nempe Rabi Davidis Kimhi in Genesin, Iosuae, Iudicum, Samuelis, Regum, Isajam, Ieremiam, Ezechielem, 12. Prophetas minores, & totum Psalterium. Item totum Rabi Abraham Aben Ezra, in 14 libros Canonicos: juxta editionem secundam, Danielis Bombergi. Denique Rabi Salomonem Iarchi, Gallum, similiter in omnes Canonicos: Item, Rabi Levi ben Gersom, in parabolas Salomonis, & Danielem, plurimaque in Iosuae, Iudicum & Samuelis &c. Item Rabi Mosen Gerundensem in librum Iob. Rabi Abraham Prixol in Iob, usque ad vigesimum caput Commentarium quoque in Salomonis parabolas appellatum Kabunki (melius Kabbivena Ki) Rabi Simeonem quoque in verba dierum, insertum Rabi Salomoni Gallo, in editione prima Bombergi. Transtulit quoque ordinariam glossam in totum Pentateuchum, dictam Arefit Rabba, multae authoritatis apud Iudaeos. Fasciculum quoque myrrhæ in totum Mosen; Rabi Abraham Hispani: item Capitula vel pirKe Rabi Eliezer, filij Hircani Magni, continentia Theologiam Iudaicam, vetustum authorem à Rabinis junioribus crebrò allegatum. Gesta Regum Israel, tempore Templi secundi, usque ad ultimam Iudæorum captivitatem, sub Adriano principe. Talmudica quoque reddidit Latinè. Prologum, & introductionem Rabi Moysis bar Maymon, quem Rambam, Iudæi vocant. Ejusdem quoque Talmudicos libros multos, nempe inscriptos de doctrina capitulorum 10. Scientiarum traditio c.7. Doctrina Legis c.7. De idololatria c.12. De Oratione c.4. De pœnitentia cap.10. De cultu divino cap.8. De juramentis cap.12. De Sanhedrin cap.26. De regibus & bellis, capitulorum 12. & alia quædam. Ex Talmud Babylonico translulit Massechet berochot, cum Gamara, in duo prima capita: Item Massechet Schabbas Babylonicam cap.24. Massechet quoque Sanhedrim cum Gamara, in duo priora capita. Ex Talmud Hierosolymitano caput quoque memorabile, Heleк. Ex Babylonico Talmud, Massechet Suta: Prologum quoque Rambam in 14. lib. suos Talmudicos. Grammaticalia quoque vertit Latinè, Michlol Rabi Davidis Kimhi. Et R.Moses Punctatoris: Massoret quoque integram R. Eliæ Levitæ Germani, & pleraque alia. Hunc autem laborem pius senex, non ideo suscepit, ut Christianos studiosos ad dogmata Iudaicæ perversitatis perquirenda alliceret, quibus Talmudici isti libri, quos Cabalisticos vocant, & traditiones Patrum, refertissimi sunt, & post Christi Domini, & Apostolorum tempora inspirata, à Spiritu erroris, perversissimis Rabbinis, & pertinacissimis hostibus Christi Domini nostri. Sed ut appareat, quanta cæcitas contigerit in Israël, post negatam veritatem coram Pilato, Ut tandem vel sero nimis confundantur infelices, & revertantur, ad Canonicos utriusque Testamenti libros, & ut commendentur isti Viri docti, qui nunc & olim judicârunt sanctum & utile, ut nihil tale extaret alicubi etiam apud Iudæos, Talmudicorum errorum, & fabularum monstra, quibus à Canonicis, & sacrisabstrahuntur, & in miseria miseranda retinentur. De quibus forsan proprio volumine quisquam aliquando, quid factu opus, conscribet. Obijt Tiguri anno D. 1556, anno ætatis 79. Multis annis post ejus obitum denuò excusi sunt ejus commentarij in libros Veteris Testamenti, nempe in quinque libros Mosis. His accesit narratio de ortu, vita & obitu ejusdem, operâ Ludovici Lavateri Tigurini, jam primùm in lucem edita. In folio Tiguri excudebat Christophorus Froschouerus anno 1582. Ejusdem commentarij in libros Historicos, puta Iosuæ, Iudicum, Ruth, Samuelis, Esdræ, Nehemiæ, Esther. In sol. Tig. anno 1582. Commentarij in Iob, Psalterium, Proverbia, Ecclesiasten, & Cantica Salomonis, sol. Tig. anno 1582. In Prophetas majores, & minores, ut vulgò vocant, commentarij. Tiguri apud Christophorum Froschouerum anno 1582. Commentarios in libros Apocryphos, vel potiùs Ecclesiasticos, putà Tobiam, Iudith, Baruch, Sapientiæ, Ecclesiastici, Ezræ duos, Macchabæorum duos, & in fragmenta Danielis & Esther. In sol. Tig. anno 1582. Commentarij in quatuor Evangelistas, item in acta Apostolorum. In folio, Tiguri apud Christophorum Froschouerum, anno Domini 1582. Quae de translatis Veterum Hebraeorum libris adjiciuntur, non modo extra dubii aleam poni debent, sed & illud insuper notandum, accuratius & felicius hoc ab illo tentatum vadum, quam ab homine Christiano, & fere αὐτοδιδάκτῳ sperari posisit: ut vitio illis verti non debeat, qui hanc optimi Senis peritiam Linguarum Orientalium in dubium vocarunt. Prout memini, magnum aliquando Belgij Theologum hac ipsa de re, sive dubia, sive fidem superante, serio apud me inquisivisse. Non vertit modo, sed & descripsit integra Hebraeorum volumina; de quo ipse in vita sua. Habeo ipse versionem ejus, libri verborum dierum Mosis, Libri Eldad Danita, Epistola R. Mosis ben Majmon ad filium suum R. Abraham. Responsi ad quaestionem R. Mos. Fil. Majm. Responsi ejus ad Massilienses. Sepher Hajaschar R. Tam, Capp. 18. Libri Jirah, seu de pietate R. Jonae Gerundensis. Majm. de precibus & benedictionibus Sacerdotum.
units.tr: Pellicanus, Conradus, of Rouffach, first a Franciscan, afterwards a theologian of the Reformed religion: for some time at Basel, and at Zurich from 1526 to 1556. A man of proven piety and the most successful restorer of Hebrew studies, whom for this reason Munsterus used to call his teacher. He translated more from the thorny books of the rabbis than could have been expected at that time. I have many copies of his translations. Besides, I have his lectures, sermons and commentaries, most of Biblianderus and Bullinger, taken down with great care and written out in the hand of the same man. I also possess a large volume of letters written to him by the greatest men of the last century, which a certain grandson of his gave me as a gift. Iacobus Frisius collected a list of his works, with great diligence, in the last edition of the Gesner Library. He wrote, he says, a Hebrew grammar; he compiled a Hebrew dictionary, adding a method of making progress in that language, which Groninger later published at Strasbourg together with the Margarita philosophica. He wrote the summaries of the books of D. Augustini, printed together with Augustine at Basel in 1540. He added the Hebrew words to the works of St. Jerome, as Capnion did the Greek ones; he set out the Hebrew Psalter with a Latin translation, placing it opposite the Greek and its version, in the first and second editions of the works of St. Jerome, with an index for the second Basel edition. For the works of Cyprian, Tertullian, and the books of many other theologians, he drew up indexes. He produced commentaries on all the books of the Old Testament, divided into five volumes or parts. Froschauer printed them at Zurich in 1536 and 1538. The Index of the Bible, printed there in 1537. He wrote two books of collections on the Gospels of Matthew, John, Mark and Luke. Annotations on all the Pauline and other apostolic epistles, published at Zurich in 1537 in two volumes together. On the Apocalypse he wrote a German interpretation, which was added to Erasmus of Rotterdam's German paraphrases as a crown. He translated the Psalter into Hebrew truth and illustrated it with brief scholia, first printed at Strasbourg, then at Zurich, in 1532. He translated into Latin the Syriac Targums of Onkelos, Jonathan, and all the other Jewish interpretations, except those already translated earlier, in the work of Francis, Cardinal of Toledo, and in the work of Agostino Giustiniani on the Psalms, published long ago. Besides, he translated from the Hebrew the commentaries of several rabbis, word for word: namely, Rabbi David Kimhi on Genesis, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the twelve minor prophets, and the whole Psalter. Likewise the whole of Rabbi Abraham Aben Ezra on the fourteen canonical books, according to the second edition of Daniel Bomberg. Finally, Rabbi Salomon Iarchi, the Frenchman, likewise on all the canonical books. Also Rabbi Levi ben Gersom on the Proverbs of Solomon and Daniel, and very many on Joshua, Judges and Samuel, etc. Also Rabbi Moses of Gerona on the book of Job, and Rabbi Abraham Prixol on Job up to the twentieth chapter. Also a commentary on the Proverbs of Solomon called Kabunki (better Kabbivena Ki), Rabbi Simeon also on the Chronicles, inserted into Rabbi Solomon the Frenchman in the first Bomberg edition. He also translated the ordinary gloss on the whole Pentateuch, called Arefit Rabba, of great authority among the Jews. Also a bundle of myrrh on the whole of Moses, by Rabbi Abraham the Spaniard; also the Chapters or Pirke Rabbi Eliezer, son of Hyrcanus the Great, containing Jewish theology, an ancient author often cited by the later rabbis. The Deeds of the Kings of Israel from the time of the Second Temple to the last captivity of the Jews under the emperor Hadrian. He also rendered the Talmudica into Latin. The prologue and introduction of Rabbi Moses bar Maimon, whom the Jews call Rambam. Also many of his Talmudic books, namely those entitled on the doctrine of the chapters (10), traditions of the sciences (ch. 7), doctrine of the Law (ch. 7), on idolatry (ch. 12), on prayer (ch. 4), on repentance (ch. 10), on divine worship (ch. 8), on oaths (ch. 12), on the Sanhedrin (ch. 26), on kings and wars (12 chapters), and certain others. From the Babylonian Talmud he translated Massechet Berakhot with the Gemara, in its first two chapters; also Massechet Shabbat of the Babylonian Talmud, chapter 24; also Massechet Sanhedrin with the Gemara, in its first two chapters. From the Jerusalem Talmud also one notable chapter, Helek. From the Babylonian Talmud, Massechet Sotah. Also the prologue of Rambam to his fourteen books of Talmudic matter. He also rendered into Latin the grammatical works, Mikhlol of Rabbi David Kimhi, and of R. Moses the Punctator; also the whole Masorah of R. Elijah Levita the German, and very many others. This labour, however, the pious old man undertook not so that he might entice studious Christians to inquire into the doctrines of Jewish perversity, with which those Talmudic books, which they call Cabbalistic, and the traditions of the Fathers, are very full, and which, inspired after the time of Christ the Lord and the Apostles, came from the spirit of error, from most perverse rabbis and most obstinate enemies of Christ our Lord. Rather, so that it may appear how great a blindness has befallen Israel after the truth was denied before Pilate, that at last, though too late, these unhappy people may be confounded and return to the canonical books of both Testaments; and so that those learned men may be commended who, both now and formerly, judged it holy and useful that nothing of the kind should exist anywhere, even among the Jews, the monsters of Talmudic errors and fables, by which people are drawn away from the canonical and sacred books and kept in pitiable misery. Perhaps someone will one day write a separate volume on these matters, on what is to be done. He died at Zurich in the year of our Lord 1556, in the seventy-ninth year of his age. Many years after his death his commentaries on the books of the Old Testament were printed again, namely on the five books of Moses. To these was added an account of his birth, life and death, by the work of Ludwig Lavater of Zurich, now first brought to light. Printed in folio at Zurich by Christoph Froschauer in 1582. Commentaries of the same man on the historical books, namely Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Samuel, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther. Folio, Zurich, 1582. Commentaries on Job, the Psalter, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Solomon, folio, Zurich, 1582. Commentaries on the greater and lesser prophets, as they are commonly called, at Zurich by Christoph Froschauer, 1582. Commentaries on the apocryphal, or rather ecclesiastical, books, namely Tobit, Judith, Baruch, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, the two books of Ezra, the two books of the Maccabees, and the fragments of Daniel and Esther. Folio, Zurich, 1582. Commentaries on the four Evangelists, and likewise on the Acts of the Apostles, in folio, at Zurich by Christoph Froschauer, in the year of the Lord 1582. What is added concerning the translations of the Hebrew books of the ancients ought not only to be placed beyond the chance of doubt, but it should also be noted that this ford was attempted more accurately and happily by him than could be hoped for from a Christian and almost self-taught (αὐτοδιδάκτῳ [autodidaktō]) man. So those people should not be blamed who have called in question this good old man's skill in the Oriental languages. As I recall, a certain great Belgian theologian once seriously asked me about this very matter, whether it was doubtful or beyond belief. He not only translated but also copied out entire Hebrew volumes, as he himself says in his life. I have his version of the Book of the Words of the Days of Moses, the Book of Eldad the Danite, the Letter of R. Moses ben Maimon to his son R. Abraham, the Answer to the question of R. Moses son of Maimon, his Answer to the Marseillais, the Sepher ha-Yashar of R. Tam, 18 chapters, the Book of Yirah, or on piety, of R. Jonah of Gerona, and Maimonides on the prayers and blessings of the priests.

units.la: Pellicanus Samuel, Conradi Filius, Collegii Abbatiliani Inspector, superiori seculo. Multa, ut refert de eo Ioh: Iacobus Frisius amitinus ejus, Majorum diligenter collegit monumenta, quae intra privatos hactenus delituerunt parietes.
units.tr: Samuel Pellicanus, son of Conrad, inspector of the Abbatiana college, in the last century. As his cousin John James Frisius reports, he diligently gathered many records of our forebears, which until now have lain hidden within private walls.

units.la: Pictorius Iosue, Ecclesiae Tigurinae in agro Turgovienfi & Tigurino ab an. Chr. 1551. ad 1598. Minister, raro exemplo IV. Decanus, Dictionariolum Germanico Latinum composuit, & edidit Tiguri. Epigrammata item sacra.
units.tr: Josiah Pictorius, minister of the Church in the Thurgau and Zurich countryside from 1551 to 1598, a rare example, served four times as dean. He composed a small German-Latin dictionary and published it at Zurich, together with sacred epigrams.

units.la: Pictorius Iosue, F. Patris in Parochia Glatfeldensi successor ab an. Chr. 1598. ad 1611. Psalmos Davidis Germanice edidit cum argumentorum apparatu, & tabulis analyticis. Dissertationem de officio Auditorum verbi divini: adjectis variis precandi formulis Tig. 1609.
units.tr: Josiah Pictorius, successor of his father in the parish of Glattfelden from 1598 to 1611. He published the Psalms of David in German, with an apparatus of arguments and analytical tables, and a dissertation on the duty of hearers of the divine Word, with various forms of prayer added (Zurich, 1609).

units.la: Piscatorius, Iohannes, Lithopolitanus dedit Epitomen operum omnium Augustini, secundum locos communes distributam, Augustae 1537. & Genevae 1565. Eadem postea recognita & aucta fuit per Iohannem Pesselium Tylanum, cujus etiam opera accessit ex eodem Augustino collectus Tomus quartus, de septem Sacramentis, Coloniae 1539. Idem libellum ex Augustino collegit, in quo rationibus & authoritatibus probatur, ex immaculata semper Virgine Maria Christum, secundum Veritatem carnis suae, Veram, humanam assumfisse Creaturam: simul etiam excutiuntur loci, qui secus ac diversum sonare videntur, Augustae 1544. Claruit an. Chr. 1554.
units.tr: John Piscatorius of Lithopolis produced an epitome of all the works of Augustine, arranged according to commonplaces (Augsburg, 1537; Geneva, 1565). The same work was later revised and enlarged by John Pesselius of Thielt, whose edition also included a fourth volume, collected from the same Augustine, on the seven sacraments (Cologne, 1539). The same man collected from Augustine a little book in which it is proved, by reasons and authorities, that Christ took on a true human nature from the ever-immaculate Virgin Mary, according to the truth of his flesh; at the same time, passages that seem to sound otherwise are examined (Augsburg, 1544). He flourished in 1554.

units.la: Pontifella, Iohannes Scholae primum & Ecclesiae, circa a. Ch. 1541. Tigurinae, postea & Curiensis Minister. carmina quaedam scripsit in obitum Bullingeri.
units.tr: Pontifella, John, first teacher at the school and church of Zurich, around 1541, afterwards also minister at Chur. He wrote some poems on the death of Bullinger.

units.la: R.
units.tr: R.

units.la: Ranius Ioh. Henricus, Vir amplissimus, Comitatus Kiburgici Administrator, pro tempore, meritissimus, locuples diffusae literaturae cornucopiae, Mathematicarum cumprimis disciplinarum cultor & promotor felicissimus. Algebram scripsit Germanicam, magna cum eruditorum, eorum etiam, qui has literas ex professo colunt, admiratione. Prodijt Tigur. 1659.
units.tr: John Henry Ranius, a most distinguished man, administrator of the County of Kyburg for the time being, most deserving, a rich cornucopia of wide-ranging learning, and a most successful cultivator and promoter especially of the mathematical disciplines. He wrote an algebra in German, to great admiration from the learned, including those who cultivate these studies professionally. Published at Zurich, 1659.

units.la: Rapertus, Tigurinus, Monachus Sangallensis, scripsit librum de origine & diversis casibus Monasterij S. Galli in Alamannia, quem cum Notis edidit Melchior Haiminsfeldius Goldastus 1606. Francofurti T. I. Rerum Germanic. Abbatum primorum vitas prolixè describit, stylo, pro ratione illius temporis, satis perspicuo, & praeter Monasticae barbariei consuetudinem, satis Latino. Eundem Poetam vocat Bullingerus de reb. Tig. lib. 4. c. 13. Carmen ei, de Proto-Martyribus Tigurinis, Felice & Regula, tribuitur sequens: Deque loco ad quem truncati sua sumpta tulerunt Membra pij fratres, Felix, & Regula Felix: Partibus ablatis, multisque in munera datis, Inque loco sancto non parva parte relicta: Cum reliquis membris sacrare novam satagebat Ecclesiam, Monachis sese, clerōque sequente Virginibus Christi dicentibus eminus Amen,
units.tr: Rapertus, of Zurich, a monk of St Gall, wrote a book on the origin and various fortunes of the monastery of St Gall in Alemannia, which Melchior Goldast of Haiminsfeld edited with notes (Frankfurt, 1606, vol. I of Rerum Germanicarum). He describes at length the lives of the first abbots, in a style clear enough for its time and, apart from the usual monkish barbarism, fairly good Latin. Bullinger calls him the same poet in De rebus Tigurinis, book 4, chapter 13. The following poem on the first martyrs of Zurich, Felix and Regula, is attributed to him: "And to the place to which the pious brothers carried the mutilated limbs they had taken up, Felix and Regula Felix; with parts removed and many given as gifts, and no small part left in the holy place; with the remaining limbs he strove to consecrate a new Church, the monks following him and the clergy following after, and the virgins of Christ saying Amen from afar."

units.la: Vixit seculo nono, ut videre est apud Stumpf Hist. Helvet. pag. 426.
units.tr: He lived in the ninth century, as may be seen in Stumpf, Helvetic History, p. 426.

units.la: Rhellicanus Iohannes, ita à patria, Tigurinae ditionis pago, qui alias Iohannes Myllerus, Poeta & Graecorum authorum Interpres, Collegij Abbatisani paedagogus. Translulit Megandri Catechismum Germanicum Latinè. Homeri vitam ex Plutarcho Latinitate donavit, notisque marginalibus illustravit: in fine carmen Stockhornias; quo describit iter animi gratia factum, per montem ejus nominis in agro Bernensi, Basil. 1537. In C. Iulij Caesaris & A. Hirtij, seu Opij Commentaria de bello Gallico, Civili, Pompejano, Alexandrino, Africano & Hispanienfi; annotationes, in quibus multa contextus loca partim exemplarium collatione, partim conjecturis emendantur, Basil. 1543. Ejusdem carmen, quo Tigurum alloquitur, praefixum est annotationibus Zuinglij in Evangelistas. Item aliud de Bibliotheca Bernensi, additum est annotationibus Megandri in Epistolam ad Galatas: Item carmen de tribus Badenae ob Evangelium decollatis. Claruit an D. 1538.
units.tr: John Rhellicanus, so called from his homeland, a village in the Zurich territory, who was otherwise John Müller, poet and interpreter of the Greek authors, and teacher at the Abbatiana college. He translated Megander's German Catechism into Latin. He rendered the Life of Homer from Plutarch into Latin and illustrated it with marginal notes. At the end is a poem, the Stockhornias, in which he describes a journey made for pleasure over the mountain of that name in the Bern territory (Basel, 1537). He also published annotations on the Commentaries of C. Julius Caesar and A. Hirtius (or Opius), on the Gallic, Civil, Pompeian, Alexandrian, African and Spanish wars, in which many passages of the text are emended partly by collating copies and partly by conjecture (Basel, 1543). His poem addressed to Zurich is prefixed to Zwingli's annotations on the Evangelists. Another poem, on the library of Bern, is added to Megander's annotations on the Epistle to the Galatians, and there is a poem on the three men of Baden who were beheaded for the Gospel. He flourished in 1538.

units.la: Rubertus Iacobus, Vitoduranus; de quo in Bibl. Gesner. ex Edit. Frif. Iacobus Rubertus Vitodurensis, doctissimus juvenis, scripsit Orationes & Epistolas aliquot, eruditione singulari refertas. In Demosthenem instituerat annotationes, & quaedam alia, quae immatura morte subreptus imperfecta reliquit. Vixit annos plus minus 18 mortuus.
units.tr: James Rubertus of Winterthur, of whom the Frisian edition of Gesner's Bibliotheca speaks: a very learned young man, he wrote orations and some letters, full of singular learning. He had begun annotations on Demosthenes and some other works, which he left unfinished when an early death carried him off. He lived about eighteen years before he died.

units.la: Rueff Iacobus, Chirurgus Tigurinus, vir, Gesneri judicio, in arte sua peritissimus, eidemque amicissimus; Catalogum scripsit, quo continentur Medicorum fermè omnium, & Astrologorum nomina cum figuris: Ephemerides sive Calendaria; Comoediam de V Vilhelmo Tellio: Quatuor item alias Germanicis metris composuit,quæ in scribuntur: De felice & infelice statu fæderis Helvetici: de vinea Domini: quæ acta est Tiguri anno 1539. postridie Pentecostes: De itupro Paulinæ,nobilis ac pudicisimæ matronæ Romanæ, dolo Sacerdotum in Æde Isidis illato,cujus Iosephus meminit, & Hegesippus: De passione Domini ex quatuor Evangelistis, perpaucis,præter Historiam expressam, adjectis. Scripsit & Interpretationes ostentorum aliquot, de duplici infante, utroque fæminei sexus, Schafhusij edito anno Domini 1543. capitibus duobus, brachijs quatuor, totidemque pedibus disjunctis: uno vero solido corpore à collo ad umbilicum usque,umbilici subtus vinculo propendente: De circulo quodam, cujus pars una midium Solem distinguere visa est, per centrum verò & medium circuli transfire iris. Apparuit Glaronæ 1544. die 19. Aprilis: De Cruce alba, quæ plenam lunam obtegere visa est, Villæ (oppidum est Helvetiorum) 1544 d.7. Aprilis. Ejusdem de conceptu & generatione hominis lib.6. excusi sunt Tiguri Germanicè 1554. & Latinè, per VVolfgangum Haleram translati. Claruit anno Domini 1554.
units.tr: James Rueff, a Zurich surgeon, a man who, in Gesner's judgment, was most skilled in his art and his very close friend. He wrote a catalogue, with portraits, of almost all physicians and astrologers; ephemerides or calendars; and a comedy on William Tell. He also composed four other works in German verse: on the happy and unhappy state of the Swiss covenant; on the vineyard of the Lord, performed at Zurich on the day after Pentecost in 1539; on the violation of Paulina, a noble and most chaste Roman matron, by a trick of the priests in the temple of Isis, which Josephus and Hegesippus mention; and on the passion of the Lord, taken from the four Evangelists, with few additions beyond the narrative itself. He also wrote interpretations of several portents: of a double infant, both of the female sex, published at Schaffhausen in the year of the Lord 1543, with two heads, four arms and as many feet, separate, yet one solid body from the neck to the navel, with a growth hanging below the navel by a cord; of a certain circle, one part of which seemed to divide the sun in the middle, while a rainbow seemed to pass through the centre and middle of the circle, which appeared at Glarus on 19 April 1544; and of a white cross, which seemed to cover the full moon, at Ville (a town of the Swiss) on 7 April 1544. His six books on the conception and generation of man were published at Zurich in German in 1554, and translated into Latin by Wolfgang Haller. He flourished in 1554.

units.la: S.
units.tr: S.

units.la: Schieggius Erhardus, Steckborâ Turgæus; sed Ecclesiæ postea Tigurinæ alumnus, & Minister cætus Bubickonensis 1585. Ingenium felix, & excolendis Linguis aptum natum. Carmen scripsit Hebraicum encomiasticum in librum Mæcenatis sui, D. Guilelmi Stuckij 1582. Græcum invectivum in librum de Concordia Smidelini. Evangelia Lucæ & Iohannis Hebraicè transtulit. Orationem Græcam scripsit de varietate donorum Sp.S. quam & publicè Tiguri recitavit. Homiliam 93. Gualtheri in priorem ad Corinthios Hebraicè translatam reddidit 1583. Burckhardi Leemanni brevem Methodicamque Christianæ religionis institutionem Germanicam, Hebraicam fecit. Quæ tamen posteriora omnia sunt ἀνέκδοτα.
units.tr: Schieggius Erhardus, a Thurgauer from Steckborn, but later a student of the Zurich Church and minister of the congregation at Bubikon in 1585. He had a happy talent, born fit for cultivating languages. He wrote a Hebrew encomiastic poem on the book of his patron, Herr Wilhelm Stuckius, in 1582, and a Greek invective against the book on Concord by Smidelinus. He translated the Gospels of Luke and John into Hebrew. He wrote a Greek oration on the variety of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which he also delivered publicly at Zurich. He rendered Gualter's 93rd homily on the First Epistle to the Corinthians into Hebrew in 1583. He made a Hebrew version of Burkhard Leeman's brief and methodical German introduction to the Christian religion. All these later works, however, are [ἀνέκδοτα] (unpublished).

units.la: Schlegel, Iohannes, ex Augustiniano montis Thuricensis, Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ Ottelfingę, & Volkensch vilæ ad a. Ch. 1552. Minister; cum alijs ejusdem antea Ordinis prolixam de causis abolitæ Fraternitatis dedit Epistolam. Exemplum ex Schlegelij autographo descriptum inseruimus Histor. Eccles. T.V.p.522.
units.tr: Schlegel, Iohannes, formerly an Augustinian of the Zurich hill, minister of the Zurich Church at Ottelfingen and Volken, up to about the year of Christ 1552. Together with others of the same former order, he gave a lengthy letter on the causes of the abolished brotherhood. We have inserted a copy made from Schlegel's autograph in our Church History, vol. 5, p. 522.

units.la: Schnebergerus, Antonius, Tigurinus, Medicus, de quo Ioh: Huldricus Grobius. Dum Sneebergero currebant stamina vitæ Helvetiæ decus & gloria Gentis erat: Quin etiam donec Medicinæ fama manebit, Helvetiæ decus & gloria Gentis erit.
units.tr: Schnebergerus, Antonius, of Zurich, a physician, of whom Johann Huldrich Grob says: While the threads of Schneberger's life were still running, he was the glory and pride of the Swiss nation; indeed, as long as the fame of medicine endures, he will remain the glory and pride of the Swiss nation.

units.la: Floruit Cracoviæ in Polonia 1570. Scripsit Catalogum Plantarum LatinoGermano-Polonicum: De remedijs particularibus contra pestem: De tuenda militum valetudine: De multiplici falis usu, Cracov. 1562. Promisit etiam de aeris usu librum: Bacchanalia, quæ inscribuntur, Gemma amethystus, sive carbunculus Æthiops, & alia quædam.
units.tr: He flourished at Kraków in Poland in 1570. He wrote a catalogue of plants in Latin, German and Polish; on particular remedies against the plague; on preserving the health of soldiers; on the manifold use of salt, Kraków 1562. He also promised a book on the use of air, and others entitled Bacchanalia, The Amethyst Gem, or the Ethiopian Carbuncle, and some other works.

units.la: Similerus, simlerus, Iosias. Petri Simleri Rhinovienfis, (Viri dosti, Cœnobij Capellani in agro Tigurino Priori, ante Reformationem, postea Oeconomi & Ministri adannum Christi 1557. ætatis 71.) filius Bullingeri & Gualtheri Gener, Ecclesiæ primùm Petrinæ Minister, postea in Professione Theologica Petri Martyris successor ab an. Chr. 1563. ad 1576. d. 6. Iulij quo vitam cum morte commutavit, a. ætatis 45. Vitam ejus descripsit Ioh. Guilel. Stuckius. Theologus, Historicus, Mathematicus sui temporis cum paucis conferendus. Theologica ejus scripta sunt, Responsio de Christo Mediatore adversus maledicum libellum Francisci Stancari: De æterno Dei Filio, D. N. Iesu Christo. Adversus novos Arianos, Tritheitas, & Samosatenianos lib. 3. Item adversus eosdem de Spiritu Sanƈto lib. 1. Narratio veterum Controversiarum de una persona, & duabus Naturis Christi Servatoris, una cum collatione Controversiarum nostri temporis, edita cum Latinis veterum scriptis de eadem Controversia, quæ ab ipso recognita, summarijs & annotationibus illustrata, & in unum volumen conjuncta sunt: Scripta illa sunt Iustiniani Imperatoris, Boëthi, Cæsiani, Maxentij, Leonis, Gelasij, Fulgentij, Vigilij, Rustici. Edidit præterea Petri Martyris Commentaria in Genefin, & duos libros Samuelis: Ejusdem libellum precum ex libellis colleƈtum. Ejusdem est expositio de vera Iesu Christi secundùm humanam Naturam in his terris præsentia, 1574. Responsio ad duas disputationes Andreæ Musculi. Responsio ad Iacobum Andream, communi nomine scripta. Responsio secunda ad Iacobum Andream. Petri Martyris Epistolas, Quæstiones & responsa, item Orationes editioni paravit. Ejusdem est assertio duarum naturarum in Persona Christi Servatoris, contra Simonem Budnæum. Transtulit etiam quædam Theologica, ut est Bullingeri responsio ad 7. Capita accusationum. Ejusdem lib. 6. adversus errores Anabaptisticos. Institutio eorum, qui de fide ab Inquisitoribus examinantur, quæ est responsio ad articulos Bavaricos: Compendium Christianæ religionis. Adhortatio ad Ecclesiæ Ministros omnes, ut concordiam mutuò colant, & fidem in Christum, & veram resipiscentiam simpliciter doceant: De persecutionibus, quas Ecclesia passa est, earumque causis, & persecutorum pœnis: Ottonis VVerdmylleri Paraphrastica interpretario Orationis Dominicæ, & Symboli Apostolici. Addi potest doƈtissimus ejus Dialogus, quo disputatur, utrum campanæ pulsu, meridie, aut Vesperi audito, deteƈto capite sit orandum, quem, cum multis ejus Epistolis Theologicis, & Historicis habeo adhuc Msc. Commentaria ejus in Exodum aliquot post obitum ejus annis prodierunt per filium Iofiam; an. Chr. 1584. Rationem moræ reddidit præfatione ad lectorem Henricus VVolfius. Ad Historica pertinent variæ Orationes profopographicæ, qualis est de vita & obitu Bullingeri, Martyris, Conradi Gefneri. Epitome Bibliothecæ Gefnerianæ, magna accessione locupletata. Lib 2. de fœdere & Republica Helvetiorum, Latinè & Germanicè, Valesia, sive lib. 2. de Viberis, Sedunis, & Veragris. Descriptio ptio Rauracorum, Tulingorum, Latobrogorum, Bojororum. De Lepontijs lib. 1. in quo de Alpibus & itineribus alpinis. Historiam etiam Helvetiæ, & ejus ἀν inchoavit; sed præmatura morte præventus non absolvit. De hoc opere Vid. Meth.leg. Hist. Helvet.p.218. Ad Mathematicas lucubrationes referuntur, de Principiis Astronomiæ lib.2. Notæ in Ætici Cosmographiam antea non editam, & in Antonini Augusti itinerarium, quod collatione veterum manuscriptorum exemplarium plurimis locis emendavit. Vocabula rei nummariæ ponderum & mensurarum Græca, Latina, Hebraica, Arabica ex diversis auctoribus collecta, & in ordinem Alphabethicum disposita, cum Dictionario Latino Germanico Iohannis Frifij, sine Authoris nomine, impressa.
units.tr: Similerus, Simlerus, Josias. Son of Peter Simler of Rhinau (a learned man, who before the Reformation was prior and chaplain of a monastery in the Zurich countryside, and afterwards steward and minister; he died in the year of Christ 1557, aged 71), and son-in-law of Bullinger and Gualter, he was first minister of the church of St Peter at Zurich, and afterwards successor to Peter Martyr in the theological professorship, from AD 1563 until 6 July 1576, when he exchanged this life for death, at the age of 45. His life was written by Johann Wilhelm Stuckius. He was a theologian, historian and mathematician who can be compared with few of his time. His theological writings are: an answer on Christ the Mediator against the abusive little book of Francesco Stancari; On the eternal Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, against the new Arians, Tritheists and Samosatenes, in three books; likewise against the same on the Holy Spirit, in one book; a narrative of the old controversies on the one person and the two natures of Christ the Saviour, together with a comparison with the controversies of our own time, published with the Latin writings of the ancients on the same controversy, which he himself revised and illustrated with summaries and notes and joined into one volume. Those writings are by the Emperor Justinian, Boethius, Caesianus, Maxentius, Leo, Gelasius, Fulgentius, Vigilius and Rusticus. He also published Peter Martyr's commentaries on Genesis and two books of Samuel, and a little book of prayers gathered from various books. His also is an exposition of the true presence of Jesus Christ in this world according to his human nature, 1574; an answer to two disputations of Andreas Musculus; an answer to Jacob Andreae, written in the name of the others; a second answer to Jacob Andreae. He prepared for publication Peter Martyr's Epistles, Questions and Answers, and likewise his Orations. His is also an assertion of the two natures in the person of Christ the Saviour, against Simon Budneus. He also translated some theological works, such as Bullinger's answer to the seven chapters of accusations, and his six books against Anabaptist errors. An instruction for those who are examined on the faith by the Inquisitors, which is an answer to the Bavarian articles; a compendium of the Christian religion; an exhortation to all the ministers of the Church to cultivate concord with one another and simply to teach faith in Christ and true repentance; on the persecutions which the Church has suffered, their causes and the punishments of the persecutors; and Otto Werdmüller's paraphrastic interpretation of the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed. His very learned dialogue may be added, in which it is disputed whether one should pray with head uncovered at the sound of the bell at noon or in the evening; I still have this, in manuscript, together with many of his theological and historical letters. His commentaries on Exodus appeared some years after his death, published by his son Josias, in the year of Christ 1584; Henry Wolf gave the reason for the delay in a preface to the reader. Among his historical works are various prosopographical orations, such as those on the life and death of Bullinger, Martyr and Conrad Gessner; an epitome of the Gessnerian library, greatly enriched by additions; two books on the league and commonwealth of the Helvetians, in Latin and German; Valesia, or two books on the Viberi, Sedunenses and Veragri; a description of the Rauraci, Tulingi, Latobrigi and Boii; on the Lepontii, one book, in which he treats of the Alps and alpine routes. He also began a history of Helvetia and its annals, but, prevented by premature death, he did not finish it. On this work see the Methodus legendi historiam Helvetiae, p. 218. To his mathematical studies belong two books on the principles of astronomy; notes on the Cosmography of Aethicus, not previously published; and notes on the itinerary of Antoninus Augustus, which he corrected in many places by collating old manuscript copies. A collection of Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic terms for coins, weights and measures, gathered from various authors and arranged in alphabetical order, was printed with the Latin-German dictionary of Johann Frisius, without the author's name.

units.la: Simlerus, Iob. Rodolphus, Medicinæ Doctor, Iosiæ F. Collegij Abbatissani 1602. postea Carolini ab an. Chr. 1605. ad 1611. Artium Rhetorologicarum Professor. Edidit Archetypos Homiliarum in totum N.T. ex Rodolphi Gualtheri autographo collectos & notis auctos, Tig. 1610. In Historia etiam Helvetica laboravit, ut patet ex Method. cit. p.219. Eodem præside habitæ sunt disputationes de Philosophiæ distributione, de Natura & definitione Logicæ, de Prædicamentorum gradibus, de natura affectnum: Themata miscella.
units.tr: Simlerus, Iob. Rodolphus, Doctor of Medicine, son of Josias, of the Abbess's College from 1602, afterwards of the Carolinum from 1605 to 1611, professor of the rhetorical and logical arts. He published the archetypes of the homilies on the whole New Testament, collected from the autograph of Rudolf Gwalther and enriched with notes, Zurich 1610. He also worked on the Swiss history, as appears from the Method cited, p. 219. Under his presidency were held disputations on the division of philosophy, on the nature and definition of logic, on the degrees of the predicaments, on the nature of the affections: miscellaneous theses.

units.la: Simlerus, Iob. Guilelmus, Rodolphi F. Iosiæ nepos, Ecclesiæ ante hac Herlibergensis ad lacum Tigurinum Minister, jam Collegij Abbatissani superioris Inspector, Poeseos Germanicæ cultor non minus facilis, quàm sententiosus. Volumine integro, Variorum carminum, abundè probavit Linguæ Germanicæ ad tornandos versus nihil deesse. Tertia nuper prodijt editio, magnâ auctior mantissâ.
units.tr: Simlerus, Iob. Guilelmus, grandson of Josias and son of Rudolf, formerly minister of the church of Herrliberg on Lake Zurich, now inspector of the upper Abbess's College, a cultivator of German poetry no less fluent than sententious.
