A Synopsis of Practical Matters [Συνοψις πραγματων], begun in 1559. His Practice from 1592. Various medical consultations, diligently written out: a volume in quarto. On the books of the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, taken down by Ludovicus Duret. A book of Various Readings, written at Paris, in quarto. On the powers of simple medicines, taken down in his own hand at Paris from the mouth of Johannes Montanus. Very many other manuscripts of his survive, some of which have perished through a certain carelessness, others are unfinished. I myself also have some of his Epitomes [Ἐπιτομαί], some taken down at the academies and some composed by his own effort.

units.la: Volphius Iohannes, Ecclesiae ad Praedicatores primum & primus, 1544. postea Abbatissanae Pastor ab an. Chr. 1551. ad 1571. Theologiae etiam in Schola 1565. Professor, vir in omni literatura (vide encomium Guilelmi Stuckij, Orationi Bullingeri funebri, insertum) exercitatissimus, & Ecclesiasticae non minus, quam Scholasticae Cathedrae aptus natus. Collegit indicem Graecorum nominum, quae ad Geographiam pertinent ex Ptolemaeo, Pausania, Stephano, Strabone, Eustathio & nonnullis aliis. Idem excudi curavit, additis praefationibus suis, Petri Martyris Vermilij disputationem de Coena Domini in Anglia habitam; & ejusdem librum de Sacramento Eucharistiae, Tiguri per Andream Gessnerum, & Rodolphum VVyssenbachium. Confessionem Anglicam, cam, & quosdam alios libellos ex Latino sermone in Germanicum transtulit. Præterea scripsit præconem Evangelicum, sive de officio concionatoris sacri Orationem. De Sabbatho libellum Germanicum. Commentaria in 14 ultima capita. 1. lib. Melachim i.e. Regum, addita Commentariis in primum librum totum, & secundi capp 11. Commentaria in Nehemiam. De Christiana perseverantia, commendationes consolatoriæ ad N. captivos fratres lib. 1. Tiguri apud Froschouerum. Scripsit etiam Commentarios in Esdram; in librum Esther, in Ionam Prophetam. Considerationes domesticas: In Genesin Bibliandri & Numeros sermones & Conciones. Deuteronomium, librum Iosuæ, Iudicum, Hesther, Ruth. In Psalmos, Esdram, Prophetas, Ionam, Nahum, Ioelem, prælectiones & repetitiones in Ecclesiasten Salomonis: Item Conciones in Matthæum, Iohannem, & Acta Apostolorum memorialia. In Marcum & Lucam: Conciones matutinas & vespertinas in acta Apostolorum. Conciones in Epistolas D. Pauli ad Philippenses, Colossenses, Thessalonicenses, ad Timotheum, Philemonem. In D. Petri & Ioannis Epistolas, & variarum Concionum volumen. Præfationem in Psal. 109. Item libellus, de conferendis Bibliorum translationibus. De conficiendis succinctis Commentarijs in Biblia. De Ecclesia militante, ubi in his terris reperienda fit. De constitutione Scholæ Tigurinæ. De petra salutis. Opusculum affectum. Scripsit etiam locorum communium ex lectionibus quotidianis collectorum volumen ingens à filio, Henrico ad lucem paratum: Est & alius locorum communium susius de doctorum Tomus, præsertim de Scriptura, creatione, Prædestinatione &c. Librae aliquot Epistolarum. Librum Orationum. Decadum D. Henr. Bullingeri Conciones octo transtulit in sermonem Germanicum, & Plutarchi vitam Dionis è Græco in Latinum. Item Isagogen Germanicam in studia juris civilis. Comment. in Aphtonium, in lib. 2. Epistol Fam. Cicer. in ejusdem Orat. 3. pro Archia; Onomasticon Physicum, & Topologicum, Onomast. HebræoLatinum Palæstinæ. Annotationes in libros Aristotelis decem de moribus. In Analytica posteriora. Quæ omnia partim in privatum usum conscripta, partim editioni pridem erant parata. Pleraque tamen adhuc ἀνέκδοτα, cum reliqua ejusdem supellectili libraria, Patristica præsertim & Classica (Patrum enim & Authorum Classicorum, Græcorum & Latinorum optimas fere suo tempore collegerat editiones) ab hæredibus custodiuntur. Epistolarum doctissimarum farraginem magnificimus, eas præsertim, quas de Ecclesia ad Dudithium, Fratres Polonos, & in causa Sociniana scripsit. Chronologia adhuc ejusdem manu exarara asservatur, ab initio Mundi.
units.tr: John Wolf, first minister of the church of the Preachers and its first incumbent, 1544; afterwards minister of the Abbatissana church from 1551 to 1571. He was also professor of theology in the school from 1565. He was a man most practised in all literature (see the encomium of Wilhelm Stuck, inserted in Bullinger's funeral oration), and naturally suited to the ecclesiastical chair no less than the scholastic one. He compiled an index of Greek geographical names from Ptolemy, Pausanias, Stephanus, Strabo, Eustathius and some others. He also had printed, with his own prefaces added, Peter Martyr Vermigli's disputation on the Lord's Supper held in England, and the same author's book on the Sacrament of the Eucharist, at Zurich by Andreas Gessner and Rudolf Wyssenbach. He translated the English Confession and some other little books from Latin into German. He also wrote a Evangelical herald, or an oration on the office of the sacred preacher; a German book on the Sabbath; commentaries on the last fourteen chapters of the first book of Melachim, that is Kings, with commentaries on the whole first book and on chapters 11 of the second; commentaries on Nehemiah; a book on Christian perseverance, and consolatory exhortations to our captive brothers N., one book, at Zurich at Froschauer's press. He also wrote commentaries on Ezra, on the book of Esther, and on the prophet Jonah; household considerations; sermons and homilies on Genesis (after Bibliander) and Numbers; and lectures on Deuteronomy, the book of Joshua, Judges, Esther and Ruth. He wrote lectures and repetitions on the Psalms, Ezra, the Prophets, Jonah, Nahum and Joel, and on the Ecclesiastes of Solomon; likewise sermons on Matthew, John and the Acts of the Apostles, and memorial notes on Mark and Luke; morning and evening sermons on the Acts of the Apostles; sermons on the Epistles of St Paul to the Philippians, Colossians, Thessalonians, to Timothy and to Philemon; on the Epistles of St Peter and John; and a volume of various sermons. He also wrote a preface to Psalm 109, and a little book on comparing the translations of the Bible, and on preparing brief commentaries on the Bible. He wrote on the militant Church, and where on earth it is to be found; on the constitution of the Zurich school; on the rock of salvation; and a small work on the affections. He also left a huge volume of common places, collected from his daily readings, which his son Henry prepared for publication. There is also another, fuller common-places book of his, on the teachings of the doctors, especially on Scripture, creation, predestination and so on. Several volumes of letters, and a book of orations. He translated eight sermons from the Decades of Heinrich Bullinger into German, and Plutarch's Life of Dion from Greek into Latin. Likewise a German introduction to the study of civil law; commentaries on Aphthonius, on the second book of Cicero's Epistles to Friends, and on his oration 3 for Archias; a Physical and a Topological Onomasticon; a Hebrew-Latin Onomasticon of Palestine; annotations on Aristotle's ten books of Ethics; and on the Posterior Analytics. All of these were partly written for private use and partly already prepared for publication. Most of them, however, remain unpublished [ἀνέκδοτα], and together with the rest of his library, especially the patristic and classical works (for he had gathered together, in his time, almost the best editions of the Greek and Latin Fathers and classical authors), they are kept by his heirs. We have a great store of his most learned letters, especially those he wrote on the Church to Dudith, to the Polish Brethren, and on the Socinian controversy. A chronology written in his own hand, from the beginning of the world, is still preserved.

units.la: Wolfius Henricus, Iohannis F. Novi Testamenti Professor, & Pastor Ecclesiæ Dieticonensis 1581. Zolikonensis, 1582. Diaconus Templi majoris 1586. & tandem Pastor Abbatissanæ, adeoque & provinciæ, & eruditionis paternæ hæres, ab an. Chr. 1592. ad 1594. Opera aliquot paterna edidit præfationibus munita. Sed & commentarijs Simlerianis posthumis in Exodum præfixit prologum. Chronologiam item, sive tractationem Theologicam, de tempore & mutationibus ejus Ecclesiasticis: Disputationem de Antichristo cum corollario, de duobus testibus. Ejusdem est piû, & nostratium manibus tritissimum, adeóque sæpius præ lo iteratum Euchologion Germanicum. Tandem carmina nonnulla in Epistolas Gessneri, Psalterii Paraphrasin Rodolphi Leemanni: Insignia Serenissimi Regis Poloniæ, Stephani. In obitum Iohannis VVolfiij, & Regulæ Hegneræ, Parentum, ad Threcium: in obitum Iosiæ Simleri. Extat ejusdem manu scriptus apud hæredes doctus tractatus de Calendario Gregoriano non recipiendo. Explicatio Confessionis Helveticæ, Compendium Theologicum Msc. Methodus studendi: Methodus Apodemica, sive peregrinandi. Varii loci communes. Conciones in Ierem. In I. Epist. ad Corinthios: in Epistol. Iacobi, Lat. & Germ. Chronologiæ aliquot libri prolixè, ab initio Mundi tractati. Analysis Orationis pro Ligario: Pugna Davidis cum Goliatho, carminicè Scripsit & alia carmina.
units.tr: Wolf, Henry, son of John, Professor of the New Testament, and minister of the church at Dietikon in 1581, of Zollikon in 1582, deacon of the Great Minster in 1586, and finally minister of the Abbatissana church, and so of the province, and heir of his father's learning, from 1592 to 1594. He published several of his father's works, equipped with prefaces. He also prefixed a prologue to the posthumous Simler commentaries on Exodus. Likewise a chronology, that is a theological treatise on the times and ecclesiastical changes of the age; a disputation on Antichrist with a corollary, on the two witnesses. His is the German Euchologion, very well known to our people and handled so often that it has been reprinted many times. Finally, several poems: on Gessner's Epistles; a paraphrase of the Psalter by Rudolf Leemann; the arms of the most serene King of Poland, Stephen; on the death of John Wolf; and the Regulae of Hegner, for his parents, to Threcius; on the death of Josias Simler. There exists, in his own hand, among his heirs, a learned treatise against accepting the Gregorian Calendar. An explanation of the Helvetic Confession; a theological compendium, in manuscript; a method of study; the Methodus Apodemica, or on travelling abroad; various common places; sermons on Jeremiah; on the First Epistle to the Corinthians; on the Epistle of James, in Latin and German. Several books of chronology, treated at length from the beginning of the world. An analysis of Cicero's oration for Ligarius; the Battle of David with Goliath, written in verse; and he wrote other poems as well.

units.la: VVolfius Iob. Huldricus, Comitatus Kiburgici Administrator 1600. Prætor Vrbanus 1608. Proconsul 1609. & Quæstor ad 30 April. 1624. ætat. 65. Psalterium Davidis ex optimis Translationibus rhythmicè reddidit, inter molestissimas Provinciæ Kiburgicæ occupationes 1604.
units.tr: Wolf, John Ulrich, administrator of the county of Kyburg in 1600, city praetor in 1608, proconsul in 1609, and quaestor until 30 April 1624, aged 65. In 1604, amid the most troublesome duties of the province of Kyburg, he rendered the Psalter of David rhythmically from the best translations.

units.la: VVolfius Iob. Iacobus, Viri Amplissimi, D. Ioh. Huldrici, literarum & literatorum magni Mæcenatis, filius, Iohannis Theologi nepos, Linguarum Hebraicæ 1617. in utroque Collegio: Græcæ & Latinæ in Collegio Humanitatis 1630. Græcæ verò & Hebraicæ in Auditorio publico ab ann Chr. 1638. ad an. Chr. 1641. Professor, quo, magno sui apud nos relicto desiderio, cum vix triennio ante in Collegium Canonicorum, eximio suo merito, adoptatus fuisset, in Sanctorum Panegyrim, receptus fuit. Felix studij Linguarum propagator, publicis paulatim speciminibus probavit, quid in secretoribus etiam Studiorum illorum recessibus expectari à se potuisset. Prodierunt autem doctissimæ ejus aliquot disputationes Synodales, de integritate contextus sacri, Hebræi V. & Græci N. T. Anchora fidelium ex Iob. 19. de Sacerdotio Melchisedeki &c. Extant manu ejus scriptæ observationes textuales in quatuor Evangelia, ad D. Breitingerum. Ejus potissimum tum exemplo, tum hortatu ardor mihi, tum adhuc juveni, crevit excolendi studij Linguarum. Primas, quod sciam, literas Arabicas vidi in Erpenii Grammatica Arabica, ab eodem mihi mutuata: sed ita tum horridas, ut lectionem earum penè desperârim. Memini, cum aliquando deplorarèt neglectum illius Linguæ, quæ & ipsum Deum habueret authorem, & quâ divina nobis expositæ essent oracula, tandem eum ad Dei recurrisse liberrimam, horum etiam Charismatum, dispensationem: Non omnibus datum esse! Iohannes Iacobus, Caspari F. Medicus Tigurinus, Petri Hafneri Chirurgi & Lithotomi celeberrimi gener. Scripsit Prognostica in an. Chr. 1603. De quo Grotius noster: Herbarum vires, Linguas, artémque medendi Ut discas semper, cura labórque fuit. Discere conanti fecit facunda Minerva, Et pulchré fecit clarus Apollo Tibi, Gaude, docte parens, omnes lætamini amici, Solvitéque æterno debita vota Deo. Accesit vestro generi, Gentique vetustæ En nova gemma, decus, gloria, fama nova.
units.tr: Wolf, John James, son of the most distinguished man, Mr John Ulrich, great patron of letters and of learned men, grandson of John the theologian, Professor of Hebrew in 1617 in both colleges, of Greek and Latin in the College of Humanity in 1630, and of Greek and Hebrew in the public lecture hall from 1638 to 1641. He was received, with great regret left among us, after being adopted, by his outstanding merit, into the College of Canons scarcely three years before, into the assembly of the saints. As a happy propagator of the study of languages, he gradually showed by public specimens what might have been expected from him even in the more secret recesses of those studies. Several of his most learned synodal disputations were published: on the integrity of the sacred text, of the Hebrew Old and Greek New Testament; the Anchor of the faithful, from John 19; on the priesthood of Melchizedek, and so on. His manuscript textual observations on the four Gospels, addressed to Breitinger, survive. It was especially by his example and his exhortation, while I was still young, that my zeal for cultivating the study of languages grew. As far as I know, I first saw Arabic letters in Erpenius' Arabic Grammar, which he lent me; but they seemed so rugged that I almost despaired of reading them. I remember that when once he lamented the neglect of that language, which had God himself as its author and through which the divine oracles had been set out for us, he at last had recourse to God, the most generous dispenser of these gifts too: "It is not given to all!" John James, son of Caspar, Zurich physician, and son-in-law of the most celebrated surgeon and lithotomist Peter Hafner. He wrote Prognostics in 1603. Of him our Grotius says: "Your care and labour have always been to learn the powers of herbs, languages and the art of healing. Eloquent Minerva made you eager to learn, and bright Apollo made you fair. Rejoice, learned parent; rejoice, all friends, and pay your long-owed vows to the eternal God. A new jewel has been added to your family and to your ancient people: a new honour, glory and fame."

units.la: Vvyßius Iob. Caspar, P. Scholæ primum Abbatissanæ Parallelæ, & Ecclesiæ Minister: Professor postea in Collegio Humanitatis Linguarum: In Collegio denique Carolino Græcus ab a. Ch. 1644. ad an. 1659. Dialectologiam scripsit Græcam, molestum satis & laboriosum scriptum. Et ut purioris Germanismi fuit observantissimus, ita ex Gallica Lingua non pauca transtulit; Drelincurti meditationes præparatorias ad S. Cænam, Praxin tranquillitatis: Confessionem Parlamenti Anglicani nomine editam.
units.tr: Wyss, John Caspar, first Parish minister of the Abbatissana church, then minister of the church; afterwards professor of languages in the College of Humanity, and finally Greek professor in the Carolinum from 1644 to 1659. He wrote a Greek dialectology, a rather tiresome and laborious work. And as he was most careful of purer German usage, so he translated not a few things from the French language: Drelincourt's preparatory meditations for the holy Supper, the Practice of Tranquillity; and the Confession of the English Parliament, issued in its name.

units.la: Vvyßius Iob. Caspar, Fil. V.D. Minister & ordinarius Professor Philosophiæ in Academia Genevensi. Variæ ejus extant theses Philosophicæ, Logicæ præsertim & Physicæ, quarum integrum jam ordinariis pensis Gymnasium, sive Systema percurrit. Deus laboribus ejus porro benedicat.
units.tr: Wyss, John Caspar, son of the most worthy Mr (Dr) and ordinary professor of philosophy in the Academy of Geneva. Several of his philosophical theses survive, chiefly on logic and physics, through which the school, or system, now runs entirely through the ordinary exercises. May God further bless his labours.

units.la: Vvyßius Felix, Natus est d. 8. Decembris 1596. Post peregrinationem literariam, quâ & Lauream Poeticam, promotore Clarissimo Viro, Domino M. Ioh. Philippo Pareo, magni illius Theologi Dav. Filio, tum temporis Gymnasii Neostadiani Rectore, obtinuit, ad S. Sanctum Ministerium fuit admissus. Ex Diacono primum, post Pastore VVeningano, ab anno 1618. ad 1631. Lithopolin ad Ecclesiæ illius curam Pastoralem suscipiendam vocatus, paulo post Capituli Decanus designatur, ad an. 1638. Inde Amplifs. Magistratus Tigurum illum vocavit, ut Diaconatum Ecclesiæ Abbatissanæ, & Professionem Theologiæ Catecheticæ in Collegio Humanitatis in se suscipéret, ad an. 1646. Post piè defunctô, Domino Rodolpho Suarzenbachio, Ecclesiæ Abbatissanæ Pastore, in locum ejus subvectus stationem illam, quousque Deo benignè visum fuerit, adhuc obtinet, simul rei Eleemosynariæ Curatoris, atque Scholæ Intendentis, demum Scholarchæ officio defunctus. Ex lucubrationibus ipsius lucem viderunt. 1. Dissertatio de testibus sive sponsoribus ad S. Baptismum, Germanicè, Basileæ 1637. 2. Conciones duæ dedicatoriæ, in Consecratione novi Templi Gynopediani, jussu superiorum ab illo ibidem habitæ, Tiguri 1646. 3. Tigurini Catechismi Analysis, Thesibus CCLXII. & totidem Antithesibus illustrata, Tig 1648. 4. Funda Davidis, authore Clarissimo viro Domino Henrico à Diest, Academiæ Daventriensis Theologo, é Latino idiomate in Germanicum translata. Translationi Hecatostichon in laudem Authoris & operis præmisit, Tiguri anno eodem. 5. Centuria Sermonum Festalium in decem decades divisa, Tig. 1650. 6. Abominatio desolationis, sive sermones viginti in Cap. XIII. S. Marci Evangelistæ, Tig. 1655. 7. Florilegium Pastorale, sive Centuria selectiorum de munere Pastorali locorum, ex operibus S. Patris Ioh. Chrysostomi excerpta, Tig. 1659. 8. Centuria Precationum quadripartita, Germanicè, Tig. 1661. 9. Varia variorum generum poemata, tam Sacra, quàm profana, Eucharologia, Epithalamia, Epicedia, Propemptica, gratulatoria alia, occasionaliter scripta. 10. Disputationes publicas quinque sustinuit. a. De Mundo Heidelbergæ. b. De peccato in Spiritum S. Marpurgi, sub Clarissimi Domini Doctoris Eglini præsidio. c. De natura hominis mirabili, & causa lapsûs, celeberrimo Philosopho Domino Goclenio Præside. d. e. De προωπκπισία, clarissimo Scholæ Tigurinæ Theologo, Domino Henrico Ernio, Moderatore. f. De perseverantia Sanctorum in fide, Præside eodem. Hæ tres postremæ Synodales erant, ubi semel atque iterum Thesis ipse adornavit. Ἀνέκδοτα sunt: Sermones in Exodum, Proverbia, Ionam; in 4. Evangelia, Acta Apostolorum, Epistolam ad Romanos, Ephesios, Philippenses, Colossenses, utramque ad Thessalonicenses, utramque ad Timotheum, ad Titum, ad Philemonem, in primam, secundam, & tertiam Iohannis, Iudæ. Breves annotationes in N.T. precibus vespertinis destinatæ; quæ serio desiderantur.
units.tr: Felix Wyßius, was born on 8 December 1596. After a journey for study, during which he also won the laurel of poetry under the sponsorship of the most distinguished Mr. Johann Philipp Pareus, son of the great theologian David Pareus and at that time rector of the Neustadt Gymnasium, he was admitted to the holy ministry. He was first a deacon, then pastor at Weningen from 1618 to 1631. He was then called to Lithopolis to take up the pastoral care of that church, and shortly afterwards was appointed dean of its chapter, serving until 1638. From there the most honourable magistracy called him to Zürich to take up the diaconate of the Abbey church and the professorship of catechetical theology at the College of Humanity, which he held until 1646. After the pious death of Mr. Rudolf Suarzenbach, pastor of the Abbey church, he was promoted to succeed him, and he still holds that post, for as long as God graciously sees fit. At the same time he serves as curator of the almonry and superintendent of the school, and he has finally discharged the office of scholarch. Of his writings the following have come to light: (1) a dissertation on witnesses or sponsors at holy baptism, in German, Basel 1637; (2) two dedicatory sermons, delivered by him there by order of the authorities at the consecration of the new Gynopedium church, Zürich 1646; (3) an analysis of the Zürich Catechism, illustrated by 262 theses and as many antitheses, Zürich 1648; (4) Funda Davidis, by the most distinguished Mr. Henry à Diest, theologian of the Academy of Deventer, translated from Latin into German; he prefixed to the translation a hecatostichon in praise of the author and the work, Zürich the same year; (5) a centuria of festal sermons divided into ten decades, Zürich 1650; (6) Abominatio desolationis, or twenty sermons on chapter 13 of St. Mark's Gospel, Zürich 1655; (7) Florilegium Pastorale, a centuria of selected passages on the pastoral office, excerpted from the works of St. John Chrysostom, Zürich 1659; (8) a centuria of prayers in four parts, in German, Zürich 1661; (9) various poems of many kinds, sacred and profane, eucharistic, epithalamia, epicedia, propemptica, and other congratulatory pieces, written on various occasions. (10) He has defended five public disputations: (a) on the world, at Heidelberg; (b) on the sin against the Holy Spirit, at Marburg, under the presidency of the most distinguished Dr. Eglin; (c) on the wonderful nature of man and the cause of the fall, with the renowned philosopher Mr. Goclenius presiding; (d) and (e) on predestination [προωπκπισία], with the most distinguished theologian of the Zürich School, Mr. Henry Ernst, as moderator; (f) on the perseverance of the saints in faith, under the same president. These last three were synodal disputations, for which he himself prepared the thesis once and again. The following remain unpublished: sermons on Exodus, Proverbs and Jonah; on the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, the Epistles to the Romans, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, both to the Thessalonians, both to Timothy, to Titus, to Philemon, the first, second and third of John, and Jude; and brief notes on the New Testament intended for evening prayers. These are earnestly to be desired.

units.la: Wyßius Melchior, Verbi apud Glaronenses primum, postea Abbatiscellanos, Klotæ jam, in agro Tigurino Minister, concionem edidit Valedictoriam.
units.tr: Melchior Wyß, minister first among the people of Glarus, later at Abbatiscella, and now at Kloten in the Zürich territory, published a farewell sermon. ## Z.

units.la: Z.

Zellerus Ioh Henricus, Scholæ Carolinæ Moderator nuper felicissimus & dexterrimus, jam S.S. Theologiæ Professor ordinarius, Collega & amicissimus, & honoratissimus, disputationes aliquot dedit Synodales de Prædestinatione, Missa, Staurolatria, Ἀδυναμία implendi Legem &c. Spartam hanc, suscepit ab anno 1660. quo, d. 27 April. æt. 65 diem suum clausit celeberrimus, & solidissimus Antecessor, Ioh. Rodolphus Stuckius; quem beata analysi, biennio antevertit, Collega conjunctissimus, Joh. Winzius 1658. d. 6. Septemb. anno vero uno, clarissimus Græcæ Linguæ Professor, Joh. Caspar Wyßius, 1659. Sequutus deniq. d 13. April. 1662. ætat. 59. meritissimus urbis nostræ Archiat. Collegii Præpositus, & Physicus ordinarius, D Gygerus. Id quod vel ideo hoc loco obiter moneo, ut quantam, juxta Rempublicam, cujus intra octennium insolitam ferè vidimus Metamorphosin, brevi tempore Collegium nostrum acceperit cladem, & constaret, & nostræ fortis atque fragilitatis memores, Deum pro operariorum superstitum salute tanto rogaremus ardentius. Certum est, vix tantùm, rem familiarem, ex præmaturo patris aut matris familiâs discessu pati dispendium; quantum, ex obitu fidorum vel Politiæ, vel Ecclesiæ Ministrorum, ad Rempublicam redundat incommodi. Non annuatim succrescunt, neque unius noctis Kikajon sunt Proceres & columnæ publicæ! Deo ergo potius sedulis sunt commendandæ precibus, quàm invidiâ opprimendæ.
units.tr: Johann Heinrich Zeller, recently the most fortunate and skilful moderator of the Carolina school, now ordinary professor of holy theology, a colleague, most dear friend and most honoured man, gave several synodal disputations on predestination, the Mass, the worship of the cross, the inability to fulfil the law, and so on. He took up this Sparta in 1660, the year in which, on 27 April, in his sixty-fifth year, the most celebrated and solid predecessor Johann Rudolf Stuck closed his days. Two years earlier, in 1658 on 6 September, Stuck had been gone before by his closest colleague Johann Winz, who died in a blessed analysis; and in the following year, 1659, by the most distinguished professor of Greek, Johann Caspar Wyß. Finally, on 13 April 1662, in his fifty-ninth year, the most meritorious archiater of our city, provost of the College and ordinary physician, Dr. Gyger, followed. I note this here in passing, so that we may understand how great a loss our College has suffered in a short time, in the course of the public affairs whose unusual metamorphosis we have seen almost within the last eight years, and so that, mindful of our strength and our frailty, we may pray all the more earnestly to God for the safety of the workers who survive. It is certain that a household scarcely suffers so much loss from the untimely departure of its father or mother as the commonwealth suffers harm from the death of the faithful ministers of the state or of the Church. They do not grow up year by year, and the leaders and pillars of the public are not a gourd of a single night! They are therefore to be commended to God with earnest prayers rather than overwhelmed with envy.

units.la: Zieglerus, Adrianus: Edidit Pharmacopeam Spagyricam.
units.tr: Adrian Ziegler published a Spagyric Pharmacopoeia.

units.la: Zieglerus Iacobus, Medicus, ingeniosum de fermentatione dedit tractatum, Lingua vernacula.
units.tr: Jacob Ziegler, a physician, wrote an ingenious treatise on fermentation in the vernacular.

units.la: Zublerus, scripsit de bombardarum Pyrotechne Geometrica.
units.tr: Zubler wrote on the geometrical pyrotechny of bombards.

units.la: Zuinglius Huldricus, Toggius, exeunte seculo 15. ex Domo Sylvestri natus, μέγας, καὶ πολλῶν ἀγαπητὸς ἄλλων, singulare honoris divini organum, non eruditione tantùm; sed & fortitudine ad Reformationis aggrediendum opus sufficienter instructum. Opera ejus, & res præclarè gestas alibi enarrari potuerunt. Plebanus fuit primùm Glaronensis, postea Eremitanus, tum denique Tigurinus. Ecclesiæ non nostræ tantùm; sed & puriorum omnium Reformator; Antistes, Theologiæ Professor & Scholarcha ab an. Chr. 1525. ad 1531. Plurima scripsit, quæ primùm separatim, post mortem autem ejus in quatuor tomos digesta, Tiguri apud Froschouerum, anno 1555 excusa sunt.
units.tr: Ulrich Zwingli, of Toggenburg, born at the end of the fifteenth century in the house of Sylvester, great and beloved of many others, a singular instrument of divine honour, equipped not only with learning but with the courage to undertake the work of the Reformation. His labours and his notable deeds could be recounted elsewhere. He was first parish priest at Glarus, afterwards a hermit, and finally at Zürich. He was the reformer not only of our Church but of all the purer churches; antistes, professor of theology and scholarch from 1525 to 1531. He wrote a great deal, which was first published in separate pieces, but after his death was arranged in four volumes and printed at Zürich by Froschauer in 1555.

units.la: In primo tomo continentur, opus articulorum, sive conclusionum 76. Paraenesis ad communem Helvetiorum civitatem, ne Evangelicæ doctrinæ cursum impediant, nec licitis sacerdotum conjugijs offendantur. Supplicatio quorundam apud Helvetios Evangelistarum ad R.D. Hugonem Episcopum Constantiensem, ne se induci patiatur, ut quicquam in præjudicium Evangelii promulget, neve scortationis scandalum ultrà ferat, sed presbyteris uxores ducere permittat. Apologeticus Archeteles appellatus, quo respondetur paraenesi R.D. Constantiensi ad senatum præposituræ Tigurinæ missæ. Suggestio deliberandi super propositione Hadriani Pont. Rom Nerobergæ facta, ad Principes Germaniæ. Apologia, qua in publicis Helvetiorum comitiis Bernæ congregatis, ad quædam falsò sibi intentata crimina respondit. Epistola ad Senatum, & populum totámque Ecclesiam Toggiorum. Epistola ad communem Helvetiorum societatem, quâ docet, compaternitatem matrimonii usum non impedire, simúlque monet, ne sese externorum insidiis turbari patiantur. Paraenesis, ad vetustissimam Suitzensium Remp. ut Principum amicitias & insidiosa alienigenarum munera caveat. De certitudine & claritate verbi Dei lib. I. De Canone Missæ epicheresis. De Canone Missæ libelli Apologia. Adversus Hieronymum Emserum Canonis Missæ assertorem, Antibolon. Ad Fridolinum Lindoverum Bremogartensem concionatorem super publica, de gratia per Christum, hallucinatione, expostulatio. Christiana & Orthodoxa Prudentia Tigurinorum Cos totiusque Senatus responsio, ad Constantiensem Episcopum, de idolis & Missa. Ad Valentinum Comparem, Archi Grammateum Vraniensem responsio de Evangelio, Doctoribus, vel Patrum authoritate, de imaginibus & Purgatorio. Isagoge in Evangelicam doctrinam à Prudentiss. Tigurinorum Senatu cunctis Ecclesiarum tam in urbe quàm in agro ministris exhibita, ut ea instructi Evangelium purè prædicent. Quo pacto ingenui adolescentes informandi sint, præceptiones. Pastor, quo docetur, quibus notis veri pastores, à falsis discerni possint, & quid de utrisque sit statuendum. De duplici justitia, divina & humana, lib. 1. De delectu & libero ciborum esu, de offendiculo item & scandalo liber. De casta, intemerata, semperque Virginis Maria sermo. Anamnema de providentia Dei, ad illustrissimum Cattorum Principem.
units.tr: The first volume contains: a work of 76 articles or conclusions; an exhortation to the common state of the Swiss, that they should not hinder the course of evangelical doctrine, nor take offence at the lawful marriages of priests; a supplication of certain evangelical preachers among the Swiss to the most reverend Hugo, Bishop of Constance, that he should not allow himself to be induced to publish anything to the prejudice of the Gospel, nor bear further the scandal of fornication, but should permit priests to take wives; an apologetic called Archeteles, in reply to the exhortation of the most reverend Bishop of Constance sent to the senate of the Zürich provostry; a suggestion for deliberation on the proposal of Pope Adrian, made at Nerobergae, addressed to the princes of Germany; an apology, by which, in the public assembly of the Swiss gathered at Bern, he answered certain crimes falsely charged against him; a letter to the senate, the people and the whole Church of the Toggenburgers; a letter to the common society of the Swiss, in which he teaches that spiritual kinship does not impede the use of marriage, and at the same time warns them not to suffer themselves to be disturbed by the snares of outsiders; an exhortation to the very ancient republic of Schwyz, that it beware of the friendships of princes and the insidious gifts of foreigners; on the certainty and clarity of the Word of God, book I; on the Canon of the Mass, an epicheresis; an apology for the booklet on the Canon of the Mass; against Hieronymus Emser, defender of the Canon of the Mass, an antibolon; to Fridolin Lindover, preacher at Bremgarten, a remonstrance concerning his public hallucination about grace through Christ; the Christian and orthodox prudence of the Zürich burgomaster and of the whole senate, a reply to the Bishop of Constance about images and the Mass; to Valentin Compar, chief secretary of Uri, a reply concerning the Gospel, the teachers, or the authority of the Fathers, about images and purgatory; an isagoge into evangelical doctrine, presented by the most prudent senate of Zürich to all the ministers of the churches, both in the city and in the countryside, so that, instructed by it, they may preach the Gospel purely; precepts on how ingenuous young people are to be taught; the Pastor, in which it is taught by what marks true ministers may be distinguished from false ones, and what is to be decided about each; on the twofold justice, divine and human, book I; on the choice and free eating of foods, and likewise on stumbling and offence, a book; a sermon on the chaste, undefiled and ever-virgin Mary; an Anamnema on the providence of God, addressed to the most illustrious Prince of the Hessians.

units.la: Tomus secundus continet τὰ πολεμικὰ, i. e. pugnas, quæ ipsi cum adversariis suis intercesserunt, ut est liber, in Catabaptistarū seditiosas conciones conscriptus. De Baptismo, & ejus prima institutione, Anabaptismo, & Pædobaptismo, i. e. parvulorum & infantum Baptismo, liber, divisus in 3. tractatus, ad Balthasaris Hubmeyer Pacemontani libellum de Baptismo editum responsio. Ad Petrum Gynoræum Epistola, in qua de Fabro, Eccio & Balthasare Catabaptista, quædam comperies. De peccato originali declaratio ad Vrbanum Rhegium. De tumultuum & seditionum authoribus, & quinam seditiosi merito dicendi sint, quâ denique via ad Christianam pacem commodè perveniri possit. Ad Matthæum Albertum Rutlingensium Ecclesiasten, de Cœna Dominica. De vera & falsa religione commentarius ad Franciscum Galliarum Regem. Subsidium, sive Coronis de Eucharistia. Ad Ioh. Bugenhagii Pomerani Epistolam, contra novum errorem, ut ille scripserat, responsio: qua Eucharistiæ negotium & Christi verba, hoc est corpus meum, declarantur. Ad Theobaldi Billicani Epistolam responsio, ejusdem argumenti. Ad Vrbanum Rhegium Epistola, super eadem re. De Cœna Domini plana brevisque institutio, in simplicium quorundam usum conscripta, ne argutis aliorum fallaciis decipiantur. Epistola ad celeberrimam quandam Germaniæ civitatem, quæ tam ipsius, quàm Oecolampadii scriptis aditum ad se præcluserat. Ad libellum Doctoris Ioh. Struthionis de Cœna Domini, contra se scriptum responsio. Responsio brevis ad Epistolam satis longam amici cujusdam haud vulgaris, in qua de Eucharistia quæstio tractatur. Amica exegesis i.e. expositio Eucharistiæ negotii, ad M. Lutheri sermonem in VVittenbergensi Ecclesia, pro substantialis corporis & sanguinis Christi in Sacramento assertione, contra Suuermeros, aut fanaticos publicè habitum, pia & amica Apologia seu responsio. Orthodoxa responsio, qua Christi verba, hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur, veterem ac unicum sensum perpetuo retinere: & M. Lutherum ultimo suo scripto de Sacramento nec suum, nec Pontificis sensum docuisse aut confirmasse docetur. Ad Mart. Lutheri librum, quem is Confessionem dixit, responsio. Ad Confessionem Mart. Lutheri responsio. Sermo primus Bernæ habitus, fidei suæ Confessionem & ejusdem expositionem continens; tractat autem expositionem totius Symboli Apostolici, & multa obiter de corporis Dominici natura, deque Eucharistia disserit. Sermo ultimus, quem apud Bernenses de constantia habuit. Ratio fidei ad Carolum V. Romanorum Imp. Epistolæ ad Illustrissimos Germaniæ Principes Augustæ congregatos, de Eccii convitiis. Christianæ fidei brevis & clara expositio, ad Francisci um Galliarum Regem scripta, paulo ante mortem ejus. Ad Ioannis Eccij Helvetiorum legatis Badenæ agentibus transmissam Epistolam, Christiana responsio, qua Zuinglio intentatæ calumniæ diluuntur: ad ejusdem Epistolam & novem Pagorum Helvetiæ consilium Frovvenfeldæ initum, brevis & extemporanea responsio, Tigurino Senatui exhibita. S.P.Q. Tigurini ad Ioannem Eccium Epistola salvum conductum ipsi promittens, adjuncto simul Huld Zuinglii Epistolio, ad duodecim Helvetiorum pagos, omnesque fœderis ejusdem socios, de Badensi disputatione Epistola. Ad Ioannis Eccii propositiones septem responsio prima. Ad Ioannis Eccij falsas & impias responsiones, in Badensi disputatione proditas, responsio secunda. Ad Ioh. Fabri μὴ ἐπισχελμένην ἀπαγορεύην i.e. nunquam transmissam Epistolam, responsio. Altera ad Io. Fabrum Epistola, qua ad Fabri scriptum, quo Zuinglij ad duodecim Helvetiorum pagos, Epistolam insectatus, respondetur. Tertia ad Ioh. Fabrum responsio, libellum ipsius mendaciorum plenissimum, quem, Novitates dixit, confutans. Ad universos Christi fideles Epistola, ut impium Fabri conatum, quo non nuper modo conscriptis libris, verum & N.T. codicibus insidiendum molitur, caveant. Quo pacto mendaciorum doli, quibus hoc seculum nostrum scatet, caveri possint, brevis, sed exacta institutio. Acta disputationis primæ, quæ R. D. Constantiensis Episcopi Legatis cum Huld. Zuinglio, & interalios complures Tigurinæ ditionis ministros extitit, anno 1522. mense Ianuario. Acta disputationis secundæ, quæ coram universo Tigurinorum Senatu, & verbi ministris circiter quingentis transacta est, anno eodem mense Octobri.
units.tr: The second volume contains his polemical works, that is, the controversies he carried on with his opponents [τὰ πολεμικά]. These include the book written against the seditious sermons of the Catabaptists; a book on Baptism and its first institution, on Anabaptism and on Pedobaptism, that is, the baptism of little children and infants, divided into three treatises; a reply to the little book on Baptism published by Balthasar Hubmeyer of Waldshut; a letter to Peter Gynoraeus, in which you will find some things about Faber, Eck and Balthasar the Catabaptist; a declaration on original sin to Urban Rhegius; on the authors of tumults and seditions, who may rightly be called seditious, and by what path Christian peace may finally be reached conveniently; to Matthew Albert, minister of the church at Reutlingen, on the Lord's Supper; a commentary on true and false religion addressed to Francis, King of the French; a supplement, or crown, on the Eucharist; a reply to the letter of John Bugenhagen of Pomerania, against the new error, as he called it, in which the business of the Eucharist and the words of Christ, this is my body, are explained; a reply to the letter of Theobald Billicanus on the same subject; a letter to Urban Rhegius on the same matter; a plain and brief instruction on the Lord's Supper, written for the use of simple people, so that they may not be deceived by the subtle tricks of others; a letter to a very famous city of Germany, which had shut its doors against him, as well as against the writings of Oecolampadius; a reply to the little book of Dr. John Strauss on the Lord's Supper, written against him; a brief reply to a rather long letter from a certain not ordinary friend, in which the question of the Eucharist is discussed; a friendly exegesis, that is, an exposition of the matter of the Eucharist, a pious and friendly apology or reply to the sermon of M. Luther, delivered publicly in the church at Wittenberg, in defence of the substantial body and blood of Christ in the Sacrament, against the Sacramentarians or fanatics; an orthodox reply, in which it is shown that the words of Christ, this is my body, which is given for you, have always retained the old and only sense, and that M. Luther, in his last writing on the Sacrament, neither set forth nor confirmed his own opinion or that of the Pope; a reply to the book of M. Martin Luther which he called a Confession; a reply to the Confession of Martin Luther. The first sermon, delivered at Bern, containing his confession of faith and its exposition; it expounds the whole of the Apostles' Creed and, in passing, discusses many things about the nature of the Lord's body and the Eucharist. The last sermon, which he delivered at Bern on constancy. The reason of faith addressed to Charles V, Emperor of the Romans; letters to the most illustrious princes of Germany gathered at Augsburg, on the insults of Eck. A brief and clear exposition of the Christian faith, written for Francis, King of the French, shortly before his death. A Christian reply, in which the slanders brought against Zwingli are refuted, sent as a letter to the envoys of the Swiss, acting at Baden, in answer to John Eck; a brief and extemporaneous reply to the letter of Eck and to the counsel of the nine cantons of Switzerland held at Frauenfeld, presented to the Senate of Zurich. A letter of the Senate and People of Zurich to John Eck, promising him safe conduct, together with a short letter of Huldrych Zwingli to the twelve cantons of Switzerland and all allies of the same league, concerning the disputation at Baden. The first reply to the seven propositions of John Eck. The second reply to the false and impious answers of John Eck, put forward in the disputation at Baden. A reply to John Faber's never-sent letter [μὴ ἐπισχεθεῖσαν ἀπαγόρευσιν]. A second letter to John Faber, in which is answered his writing against Zwingli's letter to the twelve cantons of Switzerland. A third reply to John Faber, refuting his little book, full of lies, which he called Novelties. A letter to all the faithful of Christ, that they may beware of the impious attempt of Faber, who is now plotting to lay snares not only through recently written books but also through copies of the New Testament. A brief but exact instruction on how the deceits of lies, with which this age of ours abounds, may be guarded against. The acts of the first disputation, held in January 1523 between the legates of the most reverend Bishop of Constance and Huldrych Zwingli and several other ministers of the Zurich territory, in the year 1522. The acts of the second disputation, held in the month of October of the same year before the whole Senate of Zurich and about five hundred ministers of the Word.

units.la: Tomus tertius ea, quæ in Genesin, Exodum, Esajam, Ieremiam, Prophetas, partim ex ore ipsius excepta, partim ab ipso conscripta sunt, una cum Psalterio Latinitate donato continet: Psalterium ab Huldrico Zuinglio, ex Hebraica veritate, Sermone Latino donatum. Complanationis Isaiæ Prophetæ fœtura prima, cum Apologia, cur quidque versum sit. Appositā est autem divi Hieronymi traductio é regione versioni Huldrici Zuinglij, sic ut columnæ (ut vocant) columnis respondeant. Complanationis Ieremiæ Prophetæ fœtura prima: adjecta Apologia, cur quidque sic versum sit, cum Epistola nuncupatoria ad S.P.Q. Argentoratensem.
units.tr: The third volume contains the writings that were partly taken down from his own mouth and partly written by himself on Genesis, Exodus, Isaiah, Jeremiah and the Prophets, together with the Psalter translated into Latin: the Psalter translated into Latin speech by Huldrych Zwingli from the Hebrew truth. The first draft of the paraphrase of the prophet Isaiah, with an apology explaining why each thing was rendered as it was. Moreover, the translation of St. Jerome has been placed opposite the version of Huldrych Zwingli, so that the columns (as they are called) correspond to one another. The first draft of the paraphrase of the prophet Jeremiah, with an apology explaining why each thing was rendered thus, together with a dedicatory letter to the Senate and People of Strasbourg.

units.la: Quartus Tomus complectitur Annotationes in quatuor Evangelistas, & passionis Dominicæ historiam, item in Pauli Apostoli Epistolam ad Romanos, Corinthios, Philippenses, Colossenses, Thessalonicenses, Hebræos; præterea in Canonicas D. Iacobi, & primam Ioannis Epistolas. Annotationes ex Huldrici Zuinglij ore exceptas. Brevis commemoratio mortis Christi ex quatuor Evange-
units.tr: The fourth volume comprises annotations on the four Evangelists and on the history of the Lord's Passion; likewise on the Epistles of the Apostle Paul to the Romans, Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, Thessalonians and Hebrews; moreover on the Catholic Epistles of St. James and the first Epistle of John. These annotations were taken down from the mouth of Huldrych Zwingli. A brief account of the death of Christ, drawn from the four Evange-

units.la: A a 3 Evangelistis per Huldricum Zuinglium in unam seriem concinnata. Scripsit praeterea Epistolas multas, doctrina ac pietate mera refertas, quae una cum Oecolampadij Epistolis impressae sunt Basileae apud Robertum Winter. Et hactenus de Zuinglij lucubrationibus, quas vel ipse Latinè scripsit, vel ab alijs, utpote Leone Judae, Rodolpho Gualthero, Gaspare Megandro è Germanico in Latinum sermonem transfusas habemus. Ipse verò pro aris ac focis fortiter pugnans occubuit anno 1531. Undecimo Octobris. Ejus opera denuò exeusa sunt Tiguri, anno 1581. Habeo ejusdem quasdam Epistolas MSS. auro contrà charas.
units.tr: A a 3 lists, arranged into one continuous order by Huldrych Zwingli. He also wrote many letters, full of pure learning and piety, which were printed together with the letters of Oecolampadius at Basel by Robert Winter. And so far concerning the works of Zwingli, which either he himself wrote in Latin, or which we have translated into Latin from German by others, namely by Leo Jud, Rudolf Gwalther and Caspar Megander. He himself, fighting bravely for altar and hearth, fell in the year 1531, on the eleventh of October. His works were printed again at Zurich in the year 1581. I have certain letters of his in manuscript, which are dearer than gold.

units.la: Zuinglius Huldricus, Reformatoris nepos: Huldrici, Pastoris ad Praedicatores ab a Ch. 1568 ad 1571 quo apoplexia obijt, filius: N.T. Professor, scripsit de justificatione per fidem in Epist. ad Hebraeos c. XI. Cui accesserit Petri Pictavien-sis Episcopi Chronologia Patrum à Zuinglio ad sua tempora continuata. Tig. 1592.
units.tr: Zuinglius Huldricus, grandson of the Reformer, son of Huldrych, minister to the preachers from 1568 to 1571, when he died of apoplexy; professor of New Testament, wrote on justification by faith in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter XI. To this may be added the Chronology of the Fathers by Peter, Bishop of Poitiers, continued from Zwingli down to his own times. Zurich, 1592.

units.la: Atque haec quidem de Bibliotheca Tigurina hactenus. Nonnulli forte primi per nos in apertam lucem sunt protracti: Alij sedi suae restituti: De Amando, sive Henrico Susone doctorum etiam reperias ἐπυχάς, ut ex Zæmanni carnific. pag. 182. 182. apparet. Pauca quaedam veterum exciderunt nomina, & eorum quidem, de quibus dubitari queat, qualis est Metellus, Poeta Tigurinus, apud Aventin. pag. 484. Recentiorum quorundam nomina, Floris, seu Blumij, Dasypodij, Brunneri, Apostatae, Professoris Ingolstadiensis, in literatura Graeca non malè versati, Iuliani Terentiani, qui ex Epiphanio quaedam transtulit, Matthiae Hirzgartneri, Mathematici insignis; Rodolphi Guerbij, authoris tractatus de consecrationibus sive incantationibus Magicis, Iohannis Huldrici, cujus alii quot prodierunt Conciones doctissimae, & nuperrimè tractatus de revelatione mysteriorum divinorum, Guilelmi Frey, qui Comeniana quaedam compendifecit, suis restituì facilè poterunt locis.
units.tr: So much for the Zurich library up to now. Some perhaps have been first brought by us into the open light; others have been restored to their own seat. Concerning Amandus, or Henry Suso, you may also find learned notes, as appears from Zæmann's executioner, page 182. Some names of older writers have dropped out, and indeed of those about whom doubt might be raised, such as Metellus, a Zurich poet, mentioned in Aventinus, page 484. The names of some more recent writers, Floris, or Blumius, Dasypodius, Brunner, an apostate, professor at Ingolstadt, who was well versed in Greek literature; Julian Terentianus, who translated some things from Epiphanius; Matthias Hirzgartner, an outstanding mathematician; Rudolf Guerbius, author of a treatise on magical consecrations or incantations; John Huldrych, of whom several learned sermons have appeared, and most recently a treatise on the revelation of divine mysteries; William Frey, who made an epitome of certain works of Comenius, can easily be restored to their own places.

units.la: APPENDIX II. EXHIBENS STATUM ECCLESIAE & Scholae Tigurinae, Aphoristicè.
units.tr: APPENDIX II. SETTING FORTH THE ECCLESIASTICAL AND SCHOLASTIC STATE OF ZURICH, IN APHORISMS.

units.la: I. STatus Tigurinorum Ecclesiastico-Scholasticus consideratur velin Gentilismo, vel Christianismo.
units.tr: I. The ecclesiastical and scholastic condition of the Zurichers is considered either in Gentilism or Christianity.

units.la: II. Illius eadem fuit ratio, quam caterorum, tum Gallorum, tum Germanorum. De utroque actum à nobis est in Method. legend. Hist. Helvet. De Ecclesiastico pag. 528. De Scholastico verò pag. 534.
units.tr: II. The account was the same as that of the others, both French and German. We have treated both in Method. legend. Hist. Helvet.: on the Ecclesiastical at p. 528, and on the Scholastic at p. 534.

units.la: III. Hujus distinctae ante Reformationem considerandae veniunt periodi.
units.tr: III. Periods to be considered before the Reformation are distinguished here.

units.la: IV. Prima periodus ortum nobis Christianismi pandit Seculo 3. per Legionem Thebaeam: secunda continuationem ad seculum 7. Tertia incrementa sub Carolo magno ad Reformationem usque. Incunabula Christianismi in Helvetia quidam referunt ad S Beatum, Petri discipulum, cujus in vicinia adeò venerandum erat nomen, ut paucis adhuc ab hinc annis spelunca ejus religiosè fuerit visitata. Sed vel incerta haec sunt, vel fabulosa plane, ceu diximus lib. cit. pag. 539. Certiora ostendimus incunabula in Legione Thebaea, de qua veteres parcius, recentiores prolixius & fusius: videatur Hodeg. P. I. c. 1. pag. 13. &c. ubi & nos Historiae Epitomen dedimus. Aliam interea nacti sumus, ab Henrico Glareano Lutetiae ante Reformationem scriptam; de qua, Σ. Θ. edenda, alia cogitabimus occasione.
units.tr: IV. The first period reveals to us the origin of Christianity in the third century through the Theban Legion; the second its continuation to the seventh century; the third its growth under Charlemagne down to the Reformation. Some refer the beginnings of Christianity in Helvetia to St Beatus, a disciple of Peter, whose name was so venerated in the neighbourhood that only a few years ago his cave was visited with devotion. But these are either uncertain or plainly fabulous, as we said in the work cited, p. 539. We show more certain beginnings in the Theban Legion, about which the ancients wrote sparingly and the more recent writers at greater length and in more detail. See Hodeg. P. I, c. 1, p. 13 etc., where we also gave an epitome of the history. Meanwhile we have obtained another, written by Henricus Glareanus at Paris before the Reformation; concerning its publication (Σ. Θ.) we shall consider another occasion.

units.la: V. Secunda Periodus, continuationem receptae doctrinae Christianae exhibens, fere ἀδήλος est, nisi quod pro certo habeamus;
units.tr: V. The second period, which exhibits the continuation of the received Christian doctrine, is almost obscure [ἀδήλος], except for what we hold for certain;

units.la: A. Tigurum, sive Thuricum, ut ejus aetatis scriptio habet; vel castrum Thuricinum, postquam semel suscepta sacra ad vomitum Gentilismi, aliorum Europaeorum exemplo, non redijsse, etsi vicina adhuc loca, Tuconium &c. etiam seculo septimo à Paganismo fuerint purganda. B. Anno 695. aut praeter propter, ex donatione Ruperti, & Templum Tiguri extruendum, & servitium Dei ibidem perpetualiter constituendum (non, ut Guillim. habet, construendum) decretum fuisse.
units.tr: A. Tigurum, or Thuricum, as the writing of that age has it; or castrum Thuricinum, since, once the sacred rites had been taken up, they did not return to the vomit of Gentilism, as happened elsewhere in Europe, although the neighbouring places, Tuconium and others, were also to be purged of paganism in the seventh century. B. In the year 695 or thereabouts, by the donation of Ruperti, it was decreed that a temple be built at Zurich and the service of God be permanently established there (not, as Guillim. has it, construendum).

units.la: Refert donationis instrumentum Bulling. de Antiq. Tigurin. lib.4.c.1.Guillim de reb. Helvet. lib.3.pag.336. ubi tamen in subscriptione notorius est error, de quo ijdem. Fuit autem hic Rupertus Dux Militum, Ludovici Regis III. συγγρoves frater VVighardi Presbyteri, qui Lucernensis postea Ecclesiæ fuit fundator. C. Ob antiquitatem, Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ primas post Constantiensem, in toto Episcopatu fuisse delatas. Guillim.l.c.pag.349. Rapertus, qui sub Crasso & deinceps vixit, scripsit, Episcopum Constantiensem post suam electionem, unctionemque obligatum fuisse statim Tigurum se conferre, ibidemque Sacra facere, quod antiquæ & memorabilis authoritatis argumentum.
units.tr: The deed of donation is reported by Bulling., de Antiq. Tigurin. lib. 4, c. 1, and by Guillim, de reb. Helvet. lib. 3, p. 336, where, however, there is a notorious error in the subscription, concerning which ijdem. Now this Rupert was a commander of troops, kinsman [συγγενής] of King Ludovici III, and brother of VVighardi, the presbyter, who afterwards became the founder of the church at Lucerne. C. On account of its antiquity, the church of Zurich was granted the primacy after Constance throughout the whole diocese. Guillim. l.c. p. 349. Rapertus, who lived under Crassus and after, wrote that the bishop of Constance, after his election and anointing, was bound to betake himself straight to Zurich and perform the sacred rites there, which is an argument of ancient and memorable authority.

units.la: VI. Tertia periodo, ab initio Seculi IX. sive Carolo Magno, magna Ecclesia Tigurina & honorata quidem, certis suis distincta gradibus, accepit incrementa.
units.tr: VI. In the third period, from the beginning of the ninth century, that is from Charlemagne, the great and honoured Zurich church, distinguished by its own certain grades, received its increase.

units.la: Observamus ergo,
units.tr: We observe therefore:

units.la: A. Carolum Magnum liberalissimum Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ fuisse Auctorem. Non tam fundatorem Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ, quàm Auctorem Collegij certo numero adstricti, fuisse Carolum M. ex charta donationis ejus, cujusgeminum habemus apographum, patet. Meminit enim, 1. Ille Ecclesiæ & Martyrum Thuricensium, 2. Constitutis jam fratribus vitæ Canonem & subsidia oste-ndit. 3. Et aliorum donationes confirmat, & novas ipse impertitur. 4. Sacrorum administrationem, per montes & valles, omnibus ex æquo, adeoque & honestam juventutis educationem commendat. Data est charta in Thurego (in VVighardi charta castrum Turicinum appellatur, an quòd veteres ibi Romani sua habuerunt castra, aut quod, recepto vocis usu, Tigurum jam tum satis cultum fuisse significare voluerit? Æquipollet enim ἐρύματα, ὀχυρώματα munimento, castello: Etymol. mag. κάστρον, ὀχύρωμα; Perott. Castrum significat locum muris munitum, & castello majus est, minus oppido: Quamvis & castelli alibi ei tribuatur nomen, Goldast. Rer. Germ. T.II.p.387.) A.D.DCCCX. De numero horum Fratrum charta nihil exprimit. Septendecim vel octodecim numerantur tempore Ludovici & Caroli, quorum nomina vid. apud. Stumpf. lib.6. c.14. Ad 24. revocatos ab eo esse, antiquissima traditio est Statuta Eccles. Tig. de an. Chr. 1259. Ex institutione Karoli, Imperatoris Sanctissimi, & Ecclesiæ nostræ Fundatoris, sunt 24. Canonici: sed usque ad præsens (NB.) tantummodo decem curtes habentur, quæ apud nos vulgariter Klosterhöfe vocantur. Quod ipsum Iohannes XXII. in Bulla, sua repetijt.
units.tr: A. That Charlemagne was the most generous author of the Zurich church. That Charlemagne was not so much the founder of the Zurich church as the author of a college bound to a fixed number is clear from his charter of donation, of which we have a twin copy. For he mentions, 1. that church and the martyrs of Zurich; 2. that brothers were already established in common life, and he sets out their rule and support; 3. he confirms the donations of others and grants new ones himself; 4. he commends the administration of the sacraments, through mountains and valleys, to all alike, and so also the honest education of youth. The charter was given at Thurego. (In Wighard's charter it is called castrum Turicinum. Was this because the ancient Romans had their camp there, or because, with the usage of the word received, he wished to signify that Zurich was by then sufficiently cultivated? For ἐρύματα, ὀχυρώματα [fortifications, strongholds] amount to munimentum, castellum. Etymol. mag.: κάστρον, ὀχύρωμα [castle, stronghold]; Perott. Castrum signifies a place fortified with walls, and is larger than a castellum but smaller than an oppidum; although elsewhere the name castellum is also given to it, Goldast. Rer. Germ. T. II, p. 387.) A.D. 810. The charter says nothing about the number of these brothers. Seventeen or eighteen are counted in the time of Ludovicus and Charles, whose names are given in Stumpf, lib. 6, c. 14. That they were restored by him to twenty-four is the most ancient tradition: the Statutes of the Zurich church, of the year of Christ 1259, say: By the institution of Karl, most holy emperor and founder of our church, there are 24 canons; but up to the present (NB) only ten courts are held, which among us are commonly called Klosterhöfe. John XXII repeated the same in his bull.

units.la: B. Sed & cæteros ordine Imperatores, Reges, Alemannia Duces qualibet oblata occasione affectum suum, liberalitatem prolixè in Ecclesiam Tigurinam, Collegium præsertim Carolinum, fuisse testatos.
units.tr: B. But also the other emperors in turn, kings and dukes of Alemannia, whenever any occasion offered, testified their affection and lavish generosity toward the Zurich church, and especially the Carolinum college.

units.la: Extant adhuc in archivo nostro Ecclesiastico monumenta Ottonis I Luitolfi Ducis, filij ejus; Ottonis II. circa an. Chr. 974. Henrici III. & Ducis Herimanni; Henrici IV. circa an. Chr. 1057. quibus vel privilegijs cavetur Collegij, vel lites inter ipsos clericos decidantur, cujusmodi, ut instrumentorum retineamus verba, sunt: De concambitione familiarum, de Duce Herimanno facta; De Analoia; Idem de genere quatuor Fratrum, servorum Clericorum: Notitia, de servis & ancillis in Hoinga; Notitia de contentione, quæ fuit propter decimationes, quæ pertinent ad Ecclesias Sancti Petri, & ad Ecclesiam Sanctorum Martyrum Felicis, & Germanæ ejus S. Regulæ: Notitia concambij de duabus ancillis, una Sanctorum Felicis & Regulæ; & alia S. Galli: Notitia de Concilio Cotifridi, Comitis in Civitate Turicina, publicè & legitimè facto. Traditio VVicharij Diaconi ad Altare Sanctorum Felicis & Regulæ, atque Canonicis eorum. Traditio Luitgerdæ: De contentione Ruboni. De contentione inter Turricinos, & Adilhelmm. Sunt hæc fermè, post Ruperti donationem, non postrema, quibus fides tutò poterit adhiberi, in Archivis Helveticis monumenta, quæ de statu patriæ tam Politico, quàm Ecclesiastico, qualis quidem tum sub Francorum, & primorum etiam Germanorum Imperatorum regimine, per duo integra secula, erat, nonnulla habent, alijs intacta. Constitueram, quia ne à nostris quidem, quod sciam, eruderata illa fuerunt, sive, quòd ætati nonnullæ cedentes voces difficilius legerentur, sive quòd terminorum etiam quorundam insolentia terreret, vetustatis illa Helvetica documenta, hoc loco διαρρήσὴν attexere: Quando verò tam prolixam digressionem succincta notarum brevitas non admittit, de alia nobis occasione cogitandum erit. Videamus tamen usum eorum, per quasdam observationes. Et ex Caroli Magni quidem donationis charta colligimus. I. Ecclesiam Tigurinam initio Seculi IX. satis fuisse celebrem. Meminit enim Ecclesiæ Thuricinæ: Vocat Ecclesiam matrem. Exprimit dotales donationes ab Antiquis Antecessoribus constitutas. II. Carolum M. agnovisse, Martyres, Felicem & Regulam coronas gratuitas accepisse, non verò meritis proprijs acquisivisse. Fatetur enim, miraculosam sepulturam, Christo propitio prædestinante, factam. III. Scopum hujus Collegij primarium fuisse honorem Dei, idque in solidum, & salutem Testatorum. De priori, instrumentum ita loquitur: In primordio ad incrementum congregationis Canonicorum, ut ibidem regulari disciplina viventes, die noctuque indeficiendo, septies in die, Deo laudes implendo subsisterent. Posterius, jam in valescente tu proprij meriti opinione, satis ἀχυρολόγως (calamo tamen forte magis, quam animo, superbo & exorbitante; ipse potius alicujus sui boni pleno, quam ulla plenissimæ satisfactionis Christi injuria) sic exprimitur: Propria prædia fuisse ad sepulchrum tradita ut animas à criminibus alligatas redimerent; denasse pro Deo, omniumque suorum peccatorum remedio: quæ phrasis etiam in donatione Ruperti & VVighardi occurrit. IV. Primum primi Collegij corpus in Decanum & Presbyteros fuisse distinctum. Ita enim chartæ appendix habet: Hæc sunt nomina Presbyterorum, qui in illis temporibus Regum Ludovici (vix dubito, quin intelligatur Ludovicus sive Clodovæus III. qui circa finem seculi septimi mortuus, ut circa an. Chr. 742. adeoque seculo sequenti Carolus M. fuit natus, sub quibus vel simul, vel successive illi vixerunt) sub vita Canonicorum &c. Primum Decani nomen Leidirath, Comolt &c. V. Ministerio tum Ecclesiastico nomina dedisse eos etiam, qui & generis nobilitate, & facultatibus præpollebant. In prima donatione extat mentio VVighardi Presbyteri, qui frater fuit Ruperti Ducis Alemanniæ (Militiæ tamen potius initio, quam Provinciarum Duces appellabantur; quia rei militari præerant: Paulatim vero hæc dignitas hæreditaria esse cæpit) sanguine junctus Regi Ludovico. Nemo autem miretur, inquit Bulling. de Antiq. Tig. l 4 c. 1. VVighardum, Virum adeo magnum & potentem, fuisse Presbyterum. Neque enim tum temporis Ministerium ita contemtum fuit, ut ultimis nostris & perditissimis temporibus, In charta Carolina Hilfrich vocatur clericus, qui se in congregationem fratrum commendando donavit Fratribus, quicquid ad Ruitin (jam Fallenden Brunnen) & illa Marcha possedit. Ipsum pertus Presbyter dedit in VVolasfelda (Wallisfelen) unam mansam. Comolt Presbyter donavit ad Ecclesiam Fratribus, quicquid in Flobotisreine (Stuntenreyn) & illa possedit marca. In Bozivila autem unus ex illis Fratribus unam dedit cum mancipiis mansam Ecclesiæ. VI. Ab ipsa statim prima institutione hujus Collegij fuisse discessum. In primordio, i.e. ut supra monuimus, initio constitutum, & à Carolo M. postea confirmatum fuit, ut regulari (nullius Sancti, sed Scripturæ canone) disciplina viventes, die noctuque indeficiendo, septies indie Deo laudes implendo subsisterent. Iam in hac posteriori lacinia, illud quidem plenius explicatur, ut populus Catholica fidei & Christianitatis omni tempore Ministerium quaerere, atque Deo(cui Sanctos jam addunt) & sanctis Martyribus, Felici & germana ejus, Regula, serviendo permanerem. VII. Tandem & hoc haud obscure colligimus, Carolum M. Tigurinum fuisse. Ita enim habet clausula, Imperatoris jussu coepta & scripta: Actum in Turego anno Imperii sui X. (adeoque tertio ante obitum) ipsius Caroli Imperat. indictione XIII. A.Chr. DCCC. sed & F. Martinus de Bartenstein, in Legenda sua, de Felice & Regula, refert, per eundem reliquias illic Thebaicas elevatas, Felicem & Regulam Tiguri relictas, Exuperantium vero Aquisgranum deductum, & in ejus honorem Ecclesiam collegiatam fundatam. Traditio est, habitasse e regione Templi Majoris, de qua Iohannes Fabricius, Epistola ad Andream Hyperium, de statu Ecclesiae & Scholae Tigurinae. Atque haec de charta Caroli M. Ex traditione Vuicbarij, Diaconi (qui & Canonicos Fratres suos appellat & Seniores) & Luitgardae nihil fere occurrit, quod Historiam illius seculi illustret, nisi quod, cum mentio facta ante fuerit, ex recepta veterum consuetudine, sepulchri Sanctorum; jam aliis Sanctorum Martyrum meminerit. Tertio instrumento a. XI. Ottonis, sub Duce Luitolvo, filio, lis inter Canonicos Carolinos, & Moniales ob censum quendam in Samilinis Ruitin orta, decisa fuit: Ex quo documento colligo, 1. Antiquitatem iterum Ecclesiae. Bis Ecclesia antiqua vocatur. 2. Antecessores, tum fuisse Alolfum, Thiedilant, Decanum. VVolfirath & Andream Fratres, &c. 3. Moniales eo demum tempore sedem suam ibi fixisse. Mentio quidem expressa fit Monasterij Monialium; sed non quasi, ut perperam quidam statuunt. Collegiata Ecclesia illud esset antiquius, utpote quod sub Ludovico demum Germanico, circa an. Chr. 838. fundatum fuit: ut ex donationis Collegij Abbatissani instrumento colligere est, quod, cum explicatione habet, Bullingerus lib. 4. c. 12. 4. Ordines illos valde ad rem fuisse attentos. Vix enim Monialium Collegium extrui potuit, litem statim Collegio Caroli no, ob censum, movet. 5. Ratio causarum civilium cognoscendarum, & statu Politici rudera vetusta ibidem apparent. Meminit familiarum Thuricinarum Civitatis Thuregia; Kerharti Advocati, legitimi consilij ejus. Testes, sive incolae distinguuntur in eos, qui erant a. de Fisco, Landolt, Perigher, Libo, &c. b. De monte, Thiethart, Vuinimund, Sigismunt &c. c. Ex familia Sanctorum (scil. ut alibi vocantur, Ministri & Magistri eorum Cunditonis. superioris Magistratus, Comitis (Comitatus enim antehac Tigurum erat) Luitoni, Concilij ejus, & Advocati. Comitis etiam meminit Peringeri, Herichi &c. judicum item aliorum Adilboldi, Libonis, Helmirichi, Cozperti, & de Fisco, & Monte, quibus sedentibus lis decisa, & controversia proprietas Canonicis iterum fuit adjudicata. Supremus autem tum Magistratus fuit Otto I. qui imperare coepit an. Ch. 938. & Lui. & Lutolvus felicis, tertius Alemannorum Dux. Ad ejusdem Ottonis tempora contentio etiam refertur Ruboni (ut habet inscriptio) & Adilhelmi. Controversia inter Thuricinos clericos, ut vocantur, & laicos, in Collegii favorem fuit dirempta. Ipse processus distincte proponitur, expresis testium nominibus; ubi Clerici contra Adilhelmum ut cum juramento proprietatem controversam confortarunt, ita in Altare & capsa Sanctorum Felicis & Regulae sicut in publico mallo (locus judicij est; Vid. Lexic. Martin.) Kerharti advocati, legitime populi judicaverunt. Sequitur Concambitio familiarum sub Duce Herimanno (qui Burckhardi, Ducis primi, fuit successor) facta, imperante Henrico I. Saxone, qui Ottonis I. Pater, an. Chr. 920. ad gubernacula sedit. Ubi iterum propter mancipia & familias clericales obortae inter Collegium & Moniales, lites erant sopitae. Nihil habet memorabile, quam vetustissimarum familiarum in Thurego, & vicinis Pagis, Rumilane, Suamundinga, Feniclanda, Mure, Flobotureine, Rieda nomina, utrique Collegio emancipata. Hunc autem Catalogum, qui Vestitura appellatur, ipse Dux Alemannorum, in scena Thuricina Civitatis, confecit cum licentia & petione Monialium & clericorum, in praesentia Dominae Reginlinda, Burckhardi Comitis (idem ille fuisse videtur, qui postea III. Alemannorum Dux inclaruit, quod vel ex eo utcunque manifestum est, quod Reginlinda mater ejus immediate praecedat) Tutonis, Hiltilin, Kerharti Advocati, Huozonis, Praepositae Cotisthiu cum suis familijs, familia Ducis, cum Fratribus & familijs Fratrum. In sequentibus etiam duobus Catalogis servorum Clericorum, quorum prior quatuor tantum habet; posterior servos & ancillas, in Hoinga, plures. In priori etiam occurrit nomen VVillcharti Advocati Regis Caroli; in posteriore Advocati Kerharti, Comitis Burckharti, qui regali bono praecepit, ut sine ulla contradictione eorum Fratrum subditi essent servituti. Caetera, quia vix nobis alium praebent usum, quam hactenus ostensum, hac vice suo relinquimus loco. Reliquorum Imperatorum ab Henrico V. privilegia valde sunt perspicua. Et Henricus quidem IV. jura & leges, quas praedecessores ejus, Reges ac Imperatores, Carolus & Otto, Conradus & Henricus avus, Praepositurae sua dederunt, & privilegijs suis confirmaverunt, ipse quoque confirmavit, scilicet ut liberam facultatem in claustro suo habeant eligendi Praepositum, & ut resilorum, sine dominio ullius personae, illis libere inserviant. Mortuus hic Imperator an. Ch. 1114 Henrici V. circa an. Ch. 1128. privilegia praecedentia confirmat, Canonicos immunes reddidit, penitusque absolvit à vigilijs nominatim, & omnibus aliis exactionibus, non obstante consuetudine aliqua vel statuto Consulū. Ejusdem tenoris est Lotharij a. Ch. 1130. Friderictus I. seu Barbarossa an. Chr. 1218. Brisaci & praecedentium privilegia omnia confirmat, & insuper decernit, ut bona Collegij, nulla necessitate incumbente, possint ab Imperio ullo modo abalienari. Ludovicus eadem repetit Egmundae 1255. Richardi duplex est, alterum Haganoae datum 18. Novemb. 1262. alterum Moguntiae. Rodolphi I. luculentissimum est, Viennae perscriptum 1277. de quo supra pag. 68. Alberti I. Rodolphi filij, 1301. Basil. Friderici Austriaci 1315. Caroli IV. à quo privilegium accepit Capitulum causas capitales cognoscendi & exequendi Pragae 1363. Wenceslai, qui idem roboravit privilegium 1384. quem secutus est Sigismundus 1415. ubi etiam pagi, in quos jus illud se extendebat, recensentur Fluntrein, Rieden, Ruschlikon, Meilen, Svvamendingen; quae tamen Amplissimo Magistratui tempore Reformationis sponte Capitulum resignavit. Successit Albertus II. 1439. Maximilianus I. Antverpiae 1487. Carolus V. VVormatiae 1521. C. Neque minor fuit Indulgentiarum apparatus. Catalogum dedimus in Method. legend. Hist. Helvet. pag. 582. Plerarumque autem Indulgentiarum habemus apographa.
units.tr: Still extant in our ecclesiastical archive are the records of Otto I, Duke Luitolf, his son Otto II, about the year of Christ 974; of Henry III and Duke Herimann; Henry IV, about the year of Christ 1057. These either confirm the privileges of the college or settle disputes among the clergy themselves. To give the words of the documents, they bear titles such as: On the exchange of households, made with Duke Herimann; On Analoia; The same, concerning the family of four brothers, clerical serfs; Notice, concerning male and female serfs in Hoinga; Notice, concerning the dispute over the tithes which belong to the churches of St. Peter, of the holy martyrs Felix and his sister Regula; Notice of the exchange of two maidservants, one belonging to Saints Felix and Regula and the other to St. Gall; Notice of the council of Count Cotifrid, held publicly and lawfully in the city of Zurich; The gift of Wichari the deacon to the altar of Saints Felix and Regula and to their canons; The gift of Luitgerda; Concerning the dispute of Rubo; Concerning the dispute between the Zurichers and Adilhelm. These are almost the latest of the documents after the donation of Rupert, and they can safely be trusted. In the Swiss archives there are records concerning the state of the homeland, both political and ecclesiastical, as it was under the rule of the Franks and of the first German emperors for two full centuries; some of these have been studied and some remain untouched. I had intended, since none of our own people, as far as I know, has examined these, to insert those old Helvetic documents here, as a digression. Either some words belonging to that age were harder to read, or the unfamiliarity of certain technical terms was discouraging. But since a brief note cannot admit so long a digression, we shall have to think of another occasion for it. Let us nonetheless look at their use through a few observations. From the charter of the donation of Charles the Great we gather the following. I. That the Zurich church was quite famous at the beginning of the ninth century. For it mentions the church of Zurich; it calls it the mother church. It speaks of dowry gifts established by the ancient predecessors. II. That Charles the Great acknowledged that the martyrs Felix and Regula had received their crowns as a free gift, and had not won them by their own merits. For it confesses that their miraculous burial was made by Christ's favourable predestination. III. That the chief aim of this college was the honour of God, and that wholly, and the salvation of the testators. Concerning the first point, the document speaks thus: at its beginning, for the increase of the congregation of canons, so that they might live there under a rule of discipline, continuing day and night without ceasing, offering praises to God seven times a day. Later, when the opinion of their own merit had already grown strong, it is expressed (with a boastful and extravagant pen, perhaps, rather than with a proud intention, and rather a man full of some good of his own than an offence against the most complete satisfaction of Christ) in these words, not without a certain crudeness: that their own estates had been handed over to the tomb so that they might redeem souls bound by crimes; that they had died for God and for the remedy of all their sins. This phrase also occurs in the donation of Rupert and Wichard. IV. That the first body of the early college was divided into a dean and presbyters. For the appendix to the charter reads: These are the names of the presbyters who, in the times of King Louis (I scarcely doubt that Louis or Clovis III is meant, who died near the end of the seventh century, so that Charles the Great was born about the year of Christ 742 and in the following century; under these men they lived either together or in succession) during the lifetime of the canons, etc. The first name of dean is Leidirath, Comolt, etc. V. That those who excelled both in nobility of birth and in wealth also gave their names to the ministry of the Church at that time. In the first donation there is mention of Wichard, a presbyter, who was the brother of Duke Rupert of Alemannia, related by blood to King Louis. (Yet at first they were called rather military than provincial dukes, since they commanded the military affairs; but gradually this dignity began to become hereditary.) No one should be surprised, says Bullinger (On the Antiquities of Zurich, book 4, chap. 1), that Wichard, a man so great and powerful, was a presbyter. For at that time the ministry was not so despised as in our last and most wretched times. In the Carolingian charter, Hilfrich is called a clergyman, who, commending himself to the brotherhood, gave to the brothers whatever he possessed at Ruitin (now the Falling Spring) and in that march. The presbyter Pertus himself gave one farm at Wolasfelda (Wallisfelen). The presbyter Comolt gave to the church for the brothers whatever he possessed in Flobotisreine (Stuntenreyn) and in that march. In Bozivila one of those brothers gave to the church one farm with its serfs. VI. That there was a departure from the very first institution of this college. In its beginning, that is, as we noted above, it was established and later confirmed by Charles the Great, that they should continue to live under a rule of discipline (not of any saint, but by the canon of Scripture), continuing day and night without ceasing, offering praises to God seven times a day. Now, in this later fragment, the matter is more fully explained: that they should remain seeking the ministry at all times for the Catholic people of the faith and of Christianity, and serving God (to whom they now add the saints) and the holy martyrs Felix and his sister Regula. VII. Finally we gather this too, not obscurely: that Charles the Great was a Zurich man. For the closing clause, begun and written at the emperor's command, reads: Done at Zurich in the tenth year of his reign (that is, three years before his death) in the thirteenth indiction of Charles the emperor himself, in the year of Christ 800. Also Friar Martin of Bartenstein, in his legend of Felix and Regula, reports that the Theban relics were raised there by the same emperor, that Felix and Regula were left at Zurich, and that Exuperantius was led to Aachen, where a collegiate church was founded in his honour. There is a tradition that they dwelt opposite the Great Minster, which Johannes Fabricius mentions in his letter to Andreas Hyperius, concerning the state of the Church and School of Zurich. So much for the charter of Charles the Great. From the tradition of Wicbari, the deacon (who also calls his canonical brothers elders), and of Luitgarda, there is almost nothing that illustrates the history of that century, except that, since mention was made earlier, according to the received custom of the ancients, of the tombs of the saints, now he mentions other holy martyrs. In the third document, of the eleventh year of Otto, under Duke Luitolf, his son, a dispute between the Carolingian canons and the nuns over a certain census in Samilinis Ruitin was settled. From this document I gather the following: 1. The antiquity of the church again: it is twice called an ancient church. 2. The predecessors at that time were Alolf, Thiedilant, the dean, Wolfirath and the brothers Andreas, etc. 3. The nuns had at last fixed their seat there. Indeed, the monastery of nuns is expressly mentioned; but not as some have wrongly supposed, as though the collegiate church were older, since it was founded only under Louis the German, about the year of Christ 838, as may be gathered from the instrument of the donation of the abbess's college, which Bullinger explains in book 4, chap. 12. 4. That those orders were much attended to in the matter. For the college of nuns could hardly have been built before it began a suit against the Carolingian college over a census. 5. The method of hearing civil causes, and the ancient remnants of the political state, appear there. It mentions the families of the Zurich citizens of the city of Thuregia; Kerhart the advocate, his lawful counsel. The witnesses, or inhabitants, are distinguished into those who were a. of the fisc: Landolt, Periger, Libo, etc.; b. of the mountain: Thiethart, Wuinimund, Sigismund, etc.; c. of the family of the saints (namely, as they are called elsewhere, ministers and masters of their property). The superior magistrate was the count (for the county was formerly Zurich): Luitho, his counsellor, and the advocate. He also mentions the count Peringer, Herich, etc., and the judges, likewise Adilbold, Libo, Helmerich, Cozpert, and of the fisc and the mountain, by whose sitting the suit was decided and the ownership of the property was again adjudged to the canons. The supreme magistrate at that time was Otto I, who began to reign in the year of Christ 938, and Luitolf, the fortunate, the third Duke of the Alemanni. The dispute with Rubo (as the inscription says) and Adilhelm is also referred to the time of this same Otto. The controversy between the Zurich clergy, as they are called, and the laymen, was settled in favour of the college. The very proceedings are set out clearly, with the names of the witnesses named; where the clergy, against Adilhelm, confirmed the disputed ownership with an oath, and so at the altar and the chest of Saints Felix and Regula, as in the public court (the place of judgment; see the Martin lexicon) the advocate Kerhart and the people lawfully judged. Next follows the exchange of households, made under Duke Herimann (who was the successor of Burkhard, the first duke), in the reign of Henry I the Saxon, who was the father of Otto I, about the year of Christ 920, when he sat at the helm.
