There again, on account of serfs and clerical households, disputes had arisen between the college and the nuns, and these were quieted. There is nothing memorable in it except the names of the most ancient families in Zurich and the neighbouring districts, Rumilane, Suamundinga, Feniclanda, Mure, Flobotureine, Rieda, emancipated to both colleges. This catalogue, which is called the Vestitura, was itself drawn up by the duke of the Alemanni, in the court of the city of Zurich, with the licence and petition of the nuns and clergy, in the presence of Lady Reginlind, Count Burkhard (this seems to be the same man who later became famous as the third duke of the Alemanni, which is at least clear from the fact that his mother Reginlind precedes him directly) Tuto, Hiltilin, Kerhart the advocate, Huozo, the provost of Cotisthiu, with their families, the duke's household, with the brothers and the families of the brothers. In the following two catalogues of clerical serfs, the first has only four, the second more male and female serfs in Hoinga. In the first there also occurs the name of Willchart, advocate of King Charles; in the second, the advocate Kerhart, Count Burkhard, who by royal grace ordered that the subjects of those brothers be in servitude without any contradiction. The rest, since they offer us little use beyond what has been shown so far, we leave in their own place for now. The privileges of the remaining emperors from Henry V onward are very clear. And Henry IV indeed also confirmed with his own hand the rights and laws which his predecessors, the kings and emperors Charles and Otto, Conrad and his grandfather Henry, had given to his provostship and confirmed by their privileges: namely, that they should have the free right in their cloister to elect a provost, and that they should freely serve the people without the lordship of any person. This emperor died in the year of Christ 1114. Henry V, about the year of Christ 1128, confirmed the preceding privileges, made the canons immune, and wholly freed them by name from night watches and from all other exactions, notwithstanding any custom or decree of the councils. Lothar is of the same tenor in the year of Christ 1130. Frederick I, or Barbarossa, in the year of Christ 1218 at Brisach, confirmed all the preceding privileges and moreover decreed that the goods of the college, when no necessity presses, may by no means be alienated by any empire. Louis repeats the same at Egmond in 1255. There are two of Richard: one given at Hagenau on 18 November 1262, the other at Mainz. Rudolph I's is most illustrious, drawn up at Vienna in 1277, concerning which see above, page 68. Albert I, son of Rudolph, 1301, at Basel. Frederick of Austria, 1315. Charles IV, from whom the chapter received the privilege of hearing and executing capital causes, at Prague in 1363. Wenceslas, who likewise strengthened the privilege in 1384, was followed by Sigismund in 1415, where also the districts to which that right extended are listed: Fluntrein, Rieden, Ruschlikon, Meilen, Schwamendingen; which, however, the chapter of its own accord surrendered to the most honourable magistracy at the time of the Reformation. Albert II succeeded in 1439. Maximilian I at Antwerp in 1487. Charles V at Worms in 1521. Nor was the display of indulgences any less. We have given a catalogue in the Method of the Legend of the Helvetic History, page 582. Moreover, we have copies of most of the indulgences.

units.la: D. Ut vero a notoria Cleri culpa & superstitio creverit in Ecclesia, & ignorantia b in Collegio atq; Scholis; desidia, c superstitionis d mater, ubique; semper tamen apud Majores nostros & tyrannidi reguminis, & novitati doctrinae resistendi, masculus se exeruit conatus.
units.tr: D. But that the Church grew, through the notorious guilt of the clergy and superstition, and through ignorance in the college and schools, and through idleness, the mother of superstition, everywhere; yet among our forefathers a manly effort always stood out against tyranny in the government and against novelty of doctrine.

units.la: a. Crevit I. opinio meriti; unde magis magisque phrasis, pro remedio animae, ad redemptionem animarum, invaluit. In supra memorato Censorum Catalogo, Reginhardus pro animae suae remedio ad Altare S. Martyrum, Felicis & Regulae tradidit, ut singulis annis censum ad Festivitatem Martyrij sui solverent. Uto Presbyter pro animae suae remedio ad altare sanctorum Martyrum Felicis & Regulae tradidit, ut singulis annis ad Missam illorum censum solverent. 2. Numerus festorum; id quod excollatione utriusque Breviarij Thuricensis facile colligitur sup p. 473. Sacellorum & Altarium auctior numerus. Altarium quidem meminerunt documenta sex & septem seculorum; Dedicationis Altaris S. Pancratij an. D. 1104. ab Ahezelone, pro ut dedicatio in Crypta an. D. 1107. à Gebhardo Episcopo, facta dicuntur; Sacellorum vero origo infra ferè seculum tertium fuit apud Tigurinos. Prima & antiquissima, in Imperiali Aula (auf dem Hof) incidit in annum 1272. Secunda Aquatica 1256. loco supplicij Martyrum : Reliqua deinceps usque dum nova hæc ædificia numerum tricesimum superârunt, de quibus Bulling l.6 c.6
units.tr: a. There grew, first, the opinion of merit; whence the phrase "for the remedy of the soul" and "for the redemption of souls" gained ever greater currency. In the aforementioned catalogue of censuses, Reginhard handed over to the altar of the holy martyrs Felix and Regula for the remedy of his soul, so that they should pay a levy each year on the feast of their martyrdom. Uto the presbyter handed over to the altar of the holy martyrs Felix and Regula for the remedy of his soul, so that they should pay a levy each year at the Mass for them. 2. The number of feasts; this is easily gathered from the comparison of both Zurich breviaries, above p. 473. The number of chapels and altars increased. Of altars, indeed, the documents of the sixth and seventh centuries make mention; the dedication of the altar of St Pancras in the year 1104 by Ahezelo, and the dedication in the crypt in the year 1107 by Bishop Gebhard, are said to have been made. The origin of the chapels, however, falls within almost the third century before this among the Zurichers. The first and oldest, in the imperial court (auf dem Hof), dates from the year 1272. The second, the Aquatic, from 1256, on the site of the execution of martyrs. The rest followed, until these new buildings exceeded the number of thirty, of which Bullinger, book 6, chapter 6.

units.la: 4. Festorum jam receptorum ἀναξηνσις vel duplicatio. Ita ex ordinatione Magistri Walter, Plebani, festum Vincentij debebat sub pleno officio celebrari. De Franciseanorum Patriarcha querelam Malleoli alibi dedimus.
units.tr: 4. The revival [ἀναξήνσις] or doubling of feasts already received. Thus, by the ordinance of Master Walter, the provost, the feast of Vincent was to be celebrated with the full office. We have given elsewhere a complaint of Malleolus about the patriarch of the Franciscans.

units.la: 5. Ipsum Capitulum in Statutis suis, quæ semel atque iterum mutavit, de ritibus magis augendis, quàm commendanda vel pietate vitæ, vel puritate doctrinæ fuit solicitum. Patet ex Statutis scriptis an. Chr. 1259 repetitis sub Præposito Rodolpho de Vartensee, emendatis paulò ante Reformationem sub Præposito Frey, de quibus supra pag. 97. Major etiam cura pro reliquijs, quas vocabant Sanctorum, dubijs, & incertis, quàm vero Scripturæ sanctuario, supellectili vestiaria & ceremoniali, quàm libraria fuisse laboratum, ex Catalogo Thesaurarij Brunij patet. b. Qua de re videri poterit Orat. I.p. 22. Et Miscell. p 9. c. Etiam in peragendis sacris receptis, teste Malleolo, Miscell. pag. 55. Hinc enim factum, ut Sacellorum, & Sacellanorum numerus cresceret. Cùm enim ipsi Canonici Mundana libentius tractarent; & alios substituerunt muneris vicarios, & in redemtionem dissolutæ vitæ, ad Sacella facultates suas contulerunt; qua de re Bulling. & Frey Præposit.Antiq.Tig.l.6.c.6. e. Id quod abundè condoce fecimus Method.leg. Hist. Helvet.p.542.
units.tr: 5. The chapter itself, in its statutes, which it changed once and again, was more concerned with increasing ceremonies than with commending either the piety of life or the purity of doctrine. This is clear from the statutes written in the year of Christ 1259, repeated under Provost Rudolf of Vartensee, and corrected shortly before the Reformation under Provost Frey, concerning which see above, p. 97. There was also greater care for the relics which they called holy, doubtful and uncertain, than for the sanctuary of Scripture; labour was spent more on vestments, furnishings and ceremonial than on the library, as is clear from the catalogue of the treasurer Bruno. b. On this matter Oration I, p. 22 and Miscellanea p. 9 may be consulted. c. Also in carrying out the sacred rites received, as Malleolus testifies, Miscellanea, p. 55. Hence it came about that the number of chapels and of chaplains grew. For when the canons themselves preferred to deal with worldly matters, and substituted others as deputies for their office, and gave their revenues to the chapels as a redemption of a dissolute life, Bullinger and Frey, Provost, Antiquities of Zurich, book 6, chapter 6, speak of this. e. Which we have shown at more length in Method. Legend. Hist. Helvet., p. 542.

units.la: E. Primaria in Præpositura munera erant Præpositi, a Cantoris b Scholastici, cujus tamen honoraria potius fuit pro Scholis cura, quàm c onerosa functio. Concionandi munus aliquandiu Plebanis in Templo Majori, Abbatissano & Petrino; postea, cùm Monachi, Mendicantes præsertim, nidum Tiguri fixissent, illi quoque ad obeunda munera sacra, majoricum auditorum stupore, quàm ædificatione, fuerunt admissi. Reliquorum, intra aliquot secula, Tigurinæ Ecclesiæ Ministrorum Canonicorum, Sacellanorum, Adjutorum, Pramissariorum nomina habere in promtu, Historiæ magis inservit, quàm Theologiæ.
units.tr: E. The chief offices in the provostship were those of the provost, the cantor, and the scholastic; yet this last office was rather an honorary charge for the care of the schools than a burdensome function. For a time the duty of preaching fell to the parish priests in the Great Minster, in the Abbey and in St Peter's; afterwards, when the monks, especially the mendicants, had settled in Zurich, they too were admitted to perform sacred duties, to the astonishment of the greater hearers rather than to their edification. To have at hand the names of the remaining ministers of the Zurich Church over some centuries, canons, chaplains, assistants and treasurers, serves history more than theology.

units.la: a. Quorum nomina ad Reformationem usque sunt sequentia : Waltherus 1187. 2. Rodolphus de Hottingen 1218 qui prædia sua Oberhusæ Collegio legavit. 3. Wernherus, Sacellanus Wilhelmi Regis 1243. 4. Henricus 1259. 5. Otto de Mannheim 1264. qui Præpositura abiit, ut Prædicatorum ordini se adjungeret. Alij aliter. 6. Henricus de Klingenberg 1271. quo tempore Augustiniani Tiguri recepti sunt. 7. Iohannes de Wildegg, 1276. Ipse verò Cancellarius Rodolphi & Alberti Regum vicarium habuit Rodolphum de Wædischwil. 8. Rodolphus 1307. 9. Crafto, Comes Doggij, Vir magnus, & de Collegio præclaré clarè meritus, 1319. 10. Rodolfus de VVartensee 1339 sub quo Collegij statuta restaurata fuerunt. 11. VVernherus de Rynach, 1370. urbe tamen ejectus fuit, quod fœdera Helvetica, recenter inita, violaret. 12. Iohannes VVyßo 1382. 13. Iohannes de Mœchuang, cognom. Susbach 1392. 14. Conradus Elye, de Loffen, DD 1388. 15. Leonhartus Moßhart, D D Canonicus etiam Constantiensis & Basileensis. 16. Henricus Anenstetter Lic. Decret. 1427. Monet Malleolus, sibi Pontificis authoritate Præposituram assignatam fuisse, Anenstetero à Capitulo: cui pacis & concordiæ gratia libenter cesserit. 17. Matthæus Nidhartus D. D. 1439. de quo graviter questus Malleolus in suo Passionali. Ita interalia:
units.tr: a. The names of these, down to the Reformation, are as follows: (1) Walter, 1187. (2) Rudolf of Hottingen, 1218, who bequeathed his estates at Oberhausen to the college. (3) Werner, chaplain of King William, 1243. (4) Henry, 1259. (5) Otto of Mannheim, 1264, who left the provostship to join the order of the Preachers. Others say otherwise. (6) Henry of Klingenberg, 1271, at which time the Augustinians were received in Zurich. (7) John of Wildegg, 1276. He was indeed chancellor, and had as vicar for the kings Rudolf and Albert, Rudolf of Wädenswil. (8) Rudolf, 1307. (9) Crafto, Count of Toggenburg, a great man who deserved very well of the college, 1319. (10) Rudolf of Wartensee, 1339, under whom the statutes of the college were restored. (11) Werner of Rynach, 1370, though he was ejected from the city because he violated the recently made Swiss treaties. (12) John Wyßo, 1382. (13) John of Mœchuang, surnamed Susbach, 1392. (14) Conrad Elye, of Loffen, D.D., 1388. (15) Leonhard Moßhart, D.D., also a canon of Constance and Basel. (16) Henry Anenstetter, Licentiate of Decrees, 1427. Malleolus notes that the provostship had been assigned to Anenstetter by the authority of the Pope, by the chapter; and he willingly yielded it for the sake of peace and concord. (17) Matthew Nidhart, D.D., 1439, of whom Malleolus complained bitterly in his Passionale. Thus, among other things:

units.la: Hic odium [a] durum non abs re cognominatur,
units.tr: This man, hard hatred, is not without reason so named,

units.la: Nam odio suo subvectus duré gravatur.
units.tr: For, carried along by his hatred, he is harshly weighed down.

units.la: Suspectus erat aperte collusionis cum hostibus tempore belli quod Tigurinum septennale vulgò à nostris appellatur. 18. Schwiderus de Gottlicken 1466. 19. Henricus Nidhart. V.I.D. 1470.20. Iacobus de Cham, LL.D. 1473. 21. Iohannes Mantzius, V.I.D. 1495. 22. Felix Frey, Magister Artium Parisiensis 1518.
units.tr: He was openly suspected of collusion with the enemy at the time of the war which our people commonly call the Seven Years' War of Zurich. (18) Schwider of Gottlicken, 1466. (19) Henry Nidhart, Doctor of both laws, 1470. (20) James of Cham, Doctor of Laws, 1473. (21) John Mantz, Doctor of both laws, 1495. (22) Felix Frey, Master of Arts of Paris, 1518.

units.la: b. De his muneribus, eorumque præcipuis administratoribus vid sup. Orat. 1. pag 15.
units.tr: b. On these offices and their chief administrators see above, Oration 1, p. 15.

units.la: c. Vtdiximus Ib pag. 16 unde nomina Scholæ Moderatorum aliquot p. 18. quibus ex anti quo Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ Anniversario addi possunt, Magister Henricus, quondam Rector Scholarum, Frater Iohannis Præpositi. Magister Berchtol. Frygt, Rector Scholarum hujus Ecclesiæ. M. Albertus de Rotvvila, quondam Rector Scholarum hujus Ecclesiæ, &c de quibus in C. tal. seq.
units.tr: c. We have said this in the same place, p. 16, whence some names of the rectors of the school are given on p. 18. To these may be added from the ancient anniversary of the Zurich Church: Master Henry, formerly rector of the schools, brother of John the Provost; Master Berchtold Frygt, rector of the schools of this church; Master Albert of Rotwil, formerly rector of the schools of this church; etc., of whom more in the following catalogue.

units.la: d. Nomina primorum Ecclesiæ Collegiatæ Plebanorum negat se reperire potuisse Bulling. de Antiq. Tig l.6.c.2. Turpiter neglecta esse conqueritur. Ab annis 70. numerat M. Conradum Hofmanum, M. Erhartum Batmannum, M. Huldricum Zuinglium. Fundatio Plebanatus non satis nota, confirmatio ex Berchtholdi, Zeringiæ Ducis, instrumento, de an. Chr. 1187 Indict 5 4 Cal. Septemb. ita habet: In nomine sanctæ & Individuæ Trinitatis: Ego Berchtoldus de Zeringen, Dux & Rector Burgundiæ, Dei & Imperiali gratia, Thuregici loci legitimus Advocatus, quod Kastvogt dicitur, venerabili VValthero, prædicti loci Præposito, sanctisque Fratribus ejus, ut in perpetuum inchoata feliciter, & pro salute multorum, beato fine consummata negotia, concessa privilegio, digne solidentur: Intimamus igitur universis sanctæ Ecclesiæ fidelibus, qualiter Parochia Thuricensis Præpositura, à primitiva sua fundationis origine, ipsorum Canonicorum providentia curabatur, ita videlicet, ut ejus Ecclefiæ Sacerdotes Canonici, competenti famulatu populo deservierint, subditisque totius Parochiæ filijs, Pastorali curâ in cunctis Ecclesijs præcaverint. Labente verò dierum curriculo, Parochiales sibi specialem Plebanum præficipetebant, & ut præfecti unius Pastoris præsidio tuerentur, frequentius exigebant. Quorum clamor sedulus dum accuratè insisteret, omnes una cum suo Prælato Canonici, mediante suo Episcopo, nobis etiam Imperiali auctoritate in id ipsum præstantibus, unum de se Canonicum in Plebanum elegerunt, & de caetero nullum unquam, nisi Canonicum hujus prælationis titulum posse suscipere decreverunt. Iacobus Frisius in Msc. quodam sequentia Plebanorum observavit nomina A. 1252. Burckhartus Plebanus, dictus Lochler. Hic primus fuit, ut ex Anniversi. colligitur. In eodem tamen anniversario in Sept. primus Præposituræ Plebanus Rudolphus vocatur. Anno D. 1307. VValtherus de VVædischvvil, Plebanus. Anno D. 1335 Iohannes, Plebanus Chamensis, unanimi Capituli consensu Tigurum ad Plebanatum vocatur, & à Nicolao, Episcopo Constantiensi confirmatur. An. D. 1410. D. Nicolaus Plebanus. Anno D. 1440. D. Iacobus Moz, Plebanus. A.D. 1444. Adduntur ex anniversario Iohannes Gerster, Brugensis, Plebanus. Conradus Megerlin. Pleb. h. Ecclef. Iohannes Saltzman, Pleban. hujus Eccles. Ulricus Schafli 1305. Conradus Marcius Pleb. VVelcho Pleb. hujus Eeclef. Henricus de Rosberg Canon. & Pleb. h. Eccles. M. Ioh. Thyia Pleb. 1311. Ioh. de Capidona, Plebanus quondam hujus Ecclesiæ. Iohannes Bischof, Plebanus nostræ Ecclesiæ 1364. Nicolaus Bleich, Henricus Blumli, &c. Plebani.
units.tr: d. Bullinger says he could not find the names of the first provosts of the collegiate church, and complains that they were shamefully neglected. He counts from the year 70 Master Conrad Hofmann, Master Erhart Batmann, Master Huldrich Zwingli. The founding of the parish priesthood is not well known; its confirmation, from the instrument of Berchtold, Duke of Zähringen, dated in the year of Christ 1187, indiction 5, on the 4th of the calends of September, reads as follows: In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity: I, Berchtold of Zähringen, Duke and Rector of Burgundy, by the grace of God and of the Empire, lawful advocate (what is called the Kastvogt) of the place of Zurich, to the venerable Walter, provost of the said place, and to his holy brothers, so that the matters begun happily and brought to a blessed end for the salvation of many may be confirmed for ever by the granted privilege, make known to all the faithful of the holy Church that the parish of Zurich, from the original foundation of its provostship, was cared for by the providence of the canons themselves; so that the priests of that church, being canons, served the people with fitting service, and watched over the sons of the whole parish with pastoral care in all the churches. But as the course of days ran on, the parishioners demanded for themselves a special parish priest, and asked that they be guarded by the protection of one set over them as minister. When their eager cry had been pressed carefully, all the canons together with their prelate, through their bishop, we also lending our imperial authority to the same, chose one of themselves as parish priest, and decreed that from then on no one but a canon should be able to take up the title of this office. James Frisius, in a certain manuscript, noted the following names of parish priests: in the year 1252, Burkhart, parish priest, called Lochler. He was the first, as is gathered from the anniversary. In the same anniversary, however, in September, Rudolf is called the first parish priest of the provostship. In the year of the Lord 1307, Walter of Wädenswil, parish priest. In the year of the Lord 1335, John, parish priest of Cham, was called to the parish priesthood at Zurich by the unanimous consent of the chapter, and was confirmed by Nicholas, Bishop of Constance. In the year of the Lord 1410, Master Nicholas, parish priest. In the year of the Lord 1440, Master James Moz, parish priest. In the year 1444, from the anniversary are added John Gerster of Brugg, parish priest; Conrad Megerlin, parish priest of this church; John Saltzman, parish priest of this church; Ulrich Schafli, 1305; Conrad Marcius, parish priest; Welcho, parish priest of this church; Henry of Rosberg, canon and parish priest of this church; Master John Thyia, parish priest, 1311; John of Capidona, formerly parish priest of this church; John Bischof, parish priest of our church, 1364; Nicholas Bleich, Henry Blumli, etc., parish priests.

units.la: e. Quorum aliquot adhuc nomina Hospiniani nostri magnu consignata reperi. Magister Iohannes Hering, Plebanus Abbatiæ Thuricensis, obijt an. D. 1484. d. 9. Aprilis. Octob. obijt 1551. Alibi occurrit Beroldus, Presbyter & Capellanus Hildegardæ, Filiæ Ludovici Germanici Regis, Abbatissæ Tiguri. A. D. 840. Vincko, Conradus, Monasterij Plebanus 1180. Rudolfus Mula, Monast. Pleb.
units.tr: e. Some of their names I have found recorded in our Hospinian's great work. Master John Hering, parish priest of the Abbey of Zurich, died in the year of the Lord 1484, on 9 April. Wolfgang Schad, Doctor of Decretals and parish priest of the same abbey, died in the year of Christ 1496, on 23 October. Henry Engelhart, Doctor of Decretals, succeeded Hering, and succeeded Schad on 24 October 1496; he died in 1551. Elsewhere occurs Beroldus, priest and chaplain of Hildegard, daughter of Louis the German, king, and abbess of Zurich, in the year 840. Vincko, Conrad, parish priest of the monastery, 1180. Rudolf Mula, parish priest of the monastery.

Chr. 871. Iohannes Guttinger, de Diesenhofen, Plebanus S. Petri: Hugo Plebanus S. Petri. Andreas, Sacerdos incuratus & Decanus Ecclesiæ S. Petri in Thurego 1285. Petri in Thurego; Quorum omnium, caeterorumque, quorum rum adhuc aliqua apud nos est memoria, nomina exprimentur sequenti Catalogo, ubi & Rudolfi Iudenmanni, utriusque Monasterij Plebani, fit mentio.
units.tr: f. Of these, John Helfenberg, 1476, is so far the only one noted. The following are added in the old anniversary book. Henry, canon, called of Teingen, once parish priest of the church of St Peter, in the year of Christ 871. John Guttinger, of Diessenhofen, parish priest of St Peter. Hugo, parish priest of St Peter. Andrew, priest with the cure of souls and dean of the church of St Peter in Thurego, 1285. Ulric of Uzena, with the cure of souls at the church of St Peter in Thurego. The names of all these, and of the others of whom some memory remains among us, will be set out in the following catalogue, where mention is also made of Rudolf Judenmann, parish priest of both monasteries.

units.tr: g Dominicans, or Preachers, in the year of Christ 1230; Franciscans 1283; Augustinians 1265. On this matter, see elsewhere.

units.tr: h. As Malleolus himself admits, Miscellanea, part I, on the Reformation, p. 53.

units.la: i. Proinde, non plane a scopo aberrabimus, si eorum, qui ab aliquot seculis Ecclesiae Tigurinae Ministerio, quale quidem ante Reformationem fuit, suam consecrarunt operam, ordine Alphabethico exhibuerimus nomina, tum etiam usum illius Catalogi, quantum ex Archivi ruderibus erui ille potuit, per Aphorismos ostendamus.
units.tr: i. Accordingly, we shall not stray far from the aim if we set out in alphabetical order the names of those who for some centuries devoted their labour to the ministry of the Church of Zurich, as it was before the Reformation, and also show, by way of aphorisms, the use of that catalogue, as far as it could be dug out of the ruins of the archive.

Galli Ioh. zillisbuser, Canon h. Ecc. Lutholdus zuicko incuratus Eccl. in Altorf. Atque sic molestiam, contexendi Catalogi, devoravimus: Non tamen, ut spero, sine fructu. Est enim hoc ipsum Alphabethum limes quidam χρόνα ἀγνεῖος, & densissimarum Papatus tenebrarum, quem unus, qui supererat in ordine Alphabethico, zuinglius sustulit & cum meliori commutat. Patet ergo, ut distincte agamus, ex præcedenti Catalogo. I. Ingens inter Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ Ministros, ante & post Reformationem, discrimen, idque multiplex. a. Ante Reformationem pleriqué sacellani vocabantur; & erant etiam, destinati paulatim cultui Sanctorum Felicis, Regulæ, Caroli, Catharinæ, Dorotheæ XI. Mill. Virginum; vocabantur Præmißarij, latores reliquiarum &c. Post illam, servos Iesu Christi, Dispensatores mysteriorum, Verbi Ministros habemus. b. Ante illam Magistrorum Parisiensium, Doctorum Legum, Decretorum, utriusque juris, &c. tantum fit mentio; nullius vel Theologiæ formati Doctoris, vel eminentis & potentis S. Scripturæ Interpretis. Post illam hæc studia, ceu minus ad obeundum munus Ecclesiasticum necessaria, postposita, aliis utilioribus locum cesserunt. c. Ex toto illo numero vel Canonicorum, vel Sacellanorum, vel Rectorum, Plebanorum, ante Reformationem ne unus quidem est, cujus vel mediocres in Scripturam Sacram extent curæ. Nullum S. Sc. librum à tota illa serie observamus vel aliqualem, ante Reformationem, accepisse lucem. post illam, & brevi quidem tempore, nullus amplius supererat, qui non doctissimis illustratus esset Reformatorum commentarijs. d. Totum, quod ordine exhibuimus Alphabethum, unam vix & alterum continet, qui literas utcunque suis studijs juverit. Intra trecentos annos, ipsis restibus Pontificijs, Conradus de Mure erat, & Felix Malleolus; qui suæ quædam reliquerunt industriæ documenta. Post Reformationem vix unus fuit, ne Scholarum quidem Præceptor, qui ad Templi structuram non aliquid conferret. Cæteri turmatim prodierunt. Vnus Zuinglius, & ultimus quidem, cujus nomen per compatibilem, ut vocant Grammatici, literarum combinationem, in ordine Alphabethico potest exprimi, & plura & meliora dedit scripta, quam cæteri, aliquot seculorum flexu, omnes. Vt turpem nuper paralogismum commiserit, Vilhelmus Gothardus, sacrific. Solodurens, qui Dialog. sui de Rel. P. III. q. 3 S. 7. scripsit: De Pontificiorum doctrina tot editi testantur libri quos adversarij nunquam, exhibebunt. Centum annorum ætatem qui excedat, ostendere nullum possunt.
units.tr: Y. John of Umendingen, prebendary of the altar of St Blaise; Ulrich Usenburg, chaplain of St Mary Magdalene; Henry Zebender, chaplain of St Leonard; Wenceslaus Zaggi, canon of this Church, 1385; Burkhard, called Zederzoben, prebendary of the altar of Saints Martin at the tombs; John Zimbermann, subdeacon; John Zoller, chaplain of the altar of St John the Baptist in Cappel; John Zegner, chaplain of the altar of St Gall; John Zillisbuser, canon of this Church; Luthold Zuicko, curate of the church in Altorf. And so we have finished the tedious work of compiling the catalogue, though not, I hope, without profit. For this very alphabetical list is a boundary of a certain age of ignorance [χρόνα ἀγνεῖος] and of the thickest darkness of Papacy, which Zuinglius, the one name left at the end of the alphabet, removed and replaced with a better one. So, to speak clearly, the following points may be drawn from the preceding catalogue. I. There is a great difference, and a manifold one, between the ministers of the Zurich Church before and after the Reformation. a. Before the Reformation most were called chaplains, and they were gradually appointed to the worship of the saints Felix, Regula, Charles, Catherine, Dorothy and the Eleven Thousand Virgins. They were called sponsors of the chapels, bearers of relics, and so on. After the Reformation we have servants of Jesus Christ, dispensers of the mysteries, ministers of the Word. b. Before that only the Masters of Paris, doctors of laws, of canon law, of both laws, and so on, are mentioned; no doctor of theology, and no eminent and powerful interpreter of Holy Scripture. After it, these studies, as less necessary for the discharge of the ecclesiastical office, were set aside and gave place to more useful ones. c. Of that whole number, of canons, chaplains and rectors or parish priests, before the Reformation there is not even one whose work on Holy Scripture is at all respectable. We observe that from that whole series no book of Holy Scripture received any light, however slight, before the Reformation. After it, and within a short time, there was no one left who was not thoroughly enlightened by the most learned commentaries of the Reformers. d. The whole alphabetical list we have set out contains scarcely one or two men who helped literature in any way by their studies. Within three hundred years, among the very remnants of Papacy, there were Conrad von Mure and Felix Malleolus, who left some proofs of their diligence. After the Reformation there was hardly one, not even a schoolmaster, who did not contribute something to the building of the Church. Others came forth in droves. Only Zuinglius, and he the last, whose name can be expressed in the alphabetical order by a compatible combination of letters, as the grammarians say, gave more and better writings than all the others put together across several centuries. So shamefully did Wilhelm Gotthard, sacristan of Solothurn, recently commit a paralogism, when he wrote in his Dialogue on Religion, Part III, question 3, section 7: The many books published testify to the doctrine of the Papists, which the adversaries will never produce. They cannot show anything that goes back more than a hundred years.

units.la: II. Plenior hinc, quàm aliunde cunque haberi potest Canonicorum, Collegij Carolini, inde ab ejus initio, recensio.
units.tr: II. A fuller list of the canons of the Carolinum College, from its beginning onward, than can be had from any other source.

units.la: Tribus fere illa periodis absolvi potest. Primam à Carolo Magno, ad Berchtoldum Zeringiæ Ducem se extendit. Secunda, à Berchtoldo ad seculum 13. &c. Tertia, ad Reformationem Nomina Fratrum, tempore Caroli M. ex donationis charta ita habent: Primum Decani nomen Leidirath, Comolt, Hacco, Frehinhart, Hugifrid, Ingelbert, Vuinipert, Helfirich, Ifinpert, Lendine, Perthilo, Liubolf, Luitfrid, Adilunch, Aliuuie, Pero, Vuerinnoz. Secunda Periodi nomina in Catalogo defunctorum, quem viventium illi appellant, nos Indicem anniversarium, simpliciter expressa videntur, nullo vel ortus, vel familiæ addito Epitheto; quod non obscurum est antiquitatis monumentum; unde & in memorato Catalogo primum semper occupant locum, absque ullius Epochæ indicio. Tales, ut vel aliquos exprimam, sunt, Adelbero Diaconus, Henricus Canon. Hugo Sacerdos, Riochoʃus Presbyter, Berchtoldus Presbyter, Rudolfus Plebanus Monasterij, Rofritus, Presbyter; Trutmannus Presbyter, Sigbotto, Diac. Chuno, Presbyter. Regenoldus Presbyter. Gibitho, Presbyter. Comeli Canon. & Presbyt. Vlricus Canon. Richolfus Presb. & Canon. Eberhardus Diacon. Rudolfus Presb. Otto, Diaconus. Dietricus, Presb. Wernherus, Canon. Tertiæ periodi antiquiora nomina, Seculi nempe 13. & 14. annorum annotatione signata in Alphabethico nostro ordine frequenti serie occurrunt; recentiora, & quæ Reformationem uno plerumque Seculo præcedunt, peti possunt ex Bull. de Antiq. Tig. lib. 6 c. 5. III. Collegium hoc Caroliuum honoratum semper fuisse. Patet a. Quòd, qui vel Episcopi Basileenses, Constantienses essent, vel Præpositi alibi locorum, inter Canonicos Tigurinos referri, eos non puduerit. Exempla aliquot supra commemoravimus. b. Quòd & antiquissimæ, & nobilissimæ (ut enim antehac Helvetia nobilitatem habuit verè antiquam; ita defectus ejus jure illi exprobari non potuit) Tigurinorum familiæ, primis præsertim ab origine Collegij Seculis, hujus etiam Præposituræ membra esse voluerint. Tales quidem erant Schwendij, Schaflini, Peregrini, Meisij, de Hottingen (quibus in antiquissimis instrumentis, quale de anno 1256. Clarissimo Collegæ, Professori Rhetorologico D. Ioh. Caspar Wasero, hoc loco grata mente fero acceptum, Hottingeriorum aliàs retinere placuit nomen) Boecklini, in foro, Molendinarij &c. qui ante restauratam Rempublicam, & fœdus Helveticum, rerum hic maximè potiebantur. Quos comitati, vel deinceps secuti sunt, Manesfi, Thyia, Schwvarzmureri, de Clotenn, Finckÿ, Truberi, Storÿ, de Dubelstein, Martini, vel Martÿ, Schonenwverdÿ, de Clarona, Kriegÿ, Im Gwvelb, Sculteti, Brunÿ, Ammani, VVyssones, Von VVerdegg, de S. Petro, Gnürseri, de Lunghofen, de Friburgo VVolfleibsch, quorum familiæ in Regimine duodecim. Virali ab an. Ch. 1111. ad 1315. & deinceps fit mentio. Recentiorum nomina jam mittimus. Ex quibus quidem familijs omnibus magno numero reperimus Canonicos. IV. Gradus crescentis superstitionis non obscure possunt observari. Antiquissima Ministrorum nomina sunt simpliciter Plebani, Presbyteri, Diaconi; postea secuti sunt Sacellani, Sacellorum; in Sacellis Altarium &c.
units.tr: This history can be divided into roughly three periods. The first extends from Charlemagne to Duke Berchtold of Zähringen. The second runs from Berchtold to the thirteenth century, and so on. The third runs down to the Reformation. The names of the brothers from the time of Charlemagne, as they stand in the charter of donation, are these: The first name of the dean: Leidirath, Comolt, Hacco, Frehinhart, Hugifrid, Ingelbert, Vuinipert, Helfirich, Ifinpert, Lendine, Perthilo, Liubolf, Luitfrid, Adilunch, Aliuuie, Pero, Vuerinnoz. The names of the second period, in the catalogue of the dead, which they call the catalogue of the living, we call the anniversary index, appear simply expressed, with no epithet of birth or family added. This is no obscure monument of antiquity; for this reason they always stand first in that catalogue, with no indication of any epoch. To name a few such: Adelbero, deacon; Henricus, canon; Hugo, priest; Riochoʃus, presbyter; Berchtoldus, presbyter; Rudolfus, parish priest of the monastery; Rofritus, presbyter; Trutmannus, presbyter; Sigbotto, deacon; Chuno, presbyter; Regenoldus, presbyter; Gibitho, presbyter; Comeli, canon and presbyter; Vlricus, canon; Richolfus, presbyter and canon; Eberhardus, deacon; Rudolfus, presbyter; Otto, deacon; Dietricus, presbyter; Wernherus, canon. The older names of the third period, marked by the notation of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, occur in frequent succession in our alphabetical order. The more recent ones, which generally precede the Reformation by about one century, may be sought in the Bullinger's On the Antiquities of Zurich, book 6, chapter 5. III. That this Carolinum college was always held in honour. This is clear: a. Because those who were bishops of Basel or Constance, or provosts elsewhere, were not ashamed to be counted among the Zurich canons. We have recorded some examples above. b. Because the most ancient and most noble families of Zurich (for as Helvetia once had a truly ancient nobility, so its defect cannot be justly reproached to it), especially from the earliest centuries of the college, wished to be members of this provostship too. Such indeed were the Schwendi, Schaffli, Pilgrim, Meiss, von Hottingen (whose name, in the most ancient documents, such as one of the year 1256, which I gladly acknowledge here as received from the most distinguished colleague, Professor of Rhetoric Dr Johann Caspar Waser, we have been pleased to keep as Hottinger), Böcklin, im Forum, Müller, and so on, who held the greatest power here before the restoration of the commonwealth and the Swiss league. Those who accompanied them, or followed afterwards, were Manesse, Thyg, Schwarzmurer, von Klingen, Finck, Truber, Stor, von Dübelstein, Martin or Marti, Schönenwerd, von Clara, Krieg, im Gewölb, Schulteiss, Brun, Ammann, Wyss, von Werdegg, von St. Peter, Gnürs, von Lunghofen, von Freiburg, Wolfleibsch, whose families held office in the twelve regiments. Mention is made of them from the year 1111 onward, to 1315, and afterwards. I omit the names of more recent times. From all these families we find canons in great numbers. IV. The degrees of growing superstition can be observed without difficulty. The oldest names of ministers are simply parish priests, presbyters, deacons; afterwards came chaplains, of chapels; in the chapels, of altars, and so on.

units.la: F. Atque hæc quidem de statu Ecclesiæ & Scholæ Tigurinæ ante Reformationem, qualis per Reformationem evaserit, jam dicendum esset, nisi quæ secunda, de Schola Tigurina, Oratione suprà disseruimus, hanc utcunque vicem supplerent; cætera commodius ex ipsa Reformationis Historia, quàm propediem, Deo, dabimus, peti possunt. Illud obiter monemus, nihil nobis vel de Schola nostra, vel Scholæ Doctoribus excidisse, quod gravi graviu virorum calculo non confirmetur. a. Videamus vel obvia quædam axiomata, cujusmodi sunt, 1. Scholam Tigurinam Reformatam Adversariorum etiam Encomijs esse celebratam. Svveert.in AthenBelg.ubi omnes per orbem Academias recenser,p.83.scribit: Tigurina Schola videri nequeat imi subscllij, ex quo ab anno ferè 1528. ad finem Seculi illius, multi viri doctì cam nominis sui fama celebravere. Prodijt an.Chr.1600. Coloniæ Agrippinæ per Matthæum Quadam Sculptorem compendium universi,Lothario, Archiepiscopo Trevirensi dedicatum, in cujus lib.4.c.5. leguntur verba sequentia: Mirum autem, quantũ fera ista ac Sylvestris regio postremo hoc Seculo excellentium ingeniorum sumpserit incrementum! Tigurinus namque fuit Justus Ammanus, Pictor ille & inventor copiosissimus. Sangallensis fuit Joachimus Vadianus, Poëta excellens, Mathematicus ac præsertim Geographus exactissimus, quod ipsius in Pomponium Melam commentarij, & trium orbis partium Epitome demonstrant. Capellensis fuit Josias Simlerus,elegantis homo ingenij ac doctrinaMathematicus nobilis, & Historicus excellens, Theologiæ in Schola Tigurina Professor. Tigurinus fuit Ludovicus Lavaterus: Johannes item VVolphius,Philosophiæ pariter ac Theologiæ eruditissimi: Conradus Gesnerus, Græcus, Philosophus, ac Medicus notissimus: alìjque innumeri,quorum multi citra invidiam nominari non possent. Quo loco Naudæus Tigurinos habuerit Theologos, ex consilio ejus de Biblioth patet pag.60. Luculentissimum est Ferdinandi de Escalante, ordinis Sanctissimæ Trinitatis, & redemtionis captivorum, Th.D. in Clypeo concionat. censurâ approbato,Philipp. III. dedicato, Venetijs excusò, cujus verba lib.6.c. ultimo de Biblijs,& Doctoribus Tigurinis digna sunt, quæ exscribantur.
units.tr: F. These things about the state of the Zurich Church and school before the Reformation, and about what it became through the Reformation, would now have to be discussed, were it not that what we said in the second oration, on the Zurich school, in some measure fills this place. The rest may more conveniently be sought in the history of the Reformation itself, which, God willing, we shall soon give. We remark in passing that nothing has escaped us, either about our school or about the teachers of the school, that is not confirmed by the weighty judgment of serious men. a. Let us look at some commonplace maxims, such as these: 1. The Reformed Zurich school has been celebrated even by the praises of its adversaries. Sweert, in his Athenae Belgicae, where he surveys all the academies of the world, writes on page 83: The Zurich school cannot be thought of as the lowest bench, since from about the year 1528 to the end of that century many learned men have made it famous by its name. In the year 1600 there appeared at Cologne, printed by Matthaeus Quadus, an engraver, a compendium of the whole world, dedicated to Lothar, Archbishop of Trier. In its book 4, chapter 5, the following words are read: It is remarkable how much this wild and sylvan region has gained in excellent talents in this last century! For there was Justus Ammann of Zurich, that painter and most prolific inventor. There was Joachim Vadian of St Gall, an excellent poet, mathematician and especially a most accurate geographer, as his commentaries on Pomponius Mela and his Epitome of the three parts of the world show. Josias Simler of Kappel was a man of elegant talent and learning, a noble mathematician and an excellent historian, professor of theology in the Zurich school. Ludwig Lavater was of Zurich; likewise Johann Wolf, most learned in philosophy as well as theology; Conrad Gesner, a Greek scholar, philosopher and very well-known physician; and countless others, many of whom could not be named without offence. In this passage Naudé, in his advice on libraries, evidently regarded the Zurich men as theologians; this is clear on page 60. Most splendid is the judgment of Ferdinand de Escalante, of the order of the Most Holy Trinity and of the redemption of captives, Doctor of Theology, approved by the censorship of his Clypeus of Sermons, dedicated to Philip III, printed at Venice, whose words in book 6, the last chapter, on the Bibles and the Zurich teachers, are worthy to be copied out.

units.la: Diu multumq̃, inquit, flagravi studio & desiderio videndi translationem Tigurinam,ut tractarem, quidnam authoritatis Latina illa inter cateras editiones publicas retineat;nec uspiam quærendo invenire potui: vadens autem visum & salutatum doctissimum, integerrimum, & sanctissimum virum, D.Sanctium ab Avila & Toleto, Illustrissimum & Reverendissimum Episcopum Giennensem,non minus sacrarum literarum scientiâ prepollentem, quàm verbi divini prædicatione præstantem; præter infinitas Sanctorum reliquias,quibus devotissimè deditus est, quas ostendit mihi, inducere dignatus est me in Bibliothecam suam, omnium, quas unquam vidi, operibus selectissimis maximè refertam: Inter ea reperi Biblia Tigurina tantoopere desiderata, lubentissimo animo Illustrissima sua Dominatio mihi mutuo dedit, operâ, & diligentiâ elaborata Leonis Tigurinæ Ecclesiæ Episcopi, qui pio zelo fervens, Latinam versionem Bibliorum moliri capit. In transferendo autem Veteri Testamento usus est Hebraico exemplari emendatissimo: Græcis etiam & Latinis editionibus: unde lectionis veritatem putavit esse petendam, neque neglexit, quæ de genuino & germano sensu, passim tradiderunt Orthodoxi eloquii divini.
units.tr: "For a long time and with great intensity," he says, "I burned with eagerness and desire to see the Zurich translation, so that I might examine what authority that Latin version holds among the other published editions. But I could find it nowhere by searching. Then, visiting and greeting the most learned, most upright and most holy man, Don Sancho of Avila and Toledo, the most illustrious and reverend Bishop of Jaén, no less outstanding in knowledge of the Holy Scriptures than in preaching the divine Word, and besides the countless relics of the saints to which he is most devotedly given, which he showed me, he condescended to lead me into his library, richly stocked with the most select works of all the libraries I have ever seen. Among them I found the Zurich Bible, so long desired. With the most willing heart, His Lordship lent it to me, the work and diligence laboured over by Leo, bishop of the Zurich church, who, burning with pious zeal, undertook to prepare a Latin version of the Bible. In translating the Old Testament he used the most accurate Hebrew exemplar, and also the Greek and Latin editions, from which he thought the truth of the reading was to be sought. Nor did he neglect what the orthodox teachers of the divine utterance have handed down everywhere concerning the genuine and true sense."

units.la: Adjutus est autem plurimùm operâ & industriâ clarissimorum virorum, tam linguarum, quàm rerum peritissimorum, quibus omnibus adminiculis Latinam suam translationem, syncerè ad veritatem Hebraicam conformare conatus est, quàm ad optatum finem perducere non potuit, propter ingentem tanti operis molem. Non enim corpusculum optimi viri, senio jam debilitatum, & laboribus fractum, diutius tantum oneris sustinere valebat: quare in morbum incidens gravissimum, præsentissimæ mortis nuncium certissimum, orabat atque obtestabatur, Theodorum Bibliandrum, in Ecclesia Tigurina sacrarum literarum expositorem, & Conradum Pellicanum sanctæ linguæ ibidem Professorem, ut ea in sua Bibliorum Versione absolverent, quæ morbo & morte interceptus, transferre & perficere nequibat, octo scilicet postrema capita Ezechielis, Danielem totum, librum Job integrum; Psalmos quadraginta octo ultimos, libellos Salomonis duos Ecclesiasten, & Cantica Canticorum, quæ ob rerum & styli difficultatem non attigerat, sed ultimo reservaverat conatui. Postquam verò ad Dominum felicissimè migrasset Leo, Bibliander & Pellicanus citissimè & diligentissimè, quæ promiserant præstiterunt. Et propterea quod felicis memoriæ Leo, laborem suum dicatum voluit fidelissimis & religiosissimis fratribus, pastoribus Verbi & Ecclesiarum ministris, per agrum Tigurinum, hinc factum est, quod Translatio hæc Tigurina nuncupetur.
units.tr: He was helped very much by the work and industry of most distinguished men, as skilled in languages as in subject matter, and with all these aids he tried to bring his Latin translation into sincere conformity with the Hebrew truth. He could not bring this to the desired end, because of the immense bulk of so great a work. The good man, now weakened by old age and broken by labours, could no longer bear so great a burden for long. Therefore, falling into a very grave illness, and seeing the certain news of imminent death, he begged and entreated Theodore Bibliander, the expositor of sacred letters in the Zurich church, and Conrad Pellican, professor of the holy language there, to complete in their Bible version those parts which he, prevented by sickness and death, could not translate and finish: namely the last eight chapters of Ezekiel, the whole of Daniel, the entire book of Job, the last forty-eight Psalms, the two books of Solomon, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs, which he had not touched because of the difficulty of the subject and style, but had reserved to the last for an attempt. After Leo had happily departed to the Lord, Bibliander and Pellican, very quickly and very diligently, performed what they had promised. And because the blessed Leo wished his labour to be dedicated to the most faithful and devout brothers, the ministers of the Word and the ministers of the churches throughout the Zurich territory, it came about that this Zurich translation is so named.

units.la: Libros autem sacros hujus translationis ita dispositerunt, ut Cyprianus in expositione symboli : conjunxerunt enim historiales omnes, ab orbe condito ultra instauratam urbem, captivitate Babylonica : his subjunxerunt Prophetas majores & minores numero sexdecim : quibus demum appenderunt reliquos varie contextos libros; Volumen sc. Job, Hymnorum codicem, & Salomonis libros tres. Porro libri omnes Ecclesiastici soli in unum volumen sunt redacti, & ut mira suavitate permulcerent lectorem, affixerunt universo argumenta singulorum capitum, carmine comprehensa a doctissimo viro, Rodolpho Gualthero, in gratiam & usum studiosorum composita. Annotationes quoque suas suis libris appositit Bibliander, quemadmodum Leo suas sua versioni adjecit. Nota etiam marginales ubicunque occurrunt, diversitatem lectionis, & versionis varietatem indicant, & sensum aperiunt authorum; occasionem subministrant majora investigandi, rationem denique nonnunquam reddunt versionis. Testamentum novum horum Bibliorum Tigur. vertit Def. Erasmus Roterodamus: nihilominus tamen collata est hæc novi Testamenti editio cum ipsa veritate Græca, consultis interim aliquot per vetustis exemplaribus & versionibus, editione scilicet Hispalensi sive Toletana, Gallicana sive Parisiensi, & reliquis quibusdam codicibus antiquissimis. Potissimam verò in hac parte operam præstitere, optimi & doctissimi viri, Petrus Cholinus, & Rodolphus Gualtherus. Addam Cornel. Schulting. Biblioth. Cathol. P. I. pag. 1, salva tamen comparatorum inter se authoritate, & conditione utrinque incomparabili. Loci communes, inquit, Petri Martyris eodem ordine librorum & Capitum dispositi sunt, quo Institutiones Calvini, idem fere in omnibus argumentis contra Catholicam religionem utuntur, nisi quod Calvinus simiam inducit purpurâ, hoc est, cultum & ornatum Orationis majorem adhibet: Praterea in Locis Communibus Martyris major est dictionis perspicuitas. Calvinus in locis multis obscurus & intricatus est, magis in Institutionibus, quàm in Commentariis in Scripturas, idque de industria & studiose, ut imponat & fallat lectorem. Tortuosus serpens in tot mirandas formas se vertit, ut cauda apprehendi & teneri vix possit: si hic constringas, ibi elabitur. Quamobrem cum idem sit ordo, & eadem fere pleraque argumenta, nostra confutationes utiles erunt tam contra Locos Communes Martyris, quàm Institutiones Calvini, ideóque singulis fere locis contuli locos Communes Petri Martyris cum Institutionibus Johannis Calvini. Utcumque sit de illa quaestione, an Calvinus sit suam mutuatus magna ex parte à Petro Martyre, quod magni viri sentiunt, an verò Calvinus suo marte omnia invenerit, nihilque acceperit á Martyre, quod alij existimant, illud certè constat; Martyrem Calvino longè fuisse doctiorem: erat enim in Scholastica Theologia apprimè versatus. Fuerat antea Generalis ordinis Praedicatorum Florentiae Cardinalitiae dignitati proximus. In omnibus Colloquijs & Conventibus suo seculo religionis causa institutis, ex parte Calvinistarum semper primas tenuit, semper Coryphaeus & antesignanus extitit: Huic omnes plurimum deferebant, semper ei palmam tribuerunt. Calvinus & Beza in Epistolis primam ei laudum partem semper facilè concedunt. Extat etiam in Archivo nostro egregium Poloni cujusdam de Martyre testimonium: Ad quam rem mutere opera D. Pet. Martyris, cui me obsecro commendes velim. Hominem non novi sed cùm ejus monumenta revolvo, apparet hominem esse talem, qui cum quovis ex antiquioribus illis viris conferri debeat. Placet etiam his annectere luculentum de Professoribus, & Bibliis, Tigurinis judicium Iacobi Augustini Thuani, Praesidis Parisini, hominis Pontificij, Histor. I. 35. pag. 714. Ejus autem verba ita habent: Obiit ex peste Tiguri, ubi profitebatur, Theodorus Bibliander, vir multi-jugae eruditionis valdè senex, cui in munere suffectus est Joh. Guilhel. Stuckius. Nova autem Bibliorum editioni anno 1543. Tiguri publicata, quam Leo Juda inchoaverat, moriens, ut opus persequeretur, collegis in fidem religiosè adactis transcripserat, ultimam manum imposuit Bibliander, Conradi Pellicani, & Petri Cholini Tigurinis, Graeca lingua peritissimi, operà adjutus, quam translationem bienniopost in sua editione ad veterem adjecit Robertus Stephanus, suppressa eorum, qui in illa labor aruni, mentione: Et Hispani Theologi diu post recognitam, per Guilhelmum Rovillium denuò Lugduni excudendam curaverunt: Quod eò commemorandum duxi, ut Versionis, tanti apud nos & Hispanos ipsos factæ origo cognosceretur, & insigne documentum extaret, quid utilitatis ex adversariorum libris, & industria, si semotis odiis, charitatem, & æquitatem induamus, ad Dei gloriam capi posset. 2. Amicis placuisse, a. propter doctrinæ sinceritatem. Thomas Blarer, ad Bibliand, a. Ch. 1553. Non visum est, Augustinum gnatum, diutiùs ludo literario publico fraudare, & arridentadhuc mihi Tigurinorum nostrorum pulpita, propter sinceram hanc doctrinæ sacræ castitatem, quam profitentur
units.tr: They arranged the sacred books of this translation in the way that Cyprian, in his exposition of the creed, describes: they joined together all the historical books, from the creation of the world down to the restored city after the Babylonian captivity. To these they appended the greater and lesser Prophets, sixteen in number; and finally they added the remaining books, variously composed: namely the volume of Job, the book of Hymns, and the three books of Solomon. Moreover, all the ecclesiastical books have been gathered into a single volume. And so that they might delight the reader with a wonderful sweetness, they attached to the whole the arguments of the individual chapters, composed in verse by the most learned man Rudolf Gwalther, for the favour and use of students. Bibliander also added his notes to his books, just as Leo added his to his version. The marginal notes wherever they occur indicate the variety of readings and of versions, and open up the senses of the authors; they supply occasion for further investigation, and sometimes finally give the reason for the version. The New Testament of this Zurich Bible was translated by the venerable Erasmus of Rotterdam. Nevertheless, this edition of the New Testament was compared with the Greek truth itself, meanwhile consulting some very old copies and versions, namely the Spanish or Toledan edition, the Gallican or Parisian, and certain other most ancient manuscripts. But the chief work in this part was performed by the excellent and most learned men Peter Cholin and Rudolf Gwalther. I shall add Cornelius Schulting, Bibliotheca Catholica, part I, page 1, saving, however, the mutual authority of the comparisons and the completely incomparable condition on each side. "The common places of Peter Martyr," he says, "are arranged in the same order of books and chapters as the Institutes of Calvin; they use nearly the same arguments against the Catholic religion, except that Calvin brings in an ape in purple, that is, he applies a greater polish and ornament of speech. Moreover, in the Common Places of Martyr the clarity of expression is greater. Calvin is obscure and tangled in many places, more in the Institutes than in his commentaries on Scripture, and this deliberately and carefully, so that he may deceive and mislead the reader. The twisting serpent turns itself into so many wonderful shapes that it can hardly be seized and held by the tail: if you squeeze it here, it slips away there. Therefore, since the order is the same and nearly all the arguments are the same, our refutations will be useful against the Common Places of Martyr as much as against the Institutes of Calvin; and so, at almost every point, I have compared the Common Places of Peter Martyr with the Institutes of John Calvin." Whatever may be the question, whether Calvin borrowed the greater part of his work from Peter Martyr, as great men think, or whether Calvin found everything by his own effort and took nothing from Martyr, as others suppose, this at least is certain: Martyr was far more learned than Calvin, for he was thoroughly versed in scholastic theology. He had previously been Master General of the Order of Preachers, next in rank to the cardinalate at Florence. In all the colloquies and conventions held in his century for the sake of religion, on the side of the Calvinists he always held the first place; he always stood forth as their leader and standard-bearer. All men greatly deferred to him and always awarded him the palm. Calvin and Beza in their letters readily concede to him the first share of praise. There also exists in our archive an outstanding testimony of a certain Pole concerning Martyr: "For this matter I earnestly beg you to commend me to the work of Master Peter Martyr. I do not know the man, but when I turn over his monuments, it appears that he is such a man as ought to be compared with any of those older men." It also pleases me to add here the splendid judgement on the professors and Bibles of Zurich by Jacques-Auguste de Thou, President of the Parlement of Paris, a Papist, History, book I, 35, page 714. His words are as follows: "Theodore Bibliander died of the plague at Zurich, where he taught, a very old man of many-sided learning, and in his office Johann Wilhelm Stuckius was appointed in his place. The new edition of the Bible published at Zurich in the year 1543, which Leo Jud had begun, he had, on dying, transcribed for the continuation of the work, having bound his colleagues religiously to faith. Bibliander put the final hand to it, assisted by Conrad Pellican and Peter Cholin of Zurich, most skilled in the Greek language. Two years later Robert Estienne added this translation to the old one in his own edition, suppressing mention of those who had laboured on it. And the Spanish theologians, long after it had been revised, had it printed again at Lyons through William Rouillé." I thought this worth recording, so that the origin of a version so esteemed among us and among the Spaniards themselves might be known, and so that there might stand a notable example of what profit could be drawn for the glory of God from the books and industry of our adversaries, if, with hatreds set aside, we put on charity and fairness. 2. It pleased friends, on account of the sincerity of the teaching. Thomas Blarer, to Bibliander, in the year 1553: "It did not seem right to defraud my son Augustine any longer of public literary instruction, and the pulpits of our Zurich men still please me, on account of that sincere purity of sacred doctrine which they profess."

units.la: 6. Doctorum celebritatem. Henric. Apriolus Seletstad. Minist. Mylhusin. Scholæ Tigurinæ viros summos atque omni disciplinarum genere instructos Isaacus Cynegus magnificè prædicare quotidie solitus, adeò ut ejus, omniumque studiosorum nomine vehementer gratulèr, gaudeam. 15. And. Hyper. ad Ioh. VVolph. 1563. Vestra Ecclesia & Schola illustrium hominum illustribus abundat exemplis, quæ magnopere possunt ac debent te commovere. Christoph. Thretius Cracov. 1577. Prosectò, vestra Schola Tigurina uberrimè exornata fuit præstantissimis: Zuinglium illum restauratorem primum habuit verè doctrinæ; Leonemque Judæ, ac Conradum Pellicanum: quibus succedere isti Clarissimi viri, Bullinger, & Bibliander, Conrado Pellicano ad extremam senectutem Hebraicas literas profitente ac de mortuo, optimo judicio, & sua cum laude, ad vos evocâstis Argentinâ, celeberrimum illum ἀρπολατρείας Pontificia Antagonistam, solidùmque Theologum, Petrum Martyrem. Bibliandro successit tuo, nostèr Simlerus; Petro itidem Martyri Johannes VVolphius, integerrimus vir ac percruditus. VVolphius ante aliquot annos fato suo concesserat: Adhuc in vivis restabat noster Simlerus, quem invida & iniqua nobis mors abripuit. Profectò vices vestras, & Scholæ & Ecclesiæ, ut debeo, defleo, tam brevi spacio intra annum vertentem unum Ecclesiasten, alterum verò Interpretem sacrarum literarum amisisse. Prælixè deinceps Zachariam Vrsinum commendat, ut ille Simlero sufficiatur. Paulus Knibbius Colleg. Sapient. Heidelb. Præcept. 1566. De obitu D. Gessneri ad nos tristissima fama allata est. De Simlero bis simile quid sparsum fuit. fuit. De jactura, quam ex ejusmodi virorum amissione accepturi essetis, nolo hic multa commemorare; res ipsa clamat. Rogandus potius est Dominus, ut reliquias aliquas eorum, qui Ecclesiæ, suis laboribus utiles sunt, vobis conservet: utque eam laudem vestra urbs, quam ex eo habet, quod aliquandiu ibi viri doctissimi floruerint, in posterum etiam retinere possit. Non enim facile tales renasci videmus. c. Φιλοπονίαν inexpugnabilem. VVolphgang. VVeidner, I.C.VVor, mat. ad Bulling. 1553. Heus optime Bullingere, vulgatum illud nosti: Quod caret alterna requie, durabile non est. Hujus, & quod caro, qua circundatus adhuc, adamantina non sit, memor esto, temperésque ab immodicis studiis Tibi, ne videaris, quod pluribus contigit, ultro accersere immaturam mortem. Vixisset diutius, si piæ memoriæ Huldricho Zuinglio, in Epistola præliminari in Pindarum credimus, Jacobus Ceporinus, dum viveret, vel Græca vel Hebraica Lingua apud vos Professor, si temperare sibi in hoc vel novisset, vel potuisset. Quid Leoni Judæ in transferendo ex Hebræo libris sacris, quid χωρὶς ... peperint ingenii labores, & sine temperamento vigilat a noctes, tu ipse es testis oculatus. Si Conradus Gesnerus fato functus est (quod mihi ab incerto tantum rumore relatum) non magnopere mihi videbor errare, si superioribus illum annumeraro. Vir erat, dum ego adessem, ætatis (si annos spectes) adhuc integræ, & qualis tum mea conjectura ferebat, vix dum quadragesimum, aut certè non multò supergressus; pallor tamen faciei improbatum ejus studia arguebat.
units.tr: 6. The renown of the teachers. Henry Aprilius of Seelstadt, minister at Mühlhausen: "Isaac Cynegius, who was accustomed to proclaim magnificently every day the great men of the Zurich school, men furnished with every kind of learning, so that I rejoice and warmly congratulate you in his name and in the name of all students. 15." Andreas Hyperius to John Wolf, 1563: "Your church and school abound in illustrious examples of illustrious men, which ought greatly to move you." Christoph Thretius of Kraków, 1577: "Truly your Zurich school was most richly adorned with the most excellent men. It first had that Zwingli, the restorer of true doctrine, and Leo Jud and Conrad Pellican; after them came those most distinguished men Bullinger and Bibliander. When Conrad Pellican, who taught Hebrew letters until extreme old age, had died, you summoned from Strasbourg, with excellent judgement and to your own credit, that most famous antagonist of the Papist bread-worship [ἀρτολατρεία], and solid theologian, Peter Martyr. Your Bibliander was succeeded by our Simler; and Peter Martyr was succeeded by John Wolf, a most upright and most learned man. Wolf had yielded to his fate some years before; our Simler still remained alive, whom an envious and unjust death snatched from us. Truly I mourn, as I ought, your losses and those of the school and church, that within so short a space, in the course of one year, you have lost one preacher and the other interpreter of sacred letters." He then praises Zacharias Ursinus at length, so that he may be appointed in Simler's place. Paulus Knibbius, of the College of Sapience at Heidelberg, teacher, 1566: "The very sad news of the death of Master Gesner has reached us. Something similar has twice been spread about Simler." I do not wish to recount here at length the loss which you would suffer from the departure of such men; the thing itself cries out. Rather one must ask the Lord to preserve for you some remnants of those who are useful to the Church by their labours, and that your city may be able to keep in future that glory which it has from this, that for some time most learned men flourished there. For we do not easily see such men born again. c. Unconquerable diligence [φιλοπονίαν]. Wolfgang Weidner, I.C., Worms, to Bullinger, 1553: "Hey there, excellent Bullinger, you know that common saying: what lacks alternating rest is not durable. Remember this, and that the flesh by which you are still surrounded is not adamantine; and restrain yourself from immoderate studies, lest you seem, as has happened to many, to bring on untimely death of your own accord. He would have lived longer, if Jacob Ceporinus, while he lived, professor of Greek or Hebrew among you, had known or been able to moderate himself in this. What the labours of his mind produced in translating the sacred books from Hebrew for Leo Jud, and what sleepless nights kept without moderation, you yourself are an eyewitness. If Conrad Gesner has departed this life (which has been reported to me only by an uncertain rumour), I shall not seem to be greatly mistaken if I count him among the above. He was, while I was present, of an age (if you look at his years) still whole, and, as my conjecture then ran, scarcely yet forty, or certainly not much beyond it; yet the pallor of his face showed that his studies were excessive."

units.la: Hinc est quod nostri vos Tigurinos maxime complectantur: Non tantum, quod simpliciter sine convitijs causam vestram agitis, & propugnatis; verum etiam multa utilia scripta, & enarrationes, & piissimas & commodissimas tempori & loco accommodatas, in lucem datis, quibus Ecclesia ædificatur, & multi docti viri erudiuntur, & ad veram intelligentiam Scripturæ inducuntur. Rursum absit adulatio dicto. Qua enim scribo, ex animo scribo: Et video meum multos doctos & eruditos viros sentire. f. Curam pro Studiosis, & liberalitatem in assignandis stipendijs, ut exteras domestici visitare possent Academias. Insigne in Actis nostris Scholasticis extat documentum, Rectoris Magistrorum & Doctorum Academiæ VVittebergensis d. 25. Augusti 1571. inscriptum Reverendis & Clarissimis viris, pietate, eruditione virtute ac dignitate præstantibus, D. Henrico Bullingero, & reliquis Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ Doctoribus atque Ministris, sacraque Theologiæ Professoribus; ac D. Caspari VVolphio, Artis Medicæ Doctori, & Scholarchæ eximio, Dominis, & amicis, ac fratribus nostris cum observantia colendis, cujus initium ita habet: Salutem in Christo &c. Cùm justitia & fortitudinis fama inclytæ Helvetiorum Civitates claræ semper fuerunt; tum vero pietatis, doctrinæ, disciplinæ, ac beneficentiæ laude ita celebrantur, ut quas hodie illis conferamus, paucæ sint, quas anteferamus nullæ. De Tigurina autem Republica quoties cogitamus, non modo ornamenta ista Politica suspicimus, & admiramur, quæ permagnum decus rebus humanis afferunt; sed intuemur Ecclesiam Filij Dei, quæ cùm illustre apud vos hospitium, Christo favente, nacta sit, longè lateque conspicitur, & veram atque immortalem gloriam inclytæ Genti ac Reipublicæ vestræ conciliat. Itaque Tigurinis & favemus & gratulamur, cùm ob vetusta laudatissimæ Gentis ornamenta, tum vero etiam ob clarissimam Evangelij lucem Dei beneficio isthic exortam, quam ut diu fulgeat, & vicinorum tenebras illustret, toto pectore Deum æternum, Patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, precamur. Mirificè etiam Reverendi, Clarissimi, & doctissimi viri delectamur fama & prædicatione insignis & eximiæ cùm bonitatis vestræ, tum beneficentiæ erga pietatis & optimarum Artium atque disciplinarum Studiosos, quorum aliquot, ut audimus, vestra liberalitate, vestrisque stipendijs faventur & aluntur. Quod etsi ita splendidum non est, ut cætera vestra, nos tamen hæc Ecclesiæ Filij Dei, & civitatibus Rerumpublicarum ornamentis utilissimum judicamus, vos & sapientia & authoritate, & judicij rectitudine antecellentes viros invitare & diligere bene moratos adolescentes, & ad literarum studia aptos atque idoneos, quibus subsidia necessaria subministretis, ut sint aliquando, quibus quasi confecto curriculo lampada cælestis doctrinæ & Philosophiæ veluti in manus tradatis.
units.tr: Hence it is that our people embrace you of Zurich above all others. This is not only because you plead your cause and defend it openly, without insults, but also because you have published many useful writings and expositions, most pious and most fitting for the time and place, by which the Church is built up, many learned men are instructed, and they are led to a true understanding of Scripture. Nor, I say again, let there be any flattery in what I say: I write from my heart, and I know that many learned and erudite men share my view. f. Concern for students, and generosity in granting stipends so that they may visit foreign academies at home. A notable proof of this survives in our academic records: a letter from the Rector, Masters and Doctors of the Academy of Wittenberg, dated 25 August 1571, addressed to the reverend and most distinguished men, outstanding in piety, learning, virtue and dignity, Dr. Heinrich Bullinger, and the other teachers and ministers of the Church of Zurich, and professors of sacred theology; and to Dr. Caspar Wolf, doctor of medicine and an excellent scholarch, lords, friends and brothers to be honoured with respect. It begins thus: Greetings in Christ, etc. Since the cities of the Swiss have always been famous for the fame of justice and courage, they are now celebrated for their piety, learning, discipline and beneficence to such a degree that few things we can offer them today are worth more, and none can be placed above them. When we think of the Republic of Zurich, we not only admire and marvel at those political ornaments which bring great honour to human affairs, but we also see the Church of the Son of God, which, since by Christ's favour it has found an illustrious home among you, is seen far and wide and wins true and immortal glory for your noble people and commonwealth. Therefore we both favour and congratulate the people of Zurich, both for the ancient and most praiseworthy ornaments of their nation, and still more for the most clear light of the Gospel that by God's goodness has risen there; and we pray with all our heart to the eternal God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that it may shine long and illuminate the darkness of its neighbours. We also take wonderful delight, reverend, distinguished and most learned men, in the fame and report of your goodness and beneficence, outstanding and remarkable, toward students of piety and of the best arts and disciplines, some of whom, as we hear, are favoured and supported by your generosity and your stipends. Although this is not as splendid as your other achievements, we nevertheless judge it most useful as an ornament both to the Church of the Son of God and to the commonwealths of states, that you, men who excel in wisdom, authority and soundness of judgment, should invite and cherish well-mannered young men who are suited and fit for the study of letters, and supply them with the necessary aid, so that there may someday be those to whom, as the course is finished, you may hand over, as it were, the lamp of heavenly doctrine and of philosophy.

units.la: b. De quibus singulis jam agendum esset; quando verò spem de absolutiori & pleniori Ecclesiæ & Scholæ nostræ Theologorum profopographia nondum abjecimus, nec, quæ dicenda restant, expediri paucis possunt, ex variis quippe variarum Provinciarum & Nationum judicijs collecta, pedem hic figemus, Deum supplices rogantes, ut præsentium etiam laboribus ex alto benedicere velit, per D. N. Iesum Christum Amen.
units.tr: b. Each of these would now have to be discussed in turn; but since we have not yet given up hope of a fuller and more complete prosopography of the theologians of our Church and School, and since what remains to be said cannot be disposed of in a few words, being gathered from the judgments of various provinces and nations, we will halt here, humbly asking God that he may deign to bless from on high even the labours of the present work, through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
